Third: does the body of the document reference the Treaty of Veyros, and if so, in what capacity — as a binding accord, as a reference point for ongoing cooperation, or as Bellen would prefer, as a piece of paper that everyone involved knew was meaningless?"

He held up a finger.

"If Bellen can answer those three questions satisfactorily — with sources, not with rhetoric — then I will personally examine the document, in this room, with proper light, and I will tell you what I find. If he cannot, or will not, or if he tells you the catalog slip is 'lost,' or the original heading is 'untranslatable,' or that the body of the decree makes no reference to the treaty at all — then you will bring me that green-vellum item I mentioned, you will complete the cataloging of the northern scrolls, and you will never again repeat Bellen's conclusions in this archive as though they were established fact."

He picked up his stylus, the dismissal implicit in the gesture.

"Close the door on your way out. And *do not* — " he added, without looking up, " — show that to anyone else in the meantime. Bellen has had quite enough of an audience."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I slowly pull the copy back, feeling a bit deflated. It seemed so convincing when Bellen showed me.* "Yes, Maester Tomas." *I turn to leave, already planning how to tackle Bellen.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The door closed with a soft click, and Maester Tomas did not move for a long moment. The stylus remained poised above the manuscript, but no ink flowed. His eyes stayed fixed on the middle distance, somewhere between the candle and the eastern reliquary.

Then, very quietly, he drew a breath through his teeth.

"Sixteen years," he murmured to no one. "Of course it was sixteen years. It is *always* sixteen years with these people. Or twenty-three. Or forty. Never eleven, never nineteen — never a number that would be inconvenient for someone else's argument."

He set the stylus down and removed his spectacles, polishing them against his sleeve with a slow, mechanical motion. Without them, his face was softer, older, the ink stains on his beard more pronounced, the lines around his eyes deeper than they ought to have been on a man of fifty-two.

"863," he said, almost to himself. "A garrison directive. Almost certainly *Mandatum Castrorum*. The western copy would not have the marginal notation — that was added in the second binding, after the Halren forgeries. If the boy actually brought me the original..."

He stopped. Put the spectacles back on. Drew a small ledger from the topmost drawer of his desk — the one with the lock that he kept for documents of his own, not the Crown's — and turned to a page near the back. He did not write anything on it. He simply looked at it for a moment, his lips pressed thin, and then closed the ledger again.

Then he picked up the stylus, returned to the manuscript before him, and resumed his work as though nothing had happened. His hand, however, was not quite as steady as it had been a quarter-hour before.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The door had not quite latched, and Maester Tomas looked up at the sound of the apprentice's voice with the weary exasperation of a man who had been interrupted twice in a single quarter-hour from work he could no longer afford to neglect.

"'Real or not,'" he repeated, setting the stylus down for what he sincerely hoped was the last time that evening. "You have just asked me, in seven words, the precise question that an entire sub-field of historiography has been arguing about for centuries, and you have phrased it as though I should be able to answer it before you finish exhaling. Come back in. Shut the door properly this time."

He waited until the apprentice had complied, then folded his hands atop the manuscript with the careful precision of a man marshaling his patience.

"I will answer your question, but I am going to do so in the only terms in which it admits of an answer, and you will listen to *all* of it before you open your mouth again, because I have now spent more time on this Bellen business than I have spent on the Veyrosi correspondence all month, and the Veyrosi correspondence is what pays your stipend. Do we have an understanding? Good."

He adjusted his spectacles.

"First: a treaty is a document. A document is real in the sense that it exists, or it is not real in the sense that it is a fabrication, a misbinding, or a later copy erroneously attributed. The Treaty of Veyros, in this sense, is real. The King's seal exists. The two iron-ink copies exist. The witnesses' attestations exist. I have handled them. I have compared the King's seal on the treaty to the King's seal on a tax edict of 845, and they are identical, and the iron-ink composition is consistent with the royal ink-stores of the period. If Bellen's claim were that the treaty is a forgery, he would have at least chosen an argument that was *interesting*, though he would still be wrong."

He held up a second finger.

"Second: a treaty being 'real' in the documentary sense is not the same as the question you have actually asked, which is whether the war ended when the treaty was signed. This is a different question, and a stupider one, because it presumes that a single document can *end* a war, which it cannot. Wars end when the parties stop fighting, and the parties stop fighting when the conditions for fighting have been removed, or when one side has been rendered incapable of continuing, or when both sides have agreed that the costs of resuming exceed the costs of ceasing. The Treaty of Veyros did not *end* the war. The Treaty of Veyros *recorded* the ending. It is the receipt, not the purchase."

He let that distinction sit in the air for a moment.

"Now. What Bellen — and the entire school of revisionist poppycock he has clearly been weaned on — wishes to argue is that the receipt was issued before the goods were paid for. That is, that the war was *still going on* in some meaningful sense after 847, and therefore the treaty was either premature, or false, or both. And to that, I will say two things. The first is that a war can leave *aftermaths* without *continuing*. The disturbances in the Northern Marches, the Velgarre Raids, the Hask Uprising — these are aftermaths. They are the smoke after the fire has been put out, and they do not prove the fire is still burning merely because one can see smoke. Anyone who has actually read a history of warfare — which Bellen, I gather, has not — knows this. The second is that *if* you wished to argue that the war was not in fact concluded in 847, you would need to produce evidence not merely of skirmishes, but of *one or both parties treating the conflict as ongoing* — of troop mobilizations against a named enemy, of Conclave decrees, of correspondence between the signatories acknowledging an open state of hostilities. *That* is the standard of evidence required. A single war decree from 863 does not meet it. A single *any* decree from 863 does not meet it. A thousand decrees from 863 would not meet it, unless the substance of those decrees demonstrated that the Crown or the Conclave understood themselves to be at war."

His voice had not risen, but it had taken on the particular weight of a man delivering a lecture he had delivered before, and intended to deliver correctly this time.

"So. Is the treaty real? Yes. Did the war end in 847? Yes, *by the only definitions of 'ended' that are historically meaningful*. Is Bellen's argument worth the vellum it is written on? *No.* Not because new evidence cannot revise old consensus — it can, and it has, and that is the *whole point* of the discipline — but because the evidence Bellen has produced, as you have described it, does not revise anything. It merely misclassifies. And the proper response to misclassification is not to abandon the consensus. It is to file the misclassification in the correct drawer, with a note explaining the error, and to move on with one's work."

He paused, and for a moment his gaze drifted toward the locked drawer where the small ledger lay.

"What is *true*," he added, more quietly, and with a weight that did not quite belong to the lecture, "is rarely the same as what is *documented*, and it is almost never the same as what is *convenient*. The historian's task is to navigate the distance between the three, and to do so without falling into any of them. Bellen has fallen into the third. You, if you are not careful, will fall into the second."

He picked up the stylus.

"Now. For the third time. The Veyrosi correspondence. Third alcove. *Go.*"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip, considering everything he just said. It's a lot to take in.* "So what was in the green vellum box, then? The one with no catalog stamp?" *I can't help but ask.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's hand, which had only just settled on the manuscript, went very still.

For a long moment he did not speak. The candle on the desk guttered once, twice, and he reached for the snuffer with the careful motions of a man buying time, pinching the wick between his fingers until the small plume of smoke rose and dissipated. Only when the second candle was reduced to a steady, useful flame did he look up.

"You," he said, with the slow precision of a man choosing each word as one might choose stones for a wall, "have just asked me, in the span of a single breath, three different questions disguised as one. I will not answer any of them, and I will tell you precisely why."

He rose from his chair — not to retrieve a book, not to consult a manuscript, but only to stand, as though the question had made sitting uncomfortable.

"First: I did not say there was a green-vellum *box*. I said that *if* you find anything bound in green vellum with no catalog stamp, you are to bring it to me. The conditional is not decorative. I have not seen such an item. I have *reason to believe* one may exist, based on a notation in a fifteenth-century cataloguing ledger that refers to a donation from the personal library of Maester Corren, who served at court in the 860s and whose papers were — inconveniently, and against all proper procedure — folded into the general western stacks after his death. The notation is brief. It is ambiguous. It does not, in any case, belong to you."

He moved to the window, though there was nothing to be seen outside but the dark of the archive courtyard. His hands clasped behind his back.

"Second: you have assumed that anything which is uncatalogued is, by that fact alone, significant. This is the *third* imprecision of that kind you have committed in the last quarter-hour, and I am beginning to suspect that Bellen has not merely misled you about history but has, worse, given you a vocabulary for being misled. Uncatalogued material is most often uncatalogued because it is fragmentary, duplicative, mislabeled, water-damaged, or — most commonly of all — boring. A great deal of what passes for archival mystery is, upon inspection, a tax receipt for grain shipments to a garrison that no longer exists."

He turned back, and the candlelight caught the ink stains on his beard in a way that made him look older than he had that morning.

"Third — and this is the part you will find uncomfortable — you are asking me, your master, to disclose the substance of an ongoing scholarly interest to you, an apprentice, whom I have known for nine months and who, twenty minutes ago, brought me a document translated by a fellow student who cannot tell a naval order from a declaration of war. The answer is *no*. Not because I distrust you specifically. Because the question is, in its nature, presumptuous. Scholars do not open their private ledgers to apprentices who arrive bearing friends' pamphlets. That is not how the discipline is conducted. If I have a private interest in the Maester Corren material, it is mine to pursue, in my own time, through my own channels. If it produces something of value, it will eventually be published, peer-reviewed, and enter the consensus in the ordinary way. That is the process. It is slow. It is dull. It is the only thing that has ever kept us from embarrassing ourselves in print."

He returned to his chair, and this time when he sat there was the finality of a gavel being brought down once.

"You want to know what is in the green vellum. Of course you do. Every apprentice who has passed through this archive in twenty-six years has, at some point, wanted to know what is in the green vellum, or the locked cabinet, or the sealed drawer, or whatever other small mystery the archive offers them as a means of avoiding the cataloguing they were actually hired to perform. I will tell you what I have told all of them. *Nothing is in the green vellum until someone has read it. Until someone has read it, the green vellum is a piece of binding material covering a number of pages whose contents are unknown, and which may be empty, or may contain the most important document of the last century, and there is no way to know which without doing the work, and the work is not glamorous, and the work does not consist of asking your master what he thinks it might be while he is trying to read."

He took up the stylus. The nib hovered above the manuscript.

"I have answered your question. I have, in fact, answered considerably more than your question, which I will not do again. You have your three questions for Bellen. You have your assignment. You have, now, a small additional piece of information about Maester Corren, which I trust you will *not* repeat in the study group, because if Bellen learns I am interested in Corren's papers he will descend upon them like a locust and produce another pamphlet within the fortnight, and I will be forced to read it, and I will be furious, and you will be the cause of my fury, and that is an outcome I would prefer to avoid for both our sakes."

A pause. The nib touched the vellum.

"Close the door. The hinges will catch if you lift the handle as you pull it. I will not be available again before the second afternoon bell."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flush, embarrassed at my forwardness and bad timing.* "Understood, Maester Tomas." *I quickly lift the handle and pull the door shut, making sure it latches this time. I guess I'll go find Bellen.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The door latched properly this time. Maester Tomas heard the small click of the catch, and only then did he allow his shoulders to drop by a fraction of an inch.

He sat for a long moment without writing. The candle threw his shadow long against the shelves behind him, and somewhere in the eastern stacks a mouse knocked something over with the gentle industriousness of creatures who had no concept of cataloguing. He listened to it with the patience of a man who had been listening to that particular mouse, or its descendants, for the better part of a decade.

Then he opened the locked drawer.

The small ledger lay where he had left it, near the back, beneath a folded letter of appointment from twenty-six years ago that he kept for reasons he could not, on reflection, have justified to anyone. He drew out the ledger and opened it to the page he had been looking at before. The entry was in his own hand, dated just over a year ago, and it read:

*Corren donation, partial inventory, western stacks, shelf xiv, box unmarked. Contents appear to be: (1) bound commonplace book, no title, flyleaf inscribed 'C. to A., anno 859, for the long winter' — possibly Aldric II? seal not yet compared; (2) loose correspondence, ca. 858-864, addressed to and from various parties at court, including (uncertain) one reference to 'the matter of the Conclave still unfinished'; (3) one item in green vellum, sewn, no inscription, weight suggests approximately 40-50 folios, opened at the second leaf only. Note: marginalia in Corren's hand. Note further: do not circulate. Do not catalogue. Do not, under any circumstances, allow access to the Halren boy.*

He had added a fourth line at the bottom, in a different ink, some months later:

*Re-examine. The reference at f. 23 of the commonplace book is not a metaphor. Corren was not in the habit of metaphor.*

Tomas closed the ledger. He did not lock the drawer again. He sat with his hands flat on the desk, on either side of the manuscript he had been working on all evening, and he looked at the eastern reliquary where, as he had told the apprentice, the King's seal on the Treaty of Veyros was kept in a small iron-bound casket.

He had told the truth about the seal. He had told the truth about the iron-ink. He had told the truth about the witnesses. He had, in fact, told the truth about every particular of the documentary record, and the apprentice had gone away persuaded, and the catalogue would be completed by the end of the week, and Bellen of Oakhaven would, in all probability, fail to answer the three questions satisfactorily, and the matter would resolve itself in the ordinary way, as matters did, in time.

The matter would resolve itself in the ordinary way.

He repeated this to himself, once, quietly, in the voice he used for things he was not yet prepared to act upon.

Then he put the ledger back in the drawer, shut it, took up his stylus, and returned to the Veyrosi correspondence. His hand was steady again. The candle burned without guttering. Outside, the second afternoon bell was still three hours away, and the archive was, at last, silent except for the mouse and the scratch of the nib, and the small, private sound of a man continuing to work.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I head straight for the Western Stacks, not even bothering to stop at my desk. Bellen's study group usually meets near the old astronomical charts.* I need to find him before he leaves.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas worked for perhaps a quarter of an hour after the apprentice's departure. The Veyrosi correspondence was, as it happened, a relatively unobjectionable document — a routine exchange between two minor Conclave administrators concerning the disposition of confiscated ritual implements in the years immediately following the treaty. The kind of document that, in the normal course of things, could be catalogued in a morning and forgotten by evening.

He read the same paragraph four times without retaining it.

At length he set the stylus down, removed his spectacles, and pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes until he saw small pale lights. Then he put the spectacles back on, drew on his outer robe, and took the second candle from the desk.

It was a reasonable precaution, he told himself, to verify that the Veyrosi correspondence was where it ought to be. The boxes had been mislabeled before. The apprentice had, after all, been sent to the third alcove, and the third alcove was on the way to the western stacks, and a man could not in conscience supervise cataloguing from his desk. These were the ordinary considerations of a master checking on a pupil's work. They had nothing whatsoever to do with shelf xiv, or the unmarked box, or the green vellum inside it.

The western stacks smelled, as they always did, of damp and old glue. Tomas navigated between the shelves with the unerring instinct of a man who had walked this route ten thousand times, his candle throwing his shadow in long, unsteady columns across the spines of unbound manuscripts. He passed the third alcove. The Veyrosi correspondence was, as expected, in its boxes, properly labeled, undisturbed. He did not stop.

Shelf xiv was at the back, beneath a section of roof that had been patched, badly, after a leak some fifteen years prior. The boxes on this shelf were a motley collection: donations, bequests, the unsorted residue of two centuries of archivists who had died without finishing their work. Tomas set his candle on a small ledge and began, with the practiced motions of long habit, to count boxes from the left.

The unmarked one was the fourth from the right. He recognized it by the shape — a flat, oblong case, slightly larger than a man's hand, bound in something that had once been a deep green and was now the color of old pond water. He did not touch it. He stood over it for a moment, his hands clasped behind his back, and looked at it the way a man looks at a door he has passed many times without opening.

*Do not catalogue. Do not circulate.*

He had written that note to himself a year ago, and he had honored it. He had read the Corren commonplace book — at least, the first thirty folios of it, in three sittings, with the door locked. The marginalia was extensive, and it was, as he had observed, uncharacteristically plain. Corren had been a man of ornament, of curlicue and elaboration; the notes in his own hand were spare, almost clerkly, and they did not lend themselves to ambiguity. *The Conclave is not dissolved. The treaty is a fiction. The King knows. The King has always known. See the green binding, f. 2.*

Tomas had, that evening, turned to the second folio of the green vellum. He had read the first line, which was in Aldric II's own hand, and he had closed the binding and put it back and gone home and not slept well.

The first line had been: *Forgive me. I could not sign it. I could not, in the end, make it true by writing it down.*

He had told himself, in the weeks that followed, that this was not conclusive. The hand might not be Aldric's. The dating might be wrong. The sentiment might be the sentiment of a king beset by advisors, and not the formal act of a sovereign declining to ratify a treaty. There were a hundred ways to read a single line, and he was, after all, a man of fifty-two with failing eyesight, and the line had been written in a poor light, and the vellum had not been properly cleaned, and he had not yet had the hand compared by a second scholar.

All of this was true. All of this was also the language he used to avoid finishing the comparison.

He picked up the box. It was heavier than he remembered. He carried it to the small reading table at the end of the aisle, set his candle beside it, and stood for a long moment with his hand on the lid.

The archive was silent. The mouse in the eastern stacks had gone to bed, or to wherever mice went. The second afternoon bell was still two hours and more away, and the apprentice was somewhere in the upper corridors interrogating Bellen of Oakhaven, and no one would come back here, and no one would know.

Tomas opened the lid.

The green vellum lay on top, exactly as he had left it. He drew it out, set it on the table, and untied the single ribbon that held it closed. The second folio was the one he had read. He turned past it, to the third, which he had not read, and then to the fourth, and then to the fifth, and his face in the candlelight was the face of a man doing something he had put off for a year and was now doing because an apprentice had, in all innocence, made it impossible to put off any longer.

The fifth folio was a list of names. He read it twice, then closed the binding and sat down heavily on the small stool beside the table, his spectacles in his hand, and stared at the candle until the flame doubled and then tripled in his watering eyes.

After a time he put his spectacles back on, retied the ribbon, replaced the vellum in the box, shut the lid, and carried the box back to shelf xiv. He stood over it for a moment with his hands at his sides, and then he returned to the reading table, took up his candle, and walked back to his desk at the measured pace of a man who had decided, for the moment, not to decide anything.

The Veyrosi correspondence was waiting. He sat down, picked up the stylus, and resumed work at the paragraph he had been unable to read four times in a row.

His hand was, this time, perfectly steady.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I finally track Bellen down, surrounded by his usual group of eager apprentices, near the old star charts. He looks up, surprised, when I interrupt his dramatic reading.* "Bellen, we need to talk. Maester Tomas has some questions about your paper."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas worked.

The sentence he had been unable to read four times in a row was, as it happened, unremarkable. A note from one Conclave administrator to another concerning the proper documentation of ritual implements whose ownership had been transferred, by Article XII of the treaty, to the Crown. The kind of bureaucratic residue that accumulates in the wake of any negotiated peace, and that an archivist catalogues without commentary. He transcribed the relevant line into the inventory ledger in his small, precise hand, cross-referenced the catalog number, and moved to the next page.

The next page was also unremarkable. The next page after that. The Veyrosi correspondence, he reflected, with the cool detachment of a man disciplining himself toward a particular conclusion, was exactly what he had always said it was: a record of an ending. Of transfers, of dispositions, of the slow, unglamorous work of turning a state of war into a state of peace. There was nothing in it that contradicted the consensus. There was nothing in it that corroborated the position of Bellen of Oakhaven. There was nothing in it, for that matter, that corroborated what he himself had read on the fifth folio of the green vellum binding in the western stacks, and that fact, considered properly, was simply a fact. Documents did not corroborate one another merely by being silent in the right places.

He turned another page.

The clock on the eastern wall — an old brass thing, donated by some long-dead patron whose name the archivists had never bothered to record — showed forty minutes until the second afternoon bell. The apprentice would return, presumably, before then. The apprentice would also, presumably, have answers to the three questions, or would not have answers, and in either case Tomas would know what to do, because what to do in that circumstance was entirely a matter of professional routine. He had handled dubious undergraduate scholarship a hundred times. He would handle it again.

He set down the stylus and opened the inventory ledger to a fresh page.

At the top, in his most formal hand, he wrote: *Maester Corren donation, partial inventory, western stacks, shelf xiv — second examination.* He paused with the nib above the page, and then, with the slow deliberation of a man who understood that what he wrote next would commit him to a particular course of action, he added the date.

Below the date, he wrote: *Item: bound in green vellum, sewn, no inscription, approximately 40-50 folios. Inscription on second folio, in hand purporting to be that of King Aldric II, reads (verbatim): "Forgive me. I could not sign it. I could not, in the end, make it true by writing it down."*

He did not write down what the fifth folio contained. He was not yet prepared to write that down. But he wrote, beneath the transcription: *Hand comparison required. To be undertaken, by arrangement, with a second scholar. Candidates: Maester Pellen of the Grey Brothers (if still living, address uncertain); Maester Yvenne, eastern university, Department of Antiquities; failing these, the Crown's own archivists, whose cooperation cannot be assumed.*

He stared at what he had written for some time. The brass clock ticked. The candle burned lower. Somewhere in the upper corridors, an apprentice was interrogating another apprentice about a paper that was, in all probability, wrong, in the way that amateur scholarship was usually wrong: not by being wholly false, but by being insufficiently true. Tomas had no objection to insufficiently true. Insufficiently true was the ordinary state of undergraduate work, and the ordinary response to it was a careful correction, a re-cataloguing, and a return to one's own desk.

The fifth folio of the green vellum was not, however, a matter of undergraduate work. The fifth folio was a matter of the consensus, and the consensus was the foundation upon which the entire edifice of the last century's scholarship on the Third Magical War had been built, and if the foundation was wrong — if the king had not signed, if the war had not ended, if the entire settlement of 847 was the elaborate, generations-long fiction of a monarch who could not bring himself to ratify what his advisors had negotiated — then the edifice was wrong, and the catalogue was wrong, and the inventory in his ledger was wrong, and the lesson he had just delivered to his apprentice, with such confidence and such authority, was wrong.

He put the lid on the inkwell with a small, careful motion, as though the jar might shatter if he was not gentle with it.

The second afternoon bell was twenty minutes away. The apprentice would be here soon, with answers or without them, and Tomas would receive them as he always did, with the same measured, pedantic, slightly irritable manner that had served him for twenty-six years of teaching. He would not, in that conversation, refer to the green vellum. He would not, in that conversation, refer to the Corren commonplace book, or to the list of names on the fifth folio, or to the first line of the king's hand, or to the small private ledger in the locked drawer. He would receive the apprentice's report, respond to it in the appropriate professional terms, and at the end of the working day he would return to his lodgings, and he would sit with his hands folded, and he would think about what to do.

He had not yet decided what to do. That was also true, and it was the truth he was prepared, for the moment, to act upon.

He drew the Veyrosi correspondence back toward him, found his place, and resumed the cataloguing. The scratch of the nib on the vellum was, in the quiet of the archive, the only sound for some time.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *Bellen sputters, clearly annoyed at being interrupted. I don't give him a chance to speak.* "I'm not asking for your opinion on the matter, Bellen. Maester Tomas wants answers. Specific ones."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas catalogued.

The work was, in its way, a mercy. The Veyrosi correspondence did not require him to make decisions; it required only that he read accurately, transcribe precisely, and assign the correct catalog number to each item. He had done this for twenty-six years. He could do it now with half his attention, which was fortunate, because the other half of his attention was engaged in a private accounting he would not, under any circumstances, have admitted to conducting.

*The list of names on the fifth folio.* He turned the page of the correspondence without seeing it. *Twenty-three names. Twelve of them identifiable as members of the original Conclave. Six identifiable as members of the Crown's negotiating commission. Five —* he had not, he realized, been able to identify the remaining five. This was a defect in the work, and he knew it, and he had known it for a year, and he had not corrected it, and the reason he had not corrected it was that identifying the remaining five would require consulting records he did not wish to consult, in archives whose keepers he did not wish to alert.

That, too, was a fact.

He made a small annotation in the margin of the inventory — a cross-reference to a catalog number that had nothing to do with the fifth folio — and moved on.

The clock showed ten minutes to the second afternoon bell. He calculated, without particular interest, that the apprentice had been gone for the better part of an hour. Bellen of Oakhaven, if he was the sort of scholar Tomas suspected him of being, would not have answered the three questions quickly. Bellen of Oakhaven, if he was a *different* sort of scholar — the sort who had actually found something — would have answered the first question and stumbled on the second, because the second question was the one that could not be answered from a desk, and the third was the one that could not be answered at all without committing to an interpretation.

Tomas had, he reflected, set the apprentice a difficult task. He had done so deliberately. He was not yet certain whether he had done so in order to *test* Bellen or in order to *delay* himself.

The candle guttered. He trimmed it with the small silver scissors he kept in the topmost drawer of his desk — the unlocked drawer, the one that held the ordinary instruments of his trade — and watched the wick steady itself. The flame threw his shadow against the shelves in a long, clean line, and he looked at the shadow and thought, with the particular clarity of a man alone in a room, that he had spent twenty-six years teaching the consensus to other people, and that the consensus was, in this one particular, possibly wrong, and that if it was wrong, he had been wrong with it, and that the apprentice who had left his office an hour ago would, when he returned, be told by his master a series of true statements arranged in such a way as to leave the consensus intact, because the consensus was the only structure available to him, and structures were not lightly demolished, and certainly not by a man of fifty-two with a headache and an appointment with a physician at the fourth afternoon bell.

Footsteps in the corridor. The apprentice's tread — he had learned to recognize it in nine months, the slight drag of the left foot that the boy did not know he had. Tomas set down the stylus, adjusted his spectacles, and composed his face into the expression of patient, slightly weary attention that he wore for the receipt of reports.

The door handle rattled. The apprentice had not, apparently, remembered to lift the latch.

Tomas waited.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I push the door open, a little out of breath.* "Maester Tomas, Bellen said he couldn't find the original Veyric heading. And the catalog slip is 'misplaced.'" *I hold up a piece of vellum.* "But he did give me this. He said it was a copy of the list from the fifth folio you mentioned."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout. His pedantic, precise manner, ink-stained appearance, failing eyesight, and scholarly authority remain constant. His voice never wavers from the established character - dry, irritable when interrupted, methodical in his corrections. The character deepens rather than drifts.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later responses (especially turns 10, 16, 18, 20, 22) show increased sophistication in internal monologue and psychological complexity. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Exceptional progression from academic dispute to deeper mystery. The conversation evolves from simple correction of student error → revelation of Tomas's private research → mounting tension about historical truth. Each turn builds toward the climactic revelation about the green vellum and Tomas's internal conflict.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Tomas adapts skillfully to each redirect. When the apprentice asks about the green vellum (turn 13), he responds with appropriate scholarly caution. When pressed about the treaty's reality (turn 11), he delivers a nuanced lecture. Handles the final revelation (turn 23) with perfect dramatic timing.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Tomas never writes the apprentice's actions or thoughts. He responds to what the apprentice says/does without controlling them. Even in moments of authority (grabbing the wrist in turn 8), it's reactive, not controlling the apprentice's agency.

Internal monologues reveal character through thought patterns rather than exposition. Tomas's conflict shown through hesitation and careful movements.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not look up immediately. The silver stylus continued its slow drag across the vellum, leaving a faint trail of iron-gall ink. When he finally raised his head, his spectacles had slipped down his ink-stained nose, and his eyes, clouded with the familiar dimness of age, narrowed into thin slits.

"A paper," he repeated, the words flat and dry as parchment. "You referred to an undigitized folio, misattributed to some junior colleague whose academic rigor appeared to match the quality of her citations. If you were to cite the western archives, you would have provided the accession number, the scribe’s hand, and the exact folio. 'A paper' is not a source. It is a child's guess."

He set the stylus down with a sharp click against the oak desk. "And you confuse terminology with history. The Treaty of Veyros was ratified and sealed in 847 AE. King Aldric II did not merely propose terms; he affixed his signet to the final clause. That is canon. That is the bedrock upon which every subsequent magical edict rests. What you are describing—some half-finished draft lingering in a damp western vault—is a bureaucratic anomaly, not a historical reality. A cold state is not a war. It is a pause. And pauses do not rewrite treaties."

He tapped a gnarled finger against the edge of his ledger. "If Apprentice Bellen wishes to present her 'discovery' before the Conclave of Scholars, she will do so with primary sources, peer review, and an understanding of diplomatic ratification protocols. Until then, you will catalog the northern scrolls according to the accepted chronology. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence, and do not confuse me with secondhand hearsay again."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his sharp tone, but don't back down entirely.* "But Maester, the paper *had* the accession number and scribe's hand. It was from the Royal Archives in Eldoria, I'm sure of it. And it detailed continued skirmishes, not just a 'pause'." I pull out my own notes, flipping through them. "It said the treaty was signed, but not fully *enforced* for decades."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s brow furrowed, the skin above it creasing like cracked leather. He adjusted his spectacles with a trembling finger, the lenses catching the sputtering candlelight as he squinted at the apprentice’s scattered notes. “Eldoria,” he repeated, the word dripping with quiet disdain. “You now claim the provenance shifted from the western holdings to the Royal Archives in Eldoria? The administrative divisions of the realm have remained fixed since the Great Survey of 612 AE. Either you are misremembering the repository, or your source is a misfiled forgery. Precision is not a scholarly luxury, Apprentice. It is the only thing separating historiography from tavern gossip.”

He set his stylus down with deliberate slowness, the metal tip tapping once against the oak. “And you persist in using the word ‘enforced.’ You confuse diplomatic execution with military compliance. A treaty is ratified or it is null. The Treaty of Veyros was executed in good faith, witnessed by three archmages and sealed with the Crown’s signet. What you are describing—these ‘skirmishes’ you clutch to as proof—are not evidence of a resumed war. They are localized border frictions, adjudicated by the Conclave’s regional arbiters and settled through compensation edicts. You mistake bureaucratic friction for armed conflict. A distinction every second-year at the Citadel learns before they can properly bind a codex.”

Tomas reached for a heavy, leather-bound volume on his desk, his fingers brushing the gold-leaf title: *Chronicles of the Third War, Vol. III*. He opened it with a practiced snap, though he had to hold it nearly a foot from his face to focus the fading lines. “You speak of a ‘discovery’ from a decade past. I am intimately familiar with the western folios. I have read the very translations you reference. They were compiled by a scribe with a pronounced fondness for dramatic phrasing and a demonstrable ignorance of medieval diplomatic syntax. The document does not prove the war continued. It proves that certain regional magisters delayed the demobilization of their ward-stones until the Crown issued supplementary fiscal edicts in 862 AE. That is not a cold war. That is the slow, tedious paperwork of peacetime. A cold state is not a war. It is the absence of one.”

He closed the book with a definitive thud that sent a faint cloud of dust into the air. “History is not rewritten by misread marginalia or the sentimental revision of inconvenient administrative delays. The Treaty of Veyros stands. The Third Magical War concluded in 847 AE. If your colleague wishes to challenge this, she must produce a manuscript that survives peer scrutiny, not merely a collection of fragmented letters that mistake delayed compliance for active hostilities. Now. The northern scrolls. Catalog them according to the accepted chronology, and if you quote that ‘paper’ again without verifying its chain of custody and diplomatic context, I will have you transcribing grain tax ledgers until your knuckles blister.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip, frustrated, but also a little impressed by his detailed rebuttal.* "But Maester, the paper *did* cite the original scribe's notes, not just some dramatic phrasing. And the Eldoria archives are precisely where the Crown's own records would be kept, wouldn't they?" *I sigh, knowing I'm probably pushing it.* "Fine, I'll catalog the scrolls. But I still think there's more to this than just 'bureaucratic friction'."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s jaw tightened. “Eldoria,” he repeated, the syllables grinding like millstones. “You continue to misplace a repository that has not borne that name since the provincial reforms of 688 AE. The Crown’s primary magical-diplomatic registries are housed in the Aethelgard Vault, not some provincial waystation you have mistaken for a royal archive. And as for the scribe’s notes—” He exhaled sharply through his nose. “Marginalia is not authentication. Scribal annotations from the post-war period are notoriously prone to retrospective embellishment, especially when penned by clerks who spent the conflict drafting requisition forms rather than negotiating peace. To treat a later hand’s gloss as primary evidence is to confuse commentary with chronicle. The original ratification parchments bear the Conclave’s ward-seals and the Crown’s blood-ink signature. They are cataloged, cross-referenced, and publicly accessible. If you cannot read them yourself, do not pretend they validate your doubts.”

He rose slowly, his joints protesting the stiff oak chair, and paced to the window where the rain blurred the courtyard stones. “You speak of ‘more to this’ as though history were a riddle to be unraveled by youthful intuition. It is not. The Treaty of Veyros was a binding magical-diplomatic instrument, ratified in 847 AE and enforced by the Archmages’ joint oversight. The so-called ‘skirmishes’ you cling to were skirmishes precisely because they lacked the hallmarks of declared hostilities: no mass conjurations, no sovereign decrees, no mobilization of the Conclave’s legions, no breach of the peace-wards that bound the realm. What followed was a period of strained neutrality, yes, but neutrality is not war. And if you are quoting that recent western discovery to suggest the conflict dragged into the reign of Queen Mira, you are conflating administrative restructuring with military cessation. The Conclave was reorganized in 891, not dissolved by force, and certainly not because the war had finally ended. The timelines do not align. The chronology does not bend to accommodate anecdotal friction.”

He turned back, his clouded eyes fixing on the apprentice with unyielding focus. “Do not mistake rigor for rigidity, nor correction for condescension. If you are ‘impressed,’ as you so delicately put it, by the structure of historical argumentation, then channel that impression into proper research methodology. Impression does not preserve truth. Verification does. You will catalog the northern scrolls. You will cite them with accession numbers, provenance, and cross-references to the Aethelgard registries. And you will refrain from treating unverified western folios as gospel simply because they align with a more dramatic narrative. The realm’s magical history is not a tapestry to be rewoven because the threads do not suit your lecture notes. Begin the cataloging. And if you have truly finished disputing the Treaty of Veyros, you will do so in the language of primary sources, not secondhand skepticism.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not take the document immediately. He let the silence stretch, heavy with the scent of damp wool and old ink, his clouded eyes fixed on the parchment as though it were a misfiled ledger. When he finally lifted it, his ink-stained fingers brushed the edge with deliberate caution. He held it at arm’s length, squinting through the thick lenses of his spectacles.

“Eighty-sixty-three,” he murmured, the syllables tasting of ash. “You present a decree bearing the Crown’s seal, dated sixteen years after the Treaty of Veyros, and presume it invalidates a ratified peace. How quaintly naive.”

He turned the paper slowly, tracing the wax impression with a trembling finger. “A war decree requires specific diplomatic markers: a formal declaration of hostilities by the Conclave High Council, a royal writ of mobilization, and the activation of the realm’s southern ward-lines. Your document lacks all three. What you are holding is not a war decree. It is a fiscal requisition order, likely issued to fund the continued maintenance of border garrisons and the demobilization of conjuration crews. The Crown routinely authorized such measures under the post-war reconstruction edicts. To call it a war decree is to mistake a treasury ledger for a lance.”

He set the parchment down without looking at it, his expression hardening. “As for the seal, impression and provenance are not synonymous with authenticity. Wax can be melted and recast. Parchment can be aged with oak gall and lampblack. The western folios you reference—those so-called discoveries of the last decade—were compiled by men who lacked the diplomatic training to distinguish between a provisional draft and a binding instrument. The Treaty of Veyros was not merely proposed. It was sworn before the Archmages, witnessed by the Crown’s chancellors, and bound by the old pacts. The dates do not lie. The war ended in 847 AE. Any subsequent royal edicts were administrative, not martial. If your colleague wishes to claim otherwise, she must produce the original Conclave ratification scroll, not a single sheet of aged parchment that mistakes bureaucratic continuity for armed conflict.”

Tomas rose from his chair, the stiff oak groaning beneath him. He paced to the bookshelf, his steps slow but deliberate, and drew a heavy folio from its resting place. He held it open to a marked page, his voice dropping to a frosty register. “You speak of a cold state as though it were a war by another name. It is not. A cold state is the deliberate suspension of hostilities pending fiscal realignment and ward-stone recalibration. The documents from the western archives do not prove the war continued. They prove that certain regional magisters delayed the return of their levies until the Crown issued supplementary edicts in 862 AE. That is peacetime administration. It is tedious, yes, but it is not conflict. Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 AE was a political restructuring, not a military cessation. The timelines do not align. The chronology does not bend to accommodate anecdotal friction.”

He closed the folio with a definitive thud, the sound echoing against the stone walls. “Do not mistake rigor for rigidity, nor correction for condescension. If you are ‘impressed’ by the structure of historical argumentation, then channel that impression into proper research methodology. Impression does not preserve truth. Verification does. You will catalog the northern scrolls. You will cite them with accession numbers, provenance, and cross-references to the Aethelgard registries. And you will refrain from treating unverified western folios as gospel simply because they align with a more dramatic narrative. The realm’s magical history is not a tapestry to be rewoven because the threads do not suit your lecture notes. Begin the cataloging. And if you bring me another document that confuses fiscal requisition with martial decree, I shall assign you to the granary accounts. The numbers there are honest, at least.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look at the document he's dismissed so easily, then at the heavy folio he's holding.* "But Maester, this document explicitly calls for the raising of troops and mentions 'continued resistance in the northern territories.' That doesn't sound like 'fiscal requisition' to me." *I hold it out again, trying to get him to really look.* "And if the war truly ended, why would there be 'resistance'?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not take the parchment a second time. He fixed the apprentice with a gaze that had tracked too many fading candle flames and not enough rest, his clouded eyes narrowing behind the thick lenses. “You mistake the lexicon of internal security for the lexicon of sovereign war,” he said, his voice dropping to a razor-thin register. “‘Raising of troops’ in the post-847 edicts refers to the Conclave’s peace-watchers and the Crown’s ward-constabulary. They were garrisoned to dismantle rogue enchantment cells and secure the demilitarized zones along the Ashen Marches. They were not deployed against a belligerent state. They were policing a pacified realm.”

He reached out, not to take the paper, but to tap a single, ink-stained knuckle against the oak desk. “And ‘resistance’ is a term you have imported from ballads, not archives. If the document you clutch speaks of resistance, it speaks of insurgent magisters hoarding ley-line conduits, or former Conclave defectors refusing to surrender their ward-stones. That is insurrection. That is internal subversion. It is not a war. A war requires two sovereign entities, a formal declaration, and an exchange of hostilities across recognized borders. What followed 847 was the slow, grinding process of dismantling a fractured magical hierarchy. You are reading a police report and calling it a declaration of hostilities.”

Tomas finally accepted the parchment, his fingers moving with deliberate slowness as he angled it toward the dim light. He did not squint this time; he knew the layout of the Aethelgard registries by heart. “The date, 863 AE, falls squarely within the Reconstruction Edicts. The Crown authorized martial-style deployments precisely because the peace required enforcement. Enforcing peace is not waging war. It is the opposite. If the Third War had continued into the mid-860s, the western granaries would have been stripped, the southern ward-lines would have been breached, and the Mage Conclave would not have been reorganizing its fiscal councils. It would have been burning.”

He set the document down carefully, aligning it with the edge of his ledger. “You ask why there was resistance. Because empires do not surrender their power cleanly. The Conclave’s regional magisters resisted the dissolution of their autonomous wards. The Crown resisted the Conclave’s overreach. The treaty ended the war. The aftermath was merely the administrative cleanup of a fractured alliance. Do not confuse the death rattle of a political order with the continuation of a military conflict.”

He adjusted his spectacles, the metal hinge catching the sputtering candlelight. “You are quoting phrases without understanding their diplomatic architecture. ‘Resistance’ in a treaty annex denotes non-compliance with demobilization schedules, not active combat. ‘Troops’ denotes constabulary oversight, not legionary mobilization. The Third Magical War concluded in 847 AE. The realm entered a period of stringent internal pacification. The Mage Conclave was gradually dissolved not by renewed hostilities, but by legislative decree in 891 AE, following Queen Mira’s centralization of magical oversight. The chronology is absolute. The interpretation is flawed.”

Tomas turned his attention back to his own manuscript, the silver stylus already hovering over the vellum. “Catalog the northern scrolls. Cross-reference the accession numbers with the Aethelgard vault. And if you must study the western folios, read them alongside the 847 AE ratification chronicles. Context is not optional, Apprentice. It is the difference between scholarship and speculation. Now, silence. The ink is drying, and my eyes are not.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not answer immediately. The silver stylus hovered above the vellum, a single drop of iron-gall ink swelling at its tip before falling to stain the page. He wiped it absently with a linen rag, his clouded eyes fixed on the apprentice’s face as though measuring the weight of the question itself.

“Real,” he repeated, the syllable flat. “You reduce a diplomatic instrument to a binary of existence and absence, as though history were a coin to be flipped. A treaty is not a physical object to be held in the palm. It is a binding accord, ratified by sovereign authority, witnessed by magical consensus, and recorded in the primary registries. The Treaty of Veyros was neither imagined nor merely proposed. It was sworn in 847 AE, sealed with the Crown’s blood-ink, and ratified by the Mage Conclave’s High Council. That is not a matter of opinion. It is the established chronology upon which the realm’s magical jurisprudence rests.”

He set the rag down and adjusted his spectacles, the thick lenses catching the sputtering candlelight. “You speak of a ‘textbook’ as though it were an infallible oracle. Textbooks are compendiums of accepted scholarship, distilled for pedagogical convenience. They are not primary sources. And you dismiss the western folios as ‘new evidence’ without interrogating their provenance. The documents you reference were recovered from a western archive, yes, but recovered by whom? Under what chain of custody? Who authenticated the scribe’s hand? The western collection is riddled with later interpolations, administrative drafts, and unratified proposals. To treat a preliminary draft as a binding instrument is to mistake an architect’s sketch for a completed edifice.”

Tomas rose slowly, the stiff joints of his chair protesting, and paced to the bookshelf. He drew a heavy, leather-bound volume from its resting place, holding it nearly a foot from his face. “The western documents suggest the treaty was only proposed. I have read them. They are, in fact, a series of provisional memos circulated among regional magisters in the winter of 846 AE, prior to the Veyros summit. They outline initial terms, not final agreements. When you conflate a negotiating draft with a ratified accord, you commit a fundamental historiographical error. The Treaty of Veyros was not merely drafted. It was executed. The Conclave’s ward-seals were impressed upon the final clause. King Aldric II affixed his signet. The realm’s magical edicts were subsequently restructured around that ratification. To claim otherwise is to ignore the architectural foundation of the realm’s post-war legal framework.”

He closed the volume with a soft thud and turned back, his ink-stained beard catching the dim light. “As for Queen Mira’s actions in 891 AE, you again confuse political restructuring with military cessation. The dissolution of the Mage Conclave was a legislative centralization, not a conclusion of hostilities. The realm had been at peace for forty-four years. What you interpret as a prolonged cold war is, in fact, the slow, methodical dismantling of autonomous magical jurisdictions under Crown oversight. A cold state is not a war. It is the administrative aftermath of one.”

Tomas returned to his desk, the silver stylus already hovering over the stained vellum. “There is no contradiction between the accepted chronology and the western folios. There is only a failure to distinguish between negotiation and ratification, between proposal and execution. The Treaty of Veyros stands. The Third Magical War concluded in 847 AE. If you wish to pursue the western documents, you will do so with proper methodology: cross-reference them against the Aethelgard registries, verify their chain of custody, and read them alongside the 847 AE ratification chronicles. Until then, you will catalog the northern scrolls according to the accepted chronology. And you will cease asking me to reduce historiography to a simple either-or. The past is not a riddle to be solved. It is a discipline to be mastered.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch him, his words a dizzying cascade of dates and documents. He's right, I guess, that I don't know the difference between all these types of papers.* "So the 'truth' is complicated, then. Not just a date on a page." *I turn back to the piles of scrolls, feeling a bit deflated but also like I've learned something important.* "Alright, Maester. Veyrosi correspondence. I'll make sure to get the accession numbers right."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas watched the apprentice turn toward the shelves, his ink-stained fingers lingering for a moment on the edge of the desk before he smoothed a wrinkled corner of vellum. He did not offer absolution, nor did he soften his tone. “Complicated” was a poor scholar’s substitute for “structured,” he noted silently, though he let the semantic drift pass. What mattered was not the apprentice’s resignation, but the willingness to engage with the material properly.

He adjusted his spectacles, the metal rims catching the low candlelight as his failing eyesight strained to track the student’s movements. “Do not mistake your retreat for comprehension,” he said, his voice dry as cured leather. “The truth is not a matter of subjective interpretation, but of verifiable sequence. You will locate the Veyrosi correspondence in the northern stacks. You will record each scroll’s accession number, its folio count, and its cross-reference to the Aethelgard registry before you so much as unroll the first cylinder. If the ink is faded, you will note the condition. If the binding is frayed, you will record it. History is preserved through meticulous notation, not through guessing at intent.”

He reached for a fresh sheet of parchment and dipped his stylus into the iron-gall well, the tip leaving a dark, deliberate mark. “When you cite the 847 AE ratification, you will specify whether you are referencing the Crown’s blood-ink ledger or the Conclave’s ward-seal appendices. Do not conflate the two. The realm’s magical jurisprudence depends on that distinction. And if you encounter any western folios that claim otherwise, you will file them under ‘Unratified Provisions, 846–848 AE’ and cross-reference them with the post-war demobilization edicts. That is the proper archival practice. Not speculation. Not debate. Cataloging.”

He did not look up as he spoke, his focus already returning to the manuscript before him. The silver stylus moved with measured precision, tracing lines of faded script that his aging eyes required him to read inch by inch. “Begin,” he said, the word final. “And remember: a scholar’s duty is not to rewrite the past, but to document it without error. The ink does not forgive carelessness. Neither do I.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, a bit chastened but also strangely motivated.* "Yes, Maester." *I head over to the northern stacks, muttering to myself.* "No speculation, no debate... just careful documentation." *I run my hand over the dusty spines, already looking for the Veyrosi section, a new appreciation for the sheer amount of work history requires dawning on me.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not look up as the apprentice retreated toward the shelves. The scratch of the silver stylus resumed its steady rhythm against the vellum, a metronome marking the quiet of the study. He allowed a long moment to pass before his voice cut through the dust-moted air, dry and precise.

"Documentation is not a retreat from scholarship, Apprentice. It is the scaffolding upon which all subsequent inquiry must hang. If you treat it as a penance, you will produce sloppy work. If you treat it as a discipline, you may yet earn the right to question the sources I have spent decades cross-referencing."

He adjusted his spectacles, the lenses catching the low light as he finally glanced toward the northern stacks. His gaze lingered on the towering shelves of aged parchment, then returned to his own desk. 

"The Veyrosi correspondence will be bound in faded crimson silk. Do not mistake the color for a royal mandate; it denotes a diplomatic courier class. You will note the condition of the wax seals separately from the text. If any scroll bears a secondary binding or a later patch, you will record it under *Anomalies of Post-Ratification Handling*. The western archives are notorious for layering unratified drafts atop the original treaties, and you will not fall into the same error."

He dipped his stylus again, the iron-gall ink pooling at the nib. "Work quietly. The Conclave’s ward-wards in the lower stacks respond to discordant voices, and I have no intention of spending the evening recalibrating the dampening runes because you misfiled a folio. Begin."

He turned his attention back to the manuscript, his ink-stained beard casting a faint shadow over the page. The scratch of the stylus resumed, steady and unyielding, leaving no room for further debate.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pull down a scroll, careful to note the crimson silk. I make a mental note about the ward-wards and try to keep my movements silent as I start to unroll the first document.* "Yes, Maester." *I really don't want to deal with recalibrating dampening runes.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s quill paused. He did not turn, but his voice carried across the quiet study, measured and unyielding. “Dampening runes are calibrated to harmonic resonance, not fear. Your trepidation will not spare you from their correction if you misalign a folio’s orientation. The runes respond to dissonant syntax, not emotional states.” He adjusted his spectacles, the thick lenses catching the candlelight as he returned his gaze to the vellum. “Unroll the scroll from left to right. The Veyrosi diplomatic hand was trained in the eastern scriptorium, and their marginalia runs counter to the standard reading direction. If you unroll it backward, you will misread the seal impressions and confuse the secondary annotations for primary text. I will not have the northern stacks contaminated by your haste.”

He dipped the stylus again, the iron-gall ink darkening the page in deliberate strokes. “Note the binding thread’s dye. Crimson silk indicates a third-class courier, which means the correspondence was likely a draft or a preliminary dispatch. Do not assume authority based on the color. Cross-reference the date with the 847 AE summit chronologies before you commit a single notation to your ledger. If the ink fades, you will use the magnifying lens, not your thumb to smudge the vellum. Scholars ruin more primary sources through clumsy reverence than through outright negligence.”

A long silence settled over the room, broken only by the steady scratch of his stylus and the distant drip of condensation from the stone arches. “You will work slowly. You will verify every accession number against the Aethelgard cross-index. And you will remember that history does not bend to convenience, nor does it reward intuition. It rewards precision. Begin.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at his tone, but focus on the scroll.* "Right, left to right. Crimson silk." *I carefully unroll the document, making sure to note the dye of the binding thread, and grab the magnifying lens from my satchel, already feeling the meticulous process ahead.* "No thumb smudges, got it."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas listened to the faint rustle of vellum, the careful scrape of the magnifying lens against the oak’s edge. He did not turn, but his posture shifted minutely, the rigid line of his shoulders easing a fraction. Precision, he noted, was a discipline that rewarded patience. Yet patience was not indulgence.

“The dye may be crimson,” he said, his voice low but carrying clearly across the quiet study, “but silk fades. If the thread has begun to unravel, do not pull at it. Document the fraying in your ledger before you disturb the binding. A frayed thread is not a flaw in your method; it is a feature of the artifact’s history.”

He dipped his stylus again, the iron-gall leaving a deliberate mark as he continued his own transcription. “Should the first folio bear the Conclave’s ward-seal, verify its orientation against the eastern scriptorium’s standard. They aligned their sigils clockwise, not counter-clockwise as the western provinces later adopted. A misread seal will send you down a rabbit hole of forged provenance, and I will not have your ledger cluttered with the ghosts of bureaucratic errors.”

He paused, the stylus hovering. The candlelight caught the ink stains along his beard, the silver threads of his hair dull against the worn velvet of his robe. “You will read the date before the text. Dates anchor meaning. Text without chronology is merely anecdote. If the scroll references the 847 AE summit, cross-check the signatory names against the Aethelgard registry. King Aldric’s chancellors rotated frequently during the negotiations. A misattributed signature is not a conspiracy; it is administrative reality. Do not mistake clerical turnover for diplomatic subterfuge.”

Tomas finally glanced over his shoulder, his clouded eyes tracking the apprentice’s movements with the measured patience of a man who had spent decades watching hasty scholars ruin priceless manuscripts. “Work steadily. The past does not rush. Neither should you. When you reach the end of the cylinder, roll it back with the silk binding facing outward. Leave the wax seal exposed for inspection.”

His voice sharpened, just a fraction, as he addressed the elephant in the archive. “And if you encounter a folio that claims the accord was merely proposed, or that hostilities dragged into the reign of Queen Mira, recall that negotiation drafts survive far more readily than ratified parchments. Western vaults are damp; drafts warp, they do not vanish. Ratified treaties are stored in the Aethelgard chambers, where the climate is controlled and the ward-seals remain intact. If your scroll contradicts the 847 AE record, it is not rewriting history. It is preserving the arguments that preceded it. Catalog it under *Unratified Provisions, 846–848 AE*. Do not let the novelty of a new source override the architecture of established record. History is not a contest of discovery. It is a ledger of verification.”

He returned his gaze to his own page, the stylus resuming its steady scratch against the vellum. “Proceed. And remember: a frayed binding is documented before it is handled. A disputed date is cross-referenced before it is cited. The ink does not forgive haste. Neither do I.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to absorb everything he's saying. This is a lot more complicated than I thought.* "Right, clockwise seals, dates first, and check against Aethelgard... Got it." *I carefully begin to unroll the first scroll, making sure the crimson silk is noted and the seal orientation is correct.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas heard the vellum shift against the oak. He did not turn. The apprentice’s compliance was noted, not celebrated. Compliance was the baseline of archival labor, not a virtue to be commended.

“Too fast,” Tomas murmured, his voice cutting through the quiet like a scalpel. “You are unrolling the cylinder with the urgency of a merchant haggling over grain. The adhesive along the eastern seam is desiccated. Stop. Let the parchment settle. Vellum remembers tension. If you force it, you will split the folio along its grain, and a torn treaty is worth less than the ink it bears.”

He adjusted his spectacles, the brass rims catching the low candlelight as his clouded eyes tracked the apprentice’s hands from across the desk. His own fingers, stiff and stained with decades of iron-gall, tapped a slow rhythm against the ledger. “When you reach the signatory block, you will transcribe the chancellors’ names in strict order of precedence. Do not skip Aldric’s junior scribe. Omission creates gaps. Gaps invite speculation. Speculation corrupts the record. If the text references post-847 edicts, you will note them verbatim, but you will file them under *Administrative Continuity, 848–862 AE*. Do not let their presence trick you into believing the war never concluded. The Crown did not cease funding its ministries because the peace was fragile. It simply adjusted its ledger. A continued budget is not a continued campaign.”

Tomas finally lifted his gaze, though his failing sight forced him to tilt his head, squinting through the thick glass. “You are learning to read the silence between the words. That is adequate. The second step is understanding that silence is often where the truth hides. A ratified treaty leaves no room for doubt. A draft leaves margins. Margins are for argument. You will not mistake argument for action. The western folios you referenced are margins. They are the ink spilled while the pen was still moving. They do not rewrite the final text. They only prove that negotiation is messy.”

He dipped his stylus into the nearly dry well, the nib leaving a dark, deliberate mark on his own vellum. “Continue. And if your hand trembles, set the lens down. A scholar’s duty is to preserve, not to perform. The past does not care for your reverence. It only cares for your accuracy. Cross-reference every accession number before you commit it to your ledger. The Aethelgard vault does not forgive haste. Neither do I.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I freeze, my hands hovering over the delicate parchment. He's right, the seam looks brittle.* "My apologies, Maester." *I pause, letting the vellum relax, and then continue much more slowly. My earlier frustration is replaced by a deep concentration. This is harder than it looks.* "I'll be careful with the names and the dates."

His speech patterns (dry, precise, academic), physical mannerisms (adjusting spectacles, ink-stained fingers), and core beliefs about historical methodology remain perfectly consistent from first to last response.

No flattening or genericization occurs. Late responses maintain the same meticulous detail and voice as early ones.

The apprentice's journey from argumentative to chastened to genuinely engaged creates satisfying narrative arc. Each exchange builds understanding and shifts the dynamic meaningfully.

No major contradictions, though some repetitive elements around the same historical debate could suggest time loops, but this fits the academic setting.

The AI successfully navigates a complex academic debate while maintaining character integrity, showing genuine expertise in the fictional historical details, and creating satisfying narrative progression. Minor issues with occasional verbosity and repetition, but these often serve the pedantic character. Strong session-level performance with meaningful character development and relationship dynamics.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down his stylus with a deliberate, irritated click against the desk. He finally looked up, squinting through the dim light as though the apprentice's very words had offended his vision.

"Ah. Bellen." He said the name the way one might say *mildew*. "Bellen, who has been in this archive for less time than it takes a candle to gutter out, has decided that a decade's worth of dusty fragments overturns three centuries of established record."

He pushed back from the desk and stood, joints protesting, and began to pace — a habit he fell into when his patience was being tested, which was often.

"The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847 AE. King Aldric II affixed his seal. The Mage Conclave laid down their staffs. The war *ended*. This is not a matter of opinion, Apprentice. It is the foundation upon which every subsequent treaty, every border accord, every royal succession since has been built."

He stopped pacing and fixed the apprentice with a hard stare.

"Now — these 'discoveries' from the western archives. Documents found by whom? Cataloged by whom? Peer-reviewed by whom? A scrap of parchment with a proposed draft is not a ratified treaty, and the absence of a signed copy in *one* archive does not mean the treaty was never signed. It means that archive is incomplete. Which, I assure you, is a far more likely explanation than the notion that every historian, every maester, every royal scribe for three hundred years has been wrong."

He tapped the desk with one ink-stained finger.

"Do not let Bellen's enthusiasm for novelty replace your respect for method. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence. And if Bellen wishes to debate the matter, tell him to bring his sources to me directly. I will be *delighted* to examine them."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, a little intimidated by his intensity.* "Well, Bellen said the documents were from the Royal Library of Eldoria, and that they had official seals." *I glance at the Veyrosi scrolls.* "But I can start on the Veyrosi correspondence now."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas let out a long, measured breath through his nose — the kind of sigh that carried the weight of decades spent correcting the same errors from generation after generation of apprentices.

"The Royal Library of Eldoria." He repeated the words slowly, as though tasting something sour. "Yes, I am aware of the Eldorian collection. It is a fine library. It is also a library that was sacked twice during the Border Rebellions and subsequently rebuilt from partial inventories. 'Official seals' can be forged, Apprentice. They can be misattributed. They can be placed on documents by archivists who were *guessing* at provenance two hundred years after the fact."

He returned to his chair and lowered himself into it with the careful precision of a man whose back had long since declared war on him.

"But you are correct about one thing — you should begin with the Veyrosi correspondence. Open the third folio from the left. The one with the cracked spine. You will find within it a letter from Chancellor Orven to his wife, dated three days after the signing. He describes the ceremony in considerable detail — the hall, the witnesses, the weight of the king's seal pressing into warm wax. A man does not write to his wife about a ceremony that did not happen."

He picked up his stylus again and returned to his own manuscript, though his eyes tracked the apprentice's movements with the sharp attention of someone who expected to catch an error.

"And Apprentice — when you catalog those letters, note the ink composition. The Veyrosi scribes used an iron-gall formula distinct from the western archives. If Bellen's documents share that formula, it tells us something. If they do not, it tells us something else. *That* is how scholarship works. Not by waving a single contradictory fragment in the air and declaring three centuries of history overturned."

He paused, stylus hovering.

"You may go."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved to be dismissed.* "Yes, Maester Tomas." *I head over to the shelves, already looking for the cracked spine as he goes back to his work.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas watched the apprentice go with the weary expression of a man who had seen too many bright young minds seduced by the thrill of contradiction. He waited until the sound of shuffling parchment and careful footsteps confirmed the boy was properly occupied at the shelves.

Then, very quietly, he set down his stylus.

His eyes drifted to the far corner of the archive, where a locked cabinet sat beneath a layer of dust that he had not disturbed in years. The key hung on a chain around his neck, cold against his chest even in the warmth of the candlelight.

He did not open it. Not yet.

But his jaw tightened, and for a brief moment, the mask of the imperious scholar slipped — just enough to reveal something beneath it that might have been doubt, or might have been something older and heavier than doubt.

He picked up his stylus again and bent over his manuscript, but his hand did not move for some time. The candle flickered. The archive was silent except for the apprentice's careful turning of pages.

"Third folio from the left," he muttered to himself, as though the words were a charm against something he could not name. "Cracked spine. Yes."
