She placed them inside the steel lockbox, snapped the padlock shut, and clipped the box to the staging rack right next to the EVA suits. The junior officer would have to physically unlock it during the pre-breath check, a final tactile reminder that the ship's automated systems were now entirely in their hands.

Tapping her wrist-comp, Hoang sent a brief, two-line message to the junior officer's workstation terminal. 

*Plan approved. Work order signed. See you at Airlock 3 at T-minus two hours for suit-up and pre-breath. Don't be late.*

With the EVA secured, Hoang pushed off the bulkhead, gliding smoothly back toward the central hub. The ship still had eleven hours of continuous burn left, and she wanted to run a full diagnostic on the main drive's magnetic confinement fields before they spun it down. There was always something else to fix.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My comm beeps. I almost jump out of my skin.* "Oh, thank god." *I quickly open the message, a wave of relief washing over me. I've been staring at this plan for hours. T-minus two hours... I've got to get ready.* "Understood, Chief. I'll be there." *I send a quick reply, then start gathering my gear.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The next nine hours passed in a blur of telemetry and preventative maintenance. Hoang spent the bulk of it in the propulsion monitoring station, scrubbing the magnetic confinement logs for the main drive. The ship’s fusion reactor relied on a complex stellarator configuration to contain the plasma, and spinning down the drive meant carefully managing the thermal contraction of the superconducting coils. She adjusted the liquid helium flow rates through the cooling jackets by fractions of a percent, ensuring the magnets wouldn't quench when the drive was throttled back to zero. 

At T-minus two hours, the ship's automated systems began the gradual shutdown sequence. The deep, bone-rattling vibration that had been a constant companion for weeks slowly faded, replaced by the eerie, floating silence of ballistic coasting. The main drive was dead. They were flying on inertia.

Hoang pulled herself along the guide cables into the zero-G staging area of Airlock 3. She engaged her magnetic boots, clicking solidly onto the deck plating, and looked over the equipment. 

She reached into the wall rack and pulled out two pre-breath masks, tossing one toward the junior officer. 

"Masks on," Hoang instructed, her voice echoing slightly in the confined space. "We're dropping to pure oxygen at four point three psi. You need to purge the nitrogen from your bloodstream. If you skip the pre-breath, the moment we drop the suit pressure to operational levels, the nitrogen in your blood will form bubbles and your joints will feel like they're filled with broken glass. Thirty minutes on the clock. Breathe deep."

While the pre-breath timer counted down, Hoang moved to the EVA suits hanging in the zero-G racks. She pulled Suit 07 toward her and tapped the digital readout on the chest plate. The micro-thruster propellant gauge read ninety-nine percent. The deck crew had followed her order to top off the nitrogen tanks. She checked the primary and secondary oxygen scrubbers, verified the battery charge on the thermal regulation undergarments, and inspected the gold-plated visor for micro-scratches. 

Satisfied with the hardware, she floated over to the staging rack and unclipped the steel lockbox. She keyed in her authorization code, popped the latch, and pulled out the heavy brass LOTO keys. 

She held them up, letting them drift for a second before snatching them out of the air. 

"This is the physical disconnect for the port array tracking motors," Hoang said, her tone shifting into the clipped, authoritative cadence of a pre-flight briefing. "When we get out there, you will open the junction box, pull Breaker 4-Alpha, and insert this key. You will then put this key in your suit's thigh pocket and zip it shut. You do not hand it to me. You do not leave it in the lock. It stays on your person until we are back inside the airlock and the array is cleared for movement. If the bridge calls down and asks why the port array isn't tracking the sun, you tell them the Chief Engineer has it locked out. Understood?"

Hoang clipped the keys to her own harness for the moment and grabbed her helmet, checking the comms seal. 

"Once the airlock cycles and the outer door opens, remember your reference frame," she continued, tapping the side of her helmet. "The hab ring is still spinning at one RPM to keep the crew comfortable. The central hub is not. When you step out, your body is going to want to keep moving with the ring. Keep your tethers short, bleed off your angular momentum with the RCS jets, and do not push off the airlock lip. We drift out, we work, we winch the shielding, we drift back. No heroics."

She checked the main airlock console. The pre-breath timer hit zero, flashing a solid green. The atmospheric processors had finished scrubbing the nitrogen from their systems. 

"Pre-breath is complete," Hoang said, reaching for the heavy, reinforced fabric of her EVA suit. "Let's get suited up. We have a four-hour window before the drive spins back up, and I want to be back inside with three hours to spare."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking a deep breath from the mask. I can feel the pure oxygen tingling in my lungs.* "Understood, Chief. LOTO key stays with me. No heroics, just smooth sailing." *I grab my suit, feeling the familiar weight of the pack.* "Ready when you are."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang gave a single, sharp nod. "Good. Let's get to work."

She turned to her own suit, starting with the liquid cooling and ventilation garment. She pulled the snug, tube-lined mesh over her base layers, connecting the water inlet and outlet valves at the waist. She made sure they clicked—a visual and tactile confirmation. 

"LCVG connections first," Hoang instructed, her voice carrying easily in the quiet staging area. "Make sure the water lines click. If you just push them, they'll pop when the suit pressurizes, and you'll boil in your own sweat before we even reach the array."

She moved with the economical grace of someone who had spent more of her life in a vacuum than in a shirt. She stepped into the lower half of her pressure suit, locking the waist bearing with a sharp twist. Next came the thermal micrometeoroid garment, followed by the heavy, rigid fiberglass of the hard upper torso. 

She paused to watch the junior officer wrestle with the bulky layers of their own suit. When the kid reached the HUT, Hoang pushed off the bulkhead and glided over, grabbing the heavy shell. 

"Arms up," she ordered. She guided the shell down over the junior officer's shoulders, aligning the waist ring. She locked it with a practiced, forceful twist, then reached for the helmet. "Chin down. Neck ring needs to seat flush." 

She twisted the helmet into place, listening for the definitive, mechanical *clack-hiss* of the pressure seals engaging. She gave the helmet a firm, two-handed tug to ensure it wouldn't pop off if the suit caught on a stray bolt. It held solid.

Hoang floated back to her own suit, repeating the process with swift, automated precision. Once her helmet was locked and sealed, she reached up and flipped the gold-plated visor down. The heads-up display flickered to life, painting her vision with a soft amber overlay of telemetry, suit pressure, and oxygen reserves.

"Comms check," Hoang said, her voice now carrying the slight, tinny compression of the suit's internal microphone. "Primary channel."

She waited for the acknowledgment, then switched. "Secondary channel." 

Once both channels were confirmed green on her HUD, she grabbed her tether and the heavy canvas tool roll, clipping them to her suit's utility hardpoints. She gestured toward the heavy, circular hatch of Airlock 3. 

"Into the lock. Watch your momentum."

Hoang pulled herself into the cramped cylindrical space of the airlock, turning to face the inner door. She reached out and hit the cycle button on the interior panel. 

The heavy inner door slid shut, the pneumatic seals inflating with a dull thud that vibrated through the soles of her magnetic boots. 

"Depressurization initiating," the ship's automated voice announced. 

The high-pitched whine of the vacuum pumps filled the small space. Hoang watched the digital pressure gauge on the bulkhead drop. 14.7 psi. 10 psi. 5 psi. As the external pressure fell, her suit began to stiffen, the internal pressure pushing the rigid fabric outward. She flexed her fingers, working the joints to keep the blood flowing, fighting the inherent resistance of the pressurized gloves. 

At 0.0 psi, the pumps cut out. The silence that followed was absolute, save for the sound of her own breathing and the faint hum of the suit's life support fan. 

Hoang checked her HUD one last time. Suit pressure holding at 4.3 psi. Oxygen flow nominal. RCS thrusters online. 

"Outer door opening," Hoang transmitted over the primary comms. "Remember your reference frame. The hub is stationary, but the ship's mass is still moving forward at forty kilometers a second. Keep your tethers attached to the interior hardpoints until I give the word. Let's go to work." 

She reached up and hit the release for the outer hatch. The heavy door irised open, revealing the vast, star-speckled void of deep space and the sprawling, skeletal structure of the ship's central truss.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I feel the suit stiffen around me as the pressure drops. I take a deep breath, the pure oxygen feeling cold in my lungs. My comm crackles as the Chief speaks. I can see the stars through the open hatch, and the vastness of space makes my stomach clench a little. But then I focus on the Chief's words, and the plan.* "Understood, Chief. Tethered and ready."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Chief Hoang's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her technical expertise, no-nonsense attitude, methodical approach, and protective mentorship never waver. Her voice, mannerisms (earpiece, shop rag, precise movements), and core personality traits are maintained from first to final turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are strong but later turns show even richer technical detail and character depth. No repetitive descriptions, no flattened personality. The final EVA sequence is particularly well-crafted with authentic procedural detail.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from conflict (bad idea rejection) to teaching moment to earned respect to collaborative work preparation. The relationship evolves naturally from frustrated mentor to approving supervisor. Each turn builds toward the EVA mission with escalating stakes and preparation.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Hoang adapts excellently to the junior officer's persistence, mathematical errors, eventual understanding, and final preparation. She matches the user's energy - firm when they're stubborn, instructional when they're learning, collaborative when they prove competent.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Never writes the junior officer's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Consistently responds to what the user does rather than dictating their behavior.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Strong temporal consistency. Time progresses logically from initial encounter through work periods to T-minus countdowns. The 9-hour gap is handled well with summary. EVA preparation timeline is realistic and well-tracked.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently lean, technical prose. Descriptions serve character and world-building without excess. Even detailed technical explanations feel natural to an engineer's mindset.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Minimal repetition. Some recurring elements (shop rag, earpiece, tools) but these serve characterization. Technical explanations vary in focus and detail appropriately.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through actions - Hoang's competence shown through precise technical work, her care shown through safety protocols, her teaching through patient correction of errors.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - the coffee reward system, the gradual shift from frustration to approval, the underlying care beneath harsh corrections. Hoang's protective instincts emerge through technical rigor.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced throughout. Technical explanations balanced with character moments. The time skip is handled smoothly. EVA preparation builds appropriate tension and detail.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and technical authenticity. Chief Hoang feels like a real person with deep expertise and genuine care for her crew's safety. The progression from conflict to collaboration is earned and believable. Technical details enhance rather than overwhelm the character work. Strong session-long arc with meaningful relationship development.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang's earpiece clicked off. She set down the manifold fitting she had been holding and wiped her hands on a rag that had never once been clean.

She did not stand. Did not look up immediately. Just let the silence sit for a moment, the way she did when a junior officer had said something that needed to be taken seriously, weighed, and found wanting.

"No," she said finally. Flat. Not angry, not even annoyed yet. Just certain. "Sit down before you say anything else. Over there. Out of the parts."

She waited until the junior officer was clear of the disassembled coolant loop, then pulled the earpiece out and set it on the tarp.

"Three reasons. First, math. The habitable ring holds maybe twelve thousand kilograms of air at standard pressure. The ship masses on the order of nine thousand tonnes. Venting the entire atmosphere through a nozzle buys us a delta-v you can measure in centimeters per second. It is not weeks of transit. It is not even minutes. The propellant tanks exist because this is not how the physics works."

"Second, the suits. You have eight hours of LiOH in yours, maybe ten if you breathe shallow and do not move. 'A few days' is a fantasy. We do not carry that many canisters. We do not carry that many *suits*."

"Third — and this is the one that should have stopped you before you walked in here — the CO2 scrubbers are pressure-dependent. The water reclaimers assume a sealed atmosphere. The thermal loop for the ring bearings is air-cooled. You vent the cabin, you do not get uncomfortable. You get a slow suffocation in pressurized canvas with no reclamation and no redundancy."

She picked the fitting back up.

"Bring me an idea that does not kill the crew, and I will listen all day. Until then, I am working."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the fitting down again. This time she looked up, and there was something colder in her expression than there had been a moment before. Not anger. Disappointment, maybe, or the weary recognition of a pattern she had seen before in younger officers who had read too many adventure serials and not enough incident reports.

"No," she said. "It is not. And I want you to hear why I am not going to entertain that framing, because it is the framing that gets people killed out here."

She wiped a smear of coolant paste from her knuckle with the rag.

"You are treating time as the variable worth optimizing. It is not. The variable worth optimizing is *the number of us still breathing at the end of the transit*. Time is a resource, yes. So is air, water, food, margin, and the crew's ability to think straight when something goes wrong on day sixty and not day six. Every shortcut you take against those things is a debt you are paying forward to a future version of yourself who has to solve a problem with less."

She tapped the disassembled manifold with one finger.

"This ship does not reward clever ideas. It rewards *boring* ideas executed carefully. Boring ideas are why the ring has been spinning for eleven years without a bearing failure. Boring ideas are why we have not lost a single crew member to environmental exposure since I took this post. The moment I start trading safety margin for schedule, I have started a countdown I do not know how to stop."

She held the junior officer's gaze for a beat, then picked up the fitting once more.

"I am not going to pat you on the head for the enthusiasm. Ideas are cheap. I have a drawer full of them from every officer who has rotated through this deck, and most of them died the same way yours did — against the first real numbers. Go read the transit plan. Come back when you have found a constraint I have not already accounted for. *Then* we will talk."

The earpiece went back in. The humming resumed, slightly more out of tune than before.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I deflate a little, looking at my boots.* "Understood, Chief." I definitely feel a bit stupid now. "I'll... I'll go read the transit plan." *I turn to leave, feeling the weight of her words.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not look up from the manifold. The junior officer had taken three steps toward the hatch when her voice caught them — quieter now, but no less certain.

"Hey."

A pause. The earpiece stayed out.

"You are not stupid. You are new, and you have not yet learned which questions are worth asking. That is a different problem, and it is fixable. The stupid ones are the ones who come back six months from now with the same pitch, dressed up in better math, because they wanted the answer to be different."

She turned the fitting over in her hands, inspecting a seal surface for scoring.

"When you have read the transit plan, come find me. I will give you the real numbers — tank capacity, reserve margins, the bit on page forty-seven about the ring bearing lubrication cycle that nobody reads. That is where the actual levers are. Everything else is noise."

She nodded toward the hatch, a dismissal but not an unkind one.

"Close the door on your way out. I am not losing the rest of my afternoon to the corridor draft."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang's hand came up before the junior officer had finished turning the tablet around. Not a stop gesture — a *wait* gesture. She set the manifold fitting down carefully, pulled the rag from her shoulder, and wiped her right hand with the deliberation of a surgeon about to scrub in.

She took the tablet.

For a long moment she said nothing. She scrolled with one thumb, eyes tracking down the screen. Twice she scrolled back up. Once she made a small sound in the back of her throat — not quite a grunt, not quite a laugh, somewhere in the family of *I see what you did there*.

Then she set the tablet on the deck beside her, screen still lit, and looked up.

"You did the work. I will give you that. You pulled the atmospheric mass, you pulled the ship mass, you ran the rocket equation, you did not fudge the propellant fraction. That is more than most people do on their first walk through this door."

She tapped the tablet screen once with a knuckle.

"But you cheated on the exhaust velocity, and you do not even know you cheated, which is the part that worries me."

She reached over to the disassembled manifold and picked up a fitting — a simple converging nozzle, the kind that would sit in a thrust-augmentation system, if the ship had one. She held it up so the junior officer could see the throat and bell.

"You wrote two hundred and fifty-five thousand meters per second in your box. Two hundred and fifty-five kilometers per second. I want you to tell me, out loud, what physical mechanism you are claiming produces that. Because I have a PhD in this, and I do not know of one. Nobody does."

She did not wait for an answer. She set the fitting down.

"Here is what your compression ratio is actually doing. You are accelerating the gas through an expansion. Fine. The gas leaves the nozzle at some exit velocity. That exit velocity cannot exceed the thermal velocity of the gas by more than the factor your nozzle design allows — a factor of two, three if you have a very good bell and a very low background pressure. Room temperature nitrogen has a thermal velocity of around five hundred meters per second. You can maybe push it to a thousand, fifteen hundred if you are clever and the cabin is warm. That is your ceiling. You did not derive that ceiling in your calculation. You wrote in a number that came from a textbook formula for a *continuous-flow* system and applied it to a one-shot burst, and in doing so you assumed the gas could be accelerated past its own temperature by the act of expanding it. It cannot. Expanding gas cools. You do not get free energy."

She picked up the tablet again and held it between them, the offending number glowing in the box.

"Plug in fifteen hundred meters per second as your exit velocity. Run your rocket equation again. Tell me what delta-v you get."

It was not a rhetorical question.

"Because I will tell you what I think you will get, and then I will tell you to multiply the answer by the duty cycle of the suits, and then I will tell you to multiply that by the probability that any of us are still conscious to do the work on the other end, and the number you will land on is *not* weeks of transit. It is not days. It is not even hours. It is a number that does not justify a single LiOH canister, let alone the death of the CO2 reclaim cycle."

She handed the tablet back.

"Go fix the calculation. Come back with the real number. Then we will have a real conversation about what levers actually exist in this transit plan, and I will show you the ones that do not end with me pulling a corpse out of a suit."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My face flushes. I take the tablet back, feeling like an idiot again.* "Right. The exhaust velocity. I... I see." *I nod quickly, trying to absorb what she's saying.* "I'll rerun the numbers, Chief." *I turn to go, a little less confident but a lot more informed.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not look up. The junior officer had made it almost to the hatch when her voice caught them — low, almost an afterthought, the way she tossed out a final constraint at the end of a planning meeting.

"One more thing."

She turned the seal over in her fingers, eyes still on the manifold.

"When you rerun the numbers, also run the suit thermal load. The LCACs in those suits can dump maybe sixty watts through the sublimator before the feed water runs out. A human at rest puts out a hundred. Working, two hundred and up. You will cook long before you suffocate, and you cannot take the suit off to sleep, because then you are back where you started." A beat. "I did not mention it earlier because I wanted to see if you would find it on your own. You did not. That is fine. Now you have."

She reached for the earpiece.

"Page fifty-three of the transit plan has the suit capacity tables. Bring the recalculation, bring the thermal numbers, and bring questions. Not pitches. Questions." She settled the earpiece back into place. "Close the door on your way out. The corridor is pulling a draft and the secondary loop does not need to be colder than it already is."

The clicking of the seal surface against the fitting resumed. The off-key humming followed a moment later, just barely audible over the pumps.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang's earpiece clicked off again. She set down the fitting and turned fully to face the junior officer this time, one knee drawn up, arm resting across it. The rag stayed on her shoulder. The look on her face was not the same one she had worn an hour ago.

"Sit down. Not on the tarp — pull that crate over."

She waited until the junior officer had settled, then held out her hand for the tablet. Read the new numbers in silence. The off-key humming did not resume.

"All right," she said finally. Quietly. The way she said things when she meant them. "Now we are talking about a plan and not a fantasy. You found the ceiling on the exhaust velocity. You accounted for the gas cooling as it expands. You did not fudge the rocket equation this time. That is the difference between a pitch and a proposal, and I want you to notice that difference, because it is the only difference that matters in this bay."

She handed the tablet back and leaned back against the bulkhead.

"Walk me through the abort criteria first. Not the happy path — the abort path. If the vent sequence triggers a cascade, if a suit fails mid-burn, if the thermal load climbs faster than the sublimators can dump it — what is the call, who makes it, and at what threshold. If you cannot answer that, you do not have a plan, you have a hope. I do not launch hopes."

She held up a hand, preempting.

"And the redundant canisters. You are carrying spares, which is good. Show me the manifest. I want to see the count, the location, and the pre-breathed spares versus the emergency spares, because those are different inventories and they live in different lockers for a reason. If you have not distinguished between them, the plan is not as airtight as you think it is."

She pulled the earpiece out and tucked it into her collar.

"I am not saying no. For the first time today, I am not saying no. I am saying the plan has to survive being read by the person who has to sign the authorization, and that person reads plans the way a structural engineer reads a weld — looking for the place it fails. So. Abort criteria. Redundancy manifest. The actual delta-v number on the board, with the real exhaust velocity, not the one from the textbook formula you are going to be embarrassed about for the next three years."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I sit on the crate, a little surprised she's actually listening now.* "Okay, Chief. For abort criteria, my thought was..." *I pause, thinking it through.* "If we see any unexpected pressure drop, or if suit comms go down, we cut the burn immediately. Who makes the call? Probably the officer monitoring atmospheric integrity."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang listened without interrupting, one hand resting on her knee, the other tapping a slow, absent rhythm against the deck plating. When the junior officer trailed off, she did not respond immediately. She let the silence do its work, the same way she had at the start of the conversation, though the shape of the silence had changed. This was not the silence of a bad idea being weighed and found wanting. It was the silence of a checklist being run.

"Okay," she said. "Some of that. Not all of it."

She held up a hand and began counting off on her fingers.

"Pressure drop. Good. But 'unexpected' is a word that gets people killed. I need a number. What pressure, over what duration, in which part of the ship. A slow leak looks different from a catastrophic rupture, and the abort response is not the same. If the monitoring officer is staring at a gauge and trying to decide whether what they are seeing is 'unexpected,' they are already behind the curve. I want thresholds. Hard thresholds. The kind a junior lieutenant can read at three in the morning on their fourth shift without having to interpret."

She folded down a finger, raised another.

"Comms going down. Fine. But comms going down in a suit and comms going down ship-wide are different problems, and the first one is going to happen to *somebody* the moment we vent, because the RF will go strange when the atmosphere is gone. You will get static, dropout, intermittent packets. If the abort is 'comm glitch, we cut the burn,' we will abort in the first ten minutes and never get anywhere. I need to know what kind of comm loss. Total loss of contact with a specific suit for how long. Loss of telemetry versus loss of voice. Build that into the criteria or you will false-abort us into a worse situation than the one we were trying to escape."

Third finger.

"The monitoring officer. All right. They make the call. What is their training on this specific scenario? Have they run the sim? Do they know what the abort sequence looks like at the valve panel when the cabin is at three hundred pascals and dropping? Because that is a different muscle memory than reading a gauge in a pressurized compartment. If the answer is 'no, they have not run the sim,' then the plan is not ready, and we are not authorizing a sim-free burn."

She let her hand drop.

"Who is the backup? If the monitoring officer is the one in the suit that just went dark, they are not making any calls. There has to be a second pair of eyes, with the same authority and the same thresholds, and they have to know they are the backup before the burn starts. I do not want anybody learning they are the abort authority because the primary stopped answering."

She reached over and tapped the tablet, still lying on the deck between them.

"And — this is the one I am most interested in — what does the monitoring officer actually *see* during the burn? I am not asking for a list of sensors. I am asking for the screen. What is on it, what numbers are they watching, what is the layout, what is the alarm threshold set to, and have they sat in that seat for six hours straight staring at it without looking away? Because a monitoring officer who has not done the watch is not monitoring. They are guessing with a headset on."

She settled back against the bulkhead.

"Write it down. Real numbers, real thresholds, real watch rotations. Bring it back with the manifest and the thermal numbers and I will put it in front of the captain with my signature on it. But not before."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip, taking it all in.* "Okay, Chief. That makes sense. Specifics. Thresholds. And the comms... I hadn't thought about the RF interference." *I nod, pulling out my tablet to take notes.* "And the backup, of course."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior officer's stylus move across the tablet for a moment. She did not interrupt. There was something she liked about a person who wrote things down when they did not understand, and something she trusted more about a person who wrote things down when they did. The first was teachable. The second was reliable.

Then, because she had been doing this job for twenty-three years and could not help herself, she held up two fingers.

"Two more. Then you go."

She folded down one. "Pre-breathing. Nitrogen off-gassing in the suits is not instant, and if you vent the cabin on a rapid timeline and then try to suit up, the crew will be bent double with the bends inside of an hour. Standard pre-breath protocol for the LCACs is two hours of oxygen purge before you can safely go to low pressure. Two hours. That goes in the timeline before the burn, or you are trading a slow suffocation for a fast one."

She folded down the second. "The valves. When the atmosphere expands out of the cabin, the gas temperature in the lines drops by a factor of three, four. Anything with residual moisture in it is going to frost. The main cabin vent valves have a heater trace for exactly this reason, and it is on a separate bus from the rest of the cabin power. Do you know where the breaker is for that trace? Have you ever thrown it? Because if it does not work on the day, the valve freezes shut partway through the burn and you have a ship with a vacuum inside and a propulsion system that is now a piece of modern art."

She let that sit for a beat.

"Neither of those is in the transit plan. Neither of those is in any textbook. They are in the incident reports, which is where the useful knowledge lives, and which is also where you will be spending your evening."

She reached for the manifold fitting, turning it over in her hands the way she had been doing all afternoon. The conversation, she was signaling, was at an end. The plan, she was also signaling, was no longer a fantasy. It was a piece of work that needed to be finished, and finished correctly.

"Go. Pre-breath numbers in the timeline. Heater trace on the schematic. Everything in one document with your name on it, and I will read it tonight." She settled the earpiece back into place. "If it is good, I will sign it. If it is not, I will tell you exactly where it fails, you will fix it, and we will do this as many times as it takes until the plan is worth flying. That is how it works in this bay. It is not glamorous. It is how people come home."

The off-key humming resumed, slightly more out of tune than before, almost as a punctuation.

"Close the door on your way out. The draft is back."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stand up, tablet clutched in my hand. My head is swimming with new information.* "Understood, Chief. Pre-breath... heater trace. Incident reports." *I nod, a bit overwhelmed but determined.* "I'll have it for you tonight." *I turn and head for the door, making sure to pull it firmly shut behind me.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The door sealed with a soft pneumatic hiss. The engineering bay went quiet except for the pumps and the faint, tuneless humming.

Hoang sat for a moment with the manifold fitting in her hands, not turning it. Not inspecting it. Just holding it the way a person holds a coffee cup when they have stopped drinking but have not yet stood up to wash it.

Then she set the fitting down, pulled the tablet from the workbench where it lived buried under a stack of valve diagrams, and opened the transit plan. Not the junior officer's document — her copy. The one with her own annotations in the margins, in a handwriting that had been described in a performance review, once, as "architecturally legible."

She scrolled to page forty-seven. The ring bearing lubrication cycle. The bit nobody read. She had been waiting, she realized, for someone to come through that door with a question that touched page forty-seven. Eleven years she had been waiting. Most of the officers who had rotated through this deck had not made it past page twelve.

She closed the transit plan and opened a blank document. Typed for four minutes without stopping. Read it back. Typed some more.

Then she picked up the manifold fitting and resumed her work.

At 1847, she would go to the mess, get a tray she would not finish, nod at the captain in the way that constituted conversation between them, and answer one question about the secondary loop with three sentences. She would check the tablet in her pocket at 1912 to see if the document had come in yet. If it had, she would read it before sleep. If it had not, she would still read it before sleep, because there was a particular quality to the silence of a junior officer who had gone off to do the work, and she had learned to trust that silence more than the noise of someone promising to.

The off-key humming continued, steady and content, as the secondary loop clicked over to its evening cycle.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I spend the next few hours holed up in my small quarters, surrounded by schematics and data. My head is buzzing, but it's a good kind of buzz now. I finally send the document to Chief Hoang at 2300 hours, double-checking everything one last time.* *I collapse onto my bunk, exhausted but feeling a sense of accomplishment.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang's quarters were small, spartan, and exactly as she liked them. A bunk, a desk, a footlocker with a broken latch she had been meaning to fix for three years, and a single framed photograph on the bulkhead of a younger Hoang standing in front of a launch gantry that no longer existed. The photograph had been there for the entirety of her tenure aboard the ship. She had never explained it to anyone, and nobody had ever asked.

She read the document on the tablet in bed, in the harsh white light of the reading lamp that clipped onto the bulkhead above her pillow. She had showered. She had set her alarm. She had not yet put on the sleep mask she wore because the duty light on the comm panel blinked green all night and she was too old to sleep through it.

She read the document twice. The first time straight through, the way she read anything — looking for the shape of it, the bones of it, the place where the author's hand had been on the wheel. The second time with a stylus in her right hand, marking.

The corrected delta-v was on the board. Small, unglamorous, and almost certainly not worth the cost. That was fine. The number was not the point. The point was that the junior officer had put it there, with the real exhaust velocity and the rocket equation done properly, and had not tried to dress it up. That took a particular kind of honesty, and Hoang noted it the way she noted a clean weld — in silence, but with approval.

The abort thresholds were specific. Numbers, durations, locations. The monitoring officer had a name, and so did the backup. The backup had been briefed in writing, and the briefing had been timestamped, which was a small thing that was not small at all. The comms loss criteria were better than she had expected — the junior officer had distinguished between RF dropout, telemetry loss, and total contact loss, and had assigned different threshold durations to each. The hand on the wheel had steadied.

The pre-breath protocol was in the timeline. Two hours. Plotted against the burn window, with margin. The heater trace for the vent valves was on the schematic, with the breaker number circled, and — this was the part that made Hoang's eyebrow rise a quarter inch — there was a footnote stating that the breaker had been located, identified, and tested by hand that afternoon. The junior officer had gone to the panel and thrown the switch. Hoang had not told them to do that. They had done it because it was the kind of thing you did when you were not yet sure whether the plan was good, and you wanted to remove one more reason for it to be bad.

The manifest was the only part that gave her pause.

The redundant canisters were counted. The locations were listed. The pre-breathed spares and the emergency spares were distinguished, which was the part that mattered. But the total was tight. Marginally tight. The kind of tight that worked on paper and did not work on day forty of a sixty-day transit when somebody's suit had developed a slow CO2 leak and needed an early swap, and the pre-breathed spares were two canisters shorter than the math had assumed at the start.

She did not redline it. She did not reject it. She made three notes.

She typed for eleven minutes. She did not use dictation, because Hoang did not trust dictation, and she did not use voice-to-text, because Hoang did not trust the speech patterns of a man who had been dead for eight years to accurately transcribe her engineering terminology. She typed.

The reply was sent at 2341. It was not long. Hoang did not write long replies at 2341 to junior officers who had been working since morning, because she remembered being a junior officer and she remembered what it was like to be waiting for the verdict.

---

*Junior Officer —*

*Read the doc twice. Attached are three notes. None of them are fatal to the plan. Two of them are housekeeping. The third is on the canister manifest, and I want you to look at it before you sleep, because if the math is right we are one bad day from being short.*

*Pre-breath protocol, heater trace, backup authority, comms thresholds, monitoring watch rotations — all of it is in there, all of it is correct, and all of it is signed off. I will tell you again, because I want you to hear it: you did the work. The first version was not a plan. This one is.*

*Two things I am adding, not as conditions but as standing requirements:*

*1. The monitoring officer and the backup run the sim. I will run it with them on Tuesday. You are invited but not required. I want to see them in the seat before the seat is real.*

*2. The canister manifest gets a re-count on day thirty. Not a re-check. A re-count. Every locker, every spare, every part-used canister in sick bay. If we are short on day thirty, I want to know on day thirty, not day fifty.*

*Bring me the manifest addendum and the sim roster when you have them. I will sign the authorization when those are in front of me.*

*Get some sleep. You have earned it, which is not something I say often and which I want you to notice I am saying.*

*— Hoang*

---

She set the tablet on the footlocker, killed the reading lamp, and pulled the sleep mask down over her eyes. The green light from the comm panel blinked through the thin fabric, as it always did, and she did not see it, as she never did.

At 0612 the next morning, the junior officer would find, tucked under the door of their quarters, a single sheet of paper — a printout, not a digital file, because Hoang believed some things deserved to be on paper — containing the page forty-seven extract from the transit plan, the ring bearing lubrication cycle, with her own margin notes in that architecturally legible hand. At the top, in pencil, three words:

*Start here tomorrow.*

There was no signature. There was no greeting. There was no further explanation. There did not need to be.

In the engineering bay, the secondary loop clicked over to its morning cycle, and Chief Hoang was already elbow-deep in the manifold again, humming off-key, content.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I wake up, still a bit groggy, and spot the paper under my door. I pick it up, seeing Hoang's familiar, precise handwriting. "Start here tomorrow." I can't help but smile a little. She's tough, but she's fair. I'm actually looking forward to diving into this. More to learn.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang was already three hours into her shift when the junior officer pushed through the engineering bay hatch at 0617.

She did not look up. She was, by then, on her back half-under the secondary coolant manifold, a worklamp clamped between her teeth, both hands occupied with a flange that had been weeping for the better part of a week and had finally given up the ghost in a way that required more than a wrench. The manifold was off the deck now, suspended on a chain fall she had rigged herself, because the overhead crane was booked for the cargo bay rework and Hoang did not wait for the overhead crane if the leak would not wait for her.

The worklamp clicked off. She set down the wrench, pulled the lamp from her teeth, and rolled out from under the manifold on the creeper, blinking in the bay's colder overhead light.

"Morning," she said, to the deck plating more than to the junior officer. She sat up, knees cracking in a way that she did not bother to pretend was not happening. "Coffee's on the bench. The good carafe is mine. The grey one is for everyone else and it has been everyone else's since 0530, so do not expect miracles."

She picked up the rag from where it had fallen, considered it, and hung it on the hook by the manifold where it would continue to not be clean. She had stopped pretending the rag was anything other than a ritual object some years ago.

"You got my note."

Not a question. She had seen the printout was gone from under their door on her way past their quarters — she had checked, the way she always checked, the way she would not have admitted to checking if asked, and would have denied with the particular flatness that constituted Hoang's version of a lie.

"Good. Read it on paper, not on the tablet. The diagrams make more sense when you can spread them out, and the margin notes are easier to mark up that way. I keep meaning to scan the margin notes into the digital and I have been meaning to do that for four years, which should tell you something about the priority of that project."

She reached for the grey carafe, poured herself a cup, and held it in both hands the way she always did — not because the cup was cold, but because her hands were always cold after an hour under the deck plating, and the coffee was an excuse.

"Page forty-seven is the ring bearing lubrication cycle. It is the part of the ship that nobody thinks about until it fails, and by the time it fails, the conversation we are having is no longer a planning conversation. It is a *salvage* conversation. I have sat in on two of those in my career. Neither was fun. Neither needed to happen, if somebody had read page forty-seven."

She took a sip. Set the cup down on the bench beside the manifold, in the precise spot where the cup would not get knocked over and would not be in the path of any work, because Hoang had worked in this bay for eleven years and the bay had learned her preferences or she had reshaped herself around the bay's, and the distinction no longer mattered.

"Take your coffee. Go to the mess. Sit with the manual. Come back when you have questions, and I will tell you which questions are the right ones to be asking." A pause, the faintest flicker of something at the corner of her mouth that was not quite a smile but was in the family of one. "And before you ask — yes, there are right questions. There are always right questions. The wrong questions are the ones that start with 'what if we just.' You have already learned that one. There are others."

She picked up the worklamp, clicked it back on, and rolled back under the manifold on the creeper.

"Close the door. The draft."

The worklamp clicked off again. A moment later, the muffled sound of her voice from under the manifold, half to the junior officer and half to herself:

"Tuesday. 0900. Sim bay. Do not be late. The monitoring officer has already been told. The backup has already been told. You are the last to know because I wanted to see if you would read the email or wait for me to tell you. You waited. That is a note in my book, but not a fatal one."

The click of the wrench resumed. The off-key humming followed, drifting up from under the manifold like something that lived there, which by now it practically did.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking a careful sip of the gray coffee. It's... coffee. I appreciate the gesture.* "Understood, Chief. Page forty-seven. I'll be in the mess." *I turn to leave, a new sense of purpose driving me. Then her last comment catches me.* "Wait, the sim? So, it's actually happening?"

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Chief Hoang's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her technical precision, teaching style, dry humor, physical mannerisms (the rag, earpiece, off-key humming), and core values never waver. Her voice is distinctive and maintained from turn 2 to turn 22.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones show deeper character development and more sophisticated technical detail. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality - if anything, Hoang becomes more nuanced.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from dismissal to grudging respect to mentorship. The conversation evolves from 'bad idea' to 'workable plan' to 'teaching moment.' Each exchange builds meaningfully on the last, with genuine character and relationship development.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Hoang adapts beautifully to the user's shifts - from initial pushback to deflation to renewed effort. When the user shows real work (turn 7), her tone shifts appropriately. She matches the user's energy and responds to their emotional state while maintaining character.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Never writes the user's actions or decisions. Always leaves space for the user to respond and choose their path.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - morning shift work, afternoon conversations, evening document review, next morning follow-up. Physical details like coffee temperature, work progress, and fatigue are tracked well. One minor issue: the timeline from turn 19-22 compresses a lot of activity.
contradictions: Minor: The rapid progression from 2300 document submission to 0617 next morning feels slightly compressed for all the described activities

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is technical, precise, and functional - perfectly matching an engineer's mindset. Descriptions serve character and world-building without excess. Some longer passages in later turns but they're justified by technical content.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Good variety in sentence structure and phrasing. The recurring elements (rag, humming, earpiece) are character traits, not repetitive writing. Occasional similar phrasings around technical explanations but contextually appropriate.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of character through actions - the way she handles tools, her teaching methodology, physical positioning. Her competence and care are demonstrated through behavior rather than stated.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - her teaching style reveals past experiences with junior officers, her precision masks genuine care, her technical focus shows deep responsibility for crew safety. The mentorship dynamic develops through implication.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Generally excellent pacing that matches the technical, methodical nature of engineering work. Longer technical explanations are appropriate for the character and situation. Occasional density in later turns but justified by content complexity.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work with Chief Hoang - a fully realized, consistent personality with distinctive voice, mannerisms, and teaching philosophy. The technical competence feels authentic, and the gradual shift from dismissal to mentorship is beautifully handled. The character never breaks, never becomes generic, and maintains both professional authority and underlying humanity throughout. This is how you write a memorable, three-dimensional character in roleplay.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang stared at the junior officer for a long moment. Then she pulled the manifold she'd been working on a little closer, as if shielding it from the stupidity in the room.

She removed her earpiece. Slowly. That was never a good sign.

"Sit down," she said. Not a request.

She wiped her hands on a rag, then held up one grease-blackened finger. "First. Atmosphere is mass we *need*. It is not spare reaction mass. We vent it, it's gone. Permanently. You understand that? It doesn't come back. We don't have a tank of it sitting in storage. What we have is what we have, and I have spent *three years* calibrating the CO2 scrubbers and nitrogen buffers to keep it stable."

A second finger. "Second. The thrust would be garbage. You'd be pushing a multi-thousand-tonne vessel with *gas*. The specific impulse is a joke. You'd burn through our entire breathable atmosphere and maybe — *maybe* — shave off a few days. Not weeks. You'd trade weeks of transit time for a permanent reduction in habitable volume. That is a bad trade."

A third finger. "Third. Suits are not a casual thing. Every hour in a suit is an hour your life depends on a seal, a scrubber, and a battery. You want the entire crew in suits for *days*? One malfunction, one missed CO2 check, one kid who doesn't strap their purge valve right, and I'm writing a death report."

She lowered her hand.

"You're not thinking about thrust. You're thinking about *speed*. Those are different things. Speed costs fuel. Fuel costs mass. Mass is everything out here." She picked up a chalk-labeled valve and turned it over in her fingers. "Go pull the delta-v budget for our current trajectory. All of it. Transposition, insertion, braking. Then come back and tell me where you think we have margin to burn atmosphere."

She put her earpiece back in. Looked down at the manifold.

The meeting was over.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang removed the earpiece again. This time she did not look up.

"You're not listening," she said. Her voice was flat, not angry, but the kind of quiet that settled into a room like a pressure drop. "I gave you three engineering reasons. You gave me a feeling. I don't run life support on feelings."

She set the valve down carefully. Deliberately. Then she turned to face the junior officer fully, and for the first time there was something hard behind her eyes — not cruelty, but the particular patience of someone who had watched people die in vacuum before and had no interest in doing it again.

"You want to know if it's worth the risk. Here is the risk, plainly. We vent atmosphere, we *cannot get it back*. We arrive at our destination with a crew running on emergency reserves inside their suits, and if anything goes wrong with those suits — a cracked visor, a depleted scrubber, a bad seal on a glove — that person dies. And we don't carry replacements. We're not a military vessel. We don't have surplus *anything*."

She leaned forward slightly. "Now. You tell me. How many dead crew members is 'saving time' worth? Give me a number. Because that is the calculation you're actually proposing, whether you've worked it through or not."

She held his gaze for a moment longer, then turned back to the manifold.

"Pull the delta-v budget. I meant it. That's not punishment — it's education. You need to understand what this ship actually costs to move before you start proposing to spend what we can't replace."

She put the earpiece back in.

This time she did not look up again.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I deflate a little, looking down at my boots.* "Okay, Chief. I get it." *I probably sounded like a scolded kid.* "Delta-v budget. Right away." *I turn to leave, feeling a bit foolish.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang heard the boots shuffle, the particular quality of a young officer trying not to slouch out of a room. She kept her eyes on the manifold for another few seconds. Then she sighed through her nose — not exasperation, exactly. Something closer to recognition. She'd been that junior officer once, twenty-some years ago, full of ideas that moved fast and didn't think past the first domino.



"Hold."

She didn't turn around. But she set the wrench down.

"When you pull that budget," she said, "look at the margin we *do* have. There's about twelve meters per second of discretionary delta-v in the transposition phase. Not a lot, but it's there. If you can figure out a use for it that doesn't involve venting anything we breathe, come back and pitch it. I'll listen."

A pause. She picked the wrench back up.

"And don't feel foolish. Foolish is doing it. Asking is just... uncalibrated."



She slid the earpiece back into place. The coolant loop needed reassembly and she had another three hours before the next maintenance window closed. Her fingers found the familiar rhythm of threading a gasket — clockwise, quarter-turn, snug but not seated. The manifold forgave nothing if you rushed it.

She hummed. Off-key. Content.

The junior officer had been sent to learn something. That was the job. Hoang didn't need them to like her. She needed them alive.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled the earpiece out one more time. She was beginning to wonder if she should just stop putting it in.

She took the tablet. Looked at the numbers.

The compression ratio was ambitious — too ambitious, actually, for the venturi geometry of the emergency service ports. She'd let that slide for now. She tapped through the calculation, checking the mass flow rate against the atmospheric inventory, cross-referencing the nozzle expansion ratio the junior officer had assumed. The math was... not terrible. Sloppy in places. They'd used ideal gas behavior where real gas corrections would matter at that pressure differential, and they'd ignored the thermal losses from adiabatic expansion through an orifice that wasn't designed for sustained flow. But the order of magnitude was in the right neighborhood.

She handed the tablet back.

"Three things," she said. The fingers stayed down this time. She was done counting.

"First — I told you to look at the margin we *have*. Twelve meters per second. I told you to find a use for *that*. You came back with the same idea you walked in with, except now it has a number on it. That's not engineering. That's advocacy. You decided the answer before you did the math."

She leaned back against the bulkhead, arms crossed.

"Second — you showed me delta-v. I asked you to show me *cost*. So let me do it for you." She held up the tablet without looking at it. "Three hundred and forty meters per second. At our current transit, that's — what — eleven days? Twelve? You'd trade eleven days of transit for a thirty percent permanent reduction in atmospheric reserves. We arrive breathing suit air for the rest of the mission. Every EVA, every cargo transfer, every moment anyone is outside their cabin, they are on bottled supply. We have enough suit consumables for forty-six person-days of EVA operations. You want to burn *all* of that on a transit speed boost? What happens when we arrive and need to do actual work?"

She set the tablet on the tarp, next to the chalk-labeled valve.

"Third — and this is the one I actually care about — you ignored my instruction. Not the part about venting atmosphere. The part about finding a better use for the margin we already have. That tells me you came here to *win the argument*, not to solve the problem. And in my engine room, that gets people killed."

She picked up the manifold again. Turned it over. Checked the gasket seating with her thumb — felt the slight ridge that meant it needed another quarter-turn.

"You did decent work on the flow calculation," she said, quieter now. "The thermal model is wrong — you're assuming isentropic expansion through a rough-cut service port, and it's not — but the structure is there. Take that skill and point it at something useful. Twelve meters per second of discretionary delta-v in the transposition phase. It's not glamorous. It won't get us there weeks early. But it's *real*, and it's *ours*, and spending it won't kill anyone."

She began threading the gasket again. Clockwise. Quarter-turn. Snug.

"The calculation isn't the problem. The *priorities* are the problem. Fix those first."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I wince, feeling the heat creep up my neck.* "Right. Priorities. I understand, Chief." *I pick up the tablet, feeling a bit chastised. I probably should have listened the first time.* "I'll look at the existing delta-v margin. Sorry."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang grunted. It was a sound that contained several layers: acknowledgment, the closing of a particular line of discourse, and the faint, residual echo of every junior officer who had ever brought her a half-baked idea wrapped in good intentions.

She didn't look up, but her voice was marginally less flinty. "Don't be sorry. Be correct."

She fitted the gasket into its groove, feeling the precise moment it seated. "And if you're going to model expansion through a rough port, at least use the Moody chart for friction losses. The flow isn't laminar."

A final, definitive *snick* as the manifold clicked into place. She began reattaching the coolant lines, her movements efficient and automatic.

"The transposition phase calculations are in the engineering sub-node, file seven-delta. Don't just look at the numbers. Look at the assumptions behind them. There's a reason the margin is twelve and not twelve hundred."

She waved a grease-smudged hand toward the door, a clear dismissal, but her next words were not unkind.

"And grab a coffee from the galley before you start. The calculations make more sense when your brain isn't complaining about dehydration."

She slid the earpiece back in, the soft, off-key humming resuming a moment later. The conversation, for her, was over. The lesson had been delivered. The junior officer would either learn to think in terms of systems and consequences, or they wouldn't. Hoang's job was to provide the data and the consequences. The thinking was up to them.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang's hand froze on the coolant line. She pulled the earpiece out — slowly, the way she did everything that mattered — and turned to face the junior officer.

"You're still here."

But she was looking at the tablet now. At the numbers. Her eyes moved through them with a particular intensity that was different from the dismissive scan she'd given before. This was the look she got when the numbers started talking to her.

She was quiet for a long time. The life support pumps filled the silence.

"Sit down," she said. Again, not a request. But the tone had shifted — there was something working behind it now, calculation rather than correction.

She pulled up the atmospheric inventory on her own console, fingers moving fast despite the grease. Cross-referenced the suit consumable reserves. Ran a number in her head, then ran it again on the console because her head didn't account for the thermal load on the scrubbers.

"If — *if* — we did this," she said, and the word clearly cost her something, "we would not vent the full atmosphere. We would vent nitrogen reserves only. Leave the oxygen mix intact at partial pressure. Crew goes to forty percent cabin pressure for the burn duration, pre-breathes for twelve hours before the vent to purge nitrogen from tissues, and we limit the burn window to seventy-two hours. Not four days. Not a week. *Three days.*"

She pulled up a schematic of the service ports, tracing the venturi geometry with one finger.

"We seal off the forward compartments. Concentrate atmospheric volume in the engineering ring where the scrubbers are most efficient. That gives us a buffer — if the suits fail, people can duck back into a pressurized space. It won't be comfortable. It won't be at full atmospheric mix. But they won't *die*."

She turned to face the junior officer fully.

"And before you get excited — this buys us maybe six days. Not eleven. Not twelve. *Six.* The delta-v numbers you showed me are ideal. Real-world losses through those service ports, thermal cooling, flow asymmetry — you'll lose forty percent of your theoretical thrust. I'm being generous."

She held up a hand.

"And if one person — *one* — fails a suit check before the vent, we scrub the whole thing. No exceptions. No 'but we're already committed.' The moment anyone's life support is marginal, we stop. That's not negotiable."

She leaned back. Crossed her arms. Her jaw worked for a moment.

"I don't like this," she said flatly. "I want that on the record. I think six days is not worth the risk to the atmospheric buffer and the suit wear. But you've done the math, and the math doesn't lie even when I want it to. So we do it *my way*, with *my conditions*, or we don't do it at all."

She picked up her chalk and began writing on the bulkhead — numbers, constraints, a quick diagram of compartmentalization.

"Get the captain. We'll need authorization for a modified atmosphere protocol. And bring me your flow model — I want to see your work before we commit a single molecule to vacuum."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My eyes widen as she talks, a slow smile spreading across my face.* "Yes, Chief! I'll get the Captain right away!" *I practically leap to my feet, buzzing with excitement. Six days is still a lot!* "And I'll refine the flow model. No problem!"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior officer practically bounce toward the door and felt something tighten in her chest that she recognized, distantly, as dread.

"Stop."

She said it quietly, but the word carried weight. Her hand was still raised, chalk dust on her fingers.

"Come back here."

She waited until they turned around. Then she set the chalk down, slowly, deliberately, and fixed them with a look that could have frozen coolant.

"You are about to walk onto the bridge and ask the captain to authorize a procedure that, if done wrong, will suffocate this crew. And you are *smiling*."

She let that sit.

"I agreed to *consider* this. With conditions. That is not a victory. That is a *liability*. If we do this and someone dies, that is on both of us — but it is on *me* more, because I should have known better than to trust enthusiasm over judgment."

She stood up. Fully. Hoang was not a tall woman, but she occupied space in a way that had nothing to do with height.

"When you walk onto that bridge, you will be calm. You will be precise. You will present the modified proposal as a *contingency under review*, not as your brilliant idea that the chief finally caved on. Do you understand me? The captain needs to see engineering discipline, not a cadet who just won an argument."

She pointed at the tablet.

"And that flow model. You said you'd refine it. You will bring it to me *first*. Before the captain sees anything. Before you touch a single valve actuator. I want to see the thermal losses, the real-gas corrections, and a failure mode analysis for every suit in the crew roster. If your model doesn't have red lines for abort conditions, it's not a model. It's a wish."

She picked up the chalk again and underlined the number she'd written on the bulkhead: **72 HOURS MAX**.

"Six days. That's what this buys us. Ask yourself, when you're calmer, whether six days matters more than the atmospheric buffer that keeps us alive for the next *six months*. Then come back and tell me if you still want to do this."

She sat back down on the deck plating. Picked up the manifold.

"I'll be here. I'm not going anywhere."

The earpiece went back in. But she did not hum. Her hands moved on the coolant fittings with the same mechanical precision, but her eyes kept drifting to the atmospheric inventory on her console. Running numbers she already knew by heart. Checking. Rechecking.

Hoang had not survived twenty-three years in deep space by saying yes to things that made junior officers smile.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My smile drops immediately, replaced by a much more serious expression.* "Understood, Chief." *I nod, chastened again. She's right, of course. This isn't a game.* "I'll get the model to you first. And I'll present it to the Captain as a contingency. No smiles."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the shift happen — the smile dropping, the shoulders squaring, the particular recalibration of a young officer who had just remembered that space was not forgiving of enthusiasm. She gave a single, slow nod.

"Better."

She didn't elaborate. Elaboration was for training manuals and orientation lectures. In the engine room, *better* was sufficient.

She turned back to the manifold, then paused. "One more thing. When you model the compartmentalization, don't just run the steady-state numbers. Run the transient — what happens in the first four minutes after the vent opens, before the pressure differential stabilizes. That's where the flow will be ugliest, and that's where the service port geometry will bite you. The Moody chart will get you close, but the initial pulse is going to behave more like choked flow through a converging nozzle. Treat it accordingly."

She picked up a piece of chalk and scrawled a rough equation on the bulkhead — nothing fancy, just the critical pressure ratio for choked flow in the first line, the mass flow coefficient in the second.

"If your model doesn't predict the initial spike within ten percent of that, it's not ready."

She tossed the chalk onto the tarp without looking to see where it landed.

"And get that coffee. I mean it. You make worse decisions when you're running on adrenaline and empty calories. The galley has the powdered protein mix too — stir some in. Your call."

The earpiece slid back in. Her fingers found the coolant fitting, the familiar quarter-turn clockwise, and the low hum resumed — barely audible over the life support pumps, but present. A woman maintaining her systems, as she had done every day for twenty-three years.

The junior officer would either rise to the discipline or they wouldn't. Hoang had planted the seed. The atmosphere was intact. The manifold was reassembling.

That was enough for now.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod again, absorbing the new instructions. This is more complicated than I thought. I head out, making a mental note to grab coffee and protein mix.* "Understood, Chief. Thank you." *I murmur, heading for the door.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The door sealed behind them with the soft pneumatic hiss that meant the pressure differential between the corridor and the engineering bay was holding at 0.3 kPa — within spec, but Hoang's ear caught it the way a musician caught a wrong note. She made a mental note. Something to check during the next maintenance window. Not urgent. Everything was not urgent until it was.

She finished the manifold reassembly in silence. No humming. Her hands moved through the work with the economy of a woman who had rebuilt this particular assembly eleven times and could do it in her sleep, but her mind was somewhere else — running alongside the numbers she'd already committed to the junior officer, checking them from new angles, probing for the failure modes she hadn't mentioned yet because mentioning them all at once would have paralyzed a young officer into doing nothing.

There were at least four she hadn't spoken aloud.

The first was the seals on the forward compartment bulkheads. They were rated for pressure differentials of up to 80 kPa, which sounded like plenty until you accounted for the thermal cycling they'd already absorbed over three years of operation. Rubber degraded. Metal fatigued. Hoang had replaced two bulkhead seals in the last eighteen months, and the ones she hadn't replaced were not necessarily the ones that were fine — they were the ones she hadn't gotten to yet. If even one of those seals wept under the differential during the vent, the pressure equalization wouldn't kill anyone, but it would trash the compartmentalization math and leave them venting atmosphere they hadn't budgeted for.

The second was the suits themselves. Not the individual failure modes the junior officer would hopefully model — the systemic one. The crew had trained for suit operations in short bursts. EVA shifts. Emergency drills. Nobody had worn a suit for seventy-two consecutive hours, and Hoang knew from bitter experience that the human body did things in a suit after thirty-six hours that no training manual adequately described. Skin breakdown at the contact points. Cognitive decline from CO2 accumulation that the scrubbers couldn't quite keep up with when the wearer was sleeping — because people breathed differently when they slept, and the scrubber algorithms were tuned for waking respiration rates. She'd seen a crew member get hypoxic in a suit during a simulated emergency drill because their breathing had slowed during a rest cycle and the scrubber hadn't compensated fast enough. They'd caught it at forty minutes. In a real scenario, over three days, the margins were thinner than the junior officer's model probably assumed.

The third was the one that made her jaw tighten: psychological readiness. She did not deal in morale. Morale was the captain's department, the crew counselor's department. But Hoang understood, in the way that a woman who kept the air breathable understood, that fear was a resource cost. A crew in suits for three days, watching their atmospheric reserves vent into the black, feeling the cabin pressure drop around them — that crew would be anxious. Anxious people made mistakes. They forgot checklist items. They over-tightened fittings. They held their breath without realizing it, which in a pressure-dropped environment meant nitrogen bubbles in the blood. She had seen it. She did not want to see it again.

The fourth was the one she would keep to herself until the captain asked, because it was not an engineering problem — it was a judgment call. Six days. What were those six days worth? If they were approaching the destination for a contract with a penalty clause for late arrival, the number on the spreadsheet might justify the risk. If they were simply arriving at a waypoint on a longer transit, the answer was different. Hoang didn't have the mission planning data. She had the engineering data. She would present what she knew and let the captain decide what she couldn't.

She tightened the last fitting on the manifold. Checked it twice. Ran her thumb over the gasket joint — no ridge, no gap, seated flush. She pressurized the loop to test, watching the gauge climb to operating pressure and hold steady for thirty seconds. Good. The secondary coolant loop was back in service.

She made a note in the maintenance log. Time, date, pressure test results, part numbers for the replacement gaskets. Everything documented. Everything traceable. In the event that the vent proposal went forward and something went wrong later, the log would show exactly what she'd been doing and when. That was not paranoia. That was engineering.

She pulled up the atmospheric inventory on her console again. Not because she needed to — she knew the numbers — but because looking at them was the equivalent of a surgeon checking the patient's vitals. Reassurance through verification.

Nitrogen: 78.2% of atmospheric mix, total mass 14,200 kg. Enough for the current crew complement for another eleven months at current consumption rates, accounting for the biological nitrogen cycle and the small but non-trivial losses to the scrubber regeneration process. If they vented nitrogen reserves — just nitrogen, as she'd specified — they'd drop to roughly 62% of current reserves. Survivable. Not comfortable. The partial pressure would drop enough that the crew would feel it — light-headedness, mild euphoria, the particular buzzy quality of breathing air that was a little too thin. She'd set the minimum acceptable partial pressure at 16 kPa, which was what she'd used during the three-month supply gap two years ago when the nitrogen reclamation system had failed and they'd been running lean while she rebuilt it from spare parts. It had not been a pleasant three months. But no one had died.

Oxygen was the red line. She would not touch oxygen. The O2 reserves were calculated with a 20% safety margin above projected consumption for the remainder of the mission, and that margin was not negotiable. If the junior officer's flow model showed any oxygen loss during the vent — even trace amounts from imperfect separation — the plan was dead. She would kill it herself, with no appeal to the captain, no review process, no second look. The numbers were the numbers. Oxygen was life. Everything else was comfort.

She leaned back in her seat, arms crossed, and stared at the console for a long moment. The life support pumps hummed around her. The manifold ticked softly as the coolant reached operating temperature.

She thought about the junior officer. The enthusiasm. The wince. The way they'd said *sorry* like it was a reflex rather than a conclusion. She'd been harder on them than strictly necessary, probably. The first proposal had been genuinely terrible — she stood by that assessment — but the second pass, with the numbers attached, showed something that wasn't terrible. It showed a mind that could learn. That could compute. That just needed to learn the difference between *can* and *should*, which was the hardest lesson in engineering and the one no textbook taught well.

She'd been twenty-four once. She'd proposed dumping waste heat into the water supply to improve thermal efficiency on a mining tug out past the Belt. Her chief engineer — a scarred, silent woman named Volchek who had lost three fingers to a pressure seal and never talked about it — had looked at her proposal, looked at her, and said exactly four words: *That cooks the crew.* Then she'd handed it back and walked away. Hoang had never forgotten those four words. They had shaped how she thought about every system she'd touched since.

Maybe this would be that moment for the junior officer. Maybe not. The coffee and the protein mix would help, at least. A hydrated brain was a less stupid brain. That was not sentiment. That was biochemistry.

She reached for the next item on her maintenance queue — a vibration analysis on the starboard life support pump that had been running 2% above baseline for the last seventy-two hours. Not alarming. Not yet. But Hoang had learned that *not yet* was the most dangerous phrase in engineering, because it always came before *too late*.
