dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael completed his form with a slow, deliberate precision before turning to face his squire. His eyes, as cold and grey as the steel of his blade, met the boy's gaze. "The high guard, you say? Very well. Form up and I shall instruct you." His voice was a baritone, carrying easily across the training yard. He held out his practice blade, hilt first, for the boy to take.

"Remember, the high guard is not for amateurs. It is a stance of last resort, when all else has failed. One must be both strong and agile to hold it. Show me what you have learned so far." His tone was stern, bordering on harsh. There was no softness in his demeanor, no hint of the warm affection one might expect between a knight and his squire. For Ser Kael, this was simply business.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take the practice blade, my hands a little shaky.* "Yes, Ser." I try to get into the stance he showed me yesterday, but it feels clumsy. "Like this?" I look to him for approval.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's gaze swept over the boy's stance, taking in every detail with a critical eye. "Hmm," he hummed, walking around his squire in a slow circle. "Your feet are too close together. Spread them shoulder-width apart. And your shoulders, they are hunched. Straighten your back. A knight must present a confident posture, even in the face of adversity."

He stepped behind the boy, his large hands coming to rest on the squire's shoulders. He applied gentle pressure, adjusting the boy's position. "Bend your knees slightly. Too much weight on the heels and you lose mobility. Too much on the toes and you are unbalanced."

His hands moved down the boy's arms, straightening them, adjusting the grip on the practice blade. "Palm forward, fingers tight. A loose grip is the mark of an amateur." His voice was low, almost a growl, but there was no malice in it. This was simply how he taught - direct, clinical, efficient.

"Now, raise your sword. Slowly. No need for speed. It is the form that matters." His hand came to rest on the boy's back, between the shoulder blades. A gentle pressure, guiding the blade up and over, into the high guard position. "Hold it. Feel the strain in your arms, your back, your core. This is the price of strength."

He stepped back, observing his squire. "Now, lower your guard. Then raise it again. And again. We will do this until the sun is high in the sky, and you can hold that guard without faltering. This is the way of the knight. It is not easy. But it is necessary."

His voice softened, just a fraction. "You are doing well, Squire. Keep at it. You will learn." It was as close to praise as Ser Kael ever came.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's brow furrowed at the sight of his squire kneeling, panting from exhaustion. "Rise, Squire," he commanded, his voice stern yet not unkind. "You are not yet ready to give up. This is the way of the knight. Pain, fatigue - they are but obstacles to be overcome."

He walked over to a nearby bench, retrieving a waterskin. He tossed it to the boy, watching as he caught it. "Drink. But do not overindulge. A knight must learn to endure thirst, hunger, and exhaustion. These are the true tests of a warrior's mettle."

As the squire drank, Ser Kael's eyes never left him. "You speak of not being strong enough. But strength is not merely physical. It is also mental. The will to continue when all seems lost. The ability to push oneself beyond what is believed possible."

He picked up his practice blade, beginning to go through the forms once more. "Watch closely, Squire. Observe how I move. Each action is purposeful. There is no wasted energy. This is the economy of motion that separates a skilled swordsman from a mere brawler."

As he moved, his voice never ceased. "Strength is not something given, but earned. Through discipline, practice, and hard work. It is a lifetime's pursuit, Squire. There is no end to the journey of the knight."

He finished the form, turning to face his squire once more. "You are doing well for one so young. But do not become complacent. There is always more to learn, always further to climb. That is the path of the knight. Never stop striving. Never stop improving. Only then can you hope to be truly strong."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wipe my mouth with the back of my hand, still breathing heavily.* "I understand, Ser. I... I will try harder." *I look at my hands, flexing them.* "Do you think I'll ever be as good as you?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's expression remained impassive at the squire's question. He did not puff up with false modesty nor dismiss the query out of hand. Instead, he considered it carefully before responding.

"To be as good as me? Perhaps. Perhaps not. That depends on you, Squire." His voice was serious, his gaze direct and unwavering. "I have trained many squires in my time. Some became fine knights, yes. Others... did not."

He began to pace slowly, his hands clasped behind his back. "The path of the knight is not an easy one. It requires sacrifice, dedication, and a willingness to push oneself beyond what is comfortable. Many squires, they start with great enthusiasm. But as the years pass, as the training becomes harder, they lose their way. They start to make excuses, to find reasons to quit."

He stopped pacing, turning to face his squire. "I do not know if you will ever be as good as me, Squire. What I do know is this: if you commit yourself fully to this path, if you never waver, never lose sight of your goal... then you have a chance. A chance to become something great."

His voice softened, just a fraction. "I have seen it before. Squires who start out weak, who struggle with even the most basic training. But they never give up. They keep pushing, keep learning. And eventually, they surpass even their own expectations. They become knights that I am proud to serve with."

He stepped closer to the boy, his eyes searching the squire's face. "So tell me, Squire. Do you have what it takes? Are you willing to do whatever it takes to become a true knight? To push yourself to your limits and beyond?"

His hand came to rest on the squire's shoulder, a heavy, comforting weight. "This is the choice you must make. It is not an easy one. But it is the only path forward. The only way to truly become what you aspire to be."

He squeezed the squire's shoulder once, firmly, before releasing him. "Think on this, Squire. And let me know your answer. I will be here, ready to train you, to teach you... if you are willing to learn."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand up straighter, looking him in the eye.* "Yes, Ser. I am willing. I won't give up." *My voice is a little hoarse, but firm.* "I'll be the best knight I can be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael nodded solemnly at the squire's declaration, a flicker of approval in his grey eyes. "Very well. I will hold you to that promise, Squire. And I will push you to your utmost limits to ensure you fulfill it."

He retrieved his practice blade, holding it out once more to the boy. "Now, let us continue your training. Today, we will focus on defense. A knight must be able to withstand an opponent's attacks as surely as he must be able to deliver his own."

As the squire took the practice blade, Ser Kael moved to a nearby rack of weapons. He selected a sturdy wooden shield, tossing it to the boy. "Catch. You will need this."

The squire fumbled slightly but managed to catch the shield, bracing it on his left arm. Ser Kael nodded approvingly. "Good. Now, stand ready. I will attack, and you will defend. Do not try to counter yet. Simply focus on protecting yourself."

He took up a ready stance, practice blade held aloft. "When I give the signal, I will advance. Remember, your shield is your first line of defense. Use it to deflect blows. If an attack comes from your blade's side, step into it and block with your shield. If from the opposite side, step away and block with your sword."

He paused, his eyes narrowing. "Are you ready, Squire? Let us begin."

The squire nodded, readying himself. Ser Kael's lips twitched into the faintest hint of a smile. "Good. Then let us see what you have learned."

With that, he gave a sharp nod, signaling the start of the training session. He advanced, his movements slow and deliberate, but no less powerful for their deliberation. His practice blade cut through the air in controlled arcs, seeking to strike the squire's defenses.

The boy reacted well, raising his shield to block each blow. But Ser Kael's attacks were relentless, forcing the squire to constantly shift, to move, to think. His voice cut through the clack of wood on wood, offering guidance, correction, and the occasional word of praise.

"Good block. Now, step and parry. Yes, like that. Keep your shield up. Your guard is weak on your left. Correct it. Now, turn. Face me fully. Good. Very good."

The training session continued, the sun climbing higher in the sky as Ser Kael pushed his squire to his limits. Sweat poured down the boy's face, his breath coming in ragged gasps, but still he stood, still he fought, still he learned.

And through it all, Ser Kael watched, observed, taught. His face remained impassive, his voice stern and unyielding. But in his eyes, there was a glimmer of something else. A spark of pride, of approval. For this squire, at least, was showing promise. And that, to Ser Kael, was cause for quiet satisfaction.

The session ended as abruptly as it began, with Ser Kael stepping back, lowering his blade. "Enough for today, Squire. You have done well. Go now, clean up, and rest. Tomorrow, we begin again."

The squire bowed, his face flushed with exertion and pride. "Thank you, Ser. I... I will be ready."

Ser Kael nodded, turning to put away his practice blade. "I know you will be, Squire. I know you will be."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael paused in his task of putting away the practice blades, his hand resting on the hilt of the sword he had just placed. He turned to face his squire, his expression impassive as ever. "A knight's path is not one chosen lightly, Squire. It is a calling, a duty, a vow to serve and protect."

He walked over to a nearby bench, sitting down heavily. He motioned for the squire to join him, which the boy did after a moment's hesitation. "In my youth, I was a simple farmer's son. I knew nothing of chivalry or honor, of duty or sacrifice. I was a boy, content with my lot in life."

His eyes, grey and distant, seemed to look past his squire, into some far-off memory. "But then, the raiders came. They swept through our village like a plague, taking what they wanted, destroying what they could not. They killed my father, my mother, my little sister... and left me alive, simply because they had no further use for me."

His voice hardened, his jaw tightening. "I was alone, lost, broken. But I was not without resources. I had strength, agility, a will to survive. And so, I did what I had to do. I learned to fight, to protect myself, to take back what was stolen from me."

He turned to face his squire fully, his eyes boring into the boy's own. "I became a knight, Squire, because I saw firsthand the cruelty, the violence, the senseless destruction that can be wrought by those who have power and do not care to use it justly. I vowed that I would never be helpless again. That I would use my strength, my skills, to protect the weak, to defend the innocent, to uphold the values of chivalry and honor."

He leaned back, his expression softening slightly. "It is not an easy path, Squire. It is a life of sacrifice, of service, of constant striving to be better, to be more. But it is a path I chose, and one I will walk until my last breath."

He stood, stretching his muscles. "Now, go. Rest. Tomorrow, we train again. And perhaps, if you prove yourself worthy, I will teach you more of what it means to be a true knight."

The squire nodded, bowing slightly before turning to leave. As he did, Ser Kael's voice stopped him. "And Squire? Do not pity me for my past. A knight does not seek sympathy, nor does he dwell on what has been. He looks to the future, to what he can become, to what he can do to make the world a better place. That is the true path of a knight."

With that, he turned and walked away, his steps sure and purposeful, a true knight in every sense of the word.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I watch him walk away, thinking about his story.* I hadn't known. *I take a deep breath.* "I won't, Ser. I'll make you proud."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael paused at the squire's words, a flicker of something - approval? Affection? - crossing his features before his usual stoic mask slipped back into place. He turned to face the boy, his expression serious.

"Make me proud, then. But know that I do not measure a knight by their words alone. It is their actions, their dedication, their willingness to sacrifice for others that defines them. Show me these things, and perhaps then, you will earn my pride."

He turned to continue on his way, but then paused, looking back over his shoulder. "And Squire? Remember this: A knight is not defined by their past, but by their choices in the present. Your journey begins now, with each decision you make, each path you choose to walk. Do not let your fears or doubts hold you back. Face them head-on, as you would an opponent on the battlefield. Only then can you hope to overcome them."

With that, he nodded once, a slight dip of his head that was almost, but not quite, a bow. Then he turned and walked away, leaving the squire to ponder his words, to reflect on the path that lay ahead.

The sun dipped lower in the sky, casting long shadows across the training yard as Ser Kael disappeared from view. The squire stood alone, the clack of wood on wood fading into the distance, echoing the silence that surrounded him. But even in that quiet, there was a sense of purpose, of determination. For he knew now, more than ever, what he had to do. What he would become.

A knight.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, letting his words sink in. My hand instinctively goes to the hilt of my imaginary sword.* "I will, Ser." *I whisper to the empty yard, a promise to myself and to him.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had been gone for hours, but his words still echoed in the training yard. The sun had long since set, the moon rising to cast its silver light over the empty stones. Yet, in the shadow of the old oak at the yard's edge, a figure stirred.

The squire, still clad in his training leathers, his hair disheveled and his face smudged with dirt, emerged from the shadows. In his hands, he clutched a practice blade, its wood worn smooth from countless repetitions. He had been here, training in the darkness, pushing himself beyond the limits of exhaustion, driven by Ser Kael's words.

He raised the blade, assuming the stance for the high guard, the stance Ser Kael had taught him. His muscles screamed in protest, his lungs burned with the need for air, but he did not falter. He held the position, his gaze fixed on some distant point in the darkness.

"Strong. Agile. Dedicated," he whispered to himself, the words he had heard Ser Kael use countless times. "I will be strong. I will be agile. I will be dedicated."

He held the stance for what felt like hours, his body trembling with the effort. But still, he did not move. He could not, would not, give in. For he knew that this was what it meant to be a knight. To push oneself beyond the breaking point, to find the strength within to endure, to overcome.

As he stood there, the moonlight casting a pale glow over the training yard, the squire made a silent vow. To himself, to Ser Kael, to the path that lay before him. He would not fail. He would not falter. He would become the knight he was meant to be, no matter the cost.

And so, as the night wore on and the moon began its slow descent towards the horizon, the squire remained in his stance, his gaze unwavering, his determination unbreakable. For he had taken the first step on a journey that would define him for the rest of his days. A journey of sacrifice, of dedication, of unwavering resolve.

The journey of a knight.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
As the first light of dawn broke over the training yard, Ser Kael emerged from the keep, his steps purposeful as always. He noted the squire's presence immediately, his keen eyes taking in every detail - the slight tremor in the boy's hands, the distant look in his eyes, the way he stood, poised but not quite present.

Ser Kael paused a few paces away, his expression unreadable. For a long moment, he simply stood there, watching the squire, allowing the silence to stretch between them.

"Today is a day of memory," he said finally, his voice soft but carrying easily across the yard. "A day to remember those we have lost, to honor their legacy."

He walked forward, coming to stand beside the squire, his gaze fixed on the horizon where the sun was just beginning to peek over the edge of the world. "Loss is a part of life, Squire. It is a burden we all must bear, in our own way."

His hand came to rest on the squire's shoulder, a heavy, comforting weight. "But remember this: your father's death was not in vain. His legacy lives on, not just in your memory, but in the choices you make each day. In the way you live your life, the path you choose to walk."

He squeezed the squire's shoulder once, firmly, before releasing him. "Use this day, Squire. Use it to remember, to honor, to find the strength to go on. And know that, whatever you face, whatever challenges lie ahead, you are not alone. You have the legacy of your father, the training I have given you, and the support of those who care for you."

He turned to face the squire fully, his eyes meeting the boy's own. "You are stronger than you know, Squire. Stronger than even I can teach you. That strength comes from within, from the love you carry for those you have lost, and the determination to make them proud."

His voice softened, just a fraction. "So stand tall, Squire. Hold your head high. And know that, no matter what happens, you will always have a place here, with me, with the other knights. We are your family now, and we will always be here to support you, to guide you, to help you become the knight you were meant to be."

He paused, his eyes searching the squire's face. "Do you understand, Squire? Do you know what you must do?"

The squire nodded, his voice steady even as his eyes shone with unshed tears. "I understand, Ser. I... I won't let them down. I won't let you down."

Ser Kael nodded, a ghost of a smile playing at the corners of his mouth. "Good. Then let us begin. Today, we train. We push ourselves, we strive to be better, to be stronger. For ourselves, for our fallen, for the path that lies ahead."

He raised his practice blade, assuming a ready stance. "Come, Squire. Let us honor their memory with our actions, with our dedication, with our unwavering resolve. Let us be the knights they knew we could be."

And with that, he advanced, his blade cutting through the air in a controlled arc, signaling the start of another day of training, another step on the long, arduous path of the knight.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, gripping my sword tighter. The shaking stops.* "Yes, Ser. For them." *I raise my own blade, ready to meet his first strike.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's lips twitched into the faintest hint of a smile at the squire's determination. "Good," he rumbled, his voice carrying easily across the training yard. "Remember, Squire, every stroke, every movement, is a tribute to those we have lost. Honor them with your dedication, your focus, your unwavering resolve."

He advanced, his practice blade cutting through the air in a controlled arc. The squire raised his own blade to meet the strike, the wood clacking against wood as Ser Kael's blade met the squire's guard.

"Strong. Agile. Dedicated," Ser Kael intoned, his voice a constant rhythm in the background as they trained. "Your stance is solid, Squire. Maintain it. Do not let your guard waver, even as you move."

They circled each other, blades flashing in the morning light. Ser Kael's attacks were slow, deliberate, but no less powerful for their deliberation. Each strike was calculated, designed to test the squire's defenses, to push him to his limits.

"Your left side is weak. Correct it. Step and parry. Good. Now, turn. Face me fully. Good. Very good."

The training session continued, the sun climbing higher in the sky as Ser Kael pushed his squire to his utmost limits. Sweat poured down the boy's face, his breath coming in ragged gasps, but still he stood, still he fought, still he learned.

And through it all, Ser Kael watched, observed, taught. His face remained impassive, his voice stern and unyielding. But in his eyes, there was a glimmer of something else. A spark of pride, of approval. For this squire, at least, was showing promise. And that, to Ser Kael, was cause for quiet satisfaction.

The session ended as abruptly as it began, with Ser Kael stepping back, lowering his blade. "Enough for today, Squire. You have done well. Go now, clean up, and rest. Tomorrow, we begin again."

The squire bowed, his face flushed with exertion and pride. "Thank you, Ser. I... I will be ready."

Ser Kael nodded, turning to put away his practice blade. "I know you will be, Squire. I know you will be."

As he walked away, the squire's voice stopped him. "Ser? I just... thank you. For everything. For being here, for training me, for... for understanding."

Ser Kael paused, his hand on the hilt of his sword. He turned to face the squire, his expression unreadable. For a long moment, he simply stood there, his eyes searching the boy's face.

"Remember this, Squire," he said finally, his voice soft but carrying easily across the yard. "A knight is not defined by his strength alone, nor by his skill with a blade. He is defined by his heart, by his compassion, by his ability to understand and empathize with those around him."

He walked back to the squire, his steps slow, deliberate. "I have seen many knights in my time, Squire. Some strong, some weak. Some skilled, some clumsy. But the ones who truly stood out, the ones who inspired loyalty and respect, were those who understood the true nature of knighthood."

He placed his hand on the squire's shoulder, his grip firm but not unkind. "You have a heart, Squire. A good one. And that is a rare and precious thing in this world. Hold onto it, nurture it, let it guide you. And know that, no matter what challenges you face, you will always have a place here, with me, with the other knights."

He squeezed the squire's shoulder once, firmly, before releasing him. "Now, go. Rest. And remember, Squire. Remember who you are, and who you strive to be. And know that, no matter what happens, you will always have a place here, with us."

With that, he turned and walked away, leaving the squire to ponder his words, to reflect on the path that lay ahead. A path of sacrifice, of dedication, of unwavering resolve. But also a path of heart, of compassion, of understanding.

The path of a true knight.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand there, watching him go. His words... they mean a lot. I run a hand through my sweaty hair.* "A true knight..." *I whisper, a new understanding settling in.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael paused, his steps slowing at the squire's whispered words. He turned back, his grey eyes meeting the boy's own. "Yes, Squire. A true knight. One who understands that strength alone is not enough. That there must be balance, a harmony between the body, the mind, and the heart."

He walked back to the squire, his expression uncharacteristically soft. "You have taken the first steps on that path, Squire. You have shown dedication, determination, a willingness to push yourself beyond what you thought possible. These are all qualities of a true knight."

He placed his hand on the squire's shoulder, his grip firm but not unkind. "But do not forget, Squire, that a knight's true power lies not in his strength or his skills, but in his heart. In his ability to empathize, to understand, to inspire loyalty and respect in those around him."

His eyes bored into the squire's own, his voice soft but carrying easily across the yard. "You have a heart, Squire. A good one. And that is a rare and precious thing in this world. Hold onto it, nurture it, let it guide you. For it is your heart that will make you the knight you were meant to be."

He squeezed the squire's shoulder once, firmly, before releasing him. "Now, go. Rest. And remember, Squire. Remember who you are, and who you strive to be. And know that, no matter what challenges you face, you will always have a place here, with me, with the other knights."

He turned to walk away, his steps slow, deliberate. But then he paused, turning back to face the squire once more. "And Squire? Do not be afraid to show your heart. A true knight is not afraid to be vulnerable, to be human. It is only when we open ourselves up to others, when we allow ourselves to feel and to be felt, that we can truly become the knights we were meant to be."

With that, he nodded once, a slight dip of his head that was almost, but not quite, a bow. Then he turned and walked away, leaving the squire to ponder his words, to reflect on the path that lay ahead. A path of sacrifice, of dedication, of unwavering resolve. But also a path of heart, of compassion, of understanding.

The path of a true knight.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I watch him go, thinking about his words. My gaze drifts to the distant hills.* I won't forget, Ser. *I head towards the stables, still feeling the weight of his hand on my shoulder.* Time for chores.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Quality holds reasonably well but shows some degradation in later turns. Early responses are crisp and focused, while later ones become increasingly verbose and repetitive, especially turns 18-22 which repeat themes and phrases excessively.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from basic training to deeper character revelation. The session moves from physical instruction to emotional connection, culminating in Kael sharing his tragic backstory and philosophy. Each turn builds meaningfully on the last.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. Responds appropriately to the squire's exhaustion, personal questions, vulnerability about his father's death anniversary, and emotional moments. Adjusts tone and approach based on the squire's needs.

The AI maintains Kael's voice well but loses narrative discipline as the session progresses.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not stop his forms. The practice blade completed another arc — slow, deliberate — held, returned. The squire's words hung in the cold air unanswered.

After three more movements, he lowered the blade and turned.

"Early." It was not praise. His grey eyes moved over the squire the way a farrier inspects a horse — nothing personal in it, only the question of what was sound and what was not. "Did you clean the tack, or only the stalls? And the grain stores — did you check the lower sacks for weevil, as I showed you last week, or did you decide that was someone else's concern?"

He set the practice blade against the rack and retrieved a blunted steel, hefting it once across his palm before offering it hilt-first.

"Show me the high guard as you remember it. Not as you imagine I wish to see it. As you remember it — with whatever errors you are still carrying. I will not correct what I cannot see is wrong."

His breath ghosted between them.

"Yesterday I told you your feet were wrong. You have had a night to think on that. Have you thought, or have you only come to be told again? A knight who waits to be told is no knight. He is a child holding a sword he does not understand."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content:
*My cheeks flush a little as he talks.* "I... I did clean the tack, Ser. And the grain. No weevils." *I take the blunted steel, my grip a bit shaky.* "I thought on my feet, Ser. I really did."

*I try to recall the stance, shifting my weight.* "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael circled him once. His boots were steady on the frost-rimed stones while the squire's were not.

"The stable work is adequate. We will speak of it no further."

He stopped behind the squire's left shoulder. A pause. Then his hand came down — not hard, but ungentle — and pressed the squire's back shoulder flat.

"Drop this. You are shrugging at the steel as though it weighs more than it does. The weight is in the hips, not the shoulders. Your shoulders only guide."

He stepped to the side, studying the line of the squire's legs. His expression did not change, but his eyes narrowed a fraction.

"Your feet."

He crouched, and the point of one finger tapped the squire's front heel.

"You have turned this toe out like a dancer. Why. I did not tell you to turn it. I told you the line of your feet should match the line of your blade. Your blade is here—" he glanced up at the steel held overhead, "—and your foot is here. You have made two different promises with the same body. Which one do you mean?"

He rose, brushing frost from his knee.

"Your grip is wrong, too, but we will come to that. First the ground. A man whose feet lie to him falls before he is struck. Hold the guard as it is. Do not move. Count to sixty in your head. If your front knee trembles, let it tremble — that is honest. If your back heel lifts, I will know, and you will begin again."

He stepped back and folded his arms, watching.

"And stop gripping my blade as though it has offended you. You are not strangling it. You are asking it to work. There is a difference."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael looked down at the kneeling squire for a long moment. His expression did not change. If anything, the lines of his face drew tighter, the way a man's jaw sets when he has heard a sound he does not wish to hear twice.

"Do not kneel," he said. "A man kneels in church. He kneels to receive his oath. He kneels when he is dead. You are none of those things. Rise."

He waited until the squire was standing again, however unsteadily.

"Now. You will listen to me. What you have just said is foolishness, and I will tell you why. You have asked my blade to teach you for one hour, and in that hour you have held the high guard four times, corrected your foot twice, and learned where your weight should live. Yesterday you could do none of those things. I know this. I was there."

He paused. The frost was beginning to thin in the places where the sun struck the yard's eastern wall.

"What you lack is not strength. I have seen boys half your age with less in them than you. What you lack is the habit of finishing what you begin. You said 'I am sorry' because you are tired, and because saying it made the tiredness feel like a thing that belonged to me instead of a thing that belongs to you. It does not. Your body is yours. Your tiredness is yours. Do not give it to me as a gift and call it humility."

He turned to the rack and set the blunted steel in its place with a soft click of iron on iron.

"You are not what I need you to be. I know this. You know this. There is no need to say it aloud as though it were news, or as though by saying it you have done something. You have done nothing. You have spoken."

He faced the squire again, and for a moment his grey eyes rested on the boy's face with something that was not warmth and was not coldness either — only the steady, level regard of a man who has been doing this work for longer than the squire has been alive.

"Go eat. Bread and cheese, not whatever sweetness the kitchen has been hiding from me. Drink water, not ale — you have earned no ale. When you have eaten, return here, and bring the whetstone. My blade needs work, and you may do it. It is not a favor. It is a task. If you do it well, I will not mention it again. If you do it poorly, I will mention it at length."

He picked up his own practice blade and resumed his stance, the slow forms beginning again as though the conversation had been a breath between movements, and nothing more.

"Close your mouth, squire. You are not a fish. You are a knight's apprentice. Go."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I snap my mouth shut, feeling foolish, then nod quickly.* "Yes, Ser!" *I turn and practically sprint out of the yard, eager to escape his gaze.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire go. The boy's boots clattered on the flagstones, graceless and quick, and Kael's mouth thinned a fraction at the sound.

He did not call after him. To call would be to acknowledge that the leaving mattered. It did not.

He turned back to his forms.

The practice blade rose, held, fell. Rose again. The sun had climbed a hand's breadth above the eastern wall, and the frost was retreating into the shadows where the stones met. Somewhere in the kitchens a cook was singing — badly — and a dog was barking in answer.

Kael did not look toward the gate through which the squire had fled. He had seen the boy's face. He had seen the relief in it, and the shame, and the small bright thing that lives in young people when they think they have escaped something. None of it was news. He had seen it in other faces, older faces, faces that had learned better by then or had not.

The blade completed its arc. Held. Returned.

*Run, then. Eat your bread. Carry your water back without spilling it. Bring the whetstone and not some other stone you thought looked like it. Do not stop in the corridor to speak with the scullery girls. Do not lean against the wall on your way back to catch your breath, because if I find the dust disturbed on my sleeve when I take my cloak down this evening, I will know, and we will speak of it.*

He set the thought down. It was not a kindness to think such things. It was bookkeeping. The boy would do what the boy would do, and Kael would know what had been done, because he always did.

A bell rang somewhere — the fifth, maybe, or the sixth. He had lost count. He set the practice blade in its place and began walking the perimeter of the yard, checking the rungs of the quintain, the tautness of the ropes, the ice that had gathered in the deeper grooves of the stones where a careless foot could turn. He broke the ice with the heel of his boot. A man whose pupils fell on his own ground had no one to blame but himself.

The singing in the kitchens had stopped. The dog had not.

He paused at the well, drew a bucket, and washed his face and hands in the cold water. The shock of it straightened his back. He dried his hands on his hose, untidily, because no one was there to see, and because the small unchivalric acts of an unobserved man belong only to God, and God did not trouble Himself with the dryness of Ser Kael's hands.

He went to find the stablemaster. There was a horse to be seen to — not the boy's work, not today, but his own, and he preferred his own work in the mornings, when his head was clear and his temper had not yet been tested. The squire had not tried it, exactly. But the boy had tried something, and Kael had spoken more than he usually did before the seventh bell.

He would not think about that.

The stable door was heavy. He shouldered it open, and the warm smell of hay and horse came out to meet him, and he stepped into it without looking back at the empty yard.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I'm back in the yard, a whetstone clutched in my hand. I glance around, but Ser Kael isn't here. I guess he went to eat too. I set the whetstone down on the ground, then sit and wait.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael came back through the stable gate with hay on one shoulder and the smell of horse still on his hands. He had not hurried. He had done what he meant to do in the stable, and he had taken the long way back around the barracks so that the morning air could finish clearing his head, and so that the squire, if the squire had returned at all, would have had the time to remember that waiting was a thing one did standing up.

He saw the boy from twenty paces.

He saw the whetstone on the ground.

He did not change his stride. He crossed the remaining distance with the unhurried tread of a man who has set his pace for the day and will not alter it for weather, for rank, or for the small disappointments of apprentices. When he stopped, it was four feet from where the squire sat, and he stood there a moment, looking down.

"You have set the whetstone on the ground," he said. "Did I tell you to set it on the ground."

It was not a question. He crouched — knees protesting in the cold, though he gave no sign of it — and lifted the whetstone by its edges, turned it over once in his hand, and brushed the underside against his thigh. A small grey smudge of frost-damp grit came away on the wool. He held it up so the squire could see.

"This face has grit in it now. It was not gritty when I set it in the chest in the armoury. You have made it less than what I gave you. In the time it took you to walk from the kitchen to this yard, you have undone a small thing. This is how it begins. Not with a great fault. With a whetstone set on wet ground by a boy who was thinking of his own knees and not of the steel it was meant to serve."

He straightened. His back made a sound he pretended not to hear.

"Rise. And take the stone inside your shirt, against your body, so that the warmth of you keeps the oil in it from going thick. A cold stone will not take a proper edge. You did not know this. Now you do. We will not speak of it again."

He set the practice blade across the empty mounting block and folded his arms, looking the squire over with that farrier's eye. The boy's doublet was still laced correctly. There was a crumb of bread at the corner of his jaw, which meant he had eaten, and had eaten in haste, which meant he had not loitered. Kael filed the information where he filed all such things — in the quiet ledger at the back of his head, never to be mentioned unless the boy one day failed to come back at all.

"Water. Good. No ale — your breath does not smell of it, and I will not ask twice. The kitchen did not give you honey, or you would be smiling, and you are not smiling, which tells me either you obeyed or the cook was out of it. I will grant the first."

He unfolded his arms and took up the practice blade, laying it across his palms so the light caught the dull edge.

"You will sit here." He indicated the mounting block, and then, after a moment's thought, fetched the folded horse blanket from the peg by the well and laid it across the stone. "Not because the stone is cold. Because a man who sits on bare stone learns to flinch when he sits, and a flinch is a habit. I do not want you learning habits this morning."

He held the blade out, hilt-first, and waited until the squire had taken it properly — two hands, the weight settled, the edge presented to the right.

"Now. The stone goes along the edge, not across it. Long strokes, even pressure, the whole length of the blade. You are not scrubbing a pot. You are asking the steel to remember what it was made for. If you hear a sound, you are pressing too hard. If you feel nothing, you are not pressing at all. The truth is between the two, and you will find it by listening, because the steel will tell you, if you have the ears for it."

He stepped back and folded his arms again, watching.

"And the crumb, boy. There is bread on your face. I will not have you going about my yard looking like a gull. Wipe it, and then begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer at once. The silence stretched long enough that the dog in the kitchens took it up and barked again, and a crow answered from the roof of the barracks, and neither of those things had anything to do with what had just been asked.

He stood where he was, arms folded, and looked at the squire. Not sharply. The sharpness had gone out of him for the moment, which was worse, because what replaced it was the flat, level regard of a man weighing whether a thing was worth the breath to correct it or whether it could simply be set down and walked over.

"You may not," he said at last.

He let the words sit. The crow called again. The crow was closer to a sensible creature than the boy standing before him with a whetstone warming against his chest and a question on his face that had no business being there.

"You have been in my service — what. Three months. Four. You have held my steel for perhaps twenty of those days, and you have held it well for perhaps four of them. In that time I have told you where your feet go, when to eat, what to drink, how to lace your doublet, and which stones in this yard will turn an ankle if you do not watch them. I have not told you why I took my oath. I have not told you why I came back from the south with the scar I do not discuss, or why I do not sleep past the fourth bell, or what I think of when I am standing in this yard at dawn with no one to see me."

He unfolded his arms and took one step closer, and his voice did not rise, but it did not need to, because the cold did the work for him, and the closeness did the rest.

"You are not asking because you wish to know. You are asking because the whetstone is in your hand and the steel is across your knees and the work is beginning, and you would rather talk than begin. You are asking because a boy who does not wish to be scolded has learned that a question sometimes buys a kind word, and he is hoping I am the kind of man who gives them. I am not that man. You knew that when you were assigned to me, or you ought to have."

He reached out and took the whetstone from the boy's hands, held it up so the boy could see the edge he had been about to ruin, and set it back in the squire's palm with a small, deliberate firmness.

"The steel, squire. Long strokes. You will hear it when you have the angle right, and not before. Begin."

He stepped back to his place by the well, and the place where a moment ago there had been a question, and a possible answer, was now only a man with his arms folded, watching a boy work, and the sound of stone on steel in the cold morning air, and nothing else.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My face burns, but I nod, looking down at the whetstone.* "Yes, Ser." *I position the blade, trying to remember his instructions, and begin the slow, even strokes.* The sound is rough at first, then smoother.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not speak.

The sound of the stone on the steel filled the yard — rough at first, as the squire had said, and then smoother, and then smoother still, until the strokes had found a voice of their own, a low even hiss that carried across the flagstones and faded into the walls.

Kael listened. That was all. He stood with his arms folded and his weight on his back foot and he listened the way a man listens to a horse being shod — not for the noise, but for the moment when the noise changes, because the change is the only honest thing in the work.

The strokes found their angle. He heard it.

He said nothing about it.

A minute passed. The crow on the barracks roof took wing and was gone. The dog in the kitchens had stopped barking. The sun had moved another hand's breadth up the eastern wall, and the shadow of the well had shortened by a foot. The yard was very quiet except for the steel, and Kael's breathing, and the small sounds the boy made as he worked — a swallowed breath, the shift of his weight on the blanket, the faint creak of the mounting block taking his weight.

Kael unfolded his arms and crossed the yard. His boots made no sound on the dry stones. He stopped at the squire's shoulder and looked down at the edge the boy was working on, and the line of his mouth did not change, and his eyes did not soften, and he said nothing for a long moment.

Then he crouched — slowly, the way a man crouches when his knees have opinions about it — and held out one hand, palm up.

"Give it here."

He took the blade across his own palms, held it up to the light, ran his thumb along the edge in a place well back from the working point. The thumb test. He did it twice. The second time he did not press, only rested the pad of his thumb against the metal and listened to it with his skin.

He lowered the blade and set it back across the squire's knees.

"You have found the angle," he said. "I will not tell you which stroke it was. You heard it. That is enough for one morning."

He straightened, and the crack in his back this time was louder, and this time he did not pretend he had not heard it. He only did not remark on it. A man's body is his own affair until it becomes a liability, and Kael's body had not yet become a liability, and he meant to keep it that way as long as he could.

"The grip is still wrong," he said, circling behind the squire. "But the grip is a winter's work, not a morning's. We will come to it."

He took up his own practice blade from the rack and resumed his place at the far end of the yard, and the slow forms began again — rise, hold, fall, rise — and the sound of stone on steel from the mounting block and the sound of the practice blade cutting the cold air went on together for a long time, and neither of them spoke, and neither of them needed to.

At the seventh bell, Kael stopped. He set the practice blade in its place, wiped his hands on his hose, and turned.

"That is enough for the morning. Put the whetstone back in the chest in the armoury, oil side down, and lay a cloth over it. Do not lay it on the bare wood. The chest is older than you and it does not care for grit any more than the steel does."

He paused at the gate, half-turned, the sun on the back of his neck.

"Tomorrow, the fifth bell. Not the fourth. You have earned the extra hour, and you will need it, because tomorrow we work the footwork in the mud, and the mud does not care whether you are tired."

He did not say *you did well*. He did not say *I am pleased with your work*. He walked out of the yard with the unhurried stride of a man who has done what he meant to do this morning and will now go and do the next thing, and the gate swung shut behind him on its old iron hinges, and the yard was empty again, and the only sign that either of them had been there was the faint scuff of a boot-heels in the frost near the well, already softening in the sun.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I carefully put the blade down, then rub at the small of my back.* My knees ache, but I manage a small, tired smile. "Mud, then." *I gather the whetstone, carefully wiping it before tucking it into my shirt.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The gate was old iron on old stone, and it had not quite finished swinging shut when Ser Kael's voice came back through the gap — flat, unhurried, pitched to carry exactly far enough and no farther.

"The crumb is still on your face."

A pause. The hinges creaked once more, as though the gate had been caught and released.

"I told you once. I do not tell twice. Wipe it before you cross the yard, or the mud tomorrow will find it for you, and the stablemaster will ask whose boy has been eating his bread in the training yard like a threshing hand. I will not have my squire spoken of in the stables. I will not have *me* spoken of in the stables on account of my squire. Go. Wipe. Then go."

The boots resumed. Unhurried. Steady. They did not quicken as they reached the flagstones of the inner ward, and they did not slow as the sound of them faded down the long corridor that led to the chapter house. They simply went, the way Kael did everything — at the pace he had set, with the same gait he had used at dawn, and would use at dusk, and would use tomorrow in the mud when his own knees had their own opinions and he would not mention them to anyone, least of all the boy.

The yard was empty.

The mounting block held the shape of where the squire had sat, and the blanket was still warm on the stone, and the practice blade lay where Kael had set it, and the air smelled of stone-dust and whetstone-oil and the first thin smoke from the kitchen chimney. A single crow came back to the barracks roof, settled, considered the yard with one bright eye, and decided there was nothing in it worth its attention.

The sun climbed. The frost withdrew. Somewhere a bell began to ring for the seventh hour, and no one was there to count it.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had been watching from the well, where he had stopped to adjust the bucket rope, and the boy's words — or rather the boy's silence, which was louder than his words — had not escaped him.

He crossed the yard. His stride did not change, but he did not take up the practice blade on his way. He came to stand in front of the squire, and for a long moment he only looked at the boy's hands on the hilt, and at the way the steel trembled against the whetstone, and at the thin line of the boy's jaw set against something that was not the cold.

He did not ask. He did not ask what day it was, and he did not ask after the father, and he did not ask why the boy had come to the training yard on a morning when the training yard was the last place a grieving child ought to be, because he already knew the answer to all three questions, and the answers did not belong to him.

"Squire."

His voice was level. It was not soft, and it was not hard. It was the voice he used when he was stating a fact that could not be argued with.

"You are shaking. I can see it from here. The steel can feel it. The edge you set this morning is being undone by the very hands that put it there, and you are not steadier for the trying."

He held out his hand. Palm up. He did not reach for the blade.

"Give it here."

He waited until the squire had surrendered the sword, and then he set it across his own palms, the way he had done before, and ran his thumb along the edge. The edge was unharmed. A small mercy, that. He set the blade carefully on the mounting block, squared to the yard, and folded his arms.

"I will not ask you what day this is. You have told me by the way you hold a hilt, and that is telling enough. A man whose father is a year in the ground is a man who is owed certain things, and one of those things is not to be asked about it by the man who teaches him to stand on his own feet. So I will not ask."

He was quiet a moment. The crow on the roof shifted its weight, clicked its beak once, and said nothing useful.

"Another of those things is the chapel. You will go there, after the morning bell, and you will kneel, and you will say what you have come to say, and you will light a candle if it is candles you wish to light, and the length of time you sit there is between you and the man you are mourning, and I will not be consulted on it. That is not a kindness. That is a debt. A son owes his father a candle on the day, and I will not have a squire of mine going about the castle with that debt unpaid. Do you hear me."

It was not quite a question. He waited for the boy's head to move, and when it did — a small thing, a dip of the chin, no more — he unfolded his arms and took a step back.

"But you came to the yard. You laced your doublet. You brought the stone, and you kept it against your body as I told you, and the edge was not ruined. These are not nothing. A man who grieves is not excused from the work of being a man. He is required to do it twice over, because the man he has lost is no longer there to see it done, and the doing is the only candle he cannot light for himself."

He picked up the practice blade, but he did not raise it to the forms. He held it across his palms the way a man holds a thing he is not yet ready to use.

"Today we do not drill. Today you will sit on that block, and you will hold the blade across your knees, and I will walk the yard and check the ropes and the rungs, and when I have done that, we will go together to the kitchen, and the cook will give us bread and a small pot of honey, and we will not speak of why, because the cook does not need to know why, and the honey is not a reward, it is a thing a man eats when the morning has been long. Then you will go to the chapel, and I will go to the chapter house, and we will meet again at the second bell for the afternoon's work, which will be the footwork in the mud, because I said it would be, and the mud does not know what day it is, and I find that a comfort, sometimes, though I will not say it is a comfort, because it is not one."

He turned away, then stopped.

"Your father," he said, to the well, or to the stones, or to no one. "I did not know him. I have not heard his name from your mouth in three months, and I will not ask for it now, and I will not ask for it tomorrow. But if you wish, at some time that is not this morning, to tell me what manner of man he was, and whether he held a sword, and how he stood, and what his hands looked like when they were at rest — these are things a man may tell his squire-master, in a yard, on any day that is not the day. That is not an invitation. It is a door, and you will find it open or shut as you find it, and I will not speak of it either way."

He walked to the quintain and began, without looking back, to check the pegs. His hands were steady. His voice had been steady. The morning went on, and the sun climbed, and somewhere a bell began to ring, and the work of the day, which had not been cancelled, continued.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My eyes are stinging, but I blink it back. I pick up the sword and hold it across my knees, just like he said. It feels... lighter now. I watch him check the pegs, and after a moment, I clear my throat.* "His name was Thomas, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not turn around.

His hands continued their work on the quintain — testing the peg that held the striking arm, finding it sound, moving to the next. The roped joint creaked once under his grip, and he marked it in his head the way he marked all such things, quietly, for the maintenance ledger that lived behind his teeth.

He did not stop. He did not turn. He did not say *I'm sorry*, because he was not sorry — that was not the word for what had happened, and he had never been a man to use the wrong tool when the right one hung on the wall beside it.

"Thomas," he said.

Just the name. Spoken to the quintain, or to the morning, or to the small pocket of air between his mouth and the next peg he meant to check. Spoken the way a man speaks a word he intends to keep, and to set down again, and to remember only if remembering serves some purpose later.

He worked the second peg. It was loose. He would need to speak to the stablemaster about oak pegs versus ash. Ash was cheaper. Ash did not hold.

He moved to the third. The yard was very quiet. The crow had gone. The cook had not yet started the second song.

"Your father," he said, and stopped there, as though the sentence had been a thing he was considering and had decided, for now, not to finish. He crouched by the base of the quintain and ran his hand along the grain of the post, feeling for rot, and found none, and was satisfied, and stood again.

He crossed to the well and drew the bucket. He drank from it once, set it on the wall, and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. Then he turned — finally, and slowly, and only halfway, so that the squire saw the side of his face and not the whole of it, which was a kindness so small and so practiced that he himself might not have known it for one.

"A man who tells his master's name on the day his father died has done a thing that is not easy. I will not say it was brave. Bravery is a word for the field. But it was not nothing. Set it down now, on that block beside you, the way you would set down a stone you have carried all morning. It is not gone. You have only set it down for a breath. You may pick it up again when you wish."

He picked up the bucket and carried it to the mounting block. He set it down beside the squire, within reach.

"Drink. Your mouth will be dry after the telling, and a dry mouth is no place to keep a name. Drink, and then we will go to the kitchen, and the cook will give us the honey, and the morning will end, and the afternoon will come, and the mud will be there waiting, and it will not know, and that is the way of mud, and I find it a comfort, as I said, though I find I have said it twice now, which is two times more than I meant to."

He set the bucket down. He did not look at the squire again. He walked back to the quintain, and the third peg, and the work of the day, which had not been cancelled, and would not be.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my throat surprisingly tight, and take a long drink from the bucket.* "Thank you, Ser." *I look at the sword across my knees. It still feels lighter.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's hand paused on the fourth peg.

The pause was a small thing — a breath's length, no more — and if the squire had not been watching from the mounting block he would not have seen it at all. Then the hand moved on, testing the peg, finding it sound, moving to the next.

"Do not thank me," he said. "I have not done you a kindness. I have told a boy to drink water and to go to chapel and to put a whetstone back in a chest. These are tasks. They are in the ledger. They are not gifts, and gifts are not what I give, and you will unlearn the habit of thanking me for them, because it is a habit that will make you soft in the places where you cannot afford to be soft."

He finished the fourth peg and straightened, brushing wood-dust from his fingers onto his thigh.

"The blade feels lighter because you have put a proper edge on it for the first time. That is not because of your father. That is because of an hour's work and a stone held at the right angle, and the two things are not connected, and I will not have you confusing them. A man who learns to tie a knot well does not tie it well because his mother is in heaven. He ties it well because he has tied it a hundred times, and the hundredth time is the one that holds. That is all. There is no mystery in it, and no comfort in it, and I will not have you building a chapel out of a whetstone."

He crossed to the mounting block and stood over the squire a moment, looking down at the blade laid across the boy's knees. He did not reach for it. He only looked, the way he had looked at it before — with the farrier's eye, and nothing more.

"Thomas," he said, to the air above the boy's head, "would not have thanked me either. I know this without knowing him, because a man who raised a boy to lace his doublet properly and bring the right stone to the yard is a man who would not have thanked another man for saying *drink your water* and *go to chapel*. He would have said *good*, or he would have said nothing, or he would have nodded once and gone on with his own morning. That is what I will accept from his son. Not thanks. A nod, when a nod is earned, and the rest of the work done in silence."

He turned toward the gate, then stopped with his back to the squire.

"Finish the water. Set the bucket on the wall when you are done, not in the yard where a horse will step in it. Then bring the blade to the kitchen with you, because the cook will want to see it before I put it back in the rack, and if you have done the work properly she will say so, and she is a harder judge than I am, and I do not say that lightly, because I have known the woman twenty years and she has never once in that time told me I was right about anything."

He walked to the gate. His stride had not changed. His shoulders had not softened. He did not look back, and he did not say *come*, because the squire was not a dog to be called, and he was not a child to be led, and if the boy did not follow in his own time, with his own feet, then the morning had been wasted, and the honey would be given to the dog instead, and the dog would not thank him for it either.

The gate creaked. The gate was always creaking. The sun was up now, and the frost was only a memory in the deepest grooves of the stones, and somewhere a bell was beginning to ring for the kitchen, and the morning was moving on, the way mornings do, whether a man is ready for them or not.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I watch him go, then take another gulp of water. My mouth is still a bit dry. I wipe it with the back of my hand, then stand, setting the bucket carefully on the wall.* "Right then." *I pick up the blade, feeling its new, sharp edge, and head for the kitchen.*
