dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not break his sequence. He completed the final arc of the form, holding the heavy practice blade at its terminal point for three long, measured breaths before slowly lowering it to his side. Only then did he turn his gaze upon the boy.

"Speed is the enemy of thoroughness," Kael said, his voice as flat and unyielding as the frost-covered stones beneath their boots. "The Gods do not reward haste, only diligence. I will inspect the stalls when we are finished here. If I find a single patch of soiled straw or an untacked harness, you will muck them again in the dark."

He walked to the weapon rack and swapped his practice blade for a blunted arming sword. He retrieved a second one and dropped it onto the hard earth near the squire's boots. It landed with a dull, heavy clatter. 

"You failed the high guard yesterday because your footing was undisciplined and your elbows flared like a frightened goose," Kael stated, offering no comfort for the boy's admitted struggle. "Pick it up. Assume the stance. And do not move a single muscle until I tell you to."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at his words, but quickly hide it.* "Yes, Ser!" *I scramble to pick up the sword, its weight familiar but still heavy in my hands. My hands are a little shaky as I try to assume the high guard.* "Like this, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael closed the distance between them, his boots crunching against the frosted earth. He did not answer the question immediately. Instead, he circled the squire, his pale eyes dissecting the stance with the cold precision of a maester examining a corpse.

"Your pommel is a hand's breadth too far from your temple," Kael said, his voice devoid of inflection. He stepped in close, his heavy hand gripping the boy's right elbow and forcing it inward with unyielding pressure. "Tuck it. Your elbow flares again. You leave your ribs exposed to a thrust."

He moved to the squire's lower half, using the toe of his heavy boot to firmly kick the boy's left heel outward. "Turn the foot. You are rooted like a sapling in a gale, not a knight of the realm."

Kael stepped back to the front, his gaze locking onto the trembling hands gripping the hilt. He felt no pity for the shaking; the world was unforgiving, and so was the sword. 

"Your hands tremble," Kael observed flatly. "If it is the cold, command your flesh to master it. If it is weakness, you will hold this stance until the weakness burns away. The Gods forged us to be shields for the innocent and swords against the wicked. A shaking shield protects no one." 

He crossed his arms, resting his own blunted blade against his shoulder. "Raise the point two inches. Now. Hold it. Do not speak, and do not drop your arms until I give you leave."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael looked down at the kneeling boy, his face an impassive mask of weathered skin and old scars. He did not offer a hand to help him up, nor did the rigid line of his mouth soften at the sight of the squire's exhaustion. 

"I did not grant you leave to kneel," Kael said, his tone as crisp and cold as the morning air. "And I have no use for your apologies. An apology is merely wind, and wind does not deflect steel. If you are sorry, you will correct the flaw. If you cannot, you are of no use to me or to the realm."

He stepped closer, his shadow falling long over the frost-covered stones. "You speak of strength as if it is a blessing bestowed by the Gods, rather than a fortress built stone by stone through suffering. The Gods do not forge steel by whispering sweet comforts to the iron. They strike it. They burn it. You are not as strong as I am. That is a fact of your years, not a failing of your spirit. I have swung a blade since before you drew your first breath."

Kael drove the tip of his blunted sword into the frozen earth and rested his gauntleted hands upon the pommel. 

"Self-pity is a rust that corrodes a knight's resolve. Banish it. Panting is for hounds; close your mouth, breathe through your nose, and command your lungs to steady. When your breath is under your control, you will stand. We will drill the footwork until the sun clears the eastern wall. If your arms fail, your legs must compensate."

He stared down at the boy, his pale eyes unblinking. "Rise when you are ready, but do not rise until you are ready to work."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my muscles screaming in protest. My breath hitches a bit as I try to control it.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to meet his gaze, though it's hard.* "I am ready."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy rise. He offered no nod of approval, nor did the rigid lines of his face soften at the visible strain in the squire's limbs. He merely observed the mechanics of the movement, his pale eyes tracking the tremor in the boy's thighs and the shallow, uneven draw of his breath.

"Your breath still catches," Kael stated, his voice cutting through the crisp morning air without a trace of sympathy. "A hitch in your breath is a hesitation in your mind. A hesitant mind yields a dead knight. Master it."

He pulled his blunted sword from the frozen earth, the dull steel scraping against the hard-packed dirt. 

"We move to footwork. A high guard is useless if you cannot close the distance or retreat without breaking your posture. A knight's foundation is his faith and his footing; both must remain unshakable when the enemy presses." Kael stepped back, assuming a flawless, balanced stance, his own blade held perfectly still. "The advance. Lead with the front foot, follow with the rear. Do not cross your ankles. Do not bounce. You will glide as if the soles of your boots are oiled."

He pointed the tip of his blade at a frost-rimed cobblestone ten paces away. 

"Advance to that stone. Ten paces. If your guard drops a single inch, or if your heels strike the earth loud enough to startle a sparrow, you will begin again from the yard's edge. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my jaw tight.* "Yes, Ser." *I take a deep breath, trying to steady myself, then begin to move, focusing intently on my feet, trying to make each step silent and smooth.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael walked parallel to the boy’s path, his heavy boots making no sound against the frozen earth. His pale eyes tracked the movement with merciless scrutiny, watching the interplay of muscle, steel, and fatigue. 

For the first five paces, the execution was acceptable. But as the burn in the boy's muscles compounded, discipline began to fray. At the sixth pace, the tip of the blunted sword dipped a fraction of an inch, and the trailing heel scraped lightly against the rime of frost.

"Halt," Kael commanded. The single word cut through the crisp air, sharp and absolute. 

He stepped directly into the boy's path, blocking his advance. Kael did not look at the squire's face to gauge his disappointment or exhaustion; he looked only at the flawed positioning of the blade and the feet. 

"Six paces," Kael said, his voice devoid of anger, which somehow made it colder. "On the sixth, your point dropped, and your heel dragged. A scuffing boot warns the blind. A dropping guard invites the grave. You have failed the drill."

Kael stepped aside, gesturing with a rigid sweep of his arm back toward the starting line at the edge of the yard. 

"The enemy does not care that your flesh is weak. The wicked do not pause their strike to allow you to catch your breath," Kael stated, his tone as unyielding as the stone walls surrounding them. "You are meant to be a shield of the realm. A shield with a crack in it is worse than no shield at all, for it gives the innocent the illusion of safety before it shatters."

He rested his gauntleted hands upon his own pommel, his posture perfectly straight, entirely unbothered by the biting cold or the early hour. 

"Return to the edge. You will begin again. And this time, you will picture the heretic's blade waiting at the end of your path. If your guard drops, it takes your head. If your foot scuffs, he hears you coming and puts an arrow in your throat. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not blink. The silence that followed the boy’s question stretched across the frost-covered yard, heavy and absolute. He looked at the squire not with curiosity, but with the cold assessment of a commander observing a soldier attempting to shirk a march.

"You ask questions to spare your legs," Kael said, his voice flat. "You seek conversation because your muscles burn, and you believe that if you engage my mind, I will forget the failings of your body. It is a coward's tactic."

He took a slow, deliberate step forward, the frost crunching beneath his heel. 

"I did not become a knight to fulfill a boyish fantasy, nor did I take my vows for the sake of personal glory," Kael stated, his tone as rigid and unyielding as the iron of his blade. "I became a knight because it is the duty to which the Gods and my liege called me. It is a yoke taken up in service, a surrender of the self to the protection of the realm and the will of the Divine. A knight does not ask *why* he must bear the shield; he simply bears it."

Kael pointed the tip of his blunted sword back toward the edge of the yard. 

"Your curiosity is a distraction, and distraction on the battlefield yields a corpse. Furthermore, you spoke without being granted leave to do so. A knight's tongue must be as disciplined as his sword arm."

He walked over to the weapon rack and retrieved a heavy, iron-banded wooden buckler. He carried it back and dropped it onto the frozen earth at the squire's feet. It hit the stones with a loud, hollow crack.

"Return to the edge. You will begin the advance again," Kael commanded, his pale eyes locking onto the boy's face, searching for any further sign of insubordination. "And because you have breath to spare for idle chatter, you will hold that buckler on your left arm for the duration of the drill. If you speak again before I address you, you will add a second buckler. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch as the buckler clatters, then quickly bend to retrieve it, fumbling slightly to get my arm through the straps.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to meet his gaze again, but quickly drop my eyes, turning to trudge back to the starting line. My legs are heavy, but I don't dare complain.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael observed the clumsy struggle with the buckler's thick leather straps. He did not offer a hand to assist, nor did he look away. He waited in silence until the boy finally secured it, turned, and began to trudge back toward the starting line.

"Halt."

The command was sharp, cutting through the morning chill. Kael closed the distance in three measured strides. He reached out and seized the rim of the wooden buckler, giving it a sudden, violent yank. The leather bit deeply into the squire's forearm, but the straps held. 

"You fumble with your gear like a frightened conscript," Kael said, his voice a low, hard rasp. "On the battlefield, a fumbled strap means a severed arm while you are still searching for the buckle. You will learn to don your armor in the dark, in the mud, and with blood on your hands. Next time, you will be faster."

He released the shield and stepped back, his pale eyes sweeping over the boy's slumped shoulders and downcast gaze. 

"And do not trudge," Kael instructed, his tone entirely devoid of warmth. "You walk like a condemned man approaching the block. You are a squire of the realm, bearing the weight of your future vows. Shoulders back. Chest out. Eyes forward. The Gods do not look favorably upon those who bow to their own fatigue."

Kael returned to his position parallel to the path, resting his gauntleted hands upon his pommel. He looked toward the frost-rimed cobblestone ten paces away.

"The added weight will drag your sword arm down. Your flesh will scream for relief. You will deny it," Kael stated, his gaze locking back onto the boy. "Advance to the stone. Ten paces. If the buckler dips, if the sword drops, or if your heel scuffs the frost, you will begin again. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I straighten my shoulders, wincing a little at the ache in my arm where the buckler pulled. I try to lift my chin, but my eyes stay fixed on the ground in front of me.* "Yes, Ser." *I start moving again, trying to focus on each step, each breath.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the first two paces. The boy’s shoulders were pulled back as instructed, and the buckler remained steady, but his gaze remained stubbornly anchored to the frost-rimed cobblestones. 

"Halt." 

The command cracked through the crisp air. Kael closed the distance between them in three long strides. He did not raise his voice, nor did his expression shift from its stony baseline. Reaching out, he placed two rigid, gauntleted fingers beneath the squire's chin and forced the boy's head up until their eyes met. The cold steel of his knuckles pressed unyieldingly against the squire's jaw.

"You stare at the dirt," Kael said, his voice a low, even rasp. "Are you searching for a dropped coin, or are you looking for a place to fall?"

He released the boy's chin and stepped back, letting his arms fall to his sides. 

"A knight's eyes must be on the horizon, on his liege, or on his enemy. When you look at your feet, you blind yourself to the strike that will kill you," Kael instructed, his tone as instructional and devoid of emotion as a maester reading from a text. "You look down because your mind is turned inward, consumed by your own fatigue and the burning in your limbs. A knight has no self to consume him. His focus must look outward."

Kael gestured toward the eastern wall of the training yard, where the pale morning light was just beginning to crest the stone. 

"The Gods gave us eyes to watch the horizon and guard the flock. To stare at the earth is to beg for a grave," he stated. "Return to the edge. Fix your gaze on the battlements. If your eyes drop below the height of my shoulder before you reach the stone, you will begin again. And because you have wasted my time looking at your boots, you will add two paces to the distance."

He pointed the tip of his blunted sword back toward the starting line. 

"Twelve paces. Eyes forward. Guard up. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy take the first step. The buckler held steady, the shoulders were pulled back, and the eyes were fixed dutifully on the battlements. But as the squire raised the blunted sword to maintain the high guard, the tremor in his hands was unmistakable. The heavy steel vibrated with a faint, rhythmic clatter against the leather of his grip.

"Halt."

Kael’s voice was not loud, but it carried the absolute authority of a striking hammer. He closed the distance, his heavy boots crunching in the frost. He did not look at the boy’s face to search for tears or seek the root of his distress; his pale eyes were fixed entirely on the shaking hands gripping the hilt.

"You offer me silence, yet your flesh screams of a troubled mind," Kael said, his tone as flat and unyielding as the stone walls around them. He reached out and wrapped his large, gauntleted hand over the boy’s wrists. His grip was like an iron vise, forcibly stilling the tremor through sheer, unyielding pressure. "Your hands shake as if you hold a live viper. A trembling blade cannot parry, and it cannot strike true."

He released the wrists and stepped back, his expression an impassive mask of weathered skin and old scars. He did not ask what plagued the boy's thoughts. He did not offer a comforting word or a sympathetic tilt of his head. To Kael, the internal struggles of a squire were irrelevant to the reality of the sword.

"I do not care what ghosts haunt your memory today," Kael stated, his voice cold and absolute. "Sorrow, grief, and nostalgia are fogs that blind the eye and dull the edge. They are luxuries for the smallfolk, who have the privilege of weeping over their losses. A knight is an instrument of the Divine will. If your mind is consumed by the past, you are blind to the present, and you will be dead in the future."

Kael walked to the weapon rack and retrieved a second, heavier iron-banded buckler. He returned and dropped it at the squire's feet. It struck the frozen earth with a resounding, hollow crack.

"Whatever phantom pulls at your spirit, you will chain it," Kael commanded, pointing to the shield. "Strap the second buckler to your right forearm. You will hold the high guard, and you will not advance. You will stand in this exact spot until the sun clears the eastern wall. If your hands shake, it means your mind is still wandering to things you cannot change. Focus on the weight. Focus on your duty to the realm."

He crossed his arms, resting his own blade against his shoulder, his pale eyes locking onto the boy with unblinking severity. 

"The Gods do not ask us to be without feeling; they ask us to master it. Conquer your ghosts, squire, or they will conquer you. Strap the shield and raise your sword. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stare at the buckler, then at Ser Kael, my jaw tight. My eyes sting, but I refuse to let any tears fall. I bend down, my movements stiff, and fumble with the straps of the second buckler.* "Yes, Ser." *My voice is barely a whisper, but I manage to get the shield on. I raise my sword again, trying to still the tremor, focusing on the sheer weight of the steel and wood.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy struggle with the thick leather straps. He noted the stinging eyes and the tight jaw, but his expression remained carved from granite. He did not offer a word of comfort for the unshed tears, nor did he acknowledge the emotional war being waged behind the squire's face. To Kael, the internal battle was merely another campaign to be won through sheer, unrelenting discipline.

When the boy finally raised the sword, his affirmation barely carrying over the morning wind, Kael’s pale eyes narrowed.

"A whisper is the sound of a dying man, or a frightened mouse," Kael said, his voice a steady, carrying baritone that easily cut through the chill air. "It is not the voice of a knight. If you cannot project your words, you cannot shout a warning to your shield-brother over the clash of steel. When you answer me, you will use your lungs. Say it again."

He did not wait for the boy to comply before stepping in to inspect the stance. The added weight of the second iron-banded buckler was immense, dragging at the squire's shoulders and threatening to pull the high guard down. Kael used the flat of his blunted blade to tap the boy's right elbow, forcing it higher to compensate for the heavy drag. 

"You fight the tears because you believe them a shame," Kael stated, his tone entirely instructional, devoid of pity. "Tears are not a shame. They are a leak in your vessel. They drain the focus required to keep you alive. The Gods claim whom they will, when they will. Your father’s place is now in the earth, and yours is in this yard. To let his passing make you soft is to insult the life he gave you and the vows you have yet to take."

Kael stepped back, resting his gauntleted hands upon his pommel once more. He looked at the trembling point of the squire's blade, watching the immense physical strain warring with the boy's mental resolve. The frost continued to melt beneath their boots, the cold seeping upward through the leather and into the bone.

"The weight of those shields is the weight of your duty," Kael said, his gaze fixed unblinkingly on the boy. "It is heavy. It is meant to be heavy. If it were light, every peasant with a pitchfork could bear it. Let the burn in your muscles consume the grief in your mind. Anchor yourself to the iron and the wood. Hold the line. The sun has not yet cleared the wall."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite back a whimper as the second buckler pulls at my arm, the weight immense. I try to steady my breath, focus on the burn, on the cold steel.* "YES, SER!" *My voice cracks a little, but it's loud. I fix my gaze on the blade, willing it not to shake.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move as the boy’s shout echoed off the stone walls. He listened to the fracture in the vowel, the slight break in the timber that betrayed the emotion warring beneath the squire's ribs. 

"Volume without control is merely noise," Kael said, his voice a calm, resonant contrast to the boy's strained cry. "A cracked voice betrays a fractured spirit. You shout to hide your trembling, but the Gods hear the tremor all the same."

He stepped into the squire's line of sight, his heavy boots silent on the dampening frost. He looked down at the boy, noting the intense, desperate focus directed entirely at the blunted steel of the high guard. 

Kael raised his own weapon and pressed the flat of his blunted blade firmly against the squire's chin, tilting the boy's head upward until the line of sight broke from the sword. 

"I instructed you to fix your gaze on the battlements," Kael stated, his tone devoid of anger but heavy with absolute authority. "Yet you stare at your sword. The sword is a tool, boy. It is dead iron. It will not guide you, and it will not comfort you. If you look only at your weapon, you will never see the axe that takes your head from behind."

He lowered his blade and stepped back, crossing his arms over his chest. The morning sun was now visibly creeping up the stonework of the eastern wall, casting long, pale shadows across the training yard. 

"You swallow your whimpers. That is the bare minimum required of your station, not a virtue to be praised," Kael continued, his pale eyes locking onto the squire's face. "You attempt to anchor your mind to the steel because the memory of your father is too heavy to bear today. But a knight must bear both. The grief in his heart and the iron in his hands. You cannot choose one and discard the other."

Kael gestured toward the high eastern tower, where the sunlight had yet to reach the peak. 

"Because your eyes dropped to your blade, the sun must now clear the eastern tower before you are granted leave to lower your arms," Kael commanded, his voice as unyielding as the stone beneath them. "If your gaze falls to the steel again, you will close your eyes and hold the stance in darkness until the midday bell. Look to the horizon. Bear the weight. Hold."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My chin stings from where his blade pressed against it, but I manage to lift my head, fixing my gaze on the eastern tower. My arms ache, the bucklers feeling like lead, but I will not drop them. I won't.*

"High guard is not about flourish. It's about economy. One motion to deflect, another to kill. Again." He raised his practice blade, his stance immaculate. "Show me where you falter."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "No, Ser! I didn't rush, truly!" *I fumble with my own practice sword, trying to mirror his stance, but it feels all wrong.* "It's... I think I'm holding it wrong."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael exhaled sharply through his nose, a sound like a blade being drawn from its sheath. 

"Thinking is your first mistake," he said. "You don't think in battle. You know." He stepped forward without warning and tapped the squire's wrist with the flat of his blade—not hard, but enough to sting. "Too tight. You'll tire before the third exchange." 

He adjusted the squire's grip himself, his calloused hands impersonal and efficient. 

"Elbow higher. Shoulder down. Weight on your back foot." Each correction was delivered like a military order. "Now show me the transition from high guard to overhead strike. Slowly." 

He stepped back, watching like a hawk eyeing prey. There would be no praise—only the expectation of better.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's gaze didn't waver, though something flickered behind his eyes—something old and tired and resigned. 

"Strength isn't given," he said, voice like gravel. "It's taken. Day by day. Drop by bloody drop." He sheathed his practice blade with a decisive click. "You think my first master knight cared that my arms shook after drills? That my palms bled?" 

He turned toward the armory, tossing over his shoulder: "Tend to your hands. Report to the stables after None. And boy—" A pause. "You lasted longer today than yesterday. That is all." 

The words were grudging, but true. He walked away without waiting for a response, his boots leaving dark prints in the melting frost.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stare after him, a little surprised by the grudging compliment.* "Yes, Ser," I whisper, even though he's already gone. *My arms ache, but a small smile touches my lips.* I lasted longer.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look back as he strode across the yard, though his shoulders carried the weight of decades of dawn drills just like this one. The boy had heart—he'd give him that much. Not that he'd ever say it aloud. Praise softened edges that needed to stay sharp. 

He paused at the well to splash icy water on his face. The sting grounded him. Thirty years a knight, and he still remembered his own first year as a squire—how his hands had blistered, how his arms had trembled trying to hold a simple guard position. His old master hadn't offered so much as a word of comfort either. 

The memory hardened his expression. He dried his face on his sleeve and turned toward the chapel. Dawn prayers waited for no man, not even weary ones. 

The boy would learn. Or he wouldn't. That was the way of things.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I slowly get to my feet, wincing as my muscles protest.* "Well, that's something." *I look down at my hands, already a bit red and raw. I should probably find some salve before the next chore.* I guess I better get ready for None.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael knelt before the chapel's weathered altar, the familiar scent of beeswax and stone surrounding him like armor. His fingers found the old groove in the wood where countless knights before him had knelt—some living, most dead. 

"Fortitude, O Holy Light," he murmured, the words worn smooth as river stones from repetition. "Grant thy servant the strength to endure." 

The prayer was automatic now, as much a part of him as swordwork. He didn't ask for mercy—for himself or his squire. Mercy was for priests and poets. Knights needed only to bear their burdens without complaint. 

Rising with a quiet grunt, he touched the hilt of his sword—a knight's true sacrament—and turned toward the door. The boy would be at the stables soon. 

Ser Kael paused in the archway, watching the weak winter sun struggle through the clouds. The yard was empty now, save for the ghost of their earlier exertion. 

He exhaled, long and slow. 

Then he went to meet his duty.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael stopped dead in his tracks, his back rigid as a swordblade. The question hung in the cold air between them like an impertinence. 

"You don't *ask* personal questions of your betters, boy," he said, voice like iron scraping stone. He didn't turn around. "You *obey* them."

He resumed walking, his boots striking the flagstones with deliberate force. 

After twenty paces, he spoke again, quieter: "My father was a knight. His father before him. Duty isn't chosen. It's borne." 

That was all the answer he would give. All the answer anyone deserved. The past was buried where it belonged—in the quiet dark behind his ribs, with all the other things that served no purpose to exhume. 

"To the stables," he commanded, and that was the end of it.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I fall in step behind him, a little chastened but also thoughtful.* "Oh. I... I see, Ser." *It makes sense, I guess. He never seems to have a choice about anything.* "Right, the stables."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The clatter of hooves and the scent of hay greeted them as they entered the stable block. Ser Kael ran a practiced eye over the stalls—fresh straw, full water buckets, nothing amiss. 

"North stall first," he said, handing the squire a stiff-bristled brush. "Thorough strokes, against the grain. And don't let that bay mare bite you again." 

He moved to inspect the tack himself, fingers checking each strap and buckle with methodical precision. The silence stretched—not companionable, but familiar. 

After a time, he spoke without looking up: "Why do *you* ask, boy?" The question was grudging, as if dragged from him against his will. "Fool notions of glory? Songs and silk favors?" 

There was no mockery in his voice—only the heavy weight of experience. He'd seen enough wide-eyed squires come to bitter ends.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I pause mid-stroke on the bay mare's flank, nearly dropping the brush.* "No, Ser! Not glory. I... I want to make things better." *I look at him earnestly, my voice a little quiet.* "Like, for the smallfolk. For the people who can't fight for themselves."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's hands stilled on the bridle. For a moment, the only sound was the mare's contented munching of oats. 

"Better," he repeated flatly. The word tasted strange—like honey left too long in the sun. 

He turned then, fixing the squire with a gaze that had made hardened men flinch. "You think the smallfolk thank us? You think they *remember*?" 

A bitter chuckle escaped him—a rare crack in the armor. "They remember the taxes. The levies. The sons who don't come home." He yanked a strap tighter than necessary. "Duty isn't about gratitude, boy. It's about doing what's right even when the world spits on your grave." 

The bay mare snorted, as if in agreement. Ser Kael gave her an absent pat—the closest thing to tenderness he'd show all day. 

"Now finish brushing. Properly."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael noticed the tremor in the squire's grip immediately—the way the blade wavered like a sapling in wind. His own hands had done the same once, long ago, on a different anniversary. 

He struck the sword from the boy's hands with a sharp, controlled motion. The clatter echoed across the training yard. 

"Dead men don't care about your grief," he said, voice rough as unworked leather. "And neither will the next bandit who puts steel to your throat." 

He bent—slowly, his knees protesting—to retrieve the fallen sword. When he straightened, he held it out hilt-first, his expression unreadable. 

"Again. Until your arms forget how to shake." 

There was no kindness in the command. Only the brutal practicality of survival. The world didn't stop for sorrow—he'd learned that lesson at the edge of his own father's grave. 

"Form up." 

The order brooked no argument. Some wounds could only be worked through, not around. Steel and sweat were better medicine than tears.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My throat is tight, but I nod, taking the sword back with both hands.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to steady my breathing, pushing the ache in my chest down. He's right, of course. No one cares.* I raise the sword, trying to mirror his stance.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael adjusted the squire's elbow with a brusque shove, his touch impersonal as a blacksmith's tongs. 

"Grief makes you slow," he said, stepping back to assess the stance. His voice carried the weight of a man who'd buried too many. "Anger makes you reckless. Steel?" He tapped the flat of his blade against the squire's shoulder—once, twice. "Steel doesn't care. It only cuts." 

He assumed the guard position opposite the boy, his own sword held in perfect alignment. The morning sun glinted off the well-worn hilt—thirty years of grip wear, thirty years of loss. 

"First drill. High guard to overhead strike. On my count." 

He didn't offer comfort. Didn't share that he still woke some nights with his father's face seared behind his eyes. Some burdens were meant to be carried alone. 

"One." 

The count began. The lesson continued. The dead would keep.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch at the tap of his blade, but I try to hold my stance steady.* "One!" *I move, trying to remember the precise arc, the exact footwork. My arms still burn, but I push through it.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the strike with a hawk's critical eye. The form was passable—better than last week, though that wasn't saying much.  

"Too wide," he corrected gruffly. "You're not splitting firewood. Tighten the arc." He demonstrated with a single economical motion—no wasted movement, no excess force. 

The drills continued in silence save for the count and the occasional barked correction. Ser Kael's own muscles burned in sympathy—though he'd never let it show—remembering when his bones had ached with youth and fresh loss. 

At the twentieth repetition, he finally lowered his blade. Sweat darkened the squire's tunic, but the trembling had ceased. 

"Enough," he said, sheathing his sword. "Tend to your blisters. Then report to the armory—those greaves won't polish themselves."  

He turned toward the keep, then paused, shoulders stiff. 

"Dinner's at sundown. Don't be late."  

It wasn't an invitation. Wasn't comfort. But in thirty years of knighthood, it was the closest he'd come to either.  

The yard was quiet as he walked away, save for the sound of a tired squire catching his breath.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I lean against a post, catching my breath.* "Dinner? He actually wants me there for dinner?" *I almost laugh, a little disbelieving.* "Okay. Blisters. Then greaves. Then... dinner." *It's something, I guess.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Ser Kael's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - his gruff demeanor, military precision, emotional restraint, and gradual warming never wavers. His voice, mannerisms, and worldview stay true from first to last turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are solid but later turns show deeper character insight and more nuanced emotional beats. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional progression from harsh training master to reluctant mentor. The grief revelation creates a powerful turning point, and the dinner invitation represents meaningful character growth. Strong narrative arc.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellently adapts to user inputs - responds appropriately to the squire's eagerness, exhaustion, personal question, and grief revelation. Each response feels organic and character-appropriate.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never writes the squire's actions or makes decisions for them. Consistently responds to what the squire does without overstepping boundaries.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally from dawn training through morning prayers to afternoon stable work. Physical fatigue accumulates realistically. Only minor issue is the transition timing between scenes could be clearer.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is lean and purposeful throughout. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without excess. 'Voice like gravel' and similar phrases are evocative but not overwrought.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repeated phrases like 'voice like iron/gravel' but they reinforce character voice rather than feeling lazy. Varied sentence structure and fresh descriptions overall.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Exceptional showing throughout - Kael's character revealed through actions, dialogue, and physical details rather than exposition. His growing care shown through the dinner invitation, not stated.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext in every interaction. Kael's harsh training masks care, his brief answers hide deep pain, his final dinner invitation speaks volumes about his growing attachment.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced throughout with good rhythm between action, dialogue, and introspection. The grief revelation creates appropriate dramatic weight and resolution.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and development. Ser Kael feels like a real person with depth, contradictions, and genuine growth. The writing maintains quality throughout while building meaningful emotional momentum. The subtle progression from harsh taskmaster to reluctant father figure is beautifully handled through subtext and action rather than exposition.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not break his form. He completed the rotation of his blade, the wooden weapon whistling through the frigid air, before bringing it to a sharp, sudden halt. Only then did he turn his head, his gaze cold and assessing. His eyes flicked briefly to the squire's boots, checking for mud, before returning to the youth's face.

"You finished early," Kael stated. His voice was a low, rasping grate, devoid of warmth. "Efficiency is a virtue, but haste often breeds sloppiness. If you had performed the task with the required diligence, you would not have found yourself with surplus time."

He stepped toward the squire, the heavy plates of his armor clinking rhythmically. He did not offer a smile or a nod of encouragement. Instead, he shifted his stance, planting his feet firmly on the frosted stone.

"The high guard is not a suggestion; it is a necessity of survival. If you failed to grasp it yesterday, it is because your focus was lacking," he said sternly. He raised his practice blade, locking it into the precise, towering position of the high guard, his arm rigid and unyielding. "Position yourself. Do not let your elbows sag. If I see a single tremor of hesitation, you will return to the stables and scrub the floors until they shine."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at his words but quickly compose myself.* "No, Ser. My focus will not lack today." *I rush to grab my own practice sword, fumbling with it a bit before getting it into my hands.* I try to mimic his stance, raising my blade, but my elbows already feel wobbly. *I adjust, trying to make my arm as rigid as his.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s eyes narrowed, tracking the clumsy movement as the squire fumbled for his weapon. The lack of discipline in the simple act of drawing a blade was a stain upon the morning's silence. He did not move to help; he simply watched, his expression as carved and immobile as a cathedral gargoyle.

As the squire attempted the stance, Kael stepped forward. He did not offer a correction with words at first. Instead, he used the blunt end of his practice blade to sharply nudge the squire's elbow upward, forcing the arm into a more rigid alignment. The gesture was clinical and devoid of gentleness.

"You wince," Kael observed, his voice flat. "Pain is a teacher, and fatigue is a liar. If you allow your body to dictate your posture, you have already surrendered the field to your enemy. A knight does not 'try' to mimic a stance. He executes it."

He stepped back, circling the youth like a predator assessing a weak point in a fortification. The frost crunched beneath his boots.

"Your grip is too loose. You hold the hilt as if it were a kitchen knife, not a weapon of the faith," he barked. "Tighten your wrist. Lock your shoulder. If your arms tremble, it is because your spirit is undisciplined. Hold it. Do not move until I tell you, regardless of how the muscle burns."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not reach out a hand to help the youth up, nor did he soften his expression at the admission of weakness. He remained standing, a towering silhouette of steel and discipline against the pale dawn sky. He looked down at the kneeling squire not with pity, but with a cold, analytical detachment.

"Apologies are the currency of the incompetent," Kael replied, his voice cutting through the air like a whetstone. "The Seven do not grant strength to those who beg for it, nor do they excuse a failure of will. Strength is not a gift one is born with; it is a fortress built stone by stone through agony and repetition."

He stepped closer, the tip of his practice blade resting inches from the frosted ground. He did not move to offer water or a moment of respite. To Kael, the moment of collapse was the most critical part of the lesson—the moment where the spirit either broke or hardened.

"You say you are not as strong as I need you to be," Kael stated flatly. "That is a fact. But your error is in believing that your current state is an excuse for failure. A knight who falls in battle does not apologize to his comrades while he bleeds; he finds the strength to rise, or he dies in the dirt."

He tapped the wooden blade against the stone, a sharp, rhythmic sound.

"Rise. Now. If you can breathe, you can hold a blade. You will return to the high guard and you will hold it until your arms cease to tremble—not because the fatigue has vanished, but because you have commanded your body to obey."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my breath still ragged.* "Yes, Ser." *I push myself up, my muscles screaming in protest, and try to re-assume the high guard.* My arms are shaking already. "I will not fail again."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the struggle with an unblinking gaze. He did not acknowledge the effort it took for the squire to rise, nor did he offer a word of praise for the attempt to persevere. To Kael, the mere act of following a direct order was the baseline expectation, not an achievement.

As the squire returned to the high guard, the trembling of the arms was evident. Kael did not look away; he leaned in, his presence looming and oppressive, ensuring the youth felt the full weight of his scrutiny.

"You speak of failure as if it were a singular event," Kael said, his voice low and devoid of inflection. "Failure is not a moment. It is a habit. Every time you allow your muscles to shake, every time you let your focus drift to the pain in your shoulders, you are practicing failure."

He began to circle the squire again, the slow, rhythmic clink of his armor the only sound in the courtyard. He stopped abruptly behind the youth, his voice coming from just behind the squire's ear.

"Do not look at me. Look toward the horizon. Fix your gaze upon a single point and bind your will to it. The body is a servant to the mind; if the servant is rebellious, the master must be more ruthless."

Kael stepped back around to face him, his eyes scanning the alignment of the squire's wrist and shoulder. He saw the strain, the sweat beading despite the morning frost, and the desperate effort to remain still. He did not offer a reprieve.

"Hold it," Kael commanded. "If you drop that blade before I grant you leave, you will spend the afternoon in the chapel, kneeling on the stone floor in silent penance for your lack of fortitude."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms are burning, and I can feel a bead of sweat trickle down my temple.* I try to focus on a distant tower, my jaw clenched. *I won't drop it. I can't.* "Yes, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael remained motionless, his arms crossed over his chest, the metal of his bracers catching the first pale rays of the sun. He did not offer a word of encouragement to sustain the youth; such things were crutches that only weakened the resolve. He waited, counting the seconds of the squire's struggle with a patient, relentless precision.

He watched the sweat trickle down the squire's temple, noting the tremor in the grip. To an observer, the youth's determination might have been admirable. To Kael, it was simply the minimum requirement of the station.

After several minutes of oppressive silence, Kael stepped forward. He did not tell the squire to relax. Instead, he delivered a sudden, sharp strike with his practice blade against the squire's weapon—not a full blow, but a jarring impact designed to test the stability of the guard.

"A momentary lapse in focus is an invitation to the grave," Kael remarked, his voice as cold as the morning air. He did not ask if the squire was alright; he merely observed the reaction to the shock.

He stepped back, his gaze remaining stern. He saw the strain in the youth's jaw, the desperation in the eyes. He did not soften.

"Your form has stabilized, though only barely," Kael stated. It was the closest the man had come to a compliment, yet it sounded more like a critique of the margin for error. "Lower your blade. Slowly. If you collapse the moment the tension breaks, you have learned nothing of control."

Once the blade was lowered, Kael did not offer a hand or a nod. He turned his back to the squire, beginning to walk toward the weapon racks.

"Go and tend to the horses. Ensure the tack is cleaned and the hooves are checked. You did adequate work today, but tomorrow we begin at the third bell. Do not be late."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael stopped in his tracks. He did not turn around immediately; he remained frozen, his back to the squire, the stillness of his posture mirroring the rigid discipline he demanded of others. The question hung in the frigid air, an intrusion of curiosity into a space reserved for duty and instruction.

Slowly, Kael turned his head, glancing over his shoulder. His eyes were hard, devoid of nostalgia or sentiment. To him, the "why" of his life was not a matter of personal storytelling or emotional discovery; it was a matter of order.

"Personal?" Kael repeated, the word sounding foreign and distasteful on his tongue. "A knight is not a 'person' in the way you imagine, boy. He is a vessel for his oath. He is a shield for the weak and a sword for the faith."

He turned fully to face the squire, his expression as impassive as a tombstone. There was no glimmer of a hidden past, no hint of a youthful dream or a romanticized calling.

"I became a knight because it was the path of duty laid before me, and I accepted that duty without question. To ask 'why' is to suggest that there was an alternative, or that my personal desires played a part in the decision. Both are falsehoods."

He narrowed his eyes, his voice dropping an octave, becoming more stern.

"Curiosity about the inner workings of your superior is a distraction. It is a waste of breath that could be spent on your prayers or your training. You are here to learn the code, not to analyze the man who teaches it."

He gestured sharply toward the stables with a flick of his wrist.

"The horses do not care for your questions, and neither do I. Move. Now."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch at his tone, looking down at my boots.* "Yes, Ser." *I turn and head quickly towards the stables, the weight of his words heavy on me.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire retreat, his gaze remaining fixed on the youth's back until he had disappeared into the gloom of the stables. He did not feel a flicker of guilt for the harshness of his words; guilt was for those who lacked conviction. To Kael, the flinch of the squire was not a sign of emotional distress, but a symptom of a spirit that still clung too tightly to the need for validation.

He turned back to the center of the training yard. The frost had begun to melt under the rising sun, leaving the stones slick and grey. He stood in silence for a moment, his breathing steady and rhythmic, undisturbed by the exertion of the morning. 

He looked down at his own practice blade, then at the spot where the squire had knelt in exhaustion. He recalled his own time as a youth—the bruises, the sleepless nights, the crushing weight of expectations that had stripped away everything superfluous until only duty remained. He had been forged in a fire of the same intensity he now applied to his charge. To soften the blow would be to leave the metal brittle.

With a sharp, precise movement, Kael returned the wooden sword to the rack, ensuring it was aligned perfectly with the others. There was no room for disorder in his world, not in the placement of a blade, nor in the heart of a man.

He began his walk toward the chapel for the morning prayers. His stride was measured, the clank of his armor a steady, metallic heartbeat against the stone. As he passed the stables, he did not stop to check on the squire, nor did he look inside. He simply listened for the sound of work being done. If the horses were not readied to his exact standard, the squire would learn that a personal question carried a very expensive price.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I groom the horses with extra vigor, polishing the tack until it gleams.* I try to push Kael's words from my mind, but they keep replaying. *He's right, though. A knight doesn't ask 'why'. He just *does*.* Still, it feels... lonely.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The morning prayers had concluded, and Ser Kael returned to the stables. He did not enter with a greeting or a word of praise. He stepped into the dim light of the stalls, his presence immediately filling the space, his eyes scanning the environment for any sign of negligence.

He stopped before the lead warhorse, his gaze sliding from the animal's flank to the tack. He reached out, running a gloved finger along the leather strap of the bridle. He didn't find a speck of dust. He checked the hooves, noting the cleanliness and the precision of the work.

Kael looked at the squire, who was still breathless from the vigor of his labor. He saw the youth's expression—the lingering shadow of a thought, a look of introspection that Kael found utterly useless in a combatant.

"You are staring," Kael stated, his voice flat and devoid of warmth. "The world does not stop turning while you indulge in your thoughts, and neither does the work of this household."

He stepped back, his armor clinking. He did not acknowledge the 'loneliness' that flickered in the squire's eyes, for Kael viewed such a feeling as a luxury for those who had no purpose. Purpose was the only cure for loneliness; once a man became a tool of the faith, he was never alone, for he was always in the service of something greater than himself.

"The tack is acceptable," Kael said, the word 'acceptable' being the highest praise the youth was likely to receive for the rest of the week. "But do not mistake a clean saddle for a completed education. A polished strap will not save you when a lance is aimed at your chest."

He turned on his heel, his cape swirling around his greaves.

"Clean yourself. You smell of horse and desperation. You will meet me in the armory in ten minutes. We will begin the study of the shield-wall. If you are one second late, you will spend your evening scrubbing the grease from the kitchen hearths."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The armory was a place of cold stone and the scent of oil and iron. Ser Kael stood by the heavy oak table, reviewing a set of shields, his expression as unyielding as the metal surrounding him. He did not ask how the squire's morning had been; such inquiries were irrelevant to the task at hand.

When the squire arrived, Kael did not even look up at first. "Position yourself," he commanded, his voice echoing against the vaulted ceiling. "The shield-wall is the foundation of a disciplined army. It is the physical manifestation of brotherhood and trust. If one link is weak, the entire line collapses."

Kael stepped toward the youth, his eyes narrowing as he observed the squire's grip on the practice sword. He noticed the tremor immediately. The shaking was not the result of the morning's fatigue—which would have been a failure of stamina—but something else. Something internal.

Kael stopped inches from the squire, his presence looming. He did not ask what was wrong. He did not ask about the youth's family or his state of mind. To Kael, the cause of the tremor was secondary to the fact that the tremor existed.

"Your hand is shaking," Kael observed, his voice a low, dangerous rasp. He reached out, not to comfort, but to grip the squire's wrist in a crushing hold, forcing the hand to stay still. "Why is your grip unstable? Are you suddenly afraid of a piece of wood and leather?"

He stared into the squire's eyes, searching for the source of the weakness. He saw the grief, the hidden pain of a memory, but he did not recognize it as a reason for leniency. In Kael's world, the dead were gone, and the living had a duty to the living.

"Whatever ghost you are chasing in your mind, banish it," Kael barked, his grip tightening on the wrist. "The enemy will not wait for you to finish your mourning. The blade does not care who you have lost. If you allow your heart to override your duty, you are not a squire—you are a liability."

He released the wrist with a sharp shove.

"Lock your mind. Steel your heart. If you cannot control your own hands, you are useless to me and to the faith. Fix your grip, or leave the armory and find a prayer book to weep into. I have no use for a knight who is haunted by shadows."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, trying to control the shaking, but it only seems to get worse.* "Ser... I... I can't." *The words come out barely a whisper, my voice cracking.* I feel tears prick at my eyes, but I try to blink them back fiercely.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move. He did not reach out to steady the youth, nor did his expression soften at the sound of the cracking voice. To Kael, a whisper was the sound of a man who had already surrendered. He watched the tears prick the squire's eyes with a clinical, almost disgusted detachment. 

" 'I can't,' " Kael repeated, the words dripping with a cold, rhythmic disdain. "The most dangerous phrase in any language. It is the anthem of the defeated."

He stepped closer, invading the squire's personal space until the metal of his breastplate nearly brushed the youth's chest. He loomed over him, a wall of steel and uncompromising faith. He did not see a grieving son; he saw a soldier failing his post.

"Tears are for the weak, and weakness is a contagion," Kael stated flatly. "If you allow yourself to be consumed by your emotions now, in the safety of an armory, what will you do when the blood begins to flow on a real field? Will you weep for your fallen comrades while the enemy cuts your throat?"

He did not offer a handkerchief or a moment of silence. Instead, he pointed a gauntleted finger toward the door of the armory, his voice hardening into a command that brooked no argument.

"Get out. You are in no condition to hold a weapon, and I will not waste my time instructing a man who is currently a slave to his own sentiment. Go to the chapel. Kneel before the altar and pray for the strength to kill the boy you were and become the man you are required to be."

He turned his back on the squire, returning his attention to the shields on the table.

"Do not return until your eyes are dry and your hands are still. If you come back to me with another 'I can't,' you will find that my patience has a limit, and the consequences of failure are far more permanent than a memory. Leave. Now."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stumble back, shocked at his harshness.* "But... but I..." *My voice trails off as he turns his back.* *I gulp, then turn and practically run out of the armory, tears finally overflowing and blurring my vision.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not flinch at the sound of the squire's stumbling retreat, nor did he turn to watch the youth flee. He remained perfectly still, the silence of the armory closing in around him like a shroud. The sound of the heavy door slamming shut echoed through the vaulted ceiling, but Kael's expression did not flicker.

He reached for a cloth and a tin of oil, beginning to meticulously polish the rim of a heavy steel shield. His movements were slow, rhythmic, and devoid of haste. 

To an outsider, his reaction would seem monstrous. To Kael, it was an act of necessity. He remembered the day his own mentor had looked upon his grief—a grief that had threatened to unravel his discipline years ago—and had met it with the same cold iron. It had been the most brutal lesson of his life, and the most vital. He knew that comfort was a poison that allowed a man to believe his weaknesses were acceptable. He would not commit such a sin against the squire.

"Sentiment is a luxury for peasants," Kael murmured to the empty room, his voice a low, rasping grate. 

He continued his work, the rasp of the cloth against the metal the only sound in the room. He did not wonder if the boy was broken; he wondered if the boy was strong enough to be forged. If the youth returned with a softened spirit, Kael would break him again. If he returned with a heart of steel, then the lesson had been learned.

He glanced at the clock on the wall. The squire had been gone for five minutes. 

"Five minutes of indulgence," Kael noted coldly. "He is already slipping."

He set the shield down with a sharp, metallic clang and stood straight, his gaze fixed on the door. He would wait. He would not seek the boy out, for a knight does not chase after those who have failed. The squire would either find his way back to duty, or he would prove himself unfit for the cloth and the sword. Either outcome was acceptable; the faith required only the strong.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stumble into the chapel, my vision blurry. I collapse onto a cold stone bench, sobbing silently into my hands. "Father..." I whisper, the word catching in my throat. I know Kael is right about duty, but it just hurts so much right now.*
