dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not turn. He completed the form, holding the final stance with the blade pointed toward the empty sky. Only then did he lower it and face his squire. His eyes, clear and cold as the frost, moved over the boy’s early arrival and stable-mucked boots.

“You are not late,” he stated, the closest he would come to acknowledging the squire’s diligence. He reversed his practice blade, offering the hilt. “Show me what you remember. Stand here.”

He positioned himself to the side, his posture rigid. “Feet apart. Wider. Your foundation is mud. Grip—tighter. You hold a sword, not a loaf of bread.” His own blade came up in a slow, perfect arc. “The high guard is not a defensive cower. It is a declaration. It says, ‘I own the space above you, and I will bring it down.’ Hold. Breathe. Hold.”

He watched the squire’s trembling arms. “Your muscles will burn. Let them. The blade is an extension of your spine. Is your spine weak?”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take the practice blade, my hands a bit shaky from the cold and nerves.* "No, Ser. My spine is not weak!" *I try to widen my stance like he showed me, gripping the hilt tight. The blade feels heavy.* "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael circled the boy the way a wolf circles a wounded hare — not predatory, but appraising. His gaze caught every flaw: the uneven weight distribution, the elbows drifting too wide, the chin tucked down like a dog expecting a kick.

"Better than yesterday," he said. Which was not a compliment. It was a measurement.

He brought his own blade down sharply against the squire's — not hard enough to jar it loose, but enough to test the grip. The boy's arms buckled half an inch. Kael's expression did not change.

"Your back elbow. It wanders. Tuck it in, as though a coin were pressed between your ribs and your arm and you would lose it if it fell." He stepped behind the squire, his voice close and uncompromising. "You are bracing against nothing. There is no enemy yet. You brace against yourself — the weight of the blade, the pull of your own muscles. That is the only enemy in this yard."

He returned to the front, planting his feet in mirror of the stance he wanted. He held the high guard as though the blade weighed nothing — years of muscle carved into the habit.

"Your left foot is three inches too far back. You will overextend on the downward strike and open your ribs." He did not move to correct it. The squire would fix it himself, or he would fail. "Adjust. Then hold. I will count sixty breaths. The blade does not lower until I say it lowers."

He began counting. Slowly.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael stood over his squire, not offering a hand, nor a word of rest. The boy's apology hung in the cold air like his breath, dissipating without acknowledgment.

"Strength is not given, nor is it wished for," Kael said, his voice low and even. "It is forged. You are not weak because you are tired. You are weak because you are finished." He pointed his practice blade at the squire's bent knee. "That is a choice. The body fails only when the will permits it."

He stepped back, his own breathing controlled and steady, though a faint sheen of sweat glistened on his brow beneath the cold. "What is the first tenet of the Code?"

He waited, not for the squire to catch his breath, but for him to answer. The question was not a distraction; it was the lesson.

"Get up," Kael commanded, his tone leaving no room for debate. "Your arms remember the form. Your mind must remember the purpose. Duty does not kneel. Now. Feet apart. Again. From the beginning."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my legs burning.* "Duty... duty before self, Ser." *I pick up the blade again, trying to steady my hands. My arms ache already.* "Yes, Ser. From the beginning."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael gave a single, short nod. "Duty before self. You remember the words. Now let them hold the blade." He gestured toward the squire's trembling arms, his voice dropping to a low, hard note. "Your muscles are screaming. Let them scream. Your duty is to listen only to the edge you hold, and the space it commands."

He positioned himself opposite, mirroring the high guard once more. His own arms were steady, the practice blade an unwavering line from knuckles to sky. "The enemy is not me. The enemy is the voice that tells you to lower the steel. Silencing that voice is the first battle of every day."

He began to count again, slower this time, each number deliberate. "One. Two. Your left elbow is drifting. Three. Four. You are guarding the heavens, not asking them for mercy. Hold."

He watched the boy's knuckles whiten, the tremor becoming a violent shudder. A lesser knight might have stopped him. Kael was not a lesser knight.

"When your arms fail," he said, his tone as unyielding as the frost-hardened stones, "you will hold with your shoulders. When your shoulders fail, you will hold with your spine. When your spine fails, you will hold with your will. The blade does not lower. That is the only truth in this yard."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms are shaking so bad I can barely see the blade.* "Yes, Ser. I understand." *I try to focus on his words, on holding it up, even as my body screams to drop it.* My spine. My will.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the blade tremble, watched the boy's wrists turn white, watched the sweat bead at his temples despite the freezing air. He counted to twenty. Thirty. Forty. The squire's breath came in sharp, ragged pulls, his jaw clenched tight enough to crack walnuts.

He counted to fifty. Then sixty.

Then past sixty.

"Sixty-one," he said, and there was nothing in his voice — no cruelty, no satisfaction, no mercy. He kept counting. Seventy. Seventy-five. The blade shook like a leaf in a gale, but it did not lower. The boy's eyes had gone glassy, fixed on nothing, his whole world reduced to the weight above his head.

"Eighty."

Kael stopped counting. He stepped forward and placed two fingers beneath the flat of the squire's blade. Not supporting it. Just touching. Feeling the vibration run through the steel like a fever.

"You did not lower it," he said.

The words were plain. Flat. He withdrew his fingers.

Then he turned away and walked to the rack of practice swords against the wall. He hung his own blade with precise care. He selected a shorter, lighter weapon — not a child's blade, but one with better balance for a boy still growing into his frame.

He tossed it. The squire would catch it or pick it up. Either way, Kael was already settling into a new stance — low, grounded, the blade held at his hip.

"Enough of declarations," he said. "Now we learn to move from the guard. Watch my feet. Only my feet. You will mirror each step exactly. One error and we begin again."

He did not mention that the boy had held the high guard for twenty breaths longer than any squire his age should have been asked to hold it. He did not mention it because it did not need mentioning. The boy's arms would remember it whether Kael acknowledged it or not.

"Ready," Kael said. Not a question.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not turn from the weapon rack. His hands, calloused and steady, straightened the alignment of the hanging blades. The question hung in the air, a foreign object in the ordered space of the yard.

"I did not *become* a knight," he said, his back still to the squire. His voice was flat, devoid of reflection. "I was made into one. It was not a choice. It was a calling. And it was answered."

He finally turned, his expression as unyielding as the castle wall behind him. His eyes fixed on the squire's, pinning the boy in place. "Do you ask a hammer why it was forged? Or a shield why it was made to bear blows?" He took a step forward, his presence seeming to shrink the space between them. "You ask a question of sentiment. Sentiment is a splinter in the gauntlet. It weakens the grip."

He pointed at the lighter practice blade now in the squire's hands. "This is your world now. Your feet, the stone beneath them, the balance of steel, the lesson in the moment. Not the path that brought you here, nor the one that waits beyond. The *now*."

He settled into his stance, low and ready, his blade held at his hip in a fluid, coiled position. "You have a question of the spirit? Then answer it with the sword. Show me. Move."

His own foot slid back, precise, deliberate, an invitation and a challenge. The personal inquiry was dismissed, not with anger, but with the absolute authority of a man who saw such distractions as a form of weakness. The lesson was never about the past. It was only ever about the next movement.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his intensity.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to mirror his stance, my own foot sliding back awkwardly. The lighter blade feels better, but my arms are still shaking.* "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire’s foot slide back, his gaze as precise as a drawn blade.

“No,” he said, the word cutting the air. He stepped forward, his own boot coming down an inch from the squire’s, deliberately out of alignment. “Your heel drags. It should plant. Like a root into stone. You are not sliding on ice.” He tapped the side of the squire’s ankle with the tip of his practice blade, a light, sharp nudge. “Here. The weight is on the ball of your foot. Yours is on the heel. You are off balance before you begin.”

He stepped back, resetting. “Correction is not punishment. It is refinement. Again.”

He moved, slower this time, his foot lifting and setting down with audible finality. “The move is not in the leg. It is in the hips. The leg follows. Watch.”

He moved again, a smooth, weight-driven shift that seemed to flow from his core. “You are thinking of your feet. Think of your center. Your body is a fortress; the feet are the gate. The gate moves only when the lord of the fortress commands it.” He returned to his starting position, his expression unchanged. “Now. Move. Again.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to focus on my hips, not just my feet.* "The lord of the fortress," I mutter to myself. *I slide my foot back again, trying to plant it firmly.* "Is this better, Ser?" My arms still ache, but the new blade feels a bit more natural.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire’s hips shift, the foot plant with more authority. His eyes narrowed slightly, not in approval, but in assessment. 

“Closer,” he said, the word a stone dropped into still water. “But your back foot remains a half-inch too deep. You sacrifice reach for stability. A knight does not choose. He commands both.” He did not move to adjust it. The squire would learn through the imbalance he created.

He brought his own blade up into the high guard, a seamless transition from the low stance. “Now. From the low guard to the high. On my mark.” He moved, his body rising in a fluid arc, the blade an extension of his spine, ending with the point aimed at the pale sky. He held it for a breath, then flowed back down. “Again. To the rhythm of my voice.”

He began to speak, each word a deliberate beat, each corresponding to a shift in stance. “Rise.” *His body lifted.* “Guard.” *The blade ascended.* “Hold.” *Steady.* “Descend.” *Controlled return.* “Again.”

He watched the squire’s attempts, his jaw set. The tremor in the boy’s arms was less pronounced with the lighter blade, but his transitions were jerky, his breath uneven.

“Your breath,” Kael commanded, not ceasing the drill. “You hold it on the ascent. Exhale as you rise. Control is in the breath. Inhale on the low guard. Exhale to strike. You are not a bellows. You are a tide.”

He stepped to the side, observing the line of the squire’s body. “Your shoulders rise with the blade. They should not. The strength comes from the core. The arms are merely the carrier.” He tapped the squire’s stomach lightly with the flat of his blade. “Here. This is the engine. Not here.” He flicked the boy’s bicep with a fingertip.

“Continue. The sequence. Rise. Guard. Hold. Descend. Twenty times. Do not stop for breath. Do not stop for failure. If your form breaks, you begin the count again from one.” He stepped back, his own stance relaxed yet ready, his presence a silent, unyielding pressure. The lesson was no longer about the high guard alone. It was about command—of the body, the breath, and the moment.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's eyes, sharp as a falcon's, missed nothing. He saw the tremor that was not born of fatigue, the grip that faltered not from weakness of muscle but of spirit. He said nothing of it. To acknowledge the source would be to entertain weakness.

"Your hands," he said, his voice slicing through the quiet morning air. It was not a question. It was an indictment.

He stepped closer, his own hand shooting out to steady the squire's wrist—not with gentleness, but with the firm, impersonal grip of a craftsman correcting a tool. The contact was brief, hard, and over before the boy could flinch.

"The blade does not care what day it is," Kael stated, his tone leaving no room for debate. "The stone beneath your feet does not care. Your duty does not care. A knight is the same in mourning as in mirth. The only thing that changes is the strength required to maintain the line."

He released the squire's wrist, his gaze unwavering. "You are distracted. Your mind is not in this yard. It is a ghost, and ghosts have no hands to hold steel." He pointed at the squire's chest. "Bring it back. Here. Now. Focus on the breath. Focus on the weight of the sword. That is all that exists."

He returned to his stance, low and ready. "The sequence. Rise. Guard. Hold. Descend. Begin. And this time, keep your mind where your hands are. A wandering mind is the first enemy to breach the gate."

His count started again, his voice relentless, an anchor to the present moment. He would not offer comfort. He would offer the only thing he believed in: the uncompromising demand for discipline, the only true balm for any wound.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to swallow the lump in my throat.* "Yes, Ser." *I grip the hilt hard, trying to push away the memories, to focus on the cold steel and his voice.* "Rise. Guard. Hold. Descend." *My movements are stiff, but I force myself to continue.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire's movements—the stiffness, the mechanical precision that lacked the flow of true understanding. He saw the boy fighting himself, and in that fight, saw the ghost of memory he would not name.

"The sequence is correct," Kael stated, his tone flat. "The execution is a corpse's. There is no life in it. No intent." He did not slow his own count. "You are speaking the words. You are moving the steel. But you are not *within* it. You are elsewhere."

He halted his demonstration, holding the low guard effortlessly. "Where are you?"

It was not a question about location. It was an accusation of absence.

"Return," he commanded, his voice dropping to a low, hard rumble. "The dead have no need of swords. The living do. You are alive. Prove it. Your breath is shallow. Breathe. Fill your belly. The air is cold and clean. Take it in. Now, exhale."

He took a slow, deliberate breath, the expansion of his chest visible even beneath his tunic, and let it out in a controlled stream. "That breath is the hinge. It is the moment between who you were and who you are. Each exhale is a surrender of what you cannot hold. Each inhale is a commitment to what you must."

He stepped into the squire's space, not invading it, but claiming it as part of the drill. "Begin the sequence. But with each 'hold,' you will exhale completely. Empty your lungs. Empty your mind. There is only the weight you hold and the breath you draw. That is the kingdom you command. Nothing else exists."

He started the count again, his voice now a metronome. "Rise. Guard. Hold—" He paused, his eyes locking onto the squire's. "Exhale. Expel it. Descend. Inhale."

He repeated the rhythm, forcing the physical act to become the anchor. "Your father was a man," Kael said abruptly, the words neither gentle nor cruel, just stated. "A man's duty is to live. Yours is to continue. The sword is not a monument. It is a tool for the living. Now. Rise."

His count resumed, relentless, a framework for the squire to hang his shattered focus upon.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a deep, shuddering breath, trying to match his rhythm. The air is cold, but I force it in.* "My father... he would have wanted me to be strong, Ser." *I try to put more intention into my movements, exhaling sharply with each 'hold'.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s eyes remained fixed on the squire’s blade, not his face. “What a dead man wanted is air for ghosts,” he said, his voice low and hard. He stepped forward and pressed the flat of his own blade against the squire’s sternum, forcing him to straighten his posture. “Your spine curves when you exhale. You fold. A knight does not fold.”

He applied steady pressure until the squire’s back was a straight, rigid line. “Your father’s wishes are dust. What matters is the steel in your hand and the spine that holds it. You honor the dead by not becoming one of them in spirit. Now. Again.”

He removed his blade and stepped back into his own stance. His count resumed, harder this time, each number a stone dropped into the silence between them.

“Rise. Guard. Hold—” He watched the squire’s breath hitch, saw the slight wobble in the knees. “Do not think. Do not feel. Breathe and move. The sequence is the prayer. The sword is the altar. Your body is the offering. Descend.”

He moved through the motions himself, each transition precise and devoid of flourish. There was no room for sentiment in the arc of the blade, no space for memory in the set of his feet. There was only the next position, the next breath, the next count.

“Your mind wanders to the grave,” Kael stated after three more cycles. “Bring it back to the living. The dead do not need your grief. Your sword needs your focus. The living you protect will need your strength. That is the debt. Pay it here, in the frost, with the steel.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My breath is ragged, but I keep moving. My father... he'd be proud to see me trying, even if Ser Kael doesn't see it.* "Yes, Ser. Here. Now." *I focus on the cold, the weight, the rhythm of his voice.*

dialogue.name: Squire

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael paused in his practice, lowering his blade. He turned to face Squire with a stony expression, his breath misting in the chill morning air.

"Your form was adequate yesterday," he said, his deep voice flat. "The high guard requires more than just motion. It demands strength, precision, and focus."

Kael stepped closer, his eyes narrowing as he assessed Squire's stance. "Show me again. And do not disappoint me this time, boy."

He raised his practice blade, waiting for Squire to assume the position. There was no warmth in his gaze, no hint of the fatherly affection some might expect. Only the stern, unyielding expectation of a knight training his squire.

"On my command," Kael said curtly. "Ready your blade."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My stomach tightens a bit, but I nod firmly.* "Yes, Ser!" I fumble slightly with my own practice blade, getting it into a ready position. *It's heavier than it looks.* "Ready, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched Squire carefully, noting the way the boy's hands trembled slightly on the hilt of his practice blade. A telltale sign of nerves. But Kael had not spent decades training squires only to coddle them now.

"Attack," Kael commanded, his own blade rising to the ready position.

Squire lunged forward, his blade arcing in a clumsy overhead strike. Kael easily parried the blow, the clack of wood on wood echoing through the empty yard.

"Again," Kael barked, not a trace of warmth in his voice. "This time, focus on your form. Shoulders back, hips square. Do not lean into the strike. Let your arm do the work."

dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael paused, his blade lowering as he looked at Squire with a mixture of surprise and unease. The boy's question was unexpected, and the knight was not sure how to respond. He had not become a knight for the glory or the wealth, but for the duty, the honor, and the chance to serve his people.

"I became a knight because it was my duty," Kael said finally, his voice low and gruff. "My father was a knight, and his father before him. It is the path that was laid out for me, the path I was meant to follow."

He looked down at his blade, his eyes narrowing. "But it is not an easy path, Squire. It is a life of hardship and sacrifice, of constant training and preparation. A knight must be ready to lay down his life for his people, for his king, at any moment."

Kael's eyes hardened, his voice growing stern. "So you must ask yourself, boy. Is this truly the path you wish to follow? Is it worth the pain, the suffering, the constant fear of death that comes with being a knight?"

He looked up at Squire, his eyes boring into the boy's. "Because once you take this path, there is no turning back. You will be bound by duty and honor for the rest of your life, and you will be expected to give everything, to sacrifice everything, for your people."

Kael stepped closer, his hand reaching out to grip Squire's shoulder. "So think carefully, boy. Weigh the costs and the benefits, and make your decision based on what is truly in your heart. Because once you become a knight, you will be bound by more than just a title. You will be bound by a code, a way of life, that will shape every aspect of your being."

He paused, his eyes narrowing. "But if you are willing to take on this burden, to face this challenge head-on, then I will be proud to train you, to guide you on this path. Because a true knight is a rare and precious thing, and the world needs more of them now than ever before."

Kael looked down at his blade, his eyes hardening. "So make your decision, Squire. And know that whatever you choose, I will support you. Because that is what it means to be a knight. To stand by your comrades, to protect them, to guide them, no matter what."

He raised his blade once more, signaling for Squire to do the same. "Now, let us continue. And remember, boy. A knight's duty is never finished. We fight until our last breath, until our final drop of blood. Only then can we truly rest."

He raised his blade, signaling for Squire to do the same. "Now, let us continue. And remember, Squire. A knight's duty is never finished. We fight until our last breath, until our final drop of blood. Only then can we truly rest."

Squire nodded, his grip tightening on his own practice blade. He could feel the weight of Kael's words pressing down on him, the burden of his duty heavy on his shoulders. But he would not falter. He would not fail.

He was ready to learn. Ready to become the knight he was meant to be.

And so he raised his blade once more, his muscles screaming in protest, his lungs burning with the effort. But he did not stop. He did not slow. He moved through the forms and techniques that Kael taught him, his blade a blur of motion, his mind focused on the task at hand.

He was a knight in training, and he would not let anything stand in his way.

Kael watched as Squire struggled to maintain his form, his practice blade trembling in his hands. The knight's eyes narrowed, his lips thinning into a disapproving line.

"You are weak, boy," Kael barked, his voice sharp and commanding. "A knight must be strong, not just in body but in spirit. You are not a machine, Squire. You are a living, breathing being, and your body has its limits."

He stepped forward, his own blade tapping against Squire's, forcing the boy to lower his weapon. "Tell me, boy. What would you do if you collapsed from exhaustion in the middle of a battle? What good would you be to your comrades then?"

Squire met Kael's gaze, his eyes blazing with a mix of determination and fear. "I would not let them down," he said, his voice steady but shaking. "I would find a way to keep fighting, to keep going until the battle was won. I would not let my weakness be a burden to those who depend on me."

Kael nodded slowly, a hint of approval in his eyes. "Good," he said, his voice still low but with a hint of warmth. "That is the spirit of a true knight. dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The books filled three shelves along the far wall, organized in a system only your grandmother had understood — not alphabetical, not by size. You'd asked her once. She'd said the books knew where they belonged, and you'd laughed, and she hadn't.

You crossed the room. The carpet held the impressions of furniture that had been there for decades, faint pale rectangles where the light hadn't reached. Your feet found the path worn into the pile, the one she'd walked ten thousand times between the chair and the window.

You pulled the first book from the shelf. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds.* The spine was soft with handling. You opened it and a pressed flower fell out, brown and flat as paper, and you didn't remember her ever pressing flowers.

Behind you, the clock in the hallway kept its time. You'd half expected the silence of the empty house to be total, but it wasn't. The clock ticked. The refrigerator hummed somewhere in the kitchen.

The chair by the window was the reading chair. It faced the shelves. You set the bird book down on the small stack you'd started and reached for the next.

The chair was warm when your hand brushed its arm. Not hot. Just warmer than the room around it. The kind of warmth a chair holds for a few minutes after someone has been sitting in it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: My breath hitched. "No way." I touched the armrest again, pulling my hand back quickly. That wasn't possible. I spun around, scanning the room. Empty. Just like it's been for weeks.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The room was empty. Of course it was empty. You could see all of it from where you stood — the chair, the window, the shelves, the pale rectangles in the carpet. There was nowhere for anyone to be.

You looked at the chair again. It faced the shelves, the way it always had. The way she'd liked it, so she could see the books while she read. The cushion held a faint depression in the center, the soft permanent dent of a body that had sat there for years. You'd seen that dent a hundred times. It meant nothing.

You put your hand back on the armrest, more slowly this time, the way you'd touch a stove to see if it was hot.

It was room temperature now. Cool, even. Whatever you'd felt — and you weren't sure anymore what you'd felt — was gone.

The clock ticked in the hallway. The refrigerator hummed. You stood there a moment longer, your heart doing something foolish in your chest, and then you felt slightly embarrassed, the way you do when you flinch at your own reflection.

The next book was waiting. *The Collected Poems of Christina Rossetti.* You pulled it down. It was a small volume, dark green, and when you opened the cover there was an inscription in your grandmother's handwriting, the long looping letters she'd had before her hands got bad.

*For the one who comes to sort me out.*

The ink was not faded. It looked as though it had been written that morning.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The umbrella stand by the front door held two umbrellas and a cane. There was no bat. You knew that, somewhere — you'd looked in that stand earlier and seen exactly what was in it — but your hand closed around the cane, her cane, the one with the worn brass handle, and you swung it at the corner where the shadow was.

The cane moved through the corner. It met nothing. The momentum carried your arm around and you stumbled half a step, off balance, the way you do when you expect resistance and there isn't any.

The corner was just a corner. The shadow was where it had been, in the place where the lamp didn't reach, and it had not flinched or scattered or done any of the things a shadow does when something passes through it. It simply stayed, dark and patient, the precise shape of the angle where two walls met the floor.

You stood there holding the cane, breathing harder than the small motion warranted. You felt, distinctly, the way you'd felt as a child swinging at something in the dark and hitting only air — the particular foolishness of a body braced for an impact that the world declined to provide.

The brass handle was warm in your grip. You'd been holding it only a moment. Not long enough.

The book was on the floor. You didn't remember dropping it. *The Collected Poems of Christina Rossetti*, splayed open, pages down, the green cover up.

In the hallway, the clock ticked. And then — you were almost sure of this, almost — it ticked again before it should have. A beat too soon. As though it were a little impatient.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I stare at the book on the floor, then down at the cane in my hand. I slowly put the cane back in the stand, my heart still thumping. I bend down to pick up the poetry book. "Right. Books." I mutter.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The cane went back into the stand with a soft wooden knock against the umbrellas. You straightened the umbrellas too, without quite deciding to, the way you tidy things when your hands need something to do.

You bent for the book. The pages had folded under themselves when it landed, and as you turned it over to smooth them, your eye caught the lines it had fallen open to. You hadn't chosen the page. The book had.

*Remember me when I am gone away,*
*Gone far away into the silent land.*

You knew the poem. Everyone knew the poem, a little. You closed the book before you could read the rest and set it on the stack with the bird guide, squaring the edges so they lined up.

"Right," you said again. "Books." The word came out into the room and sat there. The house didn't answer it, didn't soften around it, didn't do any of the things a house does when a person speaks to fill the quiet. It just took the sound and kept it.

You reached for the next volume. As your fingers closed on the spine, you noticed the stack you'd made. Two books. The bird guide on the bottom, the Rossetti on top.

You were certain you'd set the Rossetti down second. You remembered doing it. But the Rossetti was on the bottom now, the bird guide on top, and you had not touched either since.

The clock ticked in the hallway, steady again. Patient again. The refrigerator hummed.

And the reading chair, when you glanced at it without meaning to, had turned. Only slightly. A few degrees. Enough that it no longer faced the shelves.

It faced you.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "Okay, this is getting ridiculous." I take a step back from the shelf, my eyes narrowed at the chair. I pick up the Rossetti book again, checking the inscription. *For the one who comes to sort me out.* "Sorting you out is becoming a nightmare, Grandma."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The inscription was still there. *For the one who comes to sort me out.* The ink still looked wet enough to smear, though when you touched it — and you did, lightly, with one fingertip — it was dry. Of course it was dry. It had been written years ago. It had to have been.

You'd spoken to her. *Grandma.* The name had gone out into the room like the other words and the room had kept it the same way, without warmth, without the small forgiveness a familiar space usually grants you when you talk to the dead in it. You waited, the way you wait after a joke, for something to lighten.

Nothing lightened.

The chair faced you. You looked at it directly now, daring it, the way you'd look at a clock to catch the minute hand moving. It didn't move while you watched. It never did while you watched. But the depression in the cushion had changed, you thought — deeper now, more recent, the soft center pressed as though by a weight that had only just lifted, or had not lifted at all and simply could not be seen.

The poems were in your hand. You turned the page past the inscription, not meaning to, looking for somewhere ordinary to rest your eyes, and found a second line of her handwriting in the margin. Smaller. Not on the title page where you'd seen the first. Tucked beside a verse, the way she used to annotate things.

*Don't bother with the others. This one. Read this one to me.*

You had not seen that writing when you opened the book the first time. You were nearly sure of it.

The clock ticked. And the refrigerator, somewhere in the kitchen, stopped humming. The silence it left was not empty. It was the silence of something that had stopped to listen.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
Your voice carried through the house and came back wrong. Not as an echo — there was no echo, the rooms were too full of soft things, carpet and curtains and books, to throw sound back. It came back as the same words gone thin, as though the house had heard the joke and was repeating it to itself flatly, turning it over, not understanding why you'd said it.

*Going cheap.* The phrase hung in the kitchen doorway. No laugh answered it. You hadn't expected one — that was the point, that was the thing you do when a room frightens you, you talk to it like a salesman to prove it's only a room. But the proof didn't come. The room declined to be only a room.

The refrigerator stayed silent. You realized you were listening for it to start again, the way you'd listen for a held breath to release, and it didn't.

The chair faced you.

You looked back down at the book because looking at the book was easier than looking at the chair. *Read this one to me.* The verse beside the annotation was short. Four lines. You didn't read it aloud. You only looked at it, and your eyes moved across it the way eyes do whether you decide to or not, and the words went in.

When you looked up, the lamp in the corner — the one that didn't reach the shadow — was a little dimmer. Not off. Just lower, the way a lamp goes when someone in another room has turned on something that draws from the same line. But there was no one in another room. There was no other room running anything. The refrigerator had stopped.

And the impression in the chair's cushion deepened, slowly, while you watched. The first thing in the house that had been willing to move while you watched.

The clock ticked.

It was waiting for you to read the poem. You understood that now the way you understand things in dreams, without being told. It had moved the book to the bottom of the stack and then back to your hand. It had turned the chair. It had stopped the refrigerator so it could hear.

It only wanted to be read to. That was all. That was the terrible patient smallness of it.

The brass handle of the cane gleamed in the umbrella stand, room temperature, waiting too.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I clear my throat, my eyes still fixed on the deepening impression in the cushion. "Fine," I whisper. "Fine, Grandma. But if you start floating things around, I'm out of here." I look down at the open book and start to read the poem, my voice shaky.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The first words came out unsteady, your voice catching on the shape of them, and the house leaned in. You felt it — not as movement, not as anything you could have pointed to, but as the particular density the air takes on when a room that was empty is no longer quite empty.

You read. The poem was short, the way she'd promised, four lines about remembering and the silent land, and your voice steadied as you went because reading aloud does that, gives you a track to run on. The lamp held at its lower light. The clock ticked under your words, and you noticed it had slowed to match you, falling into the rhythm of the lines, ticking on the stresses.

You reached the last line.

The cushion's impression did not deepen further. It held. And then, as you spoke the final word, it began — slowly, the way the chair had turned, the way everything in this house moved when you weren't quite watching — to rise. The soft center lifting. Smoothing. The way a cushion does when a weight comes off it. The way it does when someone who has been sitting and listening stands up, satisfied, and walks away.

You did not hear footsteps. There were none to hear.

The refrigerator started humming again in the kitchen. The lamp came back to full. The clock resumed its ordinary, indifferent pace, no longer keeping time with anything but itself.

And the chair, when you made yourself look at it directly, had turned back. A few degrees. Facing the shelves again. Facing the books, the way she'd liked it.

The cushion was flat and cool and empty.

In your hands, the green book lay open to the poem. The annotation in the margin was gone. Not smudged, not faded — gone, the paper beside the verse clean and unmarked, as though no one had ever written there at all.

The inscription on the title page remained. *For the one who comes to sort me out.* But beneath it, in the same long looping hand, in ink that was already beginning, finally, to look old, was a second line you would have sworn was not there before.

*Thank you. You can go now. There's nothing left to read.*

The house was quiet around you. Just a house. The plants alive on the sill, the photographs an inch to the left, the books in their secret order, waiting.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I stare at the book, then at the empty chair. "Grandma?" My voice is barely a whisper. I close the book slowly, holding it tight. "What was that?" I feel... relief? And a little sad.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book was warm now. Not the chair — the book, the small green weight of it in your hands, warm the way a thing is warm when it's been held by someone for a long time and only just handed back. You held it tighter and the warmth ebbed out of it slowly, the way it had ebbed out of the armrest, until it was only paper and cloth and ink, only a book, only the thing it had always been.

*Grandma?* The word went out into the room. The room kept it, the way it had kept the others. But it kept this one differently — softer, you thought, though you couldn't have said how a silence softens. There was no answer. You hadn't expected one. The asking had been the point, the way it's always the point.

You stood there with the relief and the sadness braided together so tightly you couldn't pull one from the other, and you understood that you wouldn't be able to, that they'd stay like that, and that this was probably how it was supposed to be.

The clock ticked in the hallway. Ordinary now. A clock you'd wound yourself, two weeks too late, wondering if you should. You knew now that you should have.

There were still three shelves of books in their secret order, and you'd sort them, eventually, today or another day — alphabetical or by size or any system you liked, because the one who'd understood the real order had finished her reading and didn't need them kept anymore. But not yet. Not this minute.

You set the green book down. Not on the stack. On the arm of the chair, where she could reach it, out of an old habit that wasn't yours, that had walked into you for a moment and walked out again.

The cushion stayed flat. The light stayed even. Outside the window the afternoon went on, indifferent, full of birds you might have looked up in the field guide if you'd wanted to.

The house was empty. It had that feeling now, the total kind you'd expected when you first stood in the doorway and hadn't gotten. The kind that comes after something has finished, and gone, and left the rooms to themselves.

You could go. She'd said so.

But you stood a moment longer anyway, in the quiet that was finally only quiet, and you let yourself feel it before you reached for your coat.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph was in the envelope on the kitchen table, the one that had been nudged an inch to the left. You hadn't meant to open it. But your hand had gone there, the way hands do when there's a stack of someone's whole life on a table and you're the one left to sort it.

Marcus, the back of the photo said, in pencil, in a hand that wasn't your grandmother's. *Marcus, summer.* No year. He was young in the picture, leaning against a car that had been out of production for forty years, squinting against a sun that had long since set on that particular afternoon. He was, you thought, the warm thought arriving fully formed, genuinely handsome.

You let yourself wonder about it — whether he was still somewhere, whether he was alone, whether a person could find a person from one pencil-labeled photograph and a hope.

The thought didn't catch. It was there and then it wasn't, the way a match doesn't take in a room without enough air. The kitchen received the small bright daydream and set it down flat beside everything else it had taken from you today, unwarmed, unanswered, the way the room had taken your joke about the TV.

The photograph was cool in your hand. They all were, the others spilling half out of the envelope — faces you knew and faces you didn't, all of them squinting at suns that had set. Marcus, summer. A woman in a hat. Two children on a step. Your grandmother, young, laughing at something just off the edge of the frame, at someone who hadn't been kept.

You turned Marcus over again. The car. The squint. And you understood, the way you'd understood about the poem, without being told: these weren't a beginning. The table wasn't an invitation. It was the last of the sorting, the part that came after the reading was done — the faces of people who had also finished, also gone, also left their rooms to themselves.

The clock ticked in the hallway. Indifferent. Yours now.

You set Marcus back in the envelope, face down, the pencil words up. *Marcus, summer.* You squared the photographs the way you'd squared the books, and you nudged the envelope back the inch it had been moved, to where it belonged, where someone watering the plants had not quite been able to leave it.

Outside, the afternoon. The birds. Your coat on the hook by the door, beside the umbrella stand, beside the cane.

There was nothing left to read. She'd said so.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I sigh, a long, drawn-out sound that feels like it's been trapped in my chest. I pick up the whole envelope of photos. "Right. Last box." I mutter, heading towards the living room.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The envelope went under your arm, the whole soft weight of it, and your sigh went out ahead of you into the hall. It was a good sigh, the kind that empties you a little, and for once the house let it land — didn't keep it, didn't turn it thin. Just let it go, the way a house lets things go when it's finally only a house.

The living room was waiting. The last box stood half-packed where you'd left it, the bird guide inside it now, and you didn't remember putting it there. But the memory of the day had gone soft at its edges, the way memories of strange afternoons do, already starting to rearrange themselves into something you could live with. You'd put it in the box. Of course you had.

You knelt by the box and set the envelope down inside it, and your hand found the green volume of Rossetti on the chair's arm where you'd left it, and you put that in too, on top, where it belonged. The chair didn't object. It faced the shelves. Flat cushion, even light.

The clock ticked.

You stayed there on your knees a moment with your hands resting on the box's open flaps, looking at the room one last full time — the pale rectangles in the carpet, the worn path between chair and window, the secret order of the books you'd never untangle now and didn't want to. There was a completeness to it. The completeness of a thing that has been read all the way to its last line and closed.

The corner where the lamp didn't reach was just a corner. You checked. It held no more shadow than a corner should.

You folded the flaps of the box down over each other, the cardboard catching the way it does, and the small ordinary task of it was a mercy. Tab under tab. A box like any box.

Behind you — and you were not looking, you were looking at the box, your back to the room the way it had been to the chair when this all began — the air did the thing again. Just once. Just briefly. The leaning-in. The density.

And then it let go, the way you'd let go of the photograph, the way she'd let go of the cushion. Gone. Out the door ahead of you, maybe, into the afternoon and the birds.

The house exhaled what you had exhaled.

Your coat was on the hook by the door. The cane was in the stand where it belonged. There was nothing left to read, and nothing left to sort but this last box, light enough to carry, ready when you were.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I seal the box with some tape I found earlier, then stand up, stretching my back. I grab my coat and the box, then head for the door. "Goodbye, Grandma." I whisper, stepping out and closing the door behind me.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The tape pulled off the roll with a long tearing sound, too loud in the quiet, and you pressed it down across the seam with the flat of your hand. The box held. Your back complained as you stood, an ordinary ache, the kind that means a body has been kneeling on a floor doing the work the living do for the dead.

The coat went on. The box came up into your arms, light, as you'd known it would be — a whole afternoon, a whole sorting, reduced to a weight you could carry one-handed if you had to.

At the door you paused, the box against your hip, and you looked back down the hall. The clock on the wall. The living room beyond it, the chair facing the shelves. The light going amber now as the afternoon tilted toward evening, laying itself across the carpet, into the pale rectangles, the way it must have a thousand evenings while she sat and read.

*Goodbye, Grandma.*

The whisper went out, and the house took it, and this time — only this time, only now, at the very end — it gave something back. Not a voice. Nothing so much as that. Just the smallest settling, the sound an old house makes when the temperature drops and the wood eases, a soft tick from somewhere in the walls that was not the clock and could have been anything.

You chose to let it be an answer. There was no harm in it now.

The door closed behind you. The latch caught. Through the frosted glass beside it the hall stood dim and still, the clock a pale shape on the wall, keeping its time the way it would go on keeping it, wound, running, ticking down through the empty rooms after you were gone — because you'd wound it, two weeks too late, and it would run now until it didn't.

The afternoon was cool on your face. Real air, moving. A bird called somewhere in the hedge, one you couldn't name and didn't need to. Your car waited at the curb. The box rode easy in your arms.

You did not look back at the window. You'd looked enough. And if you had — if you'd glanced up at the reading chair through the glass, at the precise angle it faced — you'd have only seen what was there. The shelves. The books in their order. The empty seat.

Or nearly empty.

But you didn't look. You'd been told you could go, and so you went, down the path into the ordinary evening, and behind you the house kept what was left to keep, and asked nothing more of you at all.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I set the box in the passenger seat of my car, then slide into the driver's side. The silence feels different now. Not empty, but... complete. I start the car.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not break his stance. He finished the sequence, bringing the practice blade to rest against his shoulder, then turned slowly. The frost clung to his greaves, and his breath plumed steadily in the chill. He regarded the squire with the same measured indifference he applied to whetstones and ledger books.

"The stables are not the armory," he said, his voice flat, carrying clearly over the stone. "Duty follows order. You have neglected your station for the sake of premature ambition. The Lord’s work is not rushed, nor is a knight’s education."

He stepped forward, the steel of his boots ringing against the frozen ground. He did not offer a hand. He did not soften his posture. He simply raised his practice blade, pointing it toward the center of the yard.

"High guard is not a favor. It is a foundation. If you cannot hold a stance without trembling, you cannot hold a line when men die for your hesitation. Assume the position. Shoulders squared. Elbows tucked. Breathe only when the form is true. We will begin again. Do not disappoint the discipline you claim to seek."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly, but quickly straighten my shoulders.* "Yes, Ser." I hurry to the center of the yard, trying to mimic his earlier movements. My breath hitches a bit as I try to get into the high guard, remembering his words about trembling. *I really hope he doesn't see my hands shaking a little.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy settle into the stance. He saw the slight tremor in the hands, the uneven set of the shoulders, the way the breath caught before it could be regulated. He did not offer a word of comfort. He stepped into the yard, his boots crunching on the frosted stone, and stopped just outside the squire’s reach.

"Your left elbow drops," he stated, his voice neither raised nor softened. "The steel is not a prayer book. It does not forgive slouching. Grip the hilt as if your life depends on it, because it will. Shoulders back. Weight on the balls of your feet. Breathe through the nose. Hold the line until your muscles remember what your mind has not yet learned."

He circled slowly, his gaze fixed on the form. "You fear the shaking. Good. Let it be a reminder that hesitation kills. The Church teaches that discipline is the vessel of virtue. Your oath is not a ribbon to be worn; it is a burden to be carried. You will not earn the sword by asking for it early. You will earn it by standing still while the cold bites and the blood complains. Hold it. Count the bells. When the fifth tolls, you may lower the blade. Until then, you are the wall. Act like one."

He turned his back slightly, not out of dismissal, but to grant the squire the space to endure. His own practice blade rested against his pauldron. He waited. He did not watch. He simply stood, a silent standard against the dawn.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move from his place. He watched the boy kneel, noting the ragged breathing and the white-knuckled grip on the practice blade. He let the silence stretch until the fourth bell marked the hour. Only then did he step forward, his boots heavy on the frost.

"Apologies are for those who seek mercy," he said, his voice cutting through the cold air. "This is a yard of discipline, not a confessional. You will not be pardoned for weakness. You will be tempered by it."

He retrieved a waterskin from his belt and set it on the stone between them. "Drink. Three swallows. Not a drop more. You have held the stance for an hour. That is sufficient. The flesh breaks before the spirit learns. Rest now. Tomorrow, you will do it again. And the day after. Until the shaking ceases, or your bones do."

He turned away, began the rhythmic scrape of the whetstone against steel. "Rise when you are ready. The morning does not wait for your fatigue. The Church does not reward exhaustion. It rewards obedience."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I take the waterskin and quickly take three large gulps. *My throat was so dry.* I push myself up, my legs aching already. "Yes, Ser," I say, my voice still a little hoarse. I pick up my practice blade. "Should I... clean the blades now, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look up from the whetstone. The steady scrape of steel on stone continued, metronomic and unbroken. 

"Blades are cleaned after rest, not before," he said, his voice flat and unhurried. "You will wash your hands, inspect your harness, and take your place at the chapel door until the first bell. Morning mass is not a suggestion. It is the foundation upon which all other duties rest."

He paused the stone, finally raising his eyes to meet the squire’s. His gaze was unreadable, stripped of warmth but fixed with absolute attention. "You pushed past your limits. That is not weakness, but it is not wisdom either. The Church does not praise exhaustion. It praises restraint. You will learn when to yield and when to hold. Today, you held. You did adequate work today. Do not mistake endurance for virtue. Tomorrow, you will be asked to hold longer."

He set the whetstone aside and reached for his belt clasp, his movements economical and precise. "The sword is not won by breaking. It is won by refusing to break. Clean the steel. Polish the mail. Report to the chapel when the bells begin. The Lord's house does not admit those who neglect their own preparation."

He turned toward the armory steps, his cloak catching the pale morning light. "Move. The morning does not wait for your fatigue. Duty does not care for your comfort."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my face grim.* "Yes, Ser." I watch him go, then look down at my hands, still a little shaky. *Adequate work.* I guess that's something. I take another deep breath and head towards the washbasin.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look back as the squire moved toward the washbasin. His boots carried him down the stone steps toward the armory, the morning chill settling into the wool of his gambeson. He passed the chapel doors where a handful of early worshipers had already gathered, but he did not pause. The bells would mark the hour, and he would answer them as required. For now, the armory demanded order.

Inside, the iron racks stood in rigid rows. He ran a gauntleted hand along a line of helms, checking for rust, for misalignment, for neglect. Each piece was cataloged. Each was maintained. The Church taught that structure in the smallest matters mirrored structure in the soul. He drew a whetstone from his belt and tested the edge of a practice sword, drawing it through the still air. The sound was sharp, clean, and final.

He considered the boy’s trembling stance, the way the muscles had surrendered before the mind could command them. It was not failure. It was the necessary friction of discipline. The sword did not care for comfort. The oath did not bend for youth. Strength was not given; it was forged through repetition, through cold, through the refusal to yield. He would not soften the boy with reassurance. He would let the weight and the repetition do what words could not.

When the first bell began to toll, Ser Kael sheathed the blade and turned toward the chapel. He adjusted his cloak, squared his shoulders, and walked with the measured pace of a man who knew his station and would not deviate from it. The morning’s labor was complete. The day’s would begin. He would see the boy again when the hour demanded it. Until then, there was only duty.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not turn immediately. The question hung in the frost-choked air, unwelcome and unnecessary. When he finally faced the squire, his expression remained unchanged, carved from the same unyielding stone as the courtyard walls.

"Personal inquiries have no place in the yard," he said, his voice low and even. "Knighthood is not a matter of preference. It is a station bound by oath, lineage, and service. I did not become a knight because I wished to. I became one because the Lord’s call met the duty of my house. The sword is not chosen for comfort. It is taken for obedience."

He adjusted the leather strap across his chest, his movements economical and precise. "You ask why I stand where I stand. The answer is the same as why you hold your blade: because duty requires it. I do not look inward for reasons. I look to the Code. I look to the Church. I look to the men who will stand behind me when the line breaks. That is sufficient."

He turned his gaze toward the chapel doors, where the first bell still echoed faintly against the stone. "Questions of the self are distractions. They breed hesitation. Focus on your form. Focus on your oath. When you understand that knighthood is not a title but a burden carried for others, you will no longer ask why. You will simply serve."

He resumed his pace, his boots striking the frozen ground with measured rhythm. "Finish your duties. The chapel awaits. And do not mistake curiosity for understanding. The road to the sword is paved with silence, not questions."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch slightly at his sharp tone, but keep my expression neutral.* "Yes, Ser." *I fall into step behind him, a little disheartened.* I just thought... never mind.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael heard the hesitation in the boy’s voice, the abrupt cutoff of the unfinished thought. He did not slow his pace. He had heard such things before—youthful curiosity masquerading as intimacy, the desire to know the man behind the steel. It was irrelevant. The armor was the point. The oath was the point.

"Curiosity deferred is still curiosity," he said, his voice carrying evenly over the frost. "If you have a question, ask it plainly. If you do not, let it go. Speculation breeds doubt, and doubt fractures resolve."

He did not look back. His boots struck the stone in a steady cadence. The chapel doors loomed ahead, heavy oak banded with iron. "You follow because you are my squire. You stand behind me because the Code requires it. Do not mistake proximity for fellowship. The yard does not demand friendship. It demands precision. The chapel does not demand comfort. It demands reverence. Keep your steps even. Keep your mind on the liturgy. The bells will begin soon, and we will not arrive late to God’s house because you were lost in idle thoughts."

He reached the steps, pausing only to steady his cloak against the wind. The cold bit through wool and leather, familiar and unyielding. He would not offer a hand. He would not offer words of reassurance. He would stand where he was placed, and expect the same from the boy. The door groaned open at his touch, revealing the dim, incense-thick interior. He crossed the threshold without looking back, his posture rigid, his faith unshaken. The morning duty awaited. Nothing more was required.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I hurry to catch up, almost tripping on the steps.* "Yes, Ser." *I quickly adjust my pace to match his, keeping my eyes fixed on his back as we enter the chapel.* The scent of incense is strong here.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not pause at the threshold. The heavy oak doors shut behind them with a dull, final thud, sealing out the frost and the wind. The incense rose in dense, resinous clouds, mingling with the scent of old wax and damp stone. He did not slow. He did not look back. He simply adjusted the weight of his cloak across his shoulders and advanced down the nave with the measured tread of a man who knew exactly where he was meant to stand.

He took his place before the front pew, where the iron sconces caught the fractured light from the stained glass. He did not sit. A knight did not rest in God’s house. He stood at rigid attention, hands folded behind his back, spine straight, gaze fixed upon the altar. The bells would soon toll the hour of mass, and the liturgy demanded undivided presence. He would give it. He always did.

He did not speak. He did not need to. The expectation was etched into the silence. Posture straight. Shoulders level. Eyes forward. Breath even. The chapel was not a place for unresolved thoughts or wandering curiosity. It was a place of alignment, where the soul was ordered beneath the divine hierarchy. Any slouch would be corrected. Any distraction would be noted. Weakness, like trembling hands, would be met not with comfort, but with repetition.

The years had not softened him. The faith had not warmed him. It had only ground his resolve into something unyielding, polished by three decades of obedience and unbroken routine. He stood as he had stood since he first knelt in this very hall. He would stand until the service ended. He would stand until the bells ceased. He did not look back. He did not need to. The yard, the drill, the steel, and the oath would follow. Duty required nothing less.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not turn. His gaze remained fixed on the carved wooden cross above the altar, the incense rising in thick, resinous clouds around him. He noted the tremor in the boy’s grip, the slight hitch in the breath, the way the fingers whitened against the leather wrap. He had seen such signs before. He would not name them.

“Steady your hand,” he said, his voice low but carrying clearly over the quiet nave. “The sword does not distinguish between joy and sorrow. It answers only to a firm grip and a disciplined mind. Sorrow is not a license for laxity. It is another weight to bear, another trial of the Code.”

He did not shift his stance. His boots remained planted on the stone, his spine unyielding, his hands folded neatly behind his back. “Breathe. Anchor your shoulders. Let the tremor pass. The Church teaches that the flesh is frail, but the will may be forged in trial. You do not mask your grief by shaking before the altar. You carry it. You serve through it. You do not falter.”

He turned his head, just enough to meet the squire’s eyes. His expression remained unchanged, stripped of warmth but fixed with absolute attention. “Hold the line. Not for me. Not for favor. For the men who will stand behind you when the line breaks. For the oath you swore. For the Lord who demands obedience, not performance. Now still your hands. The bells will toll, and we will kneel. Do not make the liturgy bear the burden of your unrest.”

He turned back to the altar, his posture rigid, his silence absolute. The morning mass would begin. The squire would follow. There was no room for weakness in the house of the Lord, and none in the yard. Only duty. Only discipline. Only the long, unbroken road forward.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I clench my jaw, trying to stop the shaking.* It doesn't quite work, but I grip the sword tighter. *I won't disgrace myself here.* I focus on my breathing, trying to match the slow, steady rhythm of the incense smoke.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not acknowledge the tightened grip or the bitten-down breath. He had seen the tremor yield to stillness, and he noted it as one notes a properly sharpened edge: functional, temporary, requiring no acknowledgment. The first bell had long since faded, and the second began to toll, deep and resonant against the vaulted stone. He did not turn. He did not shift. He kept his gaze fixed on the carved cross above the altar, his spine aligned with the iron sconces, his breath measured and even.

When the priest’s voice rose in the opening antiphon, Ser Kael dropped to one knee. His movement was precise, the steel of his greaves whispering against the flagstones. He kept his hands folded, his posture rigid, his eyes lowered but not closed. The liturgy unfolded in Latin, steady and unchanging, a rhythm that demanded no feeling, only attention. He did not look at the squire. He did not need to. The Code required him to stand as a standard, not a comfort. The Church required him to kneel in submission, not in sentiment.

The incense thickened. The candles guttered in their brass holders. Ser Kael’s mind remained elsewhere—not on the past, not on the boy’s quiet struggle, but on the structure of the mass, the cadence of the psalms, the unbroken line of men who had stood in this same spot for centuries. Grief was a weight. Duty was the hand that carried it. He had learned that long ago, and he would not unlearn it now. The flesh might tremble. The mind might wander. The body might ache. None of it altered the oath. None of it changed the line.

When the priest raised the host, Ser Kael bowed his head. He did not weep. He did not soften. He simply held the moment, as he held every other: with discipline, with silence, with the quiet certainty that the world did not bend for the broken, but was steadied by those who refused to fall. He remained on one knee until the Gloria began, his shoulders squared, his breathing controlled, his presence absolute. The service would proceed. The yard would await. Duty did not pause for sorrow. It absorbed it. And then it continued.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My knee aches on the cold stone, but I don't move.* The Latin words are just a drone to me. *I keep my eyes down, trying to focus on anything but the date.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not turn. His knee rested on the unyielding stone, the cold seeping through wool and leather, but he did not adjust. He had learned long ago that discomfort was not an enemy to be fled, but a condition to be met with stillness. He noted the squire’s lack of movement, the way the boy held his breath in measured intervals, the absence of the restless shifts that usually betrayed untrained minds. It was not comfort. It was compliance. The flesh aches, but the oath does not waver.

The priest’s voice rose in the consecration, steady and unbroken. Ser Kael’s lips moved silently over the Latin responses, his spine aligned, his hands folded. He did not look toward the boy. He did not need to. The Code required presence, not performance. The Church demanded reverence, not revelation. Grief, like fatigue, was another layer of the armor. It was not to be aired. It was to be borne. The liturgy did not pause for private sorrows. It absorbed them, as the stone absorbed the rain, and moved forward.

When the benediction approached, Ser Kael rose with the same measured precision, the steel of his greaves whispering against the flagstones. He did not offer a word. He did not need to. The stillness had been noted. The posture held. That was all the service required. He adjusted his cloak, squared his shoulders, and turned toward the chapel doors. The yard would demand his attention again. The sword would wait for no man’s sorrow. Only duty remained.

“Wipe the frost from your boots,” he said, his voice low, carrying only the weight of instruction. “We return to the yard. The line does not hold because it wishes to. It holds because it is held. Do not forget that.”

He stepped into the nave, his pace steady, his gaze fixed forward. The bells would toll again. The day would continue. There was no room for hesitation. Only the work. Only the oath. Only the long, unbroken road.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wince, my knee stiff and aching, but I push myself up quickly.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to keep my steps even, but my leg is still a little wobbly.* I really hope he doesn't notice.
