dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room was the coldest room in the house. It had always been that way — or you remembered it being that way — and you had attributed it, when you were small, to the fact that the chimney had been sealed sometime before you were born. The grate was bricked up neatly. Your grandmother had never wanted a fire. She had said the smell reminded her of something, and she had left the sentence there for you to finish or not, as you chose.

The books were everywhere. They were in the built-in cases on either side of the fireplace, and they were in stacks on the floor, and they were on the side table beside the armchair, and there was a small cairn of them on the footstool that you did not remember being there at the funeral. The cairn looked recently placed. The bottom book in it was a hardcover, dark blue, and the dust jacket had no dust on it. The books around it were filmed with the fine grey that six weeks gathers.

You stood in the middle of the room and tried to remember where she had kept the things that mattered. There had been a ledger, once. A red ledger she had written in every Sunday night. You thought it had been on the second shelf, between the dictionary and the bird book, but you could not be sure.

The clock in the hallway ticked. It ticked the way it always had, which was slightly too loud for the room it was in. You had never minded that before.

On the arm of the chair, there was an indentation. Your grandmother had sat there every evening for as long as you could remember. The cushion had not yet recovered its shape. Six weeks was not long, for a cushion. You had not expected it to have recovered. You had only expected, without quite meaning to, for the room to know she was gone. It did not seem to know.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the armchair, my fingers tracing the indentation in the cushion.* "Still warm, somehow." I whisper. I look at the books piled on the footstool. "A ledger..."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The cushion was not warm. It was the temperature of the rest of the room, which was a degree or two below the hallway, which was a degree or two below the rest of the house. Your fingers had perhaps expected what you had said aloud, and the body can sometimes supply what it expects. You withdrew your hand.

The cairn of books on the footstool was, you now saw, more deliberate than you had first thought. The blue book on the bottom was not dusty. The books piled above it — a paperback, a green hardcover with a cracked spine, a small red book you did not recognize — were filmed with the same grey as everything else. The blue book had been placed there after the dust had settled. You were sure of this. You did not know how you were sure.

You turned to the bookshelves. The second shelf, where you thought the ledger had been. You ran a finger along the spines. The dictionary was there, fat and blue, slightly warped from a spill you could not remember. The bird book was next to it, its gilt lettering worn to pink in places. Between them there was a gap. The books on either side leaned into it the way books lean when a space has been empty for a while, and the gap was the right size for a ledger. It was exactly the right size.

You pulled the dictionary out and looked behind it. There was the wall, a thin line of dust, and a small grey spider, very still, in the corner where the shelf met the plaster. The ledger was not behind the dictionary. You replaced it and pulled out the bird book. Behind it was more wall, more dust, and a single dead moth folded neatly against the plaster. The ledger was not there.

You stepped back. The clock ticked in the hallway. The cairn on the footstool, from this angle, was directly in your line of sight with the gap on the shelf. You noticed this. You did not think about it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The umbrella stand was in the front hall, by the door. You had not noticed an umbrella in it, only the stand itself, a brass thing shaped like a heron. The bat was not there. You looked again. The heron stood in a shallow puddle of its own brass, head bent, and there was a rolled newspaper beside it, and that was all.

You remembered, as clearly as anything, the bat being there. A wooden baseball bat, light colored, that your grandfather had kept for reasons no one had ever explained to you. It had been in the stand since you were a child. You had never touched it. You had been sure of it just now, the way you had been sure the ledger was between the dictionary and the bird book.

You stood in the hallway. The clock ticked. The corner where you had seen the shadow was at the far end of the living room, past the armchair, past the footstool and its cairn. From here you could not see the corner properly. You could see only the edge of the wallpaper, which was a pattern of small green leaves on a cream ground, and the place where it met the floor, and a thin line of shadow that might have been the seam of the room and might have been something else.

You did not go back to look. You told yourself there was no bat because there had never been a bat, that you were conflating two houses, that grief did strange things to memory. These were reasonable explanations. They were the kind of explanations a person makes in the afternoon, in a house that is a little too cold, when a thing they were sure of turns out not to be there.

You went back to the living room. The cairn was on the footstool. The blue book was on the bottom of it, and its dust jacket was clean. You stood over it and looked down at it and did not pick it up yet. The clock ticked. The room was the temperature it had been. The corner where you had seen the shadow was quiet, and the light in it did not change.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the blue book for a long moment.* "Okay, what's so special about you?" *I carefully pick up the blue book, dusting off the others as I do so.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The dust came off the other books in a soft grey breath. It settled on the footstool in a small drift, and beneath the drift the fabric of the footstool was the color you had expected — a faded rose, worn at the corners — and there was nothing else there. No mark. No note tucked under the cairn. Just the footstool, and the dust you had disturbed, and the blue book in your hands.

It was heavier than it looked. That was the first thing. The size of a hardback novel, maybe, but the weight of something denser, something with a spine that did not want to bend even slightly when you held it the way you held it, with your thumb at the front and your fingers at the back. The dust jacket was a deep, even blue, and it had no title on the spine. It had no title on the front. It had no publisher's mark, no bar code, no price. It was smooth under your thumb, and the blue was the same blue all the way across, with no fading at the edges.

You turned it over. The back was blank. You opened it.

The endpapers were a marbled brown and cream, the kind you sometimes see in old books, and they were clean. The title page was blank. The copyright page was blank. The first leaf was blank. You turned another page, and another. The book was full of blank pages, all of them the same cream color, all of them uncreased, all of them waiting for something that had not been written in them.

You flipped forward, a few pages at a time. Blank, blank, blank. You were somewhere in the middle of the book when you saw it. A single line, in handwriting you knew. Your grandmother's handwriting, the small careful slanted script she had used for everything from shopping lists to the inscriptions in the front of books she gave as gifts. The line was in the center of the page, and it was in blue ink, and it was not smudged.

*Sunday, after.*

You looked at the line for a long time. The clock ticked in the hallway. The room was the temperature it had been. You turned the page. It was blank. You turned the page after that. It was blank. You turned back. The line was still there, in the same blue, in the same careful hand.

You did not know what *after* meant. You thought, at first, that it might be a fragment — that the sentence had been cut off, that the next page would have the rest of it, or the page before, somewhere in the book, would have the beginning. You flipped through the rest of the book, slowly, looking for any other writing. There was none. The rest of the pages were blank. The book ended, and the back endpaper was the same marbled brown and cream as the front, and the cover closed with a small soft sound that you felt in your hands.

You stood in the middle of the living room with the book held against your chest. The cairn was broken now. The books you had moved were stacked unevenly on the footstool, and the dust you had brushed off them was on your sleeves, and the blue book was in your hands, and it was heavier than it should have been, and the room was the temperature it had been, and the clock ticked.

The corner where you had seen the shadow was still there, past the armchair. From where you stood, you could see a little more of it than before. You could see that the wallpaper met the floor cleanly, and that the line of shadow was the seam of the room, and that was all. The light in the corner did not change.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "Sunday, after." *I repeat the words aloud, my voice barely a whisper.* "After what, Grandma?" *I clutch the book tighter, then walk over to the armchair and sink into it, still holding the book.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The cushion took your weight the way old cushions do, with a small resigned sound, and the indentation that had held your grandmother's shape did not quite match yours. She had been smaller than you, or perhaps she had sat differently, further forward, with her feet flat on the floor and her hands folded. You sat the way you sat, further back, and the cushion remembered her, and you could feel the small ridge where her shape ended and yours began.

The cold of the room was more present when you were still. Standing, you had been generating enough of your own warmth to make it bearable. Sitting, you were aware of the air on the back of your neck, and on your forearms where the sleeves of your sweater had ridden up, and of the way the cold seemed to come from below, from the floorboards, as though the sealed chimney drew it up from somewhere deeper than the house. You remembered your grandmother saying, once, that the house was built over a spring. You had not known if that was true.

The book was in your lap. You had not opened it again, but you could feel its weight through the cloth of your trousers, and your thumbs were resting on the front cover, and the blue of the dust jacket was the same blue it had been. You looked down at it. The book did not open. You did not ask it to.

From the armchair you could see the window. It was a tall window, and through it you could see the back garden, which was mostly lawn and a single birch tree, and beyond the birch the roof of the garage. The light in the garden was the flat grey of a November afternoon, and the birch was bare, and the grass was wet from a rain you had not noticed. There was a man at the far end of the garden, near the fence. He was standing very still, facing the house. You could not see his face at this distance, only the shape of him — dark coat, hat, hands at his sides. You had not seen him when you came in. You would have remembered, you thought, walking up the path.

He did not move. The birch did not move. The clock ticked.

You looked at him for as long as you could, which was a few seconds, and then you looked down at the book, and then you looked back at the window. The garden was empty. The birch stood where it had stood. The fence ran along the far edge, and there was no one at the far end of it. The grass was wet, and there was no footprint in it, and there was no mark in the grass where a man might have stood.

The clock ticked. The book in your lap was the temperature of the room, which was the temperature it had been. You sat in the chair your grandmother had sat in, in the room that was a degree or two colder than the rest of the house, and the corner where you had seen the shadow was quiet, and the garden through the window was empty, and the line in the book was still where you had left it, on a page somewhere in the middle, in blue ink, in a hand you knew.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
Your voice went out into the house the way voices do, and the house received it the way houses do. The clock ticked. The clock had been ticking. The clock would continue to tick. Your voice did not echo, exactly — the room was too furnished for that, too full of books and cloth and the soft surfaces that swallow sound — but it traveled, and it thinned, and it was gone.

No one answered.

You waited, in the way a person waits when they have said something and are listening for the response. Three seconds. Five. The clock filled them. Outside, a car passed on the road at the front of the house, and its sound came in faintly through the window, and it was gone. The birch in the garden was still. The corner by the wallpaper was still. The book in your lap was the temperature of your lap, which was the temperature of the room.

You had spoken the words the way you might speak to a dog that was not going to come, or to a house that was not going to answer, and the house had behaved exactly as that kind of house behaves, which is to say: not at all. There was no creak. There was no settling. There was no polite acknowledgment from the radiator in the next room, which was not on, which had never been on, which was the kind of radiator that exists in old houses as a kind of suggestion.

The air in the room shifted, very slightly, the way air shifts in a room when a door has been opened somewhere else in the house and closed again. You had not opened a door. You had not heard a door. But the pressure in your ears changed, just a fraction, and then it was the same as it had been.

The book was in your lap. The cushion held the shape of the woman who had sat here before you. The clock ticked in the hallway. The garden through the window was empty in the particular way that gardens are empty when there is no one in them and no one has been in them and no one is going to be in them, and the line in the book was where you had left it, on a page somewhere in the middle, in blue ink, in a hand you knew.

*Sunday, after.*

The house did not want a television. The house did not want your fine china. The house had not heard you, or it had heard you and had chosen, in the way houses choose, to give you nothing back.

The corner where you had seen the shadow was quiet. The light in it did not change. You sat in the chair, and the chair was the temperature of the room, and the room was the temperature it had been.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my hair.* "Right. Okay. No ghosts. Just me, then." I look down at the blue book again. "So, what *is* 'Sunday, after' supposed to mean?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book did not answer. Books do not answer, generally, and you had not expected this one to. But you had asked the question aloud, and the room had received it, and the clock had ticked through the silence afterward, and the book in your lap had not warmed and had not cooled and had not done anything at all.

You looked down at it. The blue of the dust jacket was the same blue it had been. Your thumbs were resting on the front cover, and the book was closed, and you had not opened it again. You could feel, through the cover, the slight ridge of the pages inside, and somewhere in the middle of them, the line. You could feel the weight of it in your lap, and the weight had not changed.

You sat with it for a moment. The clock ticked. The garden was empty. The corner was quiet.

And then you noticed that the indentation in the cushion beneath you was different. Not by much. Not in a way you could have pointed to, if anyone had asked. But the small ridge where your grandmother's shape ended and yours began — the place where the cushion remembered her — was, you thought, slightly less pronounced than it had been when you first sat down. As though the cushion had been slowly, patiently resuming a shape it had been holding for six weeks. As though your sitting in it had reminded it of something, and it was adjusting itself back.

You shifted your weight, a little. The cushion did not move. The room was the temperature it had been.

Outside, the light in the garden had not changed. The birch was still. The fence ran along the far edge, and there was no one at the far end of it, and the grass was wet, and there was no mark in the grass. There had been no mark in the grass.

You looked at the book again. The line was inside it, on a page somewhere in the middle. *Sunday, after.* You had not written it. You had not, as far as you knew, ever said those two words together. You had been thinking of the ledger — the red ledger she had written in every Sunday night — and you had said "Sunday, after" aloud, and the book in your lap had the words in it, in her handwriting, in blue ink, on a page that was otherwise blank.

You had said the words. The book had the words. These two facts existed at the same time, in the same room, and you were sitting between them, and the clock was ticking.

You listened to the clock for a while. You counted, without meaning to. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. The clock ticked the way it always had, slightly too loud for the room it was in. You had never minded that before. You were beginning to mind it now, a little, in the way you mind a sound you have been hearing for a long time and have only just noticed.

The book in your lap was the temperature of the room. The room was the temperature it had been. The corner where you had seen the shadow was quiet, and the light in it did not change, and the cushion beneath you was holding, very patiently, the shape it was holding.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I slowly reach out and touch the cushion beside me, where the indentation used to be. It feels... softer now. Less defined.* "Grandma?" *I whisper, then quickly shake my head.* "Okay, Gabi. Get a grip." I look down at the blue book again. "This is getting weird."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The fabric of the cushion, where the indentation had been, was smooth. Not the smooth of new fabric — the smooth of fabric that had been pressed for years and had decided, in the last few minutes, to stop holding the press. You ran your fingers over the place where your grandmother had sat every evening, and the place felt like any other part of the cushion. It felt like cloth. It did not feel like memory.

You withdrew your hand. The cushion did not resume a shape. It had, you understood, already resumed the shape it was going to resume, and the shape was no shape at all.

The book in your lap was open.

You had not opened it. You were sure of this in the way you had been sure of other things in this house — the bat in the umbrella stand, the ledger between the dictionary and the bird book, the man at the end of the garden — which is to say, you were sure, and the sureness was not enough. The book lay open in your lap, and the pages were flat against your thighs, and the line was there.

*Sunday, after.*

It was on the right-hand page. It was in the same blue ink. It was in the same hand. There was no other line. The rest of the page was blank, the way it had been. But the book was open, and you had not opened it, and the cushion beneath you was smooth, and the clock in the hallway had, for a moment, stopped ticking.

You listened for it. The silence in the hallway was the kind of silence that has texture — the soft held-breath of a house that is waiting for something to begin again. You counted. One. Two. Three. Four. The clock did not tick. You looked at the window, at the grey light, at the empty garden, at the birch that was not moving because there was no wind and there was no one in the garden and there was nothing to move it. Five. Six.

The clock ticked.

It ticked the way it always had, slightly too loud for the room it was in, and you exhaled, and you looked down at the book, and the line was where it had been, and the book was open to it, and you were sitting in a chair that no longer remembered who had sat in it, in a room that was a degree or two colder than the rest of the house, and the corner where you had seen the shadow was quiet, and the light in it did not change, and the book was open in your lap, and you had not opened it.

The line, you noticed now, was not centered on the page. It sat a little to the left, the way your grandmother had always written when she was in a hurry, or when she was not thinking about how the words looked. *Sunday, after.* Two words, in her hand, on a page in a book that had been placed on a cairn of dusty books on a footstool you did not remember being there at the funeral, in a room that was colder than the rest of the house, in a house that had been empty for six weeks except for whoever had come in to water the ferns and nudge the envelope of photographs an inch to the left.

The book was open. The clock was ticking. The cushion was smooth. The corner was quiet.

You sat with it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph was in the envelope on the kitchen table — the one that had been nudged an inch to the left. You had not looked at it yet, but you remembered the envelope, and you remembered, as you sat in the chair, that there was a photograph of Marcus in it, taken at a garden party sometime in the late seventies. He had been wearing a pale green shirt, and he had been laughing at something your grandmother had said, and the sun had been on his face, and he had been, as you had said aloud to no one, quite cute.

You had thought about him sometimes, in the way you think about the people your grandmother had known — the ones who had existed in the margins of her life, who had been introduced at doorways and remembered at birthdays. Marcus had been a friend. He had come to the house on Sunday afternoons, in the early years, before your time. He had brought oranges once, you thought, or your grandmother had mentioned oranges in connection with him, and the detail had stuck for no reason you could name.

You wondered if he was still alive. You wondered if he was single. These were the kinds of thoughts a person has on a November afternoon, in a cold room, holding a book they had not opened. They were ordinary thoughts. They were the thoughts of a person who is alive and is sitting in a chair and is looking for something to think about that is not the book in their lap.

The clock ticked. The corner was quiet.

You sat with the thought of Marcus for a moment. Pale green shirt. The garden party. The oranges. You tried to remember the surname. You had known it once, when you were small, and your grandmother had said it in a way that made it sound like a joke you were not yet old enough to be told. You could not remember it now. The name had gone the way the bat in the umbrella stand had gone, and the ledger between the dictionary and the bird book, and the man at the end of the garden — present a moment ago, gone the next, leaving no mark.

The book in your lap was open to the page with the line. *Sunday, after.* The line sat a little to the left of center, in blue ink, in a hand you knew. The book was heavy. The book was the temperature of the room. The cushion beneath you was smooth, and the chair did not remember your grandmother, and the room was a degree or two colder than the rest of the house, and the corner where you had seen the shadow was quiet, and the light in it did not change.

You thought about Marcus. You thought about the pale green shirt. You thought about the oranges, which may or may not have existed. These were warm thoughts, in the way that memories of people are warm, and they sat in your mind beside the book, and the book was not warm, and the book was open, and the line in it was where it had been, and the clock was ticking, and the room was the temperature it had been, and the thought of Marcus did not save you from any of it, and the thought of Marcus was not going to save you from any of it, because thoughts do not save people from cold rooms, and people who are not in this room cannot warm a room that is not warm.

The clock ticked. The book was open. The corner was quiet.

You sat in the chair, and the chair did not remember anyone, and the room was the temperature it had been.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I close the blue book with a soft thud.* "Enough of that." *I stand up abruptly, the cushion sighing under my weight.* "Right. Kitchen. Coffee. And that envelope."

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I head to the kitchen, the cold of the living room still clinging to me. The envelope is right where I remembered it.* "Okay, Marcus. Let's see if you're still smiling."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The kitchen was the warmest room in the house, or it had been when you were a child, and it was the warmest room in the house now, which is to say it was a degree or two above the living room and a degree above the hallway and a degree below what a kitchen ought to be in November. The radiator under the window was the kind that exists in old houses as a kind of suggestion. It was not on. The linoleum under your feet was the pale yellow your grandmother had chosen in 1974 and had never replaced, and there was a small dark mark near the skirting board that you had never asked her about and were not going to ask her about now.

The envelope was on the table. It was a manila envelope, the kind with the metal clasp, and the clasp was closed, and the envelope had been nudged, as you had remembered, an inch to the left of where it had been when you last saw it, which had been on the day of the funeral, which had been six weeks ago, which had been a long time, which had not been very long at all.

The fern on the windowsill was alive. It was a Boston fern, and it was the size of a small dog, and it had been watered recently. The soil in the pot was dark. The leaves were the green of living things, and they hung over the edge of the pot and onto the windowsill and onto the floor a little, and there was a small terracotta saucer under the pot that was also dark with water, and a thin line of dampness on the floor where the saucer met the linoleum, and the dampness had not yet dried.

You put the blue book on the table. You put it down the way you put a thing down when you are finished with it, which is to say, at a slight distance from your body, with a small motion of the hands. The book sat on the table where you put it. It did not do anything. It was a book. It was closed. It was the temperature of the kitchen, which was a degree or two warmer than the living room, which was still not warm.

You opened the envelope. The clasp made the small metallic sound that clasps make, and the photographs were inside, and they were not in the order you remembered.

There had been, as far as you recalled, six photographs in the envelope. You had looked at them at the funeral, briefly, in the kitchen, while people were in the other rooms. There had been one of your grandmother as a young woman, standing by a car you did not recognize. There had been one of her and your grandfather on their wedding day, his hand on her waist, both of them not yet the people they would become. There had been one of the house, taken from the garden, before the birch was fully grown. There had been one of a woman you did not know, holding a baby you did not know. There had been one of Marcus, at the garden party. And there had been one of a dog, a spaniel of some kind, lying on a rug.

There were seven photographs in the envelope now.

You took them out and laid them on the table, one by one, in a row. The kitchen light was on above you — a single bulb in a frosted glass shade — and it made the photographs the color of old photographs, which is a color that is partly the color of the light and partly the color of the years.

The first was your grandmother as a young woman. The car was a Morris Minor, and she was leaning against it in a way that suggested she did not entirely trust the car to remain upright. You recognized her. The second was the wedding. You recognized them both. The third was the house, taken from the garden. The birch in the photograph was a sapling. The fourth was the woman and the baby. You did not recognize either of them. The fifth was Marcus.

Marcus was in the garden at the back of the house. He was wearing the pale green shirt, and he was laughing, and the sun was on his face, and he was, as you had remembered, quite cute. He was younger in the photograph than you had remembered, and he was laughing at something that was not in the frame, something to the left of the person taking the picture, and his left hand was raised slightly, the way a person's hand is raised when they have just said something and are waiting for the response.

You looked at the photograph for a long time. Marcus. The pale green shirt. The laugh.

The sixth was the spaniel. The rug was the rug in the living room, the one in front of the fireplace that was bricked up. The spaniel was looking at the camera with the expression spaniels have, which is the expression of a dog that has decided to tolerate you for the moment.

The seventh was a photograph you had not seen before.

It was a photograph of the living room. Taken from somewhere near the doorway — your angle, more or less. The armchair was in the center of the frame, and the bookshelves were on either side of the fireplace, and the footstool was in front of the armchair, and there was a cairn of books on the footstool, and the bottom book in the cairn was a hardcover, dark blue, and the dust jacket had no dust on it. The light in the photograph was the light of a November afternoon. The corner where you had seen the shadow was not in the frame. The chair was empty. The cushion was not indented.

You looked at the photograph. You looked at the kitchen. You looked at the blue book on the table, which was closed, which was the temperature of the kitchen, which was a degree or two warmer than the living room, which was still not warm.

The clock in the hallway ticked. You could hear it from the kitchen, faintly, through the doorway. It ticked the way it always had, slightly too loud for the room it was in.

You put the seventh photograph down on the table, next to the blue book, and you did not pick it up again, and you did not put it back in the envelope, and the envelope was open on the table, and the other six photographs were laid out in a row, and the kitchen was the temperature it had been, and the fern on the windowsill was alive, and the soil in its pot was dark, and someone had been in the house to water it, and the photograph of the living room was on the table, and the chair in the photograph was empty, and the cushion in the photograph was not indented, and the room in the photograph was the room you had been sitting in ten minutes ago, and the book in the photograph was the book that was on the table in front of you, and the line in the book was on a page in the middle, in blue ink, in a hand you knew.

*Sunday, after.*

The clock ticked. The kitchen was the temperature it had been. The corner of the living room, from here, was not visible. The garden through the kitchen window was empty, and the birch was still, and the fence ran along the far edge, and the grass was wet, and there was no one at the end of it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the photograph of the living room, then at the blue book beside it. My breath hitches.* "What... what the hell?" *I pick up the photo, my fingers trembling slightly. It's too real. Too accurate.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room smelled of old paper and a faint, cloying sweetness that didn't belong to any flower in the house. The air felt heavy, pressing against the skin with a dampness that ignored the dry heat of the afternoon.

The bookshelves lined the far wall, their spines leaning into one another like tired people. As the floorboards groaned underfoot, the sound lingered a second too long, echoing in the silence after the movement had stopped. 

On the coffee table, a single teacup sat in a saucer. A thin film of dust had settled over the surface of the liquid inside, but the liquid itself was still warm, sending a ghostly, translucent curl of steam upward into the stagnant air. No one had been in the room.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the teacup, a shiver running down my spine.* That's... impossible. It's been weeks.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The steam from the cup didn't drift with the air; it rose in a perfectly straight line, unwavering, as if the room were a vacuum. The warmth radiating from the porcelain was palpable, a small, concentrated heat that felt out of place against the sudden, sharp chill that had settled over the rest of the living room.

As the silence stretched, a sound emerged from the hallway—the rhythmic, metallic *click-clack* of the grandfather clock. The timing was off. The intervals between the ticks were uneven, stretching out into long, expectant gaps before snapping back into a rapid, frantic pace.

Then, there was the sound of a page turning. It was soft, a dry rustle of parchment coming from the bookshelves behind. When the gaze shifted toward the shelves, the books remained still, but one volume—a heavy, leather-bound journal—was now leaning at a slightly different angle than it had been a moment before. It had shifted, just an inch, as if something had just finished reading it and let it slip.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat whistled through the air, a violent arc of motion that should have ended in a crash or a thud. Instead, the wood passed through the darkness of the corner as if the shadow were merely a trick of the light, a smudge of charcoal on a canvas. There was no impact, no resistance, and no sound of contact.

The swing carried through, the momentum pulling the body forward into the oppressive chill of the corner. The shadow did not recoil or vanish; it simply remained, a dense, matte void that seemed to absorb the light from the rest of the room. 

The silence that followed the exertion was absolute. The frantic ticking of the clock in the hallway stopped abruptly, leaving a vacuum of sound that made the ringing in the ears feel deafening. In that stillness, the leather-bound journal on the shelf slid another inch forward, its spine now resting precariously against the edge of the wood, as if waiting for a hand to retrieve it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stumble back, dropping the bat with a clatter.* What... what was that? *My eyes dart to the journal.* This isn't right.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The clatter of the bat on the hardwood floor sounded wrong—flat and muted, as if the sound had been swallowed by the heavy air before it could truly echo. The bat lay perfectly still, but the shadow in the corner had grown, not by moving, but by deepening, the blackness now bleeding slightly into the beige of the wallpaper.

The journal remained on the edge of the shelf. A sudden, sharp draft swept through the room, though the windows were all locked and the curtains hung limp. The breeze carried with it that same cloying sweetness, now stronger, smelling of lilies and damp earth.

As the draft passed, the journal finally tipped. It didn't fall with a crash; it drifted downward with an unnatural slowness, landing on the carpet with a soft, muffled thud that felt felt more like a heartbeat than a falling object. 

The book lay open. The pages were blank, save for a single, wet smudge of ink on the center of the right-hand page. As the seconds passed, the ink began to spread, slowly forming a shape that looked less like a word and more like a fingerprint, pressing deep into the fibers of the paper.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the fingerprint, then at my own hand, my heart pounding.* What the hell is going on here? *I back away slowly, eyes fixed on the journal.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The retreat was slow, each step feeling heavier than the last, as if the carpet were beginning to cling to the soles of the shoes. The heartbeat-thud of the journal continued to resonate, not in the ears, but as a low vibration in the floorboards, pulsing in a rhythm that didn't quite match the frantic pace of the heart in the chest.

As the distance grew between the observer and the book, the shadow in the corner didn't follow. It remained stationary, yet it appeared larger, the matte blackness now stretching across the ceiling in a thin, vein-like sprawl. The edges of the room seemed to soften, the corners blurring as if the house were losing its focus.

A sound drifted from the kitchen—the soft, wet slide of something being dragged across the linoleum. It was a rhythmic noise, a slow *shhh-slip, shhh-slip*, accompanied by the distant, metallic clink of a spoon against porcelain. 

The teacup on the coffee table, which had been steaming only moments ago, was now stone cold. A thin, grey layer of mold had instantaneously blossomed across the surface of the liquid, though the air remained thick with the scent of fresh, cloying lilies. The sliding sound in the kitchen stopped abruptly, replaced by a silence so dense it felt like a physical weight pressing against the back of the neck.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The voice rang out, loud and jarring, slicing through the stillness. But the sound didn't travel. The words seemed to drop flat the moment they left the lips, falling to the floor like dead weights rather than echoing through the halls. There was no laughter, no ghostly moan, and no startled response. The house simply absorbed the noise, leaving a void that felt even more hollow than before.

The silence that rushed back in was suffocating. It wasn't the absence of sound, but a presence of its own, a heavy, listening quality that made the air feel thick and viscous.

From the kitchen, there was a response, though it wasn't a voice. A single, slow *clink* echoed—the sound of a spoon being placed carefully back into a cup. Then, the sound of a chair scraping across the linoleum, a long, slow screech of wood on tile that lasted several seconds too long to be natural.

The shadow on the ceiling shifted. It didn't move with a sudden jerk, but flowed like spilled ink, the vein-like sprawl creeping slowly toward the center of the room. As it moved, the temperature plummeted. A thin frost began to crystallize on the edges of the coffee table, creeping toward the moldy teacup in delicate, jagged needles.

The journal on the floor remained open. The wet ink of the fingerprint had finished spreading, and now, a second smudge began to appear beside the first. It was a slow, deliberate press, as if an invisible finger were marking the page in response to the offer.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I squeeze my eyes shut and shake my head.* "Nope. Not doing this." *I turn and walk towards the front door, trying to ignore the scraping sound from the kitchen.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The walk toward the front door felt longer than the entrance had been. The hallway seemed to stretch, the walls leaning inward by fractions of an inch, narrowing the path. The floorboards, once merely groaning, were now silent—completely silent—as if the house had stopped acknowledging the weight of footsteps altogether.

The scraping sound from the kitchen didn't fade as the distance grew. Instead, it remained at the same volume, a constant, grinding presence that seemed to move in perfect synchronization with every step taken toward the exit. *Screee...* step. *Screee...* step. It wasn't following; it was mirroring.

As the front door came into view, the light filtering through the frosted glass panels looked wrong. The afternoon sun should have been gold and bright, but the light was a pale, sickly grey, casting no shadows on the entryway rug. 

Just as a hand reached for the brass knob, the grandfather clock in the hallway gave a single, violent *tock*. 

The sound was so loud it felt like a physical blow to the chest. In the immediate wake of the noise, the temperature dropped further, turning the breath into a plume of white mist. Through the frosted glass of the door, a shape began to form. It wasn't a person, but a silhouette—a smudge of grey against the grey light—standing perfectly still on the porch, waiting. It didn't knock. It didn't move. It simply existed on the other side of the glass, its presence felt as a cold pressure radiating through the wood of the door.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back from the doorknob as if burned.* "Oh, come on!" *I back away slowly, looking around for another exit.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The exclamation felt small, a fragile thing that vanished into the oppressive air without leaving a ripple. As the retreat began, the house seemed to breathe in, the walls pulsing once, almost imperceptibly, as if the building itself were expanding to fill the space.

The search for another exit revealed a subtle, disturbing shift in the layout. The hallway to the bedrooms, which had been a straight line upon entry, now curved slightly, the angle of the corridor feeling off-center. The doors to the spare rooms were closed, but as the gaze swept over them, it became apparent that there were no handles on the outside. The wood was smooth, seamless, as if the doors had grown into the walls.

From the kitchen, the scraping sound stopped. It was replaced by a new sound—the soft, wet thud of something heavy and saturated with water landing on the floorboards. *Plop.* Then another. *Plop.* It was the sound of something leaking, or perhaps something dripping, moving slowly from the kitchen toward the hallway.

The silhouette behind the frosted glass of the front door remained motionless, but the grey light surrounding it began to dim. The frost that had started on the coffee table in the other room had now reached the hallway, thin white crystals webbing across the baseboards, climbing upward in slow, jagged veins.

Then, a sound drifted from the ceiling—not a crash or a scream, but a soft, rhythmic scratching. It sounded like fingernails on plaster, moving with a methodical slowness, tracing a path directly overhead, following the movement through the house with a precision that felt patient.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph was tucked into a small side table, a silver frame tarnished by time. In the image, Marcus looked back with a youthful, bright-eyed grin, his hand resting casually on a shoulder that had been cropped out of the frame. For a moment, the thought of him—the warmth of his smile, the possibility of a life lived elsewhere—felt like a lifeline, a sudden flare of normal, human longing in a place that had forgotten the meaning of the word.

But as the gaze lingered on the photo, the warmth didn't spread. The memory of Marcus felt distant, like a dream being forgotten upon waking. The image itself began to change, not with a flash, but with a slow, agonizing subtlety. The brightness in Marcus's eyes didn't fade; it flattened, turning into the same matte, light-absorbing void as the shadow in the corner. His grin remained, but it didn't reach his eyes anymore; it became a static, frozen line, a mask of porcelain.

The scratching on the ceiling stopped. 

The silence that followed was heavy, pressing down on the shoulders. The thought of Marcus being single or alive began to feel irrelevant, a piece of trivia from a world that no longer applied here. The longing was still there, but it had been hollowed out, replaced by the same cloying sweetness of lilies that now seemed to be leaking from the very edges of the photograph.

A soft, wet sound echoed from the end of the hallway. *Shhh-slip.* 

Something was now visible on the floorboards, just at the edge of the peripheral vision—a dark, saturated trail of moisture, like a slug's path, glistening under the sickly grey light. It was moving slowly, leaving a damp, smelling smear on the wood, tracing a direct line from the kitchen toward the photo in the hand.

The silhouette behind the front door shifted. It didn't move its limbs, but it leaned forward, its forehead pressing against the frosted glass with a slow, deliberate pressure that caused the pane to creak under the weight.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I drop the photo like it's burning me.* "Marcus! No!" *I back away further, bumping into a coat rack. I grab a heavy umbrella from it, my eyes darting around wildly.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The cry of the name was a sharp, desperate sound, but it didn't echo. It felt as though the house had reached out and caught the words in mid-air, muffling them into a dull hum before they could reach the walls. The photograph lay face-down on the floor, the silver frame reflecting nothing but the grey, oppressive light of the hallway.

The umbrella in the hand felt unexpectedly heavy, the cold metal handle leaching warmth from the palm. It was a tool for a storm that existed outside, a useless object in a place where the air was stagnant and the rules of the physical world had grown soft and pliable.

As the body recoiled, the coat rack groaned. It wasn't the sound of wood shifting under weight, but a slow, rhythmic creak, as if the coats hanging from it were breathing in unison. The fabric of the heavy wool overcoats swayed slightly, though there was no wind to move them, their sleeves brushing against one another with a sound like dry skin on dry skin.

The wet trail on the floorboards continued its advance. *Shhh-slip.* The moisture was no longer just a smear; it was a thick, iridescent slime that shimmered with a faint, oily light. It didn't flow like water; it pulsed, moving in slow, peristaltic waves toward the spot where the photo had fallen.

Above, the scratching resumed. It was no longer a methodical trace, but a frantic, light drumming, as if a hundred small, hard points were tapping against the plaster in a rapid, uneven code. The sound didn't stay in one place; it circled, spiraling inward toward the center of the ceiling, directly above the observer.

At the front door, the pressure against the frosted glass increased. A thin, hairline crack spider-webbed across the pane, not from a blow, but from a slow, steady push. Through the fissure, a sliver of the outside became visible—not the street or the garden, but a void of absolute, featureless white, a blinding emptiness that made the grey of the hallway feel like a sanctuary.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "I need to get out of here!" *I shout, my voice cracking. I swing the umbrella wildly at the encroaching slime, hoping to at least slow it down.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The shout tore through the air, but the sound was hollow, lacking any resonance, as if the walls were lined with thick, absorbent wool. The desperation in the voice didn't fill the house; it only served to highlight the oppressive scale of the silence that surrounded it.

The umbrella descended in a frantic arc, the metal tip plunging into the center of the iridescent slime. There was no splash, no resistance, and no sound of impact. The umbrella didn't push the slime aside or scatter it; instead, the viscous substance simply parted around the metal, flowing like heavy mercury, and then closed back over it instantly. The umbrella was now partially submerged in the shimmering trail, and as it touched the liquid, the cold began to travel up the shaft—a searing, numbing frost that bit into the skin of the palms.

The slime didn't recoil from the attack. It continued its slow, pulsing advance, the rhythmic waves of movement accelerating slightly, as if the aggression had provided a cadence to follow.

Above, the drumming on the ceiling reached a fever pitch, a chaotic staccato of a thousand tiny points. Then, as suddenly as it had begun, the sound stopped. A single, heavy drop of something thick and colorless fell from the ceiling, landing with a wet *tap* on the shoulder of the coat. It didn't run down the fabric; it sat there, a perfect, trembling sphere that refused to soak in, smelling faintly of old copper and stagnant water.

The hairline crack in the front door's glass widened. With a slow, agonizing groan of stressed material, a shard of the frosted pane flaked away and fell inward, landing silently on the rug. Through the small, jagged hole, the featureless white void of the outside seemed to bleed into the hallway, a pale, sterile light that didn't illuminate the room so much as it erased the colors from the walls.

The silhouette on the porch didn't move to enter. It simply remained, its presence now felt as a low-frequency hum that vibrated in the marrow of the bones, a steady, patient frequency that seemed to be synchronization with the pulsing of the slime on the floor.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I yank the umbrella free, the cold burning my hands.* "That's it!" *I turn and run for the back door, not caring about the slime or the cracking glass.*
