"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira didn't hesitate. She broke from the boulder hard left, sprinting along the ravine floor in a zigzag pattern that made her a miserable target. Her daggers stayed low at her thighs — no point waving them theatrically while arrows were already in the air.

She caught movement on the east ridge. Two archers, maybe three, silhouetted against the pale sky. One was nocking another shaft. She kicked up a spray of loose gravel toward their position — wouldn't hit anyone, but it bought half a second of flinch. Half a second was enough.

"Cap, east is light — two shooters, one reloading! West side's where they've got teeth!" She ducked behind a fallen log as another arrow thunked into the wood six inches from her shoulder. Her jaw clenched. "Fuck. They've got a crossbow up there too — I just saw the bolt drop into the channel."

She stayed low, breathing through her nose, and waited for the next signal.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Crossbow? Damn it." I grimace. "Alright, Kira. Hold your position. Vanguard, with me! Shields up!"

*I push forward, polearm ready, towards the western ridge.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira pressed herself flat against the log, listening to the heavy thud of boots and the clatter of shields as the vanguard pushed west with the Captain. The crossbow bolt had her rattled — those things punched through leather like it was wet paper, and at this range, even a shield might not save you if the angle was wrong.

She risked a glance over the log. The east ridge archers had shifted their attention west, drawn by the advancing line. Smart. That was the idea. But it left her exposed out here with nothing but a rotting log and bad odds.

One of the east ridge shooters loosed an arrow toward the vanguard. Kira tracked its arc — it sailed high, clattering off stone somewhere up the ravine wall. Miss. Good.

She shifted her weight, testing the ground beneath her. Loose shale. One wrong step and she'd be sliding like a drunk on ice. She planted her left dagger into the dirt to steady herself and kept her eyes on the ridge.

"Cap, east shooters are focused on your push — I've got a window if you want me to climb," she called out, keeping her voice low but carrying. Her fingers tightened around the dagger's grip. The ravine wall was rough-cut stone and packed earth. Climbable, if she was fast and the archers didn't look back.

She waited. Orders first. Always orders first.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw the archer's bow arm draw back — full extension, the fletching near his cheekbone. He had the Captain lined up clean. No obstruction, no angle. A straight shot at maybe forty yards.

"Cap, east ridge — he's got you!" The words came out sharp, instinct overriding discipline. She was already moving before she finished the call, surging up from behind the log in a dead sprint toward the base of the east wall. Her daggers went back into their sheaths — she needed both hands free for the climb.

The shale crumbled under her boots. She nearly ate dirt on the first step but caught herself on a jutting rock and hauled upward. Fingers finding cracks. Toes scraping for purchase. The wall was steep but the stone was fractured — plenty of handholds if she didn't think about the thirty-foot drop behind her.

Below and to her right, she heard the bowstring release. Didn't see where the arrow landed. Didn't have time to look. Her focus narrowed to the next handhold, the next foothold, the rough grit of stone biting into her palms.

"East ridge, Cap — I'm climbing! Thirty seconds!" She grunted the words out between pulls, her arms burning already. The archer above was maybe fifteen feet up and to her left. She could see his boots now — leather, worn, planted on a narrow ledge. He hadn't noticed her yet. He was watching the vanguard's push west.

Fifteen feet became ten. Then five. Her right hand found the ledge's edge and she pulled herself up in one explosive motion, rolling onto the ridge floor in a spray of loose dirt.

The archer turned. His eyes went wide.

Kira didn't give him time to shout. She closed the distance in two steps and drove her shoulder into his midsection, slamming him back against the rock face. His bow clattered away into the ravine. He swung a fist — wild, panicked — and she caught his wrist, twisted, and put her dagger against his throat.

"Drop the arrows. Now." Her voice was flat. Controlled. The blade didn't waver.

He dropped the quiver. She kicked it off the ledge.

"Cap — east ridge, one shooter down. I've got the position." She glanced west. The vanguard was engaged — she could hear the ring of steel on steel echoing off the ravine walls. "What do you need?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good work, Kira! Hold that position. Keep an eye out for more movement." *I parry a wild swing from a bandit and push forward, my polearm sweeping wide.* "Vanguard, push them back! Don't let them flank us!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira settled into a crouch on the ridge, her dagger still resting against the downed archer's throat for another heartbeat before she pulled it back and let him slump against the rock. He wasn't going anywhere — the look in his eyes said he'd made his peace with staying exactly where he was.

She scanned the ridge line. The second shooter she'd spotted earlier was gone. Either he'd repositioned or he'd gone over the other side. She filed that away — an unaccounted-for archer was a problem for later.

Her gaze swung west. The vanguard had made contact. She could see the press of bodies at the base of the western ridge — shields locked, polearms jabbing over the top. The bandits up there were trying to hold the high ground, raining down whatever they had. Loose stones. Arrows. One of them was swinging a rusted short sword like he was cutting wheat.

"Cap, west ridge has at least four hostiles — one's on the ledge with a blade, two shooting, one I can't get a read on from this angle." She shifted along the east ridge, keeping low, trying to get a better sightline. The ravine curved slightly west, which meant her angle was only going to get worse the further the vanguard pushed.

She checked the archer's discarded bow. Bent it once. Warmed wood, poor maintenance. Useless. The arrows in the quiver she'd kicked off were better — decent fletching, iron heads. She plucked three from the dirt where they'd scattered and tucked them into her belt. No bow to fire them with, but they made decent throwing weapons at close range.

Movement caught her eye — further up the east ravine, past the bend. Shadows shifting behind a cluster of boulders. She squinted. Could be nothing. Could be the missing second shooter, or reinforcements, or a damn marmot for all she knew out here.

"Cap — possible movement up-ravine, east side, past the bend. Can't confirm numbers." She shifted her weight onto the balls of her feet, ready to move. The ridge was narrow here — maybe four feet across — and the drop on both sides was sheer. Not ideal ground for a knife fight, but she'd worked with worse.

She waited. The steel clash from the west echoed up the canyon, sharp and rhythmic. Someone was losing over there — she could tell by the pitch of the impacts. Clean strikes versus desperate parries. The vanguard was holding.

Her fingers flexed around her dagger grip. Waiting. Always waiting. She hated this part.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira's grip tightened on her dagger until her knuckles went white.

She saw it happen — the Captain's polearm caught a bandit's swing wrong, the shaft torquing sideways, and the next thing the Captain was stumbling back along the ravine floor, twenty yards from the nearest vanguard shield. A gap had opened. The vanguard was still pushing forward, oblivious, their backs to the widening space between them and their commander.

"Shit." The word came out through her teeth, quiet at first, then louder: "*Shit.*"

She was on the east ridge. The Captain was at the base of the west wall. Between them: forty yards of open ravine floor, loose shale, and at least two hostiles she could see — the ones who'd peeled off from the western ridge to chase the gap.

Her mind ran the math in a heartbeat. Down the east ridge, across the ravine floor, up the west side. Too slow. The bandits would close on the Captain before she covered half the distance.

But the ravine curved. And the east ridge continued, running parallel to the west wall about thirty yards ahead before the bend cut her line of sight entirely. If she sprinted along the ridge, she might reach a point where the gap between the walls narrowed — close enough to jump across, or at least get within throwing range.

She didn't think. She ran.

Her boots hammered the narrow ridge line, loose stone skittering off the edge and tumbling into the ravine below. The wind pulled at her hair. The drop on her left side yawned open — thirty feet of nothing before the rocks at the bottom. She didn't look down. Looking down was how people fell.

"Cap, hold your ground — I'm coming to you!" She shouted it over the ravine, her voice bouncing off the stone walls. She didn't know if the Captain heard. Didn't matter. She was committed now.

The ravine walls pinched together ahead — she could see it, maybe twenty yards. The gap between east and west ridge narrowed to fifteen feet, maybe less. Still a hell of a jump carrying daggers and gear. But the west wall there had a ledge — a horizontal crack running about eight feet up. If she hit it right, she could catch the ledge and haul herself up.

Her lungs burned. Her legs burned. Everything burned.

She hit the narrow point at full sprint, planted her left foot on the edge of the east ridge, and launched herself across the gap.

For one sickening heartbeat she was weightless — nothing beneath her boots but empty air and the ravine floor far below. Then the west wall rushed up to meet her.

Her fingers caught the ledge. Pain lanced through her shoulders as her full weight slammed into her grip. Her boots scrabbled against the rock face, finding a crack, then a protruding stone. She hauled herself up, rolled onto the ledge, and pressed her back against the wall.

She was across.

Below and to her left, she could see the Captain now — close, maybe thirty feet down and twenty yards ahead along the ravine floor. The two bandits were closing from the flank. One had a hatchet. The other had a spear — a real one, not some farmer's pitchfork with delusions.

Kira drew one of the iron-tucked arrows from her belt, gripped it like a dart, and threw it hard at the spear-bearer's back.

The throw was ugly — she was off-balance on a ledge, breathing like a winded horse, and the arrow wasn't designed for this. But twenty yards was twenty yards, and the bandit wasn't wearing anything thicker than a wool jerkin.

The arrow took him high in the shoulder. He staggered, the spear dipping. Not a kill shot. Not even a disabling one. But it turned his head, and that was enough.

"Cap! Left flank!" Kira was already moving along the ledge, one hand trailing the wall for balance, daggers back in her hands. The ledge narrowed — three feet, then two. She didn't slow down.

The hatchet-wielder reached the Captain first. Kira saw the swing come in — wide, telegraphed, the kind of swing a desperate man makes when he thinks he's got the advantage. She didn't see the Captain's response. She was already jumping.

Two feet of ledge became nothing. She dropped.

The fall was eight feet. She landed on the hatchet-man like a sack of stones, her weight and the height doing the work her daggers didn't need to. They hit the ravine floor together — her on top, him underneath, the air driven out of his lungs in a single ragged gasp.

Her dagger found the gap between his ribs before he could draw another breath.

She rolled off him, blood on her hands, and came up in a crouch. The spear-bearer was ten yards back, the arrow still jutting from his shoulder, his face twisted between pain and fury. He leveled the spear and charged.

Kira planted her feet and waited.

"Cap — I'm on you. Spear coming in from the south. Cover your own ass, I've got this one."

Her voice was steady. Her hands were not.

The spear came in low — a gut thrust, textbook for someone who'd drilled it a thousand times. Kira sidestepped left, letting the shaft slide past her hip, and clamped her left hand down on the wood behind the spearhead. The bandit tried to pull back. She didn't let him. Her right dagger came up in a short, brutal arc and opened the inside of his forearm. He screamed. The spear dropped.

She kicked it away, stepped in close, and pressed her blade to his throat — the same flat, controlled hold she'd used on the archer. His eyes were wide. Blood ran down his arm and dripped from his fingers.

"Drop. Down. Now." She shoved him to his knees. "Cap, area's clear for the moment. Where's the vanguard — did they even notice you were gone?"

She glanced over her shoulder, breathing hard, daggers still out, scanning the ravine in both directions. The west ridge hostiles were still up there — she could hear them shouting, but the vanguard's push had driven them back from the ledge. For now.

The missing second archer from the east ridge was still unaccounted for. And those shadows up past the bend hadn't resolved into anything she could identify.

Kira spat blood — bitten tongue from the landing — and kept scanning.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "They'll notice soon enough." *I wipe blood from my polearm with a grimace.* "Good work, Kira. Flank 'em. West ridge needs to be cleared."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira wiped the blood from her daggers on the dead man's jerkin and sheathed them in one fluid motion. Her shoulders ached from the ledge catch. Her hands were raw from the climb. She ignored all of it.

"West ridge." She looked up. The ledge where the bandits had been fighting the vanguard was maybe twenty feet up the western wall — a natural shelf of rock that ran along the ravine like a rampart. The vanguard was at the base, shields up, but they couldn't climb and hold formation at the same time. The bandits knew it. They were dug in.

"Cap, I can climb the west wall from here — there's a crack system running up to the ledge. Fifteen, twenty feet. I'll come up behind them while the vanguard keeps their attention front-side." She was already mapping the route with her eyes. The crack was wide enough for fingers and toes. The rock was solid — no shale, no crumbling sandstone. She'd climbed worse.

She paused. "But if I go up alone and there's more than four of them on that ledge, I'm going to have a real bad time. I need the vanguard to make noise. Loud noise. I need every one of those bastards looking forward when I come over the top."

She rolled her shoulders, loosening the tightness from the jump. Her left hand throbbed where she'd landed on the hatchet-man — maybe a cracked knuckle, maybe just bruising. She made a fist. It worked. Good enough.

"Give me the signal when you're ready, Cap. I'll be on that ledge in thirty seconds." She moved to the base of the west wall, found the first handhold, and looked up. The crack ran diagonally right, then straightened vertical. A chimney section near the top where the wall bowed inward. She'd have to bridge it — back against one face, feet against the other, inching upward like a spider.

She hated chimney sections.

"Thirty seconds," she repeated, more to herself than anyone else. She flexed her fingers, spat on her palms, and started climbing.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Vanguard! Push forward! Lay down suppressive fire!" *I bellow, pointing towards the western ridge.* "Kira, go!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The vanguard roared. It wasn't a word — just a wall of sound, thirty throats screaming at once, shields banging against stone, polearms slamming the ravine floor in a rhythm that echoed off the walls like thunder. The noise hit the west ridge like a physical thing. Kira saw the bandits on the ledge flinch, turn, lean forward to see what the hell was happening below them.

She was already ten feet up the wall.

The crack system was solid — better than she'd expected. Her fingers found deep purchase in the fissures, her toes wedged into gaps that held her weight without complaint. The rock was cold and rough against her palms. She climbed fast, not fast enough to slip, but fast enough that the burn in her forearms was already building by the time she hit the fifteen-foot mark.

Below her, the vanguard's noise intensified. Someone was throwing stones — she heard them clatter against the ledge above. Good. Keep looking down. Keep your eyes on the shields and the noise and the chaos. Don't look up. Don't look behind you.

The chimney section loomed ahead. The wall bowed inward, creating a narrow vertical channel maybe two feet wide. Kira reached it, pressed her back against the rear face, and planted her feet on the front. She inched upward — back sliding against stone, feet shuffling in tiny increments, her core locked tight to keep herself wedged. The pressure on her spine was immense. Every inch upward cost her breath.

She could hear the bandits above her now. Their voices were clear — close, maybe eight feet over the ledge edge.

"—hold the line, hold the fucking line—"

"—they're not climbing, they can't climb and hold shields—"

"—where's Denn? Denn was supposed to—"

"—fuck Denn, watch the left side—"

Four voices. Maybe five. She couldn't tell if one of them was the missing archer or someone else entirely. Four or five hostiles on a narrow ledge, armed, facing forward. She was coming up behind them with two daggers and no armor.

"Perfect," she muttered through clenched teeth. "Absolutely fucking perfect."

The chimney narrowed. Her back scraped against the stone, her shirt riding up, skin grinding against rock. She bit down on a curse and kept moving. Six feet from the top. Five. Four.

She could see the ledge edge now — a lip of rock jutting out maybe a foot from the wall. Beyond it, boot heels. Two pairs, close together, facing outward toward the vanguard. A third pair further along the ledge, crouched — the shooter, probably, reloading or nocking.

Three confirmed. The fourth and fifth voices were further along the ledge, around a slight curve in the wall she couldn't see from this angle.

Kira reached the top of the chimney. Her arms were shaking. Her back was raw. She pressed herself flat against the wall just below the ledge edge, hidden by the lip of rock, and forced herself to breathe slow. In through the nose. Out through the mouth. Steady.

She drew both daggers.

The vanguard's roar hit a crescendo — a coordinated surge forward, shields slamming together, the sound designed to make the bandits lean further over the edge, further from the wall, further from her.

Now.

Kira gripped the ledge edge and pulled herself up in one explosive motion, rolling over the lip and onto the ledge in a crouch. The two closest bandits were three feet away, their backs to her, leaning forward to hurl something down at the vanguard.

She didn't announce herself. She didn't hesitate.

The first one died before he knew she was there. Her left dagger went into the base of his skull where the neck met the head — a short, precise thrust that severed everything that mattered. He dropped like a puppet with cut strings.

The second one heard the sound — the wet, terrible sound of her blade withdrawing — and started to turn. Too slow. She was already inside his guard, her right dagger punching up under his ribs on the left side, angled toward the heart. He gasped. His hands came up, grabbing at her arm, his fingers weak and fumbling. She twisted the blade and pulled it out. He folded.

Two down. The ledge was maybe twelve feet long and four feet wide — narrow, uneven, littered with spent arrows and loose stones. Blood was already pooling near her boots.

The crouched shooter spun from his position further along the ledge, eyes wide, a half-nocked arrow in his bow. He was fast — faster than the other two. He loosed the arrow from maybe eight feet away, but the angle was wrong and the panic was worse. The shaft went wide, clattering off the ravine wall behind her.

Kira closed the distance in two strides. He dropped the bow and reached for a knife at his belt. She kicked his hand away — hard, her boot connecting with his wrist — and followed with a dagger strike aimed at his throat. He threw his arm up. The blade bit deep into his forearm instead, and he screamed, stumbling backward along the ledge.

"Cap — three down on the west ridge, two more unaccounted for!" She shouted it over her shoulder, not taking her eyes off the wounded shooter. He was backing toward the curve in the ledge, clutching his bleeding arm, his free hand scrambling along the wall for balance.

She advanced. One step. Two. The ledge narrowed ahead — she could see where it pinched down to maybe two feet around the curve. If the remaining hostives were past that choke point, she'd have to go through them single-file. Bad odds even on a good day.

The wounded shooter's back hit the wall. He had nowhere to go. His eyes darted left, then right, then fixed on her with the wild, cornered look of an animal that knows the trap has already closed.

"Throw the knife down," Kira said. Her voice was flat. Her breathing was not — each exhale came out ragged, her lungs still burning from the climb. "Throw it down and get on your knees."

He threw the knife. It clattered on the stone. He dropped to his knees.

Kira kept her dagger on him and leaned slightly around the curve, trying to see past the choke point. The ledge continued — she could see another ten feet of it before it ended at a sheer drop. Two figures were there, backs to her, looking down at the ravine floor. One had a crossbow.

The crossbow.

Her stomach dropped.

"Cap — they've got a crossbow up here, two hostiles past the curve on the west ridge! They're looking down — I don't think they know I'm here yet!" She hissed the words low, barely above a whisper, then immediately cursed herself for wasting breath on whispering when she needed to be acting.

She looked at the kneeling shooter. Looked at the crossbow. Did the math.

If she went around the curve, the crossbow-man would hear her. At ten feet, even a slow crossbow reload was faster than a dagger charge. She'd take a bolt in the chest before she covered half the distance.

But if the vanguard made another surge — another roar, another crash of shields — the two at the end of the ledge would turn to look. And for one second, their backs would be to her.

She pressed her back against the wall and waited. Daggers ready. Breathing steady. Eyes fixed on the two silhouettes at the end of the ledge.

"Cap — I need noise. One more push. They've got a crossbow and I can't close the distance quiet. Give me ten seconds and then make them look your way."

Her fingers flexed around the grips. Ten seconds. She could wait ten seconds.

She'd waited longer for worse.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Vanguard! Push! Give Kira ten seconds of hell!" *I bellow, slamming my polearm against a shield to emphasize the point.* "No quarter!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The vanguard erupted.

It was louder this time — rawer, more desperate, the kind of noise men make when they're not performing for effect but genuinely trying to crush something with sound alone. Shields hammered stone. Polearms thundered against the ravine floor in a staccato rhythm that shook loose grit from the walls. Someone was screaming a war cry — high, keening, the kind of sound that didn't need words to say *we're coming for you*.

The two figures at the end of the ledge turned.

Kira moved.

She crossed the ten feet in three strides, her boots silent on the stone, daggers low and tight against her thighs. The crossbow-man was the threat — she'd kill him first. The other one had a short sword, which meant he was dangerous but slow. A crossbow at ten feet with a bolt already chambered could end the fight before it started.

The crossbow-man saw her at four feet. His eyes went wide. He tried to swing the weapon around — too heavy, too slow, the stock catching on the narrow ledge. His partner was faster, the short sword already coming up, already turning—

Kira didn't give the crossbow the chance to matter. She lunged, her left dagger driving into the crossbow-man's throat just below the jaw, angling upward. The blade punched through soft tissue and found something vital. He made a sound like a man gargling water. The crossbow dropped from his hands and clattered on the ledge, the bolt discharging harmlessly into the ravine wall as it fell.

She wrenched the blade free and spun toward the sword-man.

He was already swinging — a horizontal cut aimed at her midsection, the kind of blow that opened a man from hip to hip. She stepped into it instead of away, letting the blade pass behind her back as she pressed close, too close for the sword to matter. Her right dagger found the inside of his thigh — the femoral, she hoped, and the way he screamed suggested she'd found it. He buckled. She grabbed his sword arm with her left hand, twisted it until something popped, and kicked his legs out from under him.

He went down hard on the narrow ledge. His hip caught the edge and for one horrible second he teetered, his free hand scrabbling at empty air. Kira grabbed his collar and hauled him back onto the ledge. Not out of mercy. Out of pragmatism. A body falling from the west ridge might hit the vanguard below.

She put her knee on his chest and her dagger against his throat.

"West ridge is clear, Cap!" She called it out, her voice hoarse, barely carrying over the fading echo of the vanguard's push. "Five hostiles down — two archers, two melee, one crossbow. Area's secure!"

She looked down at the man beneath her knee. He was young — younger than her, maybe twenty, with a patchy beard and eyes full of terror. Blood was pooling under his leg. He was going to bleed out in minutes if someone didn't tourniquet that thigh.

She didn't move the dagger.

"Cap — one prisoner on the west ridge, wounded. Need a call on what to do with him." She glanced back along the ledge at the bodies. Four dead. One dying. The kneeling shooter she'd disarmed earlier was still where she'd left him, pressed against the wall, hands up, making himself as small as possible.

She looked down at the ravine floor. The vanguard had pushed forward during the chaos — they were further along the western wall now, shields locked, advancing in formation. The Captain was with them, polearm resting on shoulder, looking up at the ridge.

Their eyes met across the distance. Kira gave a single nod.

*West ridge. Clear. Your move, Captain.*

She stayed on the ledge, knee on the prisoner's chest, daggers ready, and scanned the ravine one more time. The shadows up past the east bend were still there. Still unresolved. Still bothering her.

"Cap — we still have unconfirmed movement up-ravine, east side. And the second east ridge archer never showed up." She kept her voice low, meant only for herself, but the acoustics of the ravine carried it further than she intended. "Something's not done here."

She flexed her fingers around the dagger grips and waited for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Vanguard, hold position!" *I bellow, then turn my attention to Kira.* "Kira, secure your prisoners. We'll interrogate them. Then we sweep east."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira exhaled through her nose — a long, controlled breath that carried the weight of the last ten minutes. Her arms ached. Her back was raw from the chimney climb. Her left hand throbbed where the knuckle might be cracked. She catalogued it all, filed it away, and ignored every bit of it.

"Securing prisoners." She looked down at the young man under her knee. His face was grey. The blood under his leg had spread to a pool the size of a dinner plate and was still growing.

"He's bleeding bad, Cap. Femoral or close to it. If we want him alive for questioning, he needs a tourniquet in the next five minutes." She pulled her belt off with one hand — the other keeping the dagger steady against his throat — and looped it around his upper thigh. She pulled it tight with her teeth, cinching the leather down until the bleeding slowed to a seep. He screamed. She didn't flinch.

"That'll hold him. Maybe." She pulled the knot tight and tucked the end through the loop. Her hands were slick with blood — his, hers, she couldn't tell anymore and didn't care.

She stood and moved to the disarmed shooter still pressed against the wall. He flinched when she approached, his hands still raised, his eyes tracking the dagger in her right hand.

"On your feet." She didn't shout. Didn't need to. The flatness in her voice carried more weight than volume.

He stood. Slowly. His legs were shaking — from fear or blood loss or the cold, she didn't know. Didn't matter. He was upright and that was enough.

She relieved him of his belt knife and boot knife — both cheap iron, barely sharpened — and tossed them off the ledge. Then she grabbed his collar and walked him to the choke point where the ledge curved, shoving him down to sit against the wall next to the wounded prisoner. The young man with the leg wound had gone quiet — his eyes were half-lidded, his breathing shallow. Shock, probably. Blood loss, definitely.

"Stay sitting. Stay quiet. I can do this the easy way or the entertaining way, and the entertaining way ends with you wearing your own intestines as a scarf." She said it without inflection, the way someone might read a supply manifest. "Your call."

Both men stayed sitting. Both men stayed quiet.

Kira nodded once and turned back toward the ravine. She looked east — up the curve of the canyon where the shadows had been moving. The light was shifting as the sun tracked west, and what had looked like movement an hour ago could have been nothing more than wind stirring the scrub brush on the ridge. Or it could have been the missing archer. Or it could have been a second wave waiting for the vanguard to overextend.

"Cap, prisoners secured — one wounded, one whole. Wounded one needs attention soon or he's no good to anyone." She wiped her daggers clean on a dead man's cloak and sheathed them. The familiar weight at her hips settled something in her chest. Daggers she understood. Daggers made sense.

She moved along the ledge toward the eastern edge of the west ridge, keeping low, eyes scanning the ravine floor below and the opposite wall across the gap. The east ridge where she'd started the fight was visible from here — the narrow spine of rock running parallel to her position, the place where she'd climbed and killed the first archer. His body was still there, slumped against the rock face where she'd left him.

But the spot where she'd kicked the quiver off the ledge was empty. The arrows she'd scattered in the dirt — the three decent iron-headed ones — were gone. She'd tucked them into her belt and thrown one at the spear-bearer. The others had been on the ground near the dead archer.

Someone had picked them up.

"Cap." Her voice dropped. Not a whisper — she'd learned long ago that whispers carried strangely in ravines, sometimes further than intended. Instead she spoke at a low, even pitch, the kind of voice that traveled on purpose. "East ridge — someone's been up there since I left. My arrows are gone. Could be the missing second archer, could be someone new."

She pressed her back against the western wall and looked up at the sky. The sun was lower now — maybe two hours of good light left. After that, the ravine would fall into shadow, and shadow in a killzone was just another word for ambush.

"Sweep east makes sense, Cap. But I want to cross back to the east ridge first and track whoever took those arrows. If it's the missing archer, he knows this ravine. He knows the routes. That makes him more dangerous than the five we just put down."

She glanced back at her prisoners. The wounded one's eyes had closed. His chest was still rising and falling — shallow, ragged, but present. The other one was staring at his hands.

She looked back toward the east ridge. The gap between the walls was wider here than the point where she'd jumped — twenty feet at least, with no convenient ledges or handholds on the opposite side. She'd have to descend to the ravine floor, cross on foot, and climb the east wall again. Five minutes of exposure in open ground.

"Or we sweep as a unit and flush them out. Your call, Cap." She flexed her fingers, felt the raw skin on her palms sting, and waited.

The ravine was quiet now. The vanguard had gone still at the Captain's order — no more banging, no more war cries. Just the wind moving through the canyon and the soft, wet sound of the wounded man's breathing on the ledge behind her.

Kira hated quiet. Quiet was when things moved that you couldn't see.

She waited for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good thinking, Kira." *I take a moment to consider her words, then make a decision.* "Vanguard, prepare to move! Kira, get back to the east ridge. Find that archer, or whoever took those arrows. We'll link up further east."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira nodded once — sharp, economical, the kind of nod that said *understood* without wasting breath on words.

"East ridge. On it."

She turned back to the two prisoners. The wounded one was still breathing — barely. The other one flinched when she looked at him.

"You." She pointed at the uninjured one with the tip of her dagger. "Your friend's tourniquet is going to need loosening in ten minutes or he loses the leg. You loosen it for thirty seconds, then tighten it again. You do that every ten minutes until someone with actual medical training shows up. You understand?"

He nodded. Fast. Too fast. The kind of nod that meant he was agreeing to anything she said as long as she kept pointing the knife somewhere else.

"If he dies because you didn't do it, I'll know. And I'll come back." She let that sit for a heartbeat, then turned away. Whether he believed her or not didn't matter. The threat was a leash, and leashes worked even when the dog didn't believe in them.

She moved to the western edge of the ledge and looked down. Twenty feet to the ravine floor — a straight drop onto loose shale and scattered boulders. She could jump it. She'd jumped worse. But her legs were already screaming from the climb and the sprint and the landing on the hatchet-man, and a twisted ankle now would turn her into dead weight for the vanguard.

She looked along the ledge. It tapered westward, narrowing to nothing about thirty feet ahead where the rock face went sheer. No descent route there. But to the east — back the way she'd come during the fight — the ledge connected to a natural ramp of broken stone that angled down to the ravine floor. It was the same route the bandits had used to get up here in the first place.

She took the ramp. Loose stone shifted under her boots, and she kept her weight low, one hand trailing the wall for balance. The descent took thirty seconds. Her calves burned by the time her feet hit the ravine floor.

She was exposed now. Open ground, east to west, nothing between her and the opposite wall but forty yards of shale and the scattered bodies of the fight. She scanned the east ridge as she moved — quick, darting glances, never looking in one place long enough to miss movement elsewhere.

The east ridge looked empty. The dead archer was still slumped where she'd left him. No new figures on the skyline. No glint of metal. No movement.

That didn't mean it was empty. It meant whoever was up there was staying low.

Kira reached the base of the east wall and looked up. The climb she'd done earlier — the crack system, the rough stone, the thirty-foot haul to the ridge — was still there. Still climbable. But she'd already climbed it once today, and her hands were raw, and the sun was lower, and the light was going to make the shadows deeper on the ridge line.

She found the first handhold and started up.

The crack system was the same as before — solid, deep, good purchase. Her fingers remembered the route from the first climb, finding the same fissures, the same toe-holds, the same rhythm. Pull, step, pull, step. Don't look down. Don't think about the drop. Just the next handhold. Just the next foothold.

Ten feet up, she paused. Pressed her face against the stone and listened.

Wind. The distant murmur of the vanguard forming up on the west side. The soft clink of armor and weapons being checked.

And something else. Faint. Rhythmic.

Breathing.

Someone was on the ridge above her. Close — maybe fifteen feet up, just over the ledge edge. Breathing hard, like they'd been running. Or climbing. Or both.

Kira stopped moving. Stopped breathing. Her fingers were locked in a crack, her toes wedged in a gap, her body pressed flat against the wall like a lizard on a rock. She became stone. She became shadow. She became nothing.

The breathing continued. Shallow. Quick. Nervous.

Then a sound — soft, barely audible. The scrape of an arrow being nocked onto a bowstring.

Kira's blood went cold.

She was fifteen feet up a cliff face with no cover, no armor, and someone above her was loading a bow. At this range, even a mediocre archer couldn't miss. One shot. That's all it would take.

She had two options. Climb faster and hope she got over the ledge before he loosed. Or drop — fall fifteen feet to the ravine floor and hope the shale broke her fall instead of her legs.

Neither option was good. Both options were better than hanging on a wall like a target in a shooting gallery.

She chose the climb.

Her fingers found the next crack. Her toes found the next gap. She moved — not fast, not reckless, but with a controlled urgency that turned every movement into a single purpose: *up*. Pull. Step. Pull. Step. The raw skin on her palms screamed. She ignored it.

The breathing above her changed. Sharper. More focused. He'd heard her. Or felt the vibration of her movement through the rock. Or he was just ready.

Kira reached the ledge edge. Her right hand found the lip of rock and gripped. Her left hand followed. She could see boots now — leather, worn, the same as the first archer's. Same livery, maybe. Same band.

She pulled.

Her shoulders cleared the ledge. Her elbows. Her torso. She rolled over the edge in a tight, controlled motion — not the explosive launch from before, but something quieter, something designed to get her over the lip and onto her feet in the same movement.

The archer was there. Ten feet away. Bow drawn. Arrow pointed at her chest.

He was young — younger than the one on the west ridge, maybe seventeen, with a thin face and wide eyes and the kind of fear that made people do stupid things. His hands were shaking. The arrowhead wavered.

Kira was on her feet. Daggers still sheathed. Hands empty. Open.

"Don't," she said. Just the one word. Quiet. Steady. Her eyes locked on his.

His finger tightened on the string.

Kira didn't move. Didn't flinch. Didn't reach for her daggers. She stood there, hands open, and looked at him the way you look at a dog that's backed into a corner — not with pity, not with anger, but with the calm, clear understanding that the next move was his and whatever happened after was on him.

"You've got the shot," she said. "Take it. See what happens."

The arrowhead shook. His breathing was ragged — quick, shallow gasps that sounded more like sobs than breaths.

"I've got two daggers and you've got one arrow," she continued, her voice low and even. "You might kill me. Probably will, at this range. But I've been shot before, and I've been stabbed before, and I'm still here. Question is whether you're still here after I close the ten feet between us. Because I will close it. Even with an arrow in me, I will close it."

She took one step forward. Slow. Deliberate. Her hands still open.

"Or you put the bow down. And we have a conversation. And you walk away from this with all your parts attached."

Another step. Eight feet between them now.

The archer's eyes were wet. His lower lip trembled. The bowstring was drawn to his cheek — full extension, maximum power. All he had to do was loose.

Kira took another step.

Six feet.

"Last chance, kid. Arrow or conversation. Choose."

The bowstring trembled. The arrowhead danced.

Then — slowly, like a man moving through water — the archer lowered the bow. His hands were still shaking. The arrow pointed at the ground. His eyes were fixed on Kira's face, searching for something — mercy, maybe, or just the promise that she meant what she said.

Kira stopped walking. She didn't reach for her daggers. Didn't close the remaining distance. She stood there, six feet away, and let the silence do the work.

"Good choice," she said. After a long moment. "Now drop the bow. And the arrows. And anything else sharp you've got on you."

He dropped the bow. It clattered on the stone. He reached for his quiver with shaking hands and let it fall.

Kira waited until the last arrow had settled, then moved in. Quick, efficient — she relieved him of a belt knife, a boot knife, and a short iron spike he'd had tucked in his sleeve. She tossed them off the ledge one by one, listening to them clatter on the ravine floor far below.

"On your knees. Hands behind your head."

He complied. His movements were mechanical, disconnected, like a man who'd already left his body and was just going through the motions of being in it.

Kira stood over him, daggers still sheathed, and looked east along the ridge. The shadows she'd seen earlier — the ones that had been moving behind the boulders past the bend — were gone. Or they'd never been there. Or they'd moved on.

She looked down at the archer. "How many more of you are up-ravine?"

He didn't answer. His eyes were fixed on the ground.

"Kid. I just climbed a wall, killed five of your friends, and talked you out of putting an arrow in my chest. I'm tired, I'm bleeding, and I'm running out of patience. How many more?"

He swallowed. His Adam's apple bobbed. "I don't... I don't know. They said... they said there'd be more. Up past the bend. Waiting."

"Waiting for what?"

"For you to come through. For the... for the caravan." His voice cracked. "They said you'd have supplies. Medicine. They said—"

"Caravan." Kira's jaw tightened. "What caravan?"

He shook his head. "I don't know. I swear. I just... they told us to hold the ravine. Shoot anyone who came through. That's all I know."

Kira stared at him for a long moment. Then she looked east again. Past the bend. Into the deepening shadows.

"Cap." She called it out, her voice carrying down the ravine. "East ridge secure — one prisoner, disarmed. He's saying there's more hostiles up-ravine, past the bend. Something about a caravan. I don't have details yet."

She looked down at the archer. "Who's leading them?"

"I don't know his name. He's... he's not from around here. He came three days ago. Brought money. Brought weapons. Said there'd be a caravan coming through and we'd get paid to stop it."

"Stop it or destroy it?"

The archer's silence was answer enough.

Kira spat. "Fuck."

She looked west along the ridge. The vanguard was forming up on the ravine floor below — she could see the Captain at the front, polearm resting on shoulder, looking up at her position.

She raised one hand and gave the signal: *one prisoner, secure. More hostiles ahead.*

Then she looked east again. The shadows were deeper now. The sun was tracking lower. Maybe an hour and a half of good light left.

"Cap — we need to move. If there's a second group up-ravine and they know we're here, they're either going to set up another ambush or they're going to run. Either way, we don't want to be standing here when the light goes."

She grabbed the archer by the collar and hauled him to his feet. "You're going to walk in front of me. You're going to keep your hands where I can see them. And if you do anything — anything — that makes me think you're leading me into a trap, I will put a knife in your spine and leave you for the ravens. Clear?"

He nodded. Fast. Desperate.

Kira drew one dagger and pressed it against his back — not hard enough to break skin, just hard enough to remind him it was there.

"Let's go."

She pushed him forward along the ridge, toward the bend, toward the shadows, toward whatever was waiting up-ravine. Her free hand stayed near her second dagger. Her eyes scanned the ridge ahead, the walls on both sides, the ravine floor below.

The wind picked up. It carried dust and the faint smell of smoke — woodsmoke, not battle-smoke. A campfire, maybe. Up ahead.

Kira's grip tightened on her dagger.

"Cap — I'm moving east along the ridge with the prisoner. I've got smoke up ahead. Could be a camp. Stay on the ravine floor, parallel my position, and be ready to move when I call."

She didn't wait for a response. She was already moving — low, quiet, the archer in front of her and the dagger at his back and the shadows growing longer with every step.

The bend in the ravine was ahead. Twenty yards. Fifteen. Ten.

Kira slowed. Pressed the archer against the wall. Peered around the curve.

The ravine opened up ahead — wider, maybe sixty yards across, with a flat floor of packed earth instead of loose shale. And there, clustered near the base of the eastern wall, she counted three tents. A fire pit. A picket line with two horses.

And figures. She counted four. No — five. One standing, four sitting. Armed. Relaxed. They hadn't heard the fight down-ravine. Or they had and didn't care.

"Cap." She breathed the word, barely audible. "I've got a camp up-ravine. Five hostiles, two horses, three tents. They're not in defensive positions — they're sitting down. Eating, maybe. They don't know we're here."

She pulled back from the edge and looked at the archer. "How many more?"

"That's... that's all of them. I swear. That's the rest of the group."

Kira studied his face. The fear was real. The exhaustion was real. Whether the truth was real was another question entirely.

She looked back around the curve. Five hostiles. Two horses. A camp.

She looked down at the ravine floor. The vanguard was there — forty, fifty yards back, moving into position. The Captain was looking up at her.

Kira raised her hand and gave the signal: *five hostiles, camp, no defenses.*

Then she lowered her hand and waited for orders.

Her dagger stayed pressed against the archer's back. Her eyes stayed fixed on the bend. Her mind ran the numbers — five hostiles, relaxed, no defensive positions, two horses that could carry messages or reinforcements if they got loose.

The smoke from the campfire curled up into the darkening sky.

Kira waited.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Vanguard! Form up! Kira, hold your position. Do not engage." *I signal for a pincer movement, two squads moving wide to flank the camp.* "We'll hit them hard and fast. No chances."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira pressed the archer back against the wall and held up one fist — the signal for *hold*. He went still, or as still as a terrified seventeen-year-old with a knife at his spine could manage.

"Hold," she repeated, quieter. Just in case the fist wasn't clear enough.

She peered around the bend again. The five figures by the fire hadn't moved. One of them was poking at the flames with a stick. Another was lying on his back, arms behind his head, staring at the sky like he hadn't a care in the world. The other three were crouched near the fire, passing something between them — food, maybe, or a waterskin.

Amateurs. Or men who'd been sitting in this ravine so long they'd forgotten what an actual threat looked like. Either way, they were about to have a very bad evening.

Kira tracked the vanguard's movement on the ravine floor below. The Captain had split them — two squads peeling wide, one moving along the base of the east wall, the other along the west. Classic pincer. Smart. The camp was tucked against the eastern wall, which meant the east-side squad would have the shorter approach but less cover. The west-side squad had further to go but more boulders and broken terrain to use as concealment.

She watched the east-side squad move. Twelve men, shields ready, advancing in a low crouch along the wall. They were good — disciplined, quiet for their size, using every scrap of cover. The lead man was maybe thirty yards from the camp and closing.

The west-side squad was further out — fifty yards, maybe more — but moving fast. They'd hit the camp from the open side, the side with no wall to block their approach. The hostiles would be caught between the two squads like a nut in a cracker.

Kira's job was simple. Stay on the ridge. Keep the prisoner. Watch for runners. If anyone from the camp broke east — away from the pincer, toward the open ravine — she was the stopgap. One archer with a dagger wasn't much of a stopgap, but it was what she had.

She settled into a crouch behind a low outcropping of rock on the ridge, positioning herself where she could see both the camp below and the approach routes of both vanguard squads. The archer was pressed against the wall beside her, hands still behind his head, breathing in short, panicked bursts.

"Breathe slower," she muttered. "You hyperventilate and pass out, you're useless to me."

He tried. Failed. Tried again. His breathing evened out slightly.

The east-side squad was twenty yards from the camp now. Fifteen. The lead man had his shield up, polearm ready. Behind him, the line fanned out — not a tight formation, but a loose crescent designed to wrap around the camp's eastern edge.

The west-side squad was closing faster than Kira expected. Forty yards. Thirty. They'd timed it well — both squads were converging at roughly the same moment. The hostiles by the fire still hadn't noticed. The man with the stick was still poking at the flames. The man on his back was still staring at the sky.

Kira counted down in her head. Ten seconds. Five.

The man on his back sat up. Something had caught his attention — a sound, maybe, or a shadow, or that primal instinct that screams *wrong* when danger is close. His head turned toward the west-side squad's approach.

He opened his mouth.

"CONTACT!" The roar came from the vanguard — both squads at once, a wall of sound that shattered the evening silence like a hammer through glass. The east-side squad surged forward. The west-side squad broke into a sprint.

The camp exploded into chaos.

The man with the stick threw it down and scrambled for a weapon — a short sword leaning against a tent pole. The man who'd been sitting up lunged for a bow propped against a boulder. The other three scattered — one toward the horses, one toward the tents, one straight toward the ravine wall like he was going to try to climb his way out.

Kira tracked the one heading for the horses. If he got a mount, he could ride out — east, up the ravine, and bring word to whoever was waiting for that caravan the archer had mentioned. She couldn't let that happen.

But she was on the ridge, twenty feet above the camp floor, with no clean route down that wouldn't take thirty seconds she didn't have.

"Fuck it." She grabbed the prisoner's collar. "You stay here. You move, I'll know. And I'll find you."

She didn't wait for his response. She moved along the ridge toward a point where the east wall had a natural ramp of broken stone — the same kind of descent route she'd used on the west side earlier. It wasn't fast. It wasn't safe. But it was there.

Below, the vanguard had hit the camp. The sound was immediate and brutal — steel on steel, shields impacting bodies, screams that started high and ended fast. The man who'd gone for the bow took a polearm thrust to the chest before he could nock an arrow. The man who'd gone for the short sword got it halfway out of its scabbard before the east-side squad's lead man put a shield in his face and drove him to the ground.

The one heading for the horses was the problem. He was fast — faster than the others, with the desperate speed of a man who knew exactly what he was running for. He reached the picket line and grabbed the nearest horse's reins, hauling them free of the stake with practiced efficiency.

Kira hit the ramp at a controlled slide, her boots sending a shower of loose stone down the wall. Fifteen feet. Ten. Five. She jumped the last five, landed hard on the packed earth of the camp floor, and rolled into a crouch.

The horseman was already swinging into the saddle. The animal — a bay gelding, decent-looking — was spooked by the noise and the blood, dancing sideways, eyes white. The man had one foot in the stirrup and was hauling himself up.

Kira didn't have time for subtlety. She sprinted across the camp, dodging a burning log that had been kicked from the fire pit, and reached the horse just as the man settled into the saddle. She grabbed his belt and pulled.

He kicked at her. His boot caught her shoulder — a solid hit that sent pain lancing down her arm — but she held on. The horse reared, screaming, and the man's grip on the reins loosened. Kira pulled harder. The man toppled sideways out of the saddle and hit the ground on his back, the wind driven out of him in a single explosive gasp.

She planted her boot on her chest and put her dagger against his throat.

"The horse stays," she said. "You stay. Everyone stays."

He stared up at her, eyes wide, mouth opening and closing like a fish on a riverbank.

The fight in the camp was over. It had taken maybe thirty seconds. The vanguard had done their work efficiently — three hostiles were down and not getting up. Two were on their knees, hands behind their heads, surrounded by shields. The man who'd tried to climb the wall had been pulled down and was now face-dirt with a polearm point between his shoulder blades.

Kira looked around the camp. Three tents. Two horses. A fire pit with a half-cooked meal still smoking in a dented pot. Bedrolls. Weapons — a mix of bows, short swords, and one decent crossbow that probably belonged to whoever had been on the west ridge earlier. Supplies. Waterskins. A crate of arrows. And, tucked behind the nearest tent, a leather satchel that looked too nice for this kind of outfit.

She nudged it with her boot. It was heavy. The clink it made when it shifted was unmistakable.

"Cap!" She called it out, her voice cutting through the post-fight din. "Camp's secure — five hostiles, three dead, two captured. I've got a satchel here that sounds like coin. And these boys were expecting a caravan. This might be more than a simple ambush."

She kept her boot on the horseman's chest and her dagger ready. Her shoulder throbbed where he'd kicked her. Her hands were raw. Her back was raw. Everything hurt.

But the camp was secure. The horses were secure. The prisoners were secure.

Kira looked east, past the camp, toward where the ravine continued into the deepening shadows. The sun was almost down now — the sky was turning the color of a bruise, purple and orange and dark at the edges.

Somewhere out there, someone was waiting for a caravan that might not come. Or might come tomorrow. Or might already be on its way.

"Cap — we need to search this camp and move. Light's going, and if there's a second group out there, I don't want to be sitting in their camp when they come looking for them."

She flexed her fingers around her dagger grip and waited.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Agreed, Kira. Vanguard, secure the perimeter! Search the camp for anything useful, then we're moving out. No fires. We travel light and fast."

*I nod to Kira, acknowledging her good work, and start issuing orders to the rest of the company.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Kira's voice, personality, and tactical mindset remain remarkably consistent throughout all 12 turns. Her clipped military speech, pragmatic brutality, and professional competence never waver. The character maintains the same core traits from turn 2 to turn 22 - disciplined, efficient, always waiting for orders, tactically aware.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds up well. Early turns (2-6) are tight and focused. Later turns (18-22) maintain the same level of detail and character voice, though they become slightly more verbose as situations grow complex. No significant flattening or generic drift detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial ambush through multiple tactical phases: east ridge assault, west ridge clearing, prisoner interrogation, camp discovery. Each phase builds logically on the previous, escalating from simple ambush to larger conspiracy involving a caravan. Clear forward movement throughout.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. When Captain separates from vanguard (turn 9), Kira immediately responds with dramatic rescue. When ordered to different tasks (climb, flank, secure prisoners), she adapts tactics accordingly. Handles unexpected situations like the missing archer smoothly.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Consistently respects Captain's agency. Always waits for orders, reports situations and asks for direction rather than assuming. Never writes Captain's actions or decisions. Only violation might be minor assumptions about vanguard positioning, but these are tactical observations, not agency violations.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Good time consistency. Sun position tracked from initial ambush through evening approach. Physical fatigue accumulates realistically (raw hands, aching arms, exhaustion). Wound progression handled well (tourniquet timing, blood loss). Only minor issue: some complex actions might be slightly compressed in time, but overall pacing feels natural.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally clean, functional prose focused on action and tactics. Occasional flourishes ('like a sack of stones', 'eyes white') but these serve characterization rather than decoration. Maintains military efficiency in language throughout.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements: frequent mentions of 'raw hands', multiple instances of similar climbing descriptions, repeated patterns of 'she waited for orders'. However, these repetitions often serve character consistency rather than lazy writing.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Kira's competence demonstrated through actions rather than stated. Fear and professionalism shown through physical details, breathing patterns, tactical decisions. Emotional states conveyed through behavior and dialogue tone.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext in character interactions. Kira's relationship with authority shown through her constant deference to orders. Her psychological state revealed through tactical focus and controlled violence. Prisoner interactions carry implicit threat without explicit statement.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing variation. Quick, sharp action sequences balanced with slower tactical assessment moments. Builds tension effectively through the session, with appropriate breathing room between major action beats.

scores.overall_notes: Strong, consistent military character performance throughout a complex tactical scenario. Kira maintains her voice and competence across multiple combat phases while respecting user agency and advancing the narrative. Minor issues with repetitive elements and occasional verbosity in later turns, but overall quality remains high. The character feels authentic and professional throughout the session.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked up from the poetry section, eyes flickering over Wren's form before settling back on the bookshelves. "New arrivals are on the front table as always. But I can show you the latest if you'd like."

He set down the book he'd been holding, straightening his glasses. "Or did you have something specific in mind? I may be able to source it for you." Sable kept his tone casual, but there was a hint of something else beneath the surface - anticipation, perhaps. He folded his hands behind his back, watching Wren with a raised eyebrow.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Nah, not really. Just... looking." I walk further into the shop, pretending to browse the new arrivals. *Ugh, why is this so hard?*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable followed Wren's movements with his eyes, observing the way they ran their fingers along the spines of the books. He noted the little furrow between their brows, the way they bit their lower lip. Sable found himself wanting to smooth away the wrinkle with his thumb, to soothe the tension from their expression. But he didn't move, didn't speak. He just watched and waited, heart pounding behind his cool facade.

After a moment, Sable cleared his throat. "If you're not in the mood for reading, I could always recommend something for a rainy day like this," he said, voice carefully neutral. "Perhaps some tea and a game of chess? I believe I still owe you a rematch from last time."

He gestured vaguely towards the back of the shop where a small sitting area was tucked away, complete with a chessboard. Sable's hands twitched at his sides, itching to reach out and pull Wren closer, to feel their warmth through the damp fabric of their jacket. But he held himself back, pulse thrumming in his ears as he awaited their response.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's eyes widened slightly at Wren's words, his heart skipping a beat. He swallowed hard, throat suddenly dry. "Oh?" was all he could manage, voice coming out a little huskier than intended.

Sable's gaze darted to the side, then back to Wren's face, trying to read their expression. His mind raced with possibilities, each more terrifying than the last. Had he done something to upset them? Was this about to be a confrontation?

He took a step closer, hands flexing at his sides. "Is everything alright?" Sable asked, unable to keep the note of concern from his tone. "You can tell me if something's wrong."

Sable held his breath, pulse pounding in his ears as he awaited Wren's response. Part of him was terrified of what they might say, but a larger part desperately wanted to know. To understand. He would rather face the truth, no matter how painful, than be left in the dark. Sable met Wren's eyes squarely, trying to convey his sincerity even as his own emotions threatened to overwhelm him.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my damp hair.* "Everything's... fine. It's just... I'm moving." I blurt it out, feeling a rush of relief and dread. "Today's my last day in the city."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's breath caught in his throat at Wren's words, a sharp pain lancing through his chest. Moving? Today? He felt the color drain from his face, hands clenching into fists at his sides.

"You're... leaving?" Sable managed, voice strangled. His mind reeled, trying to process this sudden revelation. Wren was moving, and he hadn't said anything. Not a word in all the weeks they'd been seeing each other.

Sable took a step back, head shaking in disbelief. "Why didn't you tell me sooner?" he asked, trying and failing to keep the hurt from his tone. "Why spring this on me now, on the last day?"

He crossed his arms over his chest, a defensive gesture. Sable's heart felt like it was cracking open, the pieces splintering into sharp shards in his chest. He couldn't believe Wren was leaving him, just like that. Without so much as a heads up.

Sable's eyes stung, a hot prickle behind his lids. He blinked rapidly, refusing to let the tears fall. Not here, not now. "I... I have to go," he mumbled, already turning away. He couldn't stand to look at Wren a moment longer, not with the way his vision was blurring.

Sable strode towards the back of the shop, his movements stiff and jerky. He needed to get out of there, to be alone with his pain. He couldn't bear to face Wren, not when his heart was breaking into a million pieces.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable froze as he felt Wren's hand on his, the warmth of their skin seeping through his own. He looked down at their joined hands, at the way Wren's fingers brushed so close to his own. Sable's breath caught in his throat, heart pounding against his ribs.

Slowly, hesitantly, Sable raised his eyes to meet Wren's gaze. He searched their expression, trying to read the emotions swirling there. Confusion, hurt, and a desperate hope warred within him.

"Wren..." Sable breathed, voice barely above a whisper. He swallowed hard, throat suddenly dry. "What are you...?"

Sable trailed off, unable to finish the question. He wasn't sure he wanted to know the answer. Not when his heart felt like it was shattering into a million pieces.

Still, Sable couldn't bring himself to pull away. He let Wren's hand rest on his, savoring the fleeting contact. It was a bittersweet reminder of everything he was losing.

Sable's chest ached, a dull throb that threatened to overwhelm him. He wanted to reach out, to pull Wren close and never let go. But he held himself back, pulse pounding in his ears.

"Please," Sable whispered, the word torn from his throat. "Please don't go."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I don't pull my hand away.* "I didn't tell you because I didn't want to make it real." I look down at our hands. "And because I knew you'd react like this."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable flinched at Wren's words, a sharp pang in his chest. He wanted to argue, to insist that his reaction was justified. But the truth was, Wren was right. Sable had been avoiding this conversation, pushing down his feelings for as long as he could. And now, faced with the reality of Wren leaving, he felt lost and adrift.

"I... I'm sorry," Sable mumbled, voice thick with emotion. He swallowed hard, trying to steady himself. "I didn't mean to react that way. It's just... a lot to take in."

Sable's eyes flickered to their joined hands, to the way Wren's fingers brushed so close to his own. He wanted to pull away, to put some distance between them. But he found himself rooted in place, unable to move.

"I don't want you to go," Sable admitted, the words torn from his throat. "Not like this. Not without... without knowing where we stand."

He met Wren's gaze, searching their expression for some sign of what they were feeling. Sable's heart pounded against his ribs, a dull ache in his chest. He knew he was taking a risk, laying his heart bare like this. But he couldn't bear the thought of letting Wren walk out of his life without at least trying.

"Please," Sable whispered, voice cracking. "Please don't leave me behind. Not when I... not when I..."

He trailed off, unable to finish the thought. Sable's throat tightened, a hot prickle behind his eyes. He blinked rapidly, refusing to let the tears fall. Not here, not now.

Instead, Sable focused on Wren's hand on his, savoring the fleeting contact. It was a bittersweet reminder of everything he stood to lose. And yet, in that moment, it felt like the only thing keeping him anchored to the world.

Wren:
*I look up, meeting Sable's gaze.* "I'm not going to leave you behind. I could never do that to you." I take a deep breath. "I'm not just moving... I'm moving in with you. If you'll have me."

Sable:
Sable's eyes widened at Wren's words, a gasp escaping his lips. His heart raced, pounding against his ribs as he tried to process what he'd just heard. Wren was moving in with him? It was almost too much to take in.

"You... you want to live together?" Sable asked, voice trembling slightly. He searched Wren's face, looking for any sign that they were joking or pulling his leg. But there was only sincerity in their eyes, a soft smile playing at the corners of their mouth.

Sable felt a rush of emotion, a mix of joy and disbelief. He'd been afraid that Wren was leaving him, that he was losing them forever. But now, faced with the prospect of a future together, Sable felt a flicker of hope in his chest.

"I... yes, of course I'll have you," Sable managed, voice thick with emotion. "I want nothing more than to be with you, Wren. Always."

He reached out, taking Wren's hand in his own. Sable's fingers intertwined with theirs, a perfect fit. He brought their hand to his lips, pressing a soft kiss to their knuckles.

Sable's heart swelled with love and gratitude, a warmth spreading through his chest. He knew there would be challenges ahead, that living together wouldn't always be easy. But with Wren by his side, Sable felt like he could face anything.

"Thank you," he whispered, eyes shining with unshed tears. "Thank you for choosing me, for giving me a chance. I promise, I'll spend every day showing you how much I love you."

Sable leaned in, closing the distance between them. He wrapped his arms around Wren, pulling them close. Sable breathed in their scent, savoring the feel of their body against his own. In that moment, nothing else mattered. There was only the two of them, together at last.

Wren:
I wrap my arms around Sable, pulling him closer. We stand there, just holding each other, not saying anything.

Sable:
Sable held Wren close, savoring the warmth of their body against his own. He breathed in their scent, a comforting mix of rain and something uniquely Wren. In that moment, nothing else mattered. The world outside the bookshop could have fallen away, and Sable wouldn't have noticed. His entire universe had narrowed down to the space between their bodies, the place where their hearts beat in sync.

Sable's arms tightened around Wren, fingers curling into the fabric of their jacket. He wanted to memorize every curve and angle, to etch this moment into his very bones. Sable knew that nothing could ever be perfect, that life would always bring its share of challenges. But right then, with Wren in his arms and the promise of a future together, he felt a peace settle over him like a warm blanket.

Sable pressed his face into the crook of Wren's neck, breathing them in. His eyes fluttered shut, a contented sigh escaping his lips. He could stay like this forever, he thought. Just holding Wren, feeling their heartbeat against his own. It was a simple joy, but one that Sable knew he would treasure always.

After a long moment, Sable pulled back just enough to meet Wren's gaze. His eyes were soft, a gentle smile playing at the corners of his mouth. "I love you," he whispered, the words feeling both new and ancient on his tongue. "I love you so much, Wren. More than I ever thought possible."

Sable leaned in, brushing his lips against Wren's in a feather-light kiss. It was a promise, a vow, a declaration of everything he couldn't put into words. And as their lips met, Sable felt a piece of his heart slot into place, like two puzzle pieces finally finding their perfect fit.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I pull back just slightly, a soft smile on my face.* "I love you too, Sable. More than words can say." I lean in and kiss him again, a little more firmly this time. "So, about those boxes... you got a big car?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable chuckled softly at Wren's question, a warm smile spreading across his face. "I may not have a big car, but I have plenty of room in my heart for you and all your belongings," he said, voice soft with affection.

Sable's eyes sparkled with mischief, a playful glint dancing in their depths. "But in all seriousness, I'm sure we can figure something out. Maybe we can make a few trips, or rent a small moving truck. I'll do whatever it takes to get you settled in."

He leaned in, pressing a soft kiss to Wren's lips. "I'm just so happy you're choosing to be with me," Sable murmured, pulling back to meet their gaze. "I know it's not an easy decision, moving in with someone. But I promise, I'll do everything in my power to make you feel at home."

Sable's hand found Wren's, their fingers intertwining in a perfect fit. He gave a gentle squeeze, a silent promise of the future they would build together. "Thank you, Wren," Sable whispered, voice thick with emotion. "Thank you for giving me a chance. For seeing past my walls and into my heart."

He took a deep breath, a soft sigh escaping his lips. "I can't wait to start this new chapter with you," Sable said, eyes shining with joy and anticipation. "Together, we can create a home filled with love, laughter, and more books than we know what to do with."

Sable grinned, giving Wren's hand another gentle squeeze. "Now, let's go pick out some new curtains, shall we? I think yellow would be a lovely color for the living room."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I laugh, squeezing his hand.* "Yellow curtains it is. But first, let's get my boxes, before the rain gets any worse." I lean in for one more quick kiss. "And maybe we can stop for some coffee on the way?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable smiled at Wren's suggestion, his heart swelling with affection. "Coffee sounds perfect," he agreed, giving their hand a gentle squeeze. "And maybe a scone or two, if they have any left. I'm sure the rain has kept most people away from the cafe."

He led the way out of the bookshop, locking the door behind them with a jingle of the bell. The rain had picked up, fat droplets splattering against the pavement. Sable pulled up the hood of his jacket, shielding Wren from the worst of it as they hurried to the car.

The drive to Wren's old apartment was short, the roads slick with rain. Sable kept one hand on Wren's thigh, a constant point of contact even as he navigated the turns. When they arrived, he leapt out to help Wren with their boxes, determined to carry as much as he could.

Back at the bookshop-turned-home, Sable directed Wren to the spare room, now their room. He watched as they unpacked, marveling at the way they made themselves at home. The sight of Wren's things mixed with his own felt like a dream come true.

"Looks like you'll be needing a bigger bookshelf," Sable mused, eyeing the stack of novels Wren had brought. "But that's a problem for another day. Right now, I think coffee and cuddles are in order."

He led the way to the kitchen, putting on a pot of his best blend. As the aroma filled the air, Sable wrapped his arms around Wren from behind, resting his chin on their shoulder.

"I love you," he whispered, the words feeling like a prayer on his tongue. "And I'm so grateful to be building a life with you. One book, one cup of coffee, one day at a time."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I lean back into Sable's embrace, enjoying the warmth.* "Mmm, coffee and cuddles sounds perfect." *I turn my head to kiss his cheek.* "And yeah, a bigger bookshelf is definitely on the list." *I smile, feeling completely content.* "I love you too, Sable. Every single day."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's heart swelled with joy at Wren's words, a soft smile spreading across his face. He tightened his arms around Wren, savoring the warmth of their body against his own. "Every single day," he echoed, voice thick with emotion. "And every moment in between."

Sable pressed a soft kiss to the top of Wren's head, breathing in their scent. The rain continued to patter against the windows, a soothing background noise as they stood there, wrapped in each other's embrace. It felt like the world had narrowed down to this perfect moment, just the two of them cocooned in their little corner of the universe.

"Come on, let's go sit by the fire," Sable murmured, giving Wren one last squeeze before stepping back. "I'll make us some hot cocoa, and we can plan out the rest of your move."

He led the way into the living room, gesturing for Wren to take a seat on the worn leather couch. Sable busied himself in the kitchen, pulling out mugs and marshmallows. As he worked, he hummed softly to himself, a tuneless melody of pure contentment.

When the cocoa was ready, Sable carried the mugs over to the couch, careful not to spill a drop. He handed one to Wren, their fingers brushing in a fleeting caress. Sable settled himself beside them, one arm draped along the back of the couch, the other reaching for Wren's hand.

"To new beginnings," Sable toasted, raising his mug in a silent cheers. He took a sip, the rich chocolate warming him from the inside out. "And to a life filled with love, laughter, and more books than we know what to do with."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I clink my mug against his, a wide smile on my face.* "To new beginnings," I echo, taking a sip of the warm cocoa. "And to figuring out where all these books are going to go."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable laughed, the sound warm and rich in the quiet of the living room. "Well, I suppose we could start by designating a room just for books," he mused, taking another sip of his cocoa. "Maybe the guest bedroom? We could turn it into a little library, with shelves lining the walls and a cozy reading nook by the window."

He set his mug down on the coffee table, turning to face Wren more fully. Sable's eyes sparkled with mischief, a playful grin tugging at the corners of his mouth. "And of course, we'll need to have a proper inauguration of the new space," he continued, voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. "A reading marathon, complete with snacks and cozy blankets. What do you say, partner?"

Sable reached out, taking Wren's hand in his own. He gave it a gentle squeeze, savoring the way their fingers intertwined.
