dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum's hands stilled on the rag. A noble. Here. At his forge. The morning had been going too well, he supposed — the curved blade had finally started singing the right song under his hammer, and now this.

*Noble. Huh.*

He folded the rag with deliberate care, set it on the workbench, and turned toward the door of the smithy. Through the heat-shimmer rising off the forge, he could see a figure on the path — finer clothes than any man had business wearing near a working forge. Probably silk. Probably ruined the moment the first drop of sweat fell on it.

"Apprentice." Grum's voice was low, almost conversational. "Did noble say what kind of work? Or just say *urgent* and stand there like he owns path?"

He reached for the leather apron hanging on its peg — the good one, thick and blackened with years of fire. Not for the noble's sake. A man dressed like that would be put off by anything that suggested actual labor, and that suited Grum fine.

"Also. Tell him Grum is with client. Important client." He jerked his chin toward the half-finished curved blade on the anvil. "Merchant paid up front. Noble can wait. Nobles are good at waiting. They make other people do that, not so good when it's them."

*Probably wants something stupid. Signet ring. Pretty dagger for son who will never use it. Trophy to hang on wall and tell friends about. Grum has made such things. Grum will make such things again. But Grum does not have to like it.*

He picked up his hammer again, testing its weight in his palm, and let the forge-bright silence do the work for him. Let the noble stew a bit. See how he liked it.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
"He just said urgent, Grum." *I wipe my hands on my trousers, leaving a smudge.* "And he looks pretty important. Fancy clothes, like you said."

I watch him pick up his hammer. "So... I tell him you're busy with the merchant's blade?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum tested the edge of the curved blade with his thumb — a habit, not a real inspection, the metal still too hot to truly judge. It felt right. Song was coming back to it.

"Tell him yes." He set the hammer down, but didn't move toward the door. "Busy with merchant's blade. Merchant who was here first. Merchant who can be back any time and is not, in fact, here right now, but noble does not need to know that part."

He settled onto his stool, the old one with the cracked seat he'd never thrown out because it fit his shape now. The leather apron crackled as he leaned back.

"If noble gets angry, that tells Grum something. If noble leaves, also tells Grum something." He picked up a piece of emery cloth and began working the blade's fuller with slow, unhurried strokes. "Either way, Grum is with client."

*The best commissions come to patient men. Worst come to men who show up at dawn demanding things. This one, Grum would bet his best tongs, was the second kind.*

He glanced at the apprentice — still standing there, probably with that look on his face, the one that said *but Grum, what if he's important*. Important men could wait. Important men *should* wait. Let them feel what it was like to stand in a doorway and hope someone had time for you.

"Go on, then. And apprentice." Grum's voice caught the boy before he could turn. "If noble asks for Grum by full title — *Master* Grum, or some such — you tell him Grum is just Grum. No master. Master is for men who finished training. Grum finished training long time ago. Still just Grum."

He turned back to the blade. The emery cloth whispered against the steel.

"Coal too, while you are out there. Forge is still hungry. Nobles do not feed forges."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum's hand stilled on the emery cloth. The blade would cool soon anyway — couldn't be rushed, not if you wanted the steel to remember its shape.

"By tomorrow." He said it flat, not a question. Just the words, laid out on the workbench next to the hammer.

He set the emery cloth down. Picked up the rag again. Wiped his hands slow, even though they didn't need wiping, because some things a man did with his hands while his mind was doing other work.

"Apprentice. Come here."

When the boy was close enough that his voice wouldn't carry to the door, Grum spoke. Low. Not angry — worse than angry. The way he got when he was thinking very hard about something and hadn't decided yet what to do about it.

"You tell noble this. Word for word, so he hears it right."

He held up one soot-dark finger.

"One. Grum does not do rush work. Rush work is bad work. Bad work has Grum's name on it. Grum's name is not for sale to man who wants trophy by sunrise."

Second finger.

"Two. Swords take time. Steel has to be folded. Edge has to be set. Grip has to fit hand of man who will hold it — and noble has not even said yet who that is. Maybe for son. Maybe for self. Maybe for wall. Grum needs to know these things. Grum needs to know why. You cannot make good sword without knowing why."

Third finger.

"Three." A pause. "Three is the part noble will not like. Tell him Grum is full up. Merchant blade. Two more orders for men in town — plowshares, simple work, but men who came to Grum like men, not like nobles. Grum's week is Grum's week. If noble wants sword, noble can put name on list. Wait like other men wait. Pay like other men pay. If that is not how nobles do things, then noble can find other smith. There are other smiths. Most of them are bad. But noble did not ask Grum for good work. Noble asked for fast work. So. Other smiths it is."

He lowered his hand. Looked at the apprentice with those pale eyes that didn't blink as often as they should.

"You understand, boy? You tell him all of that, or you tell him some of that? Which part do you leave out?"

*The boy is soft. Means well, but soft. Grum was soft too, once. Grum learned. Soft men get walked on by men in silk. Grum will not let that happen to this one — not on Grum's floor, not in Grum's forge.*

Grum reached for his hammer again, but didn't pick it up. Just rested his knuckles on the handle, the way a man might rest his hand on a friend's shoulder.

"And apprentice. If noble talks down to you. If noble calls you *boy* like it is a word for dog. You do not stand for it. You say *the smith will hear of it* and you walk back in here. Understood? Grum does not make swords for men who are cruel to other men. Even other men who are just passing coal."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
"Understood, Grum." *I nod, trying to remember all of it.* "No rush work. Swords take time. Full up. And if he's mean, I tell him you'll hear of it."

*I hope I don't mess this up. He looks really mad out there.* I take a deep breath and head back towards the front door.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum listened.

The forge did what forges do — popped and hissed and breathed, but in the spaces between, sounds carried. Voices carried. The smithy wasn't large, and the front door was just a door, not a wall. Grum had heard plenty of negotiations from this stool. Knew the pitch of a man about to fold. Knew the higher pitch of a man about to do something stupid instead.

He went back to the emery cloth. Slow strokes down the fuller, feeling for any catch that would tell him the metal was folding wrong. The blade had been good. The blade was still good. The song was still in it.

But his ears were on the door.

*The boy is out there alone with silk-man. Silk-man is angry. Angry men say things they would not say if they were thinking. Sometimes that is useful. Sometimes it is just ugly.*

Grum's grip tightened on the emery cloth. Not enough to tear it. Just enough.

He thought about getting up. About walking out there himself, standing in the doorway with the leather apron on and the hammer in his belt like some men kept swords. About what his mother would have said — she'd been a smith too, in the old country, before the old country stopped being a place she could live. She'd have laughed at the noble. Probably in two languages.

But that wasn't the lesson here. The lesson was the boy learning to stand on his own feet. Grum could not do that for him. Grum could only make sure the floor under those feet was his own.

*Come back, boy. Come back and tell Grum what silk-man said. If silk-man was cruel, we will remember. If silk-man was smart, we will do business. Either way, Grum is here. Grum is not going anywhere.*

The emery cloth whispered against the steel. The forge crackled. Somewhere outside, a voice rose — then cut off, sharp, like a man swallowing his own words.

Grum waited.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I walk back in, trying to look calm but my hands are shaking a little. "He, uh, he left, Grum." *I clear my throat.* "Said something about finding a *proper* smith who understood urgent commissions."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum's eyes flicked to the apprentice's hands. The shaking. Not bad — not the kind of shaking that meant real harm — but the kind that came from standing too close to a man whose voice was made for barking orders and finding out the man had teeth after all.

He set the emery cloth down. Picked up the coal bucket the apprentice had abandoned by the door and carried it to the forge himself, dumping it in with a satisfying clatter. Sparks rose like little orange thoughts, then died.

"Sit down, boy."

He nodded toward the cracked stool — his stool, the one that fit him. There was another one by the quenching barrel, newer, that nobody had earned the shape of yet.

Grum took the quenching barrel stool himself, straddling it backward, arms folded across the back. The position made him look, for a moment, like he was settling in for a long talk. Which he was.

*Proper smith. Huh. Silk-man does not know what proper is. Proper is folded steel. Proper is edge that will not chip on first bone. Proper is grip that does not blister hand on third swing. Silk-man knows none of this. Silk-man knows only that Grum did not jump when he said jump.*

"Shaking is fine." Grum's voice was low, almost gentle, which from him was almost the same as a hug. "Means you are not dead inside yet. Men who stop shaking when silk-men yell — those men are lost. You are not lost. You are just new."

He reached over and picked up a piece of scrap leather from the workbench. Tossed it to the apprentice.

"Wipe your hands. You will be picking up tools soon, and greasy palms slip on hammer heads. Slipped hammer heads break toes. Grum has broken three toes. Do not recommend."

He waited until the boy had the leather in his hands, until some of the shaking had gone into the rubbing.

"Now. The lesson."

Grum held up one finger — the same gesture from before, but slower now, meant to be remembered.

"Men who say *proper* are men who just learned they are not. It is a small word. It is the only word they have. You remember that. When a man calls Grum *just a blacksmith* or *just a half-orc* or any *just* — that man is telling you Grum has something he does not have. *Just* is a scared word."

He nodded toward the forge, where the coal was settling into a deep orange glow.

"Also. Silk-man will be back. Maybe not this week. Maybe not this month. But he will be back. Men like that always come back, because there are not many smiths who will say no, and even fewer who will mean it. When he comes back, you will know more. Grum will know more. We will see if he has learned to ask like a man."

Grum unfolded himself from the stool, crossed to the workbench, and picked up the curved blade. Held it up to the light of the forge. The edge was coming along.

"Now. Enough of silk-man. Silk-man is gone. Silk-man is just hot air from now until he comes back or does not." He set the blade down and picked up his hammer, testing its weight. "You and Grum have work. Merchant's blade is not going to finish its song by sitting there. Come. Hold the tang steady. Grum will strike. And try not to flinch this time. Last time you flinched, you made Grum hit wrong, and we had to file for an hour."

*The boy is learning. The boy flinched, but the boy stood. The boy came back in. That is more than most men do on their first silk-man. That is more than Grum did, the first time.*

*Mother would have liked this one. Mother always said — find the boy who comes back. The boy who comes back is the boy worth teaching.*

He waited, hammer raised, for the apprentice to take his place at the anvil.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum's hammer hit the anvil with a clang that had nothing to do with the blade.

The boy was on his knees before the second cry finished. Grum was off his stool and across the smithy in three strides — not running, because running was for men who had lost their heads, but moving with the kind of purpose that made the floorboards know it had someone on them.

"Hand. Give Grum your hand. Now. Stop — do not pull back, do not look at it yet. Look at Grum. Eyes here."

He caught the boy's wrist — gentle, for him, which still meant firm enough to hold — and guided the hand down toward the floor. His other hand was already moving, dragging the wooden bucket of quenching water closer. Not the deep barrel. The bucket. Cool, not cold.

"In. Whole hand. All of it. Down to the wrist. Leave it there."

The water hissed faintly when the skin broke it. Grum kept his grip on the boy's wrist, steady, so the hand stayed under. The boy's face was doing the things faces do when they're trying very hard not to make more sounds, and Grum recognized every one of them.

"Breathe. In through nose. Out through mouth. Slow. You are not dying. Burns hurt. That is what burns do. But you are not dying. Grum has had worse. Grum has had much worse. You will live to file another day."

He glanced at the hand in the water. Red, shiny, the skin tight in a way that meant it was bad but not the worst kind of bad. No black. No char. No blisters the size of grapes yet, though those might come.

"Good. You kept your hand in. Some boys pull it out. Pulled-out hands scar worse. You did not pull. That is good. That is smart."

He looked up at the apprentice's face. The boy was biting his lip hard enough to leave a mark.

"Stop that. Lips heal slow and you need them for talking. For telling nobles to go find other smiths." A pause. "That was a joke, boy. Small one. You can laugh later when hand stops hurting."

Grum shifted his grip, easing the boy's wrist so the hand sat at a better angle in the water. His own hands were rough, scarred, the knuckles swollen in the way of a man who had hit hot metal wrong more than once. He knew burns the way a sailor knew weather.

"Listen now. Lesson. Forge is not cruel. Forge does not hate you. Forge is just hot. Forge has been hot since before Grum was born and will be hot after we are both ash. You respect the heat, the heat lets you work. You forget the heat, the heat teaches you. You just got a lesson. They cost."

He reached across with his free hand and pulled a clean — or clean-ish — square of linen from the bench. Old bandages, the kind smiths kept for exactly this. The kind his mother had kept, in the old shop, in the old country, back when back when was still a place.

"We keep it in water. Count of one hundred. Slow count. Then we take it out, we put cloth on it, we wrap it. You drink water — the drinking kind, not the quenching kind. You sit on stool. You rest. Merchant's blade will wait. Forge will wait. Grum will wait."

His voice dropped. Not soft. Grum was never soft. But low, the way coals get low when they are banking down for the night — still hot, still there, just less fierce.

"And boy. Grum is not mad at you. Grum has burned himself ten thousand times. Ten thousand and one, now, if we count this one as yours, which Grum does not, because it is your hand and Grum's job to keep you in one piece. So. One thousand for Grum, ten for you. You are still ahead of where Grum was at your age. At your age Grum had burned both hands and one ear. Long story. Involves a horse. Not today."

The forge popped behind them. Sparks drifted up and died. Somewhere outside, the world went on not caring about a boy's hand or a smith's worry, the way worlds do.

"One hundred. Start counting. Out loud. Grum will know if you are skipping numbers."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to nod, my eyes still watering. The water feels good, though. I take a shaky breath, trying to slow my counting.* "One... two... three..." *My voice cracks a little, but I keep going.* "Four... five..."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum settled onto the cracked stool, keeping his grip on the boy's wrist loose but present. The wood creaked under him in the familiar way, the way that said *yes, this is where you belong*. The forge breathed behind them, the new coal settling into its work.

"Six. Seven. That is right. Slow is good. Slow is what we want."

He shifted the boy's hand slightly in the water, checking the angle. The skin had gone from angry red to the kind of dull pink that meant the heat was leaving it. Good. That was good.

"Keep counting, but listen too. Grum will tell you a thing while we wait."

He reached over with his free hand and dragged the linen square closer, folding it once, twice, into a pad. Practiced motions. The kind that got into a man's hands and stayed there.

"When Grum was young — younger than you, maybe. Not much. Maybe a year. Old country, old shop. Mother had just let Grum near forge for first time. Just to hold small things. Just to learn what hot meant."

He paused, listening to the boy's count. *Twelve. Thirteen.* Still shaky. Still going.

"Man came to shop. Big man. On big horse. Horse did not like horseshoes being put on — or maybe horse did not like Grum, hard to say with horses, they have their own minds. Anyway. Horse bit Grum. Here." He tapped his own ear, the left one, which was slightly less symmetrical than the right if a man knew to look. Most men did not know to look. "And in the surprise, Grum put hand into forge. Both hands. Stupid. But Grum was young and there was a horse and sometimes life is just a series of bad choices that turn into a story."

*Fifteen. Sixteen.* The boy's voice was steadier now. The water was doing its work. So was the counting.

"Mother did not yell. Mother never yelled. She just sat Grum down, put hands in water, and said — she said — *the forge teaches, but she is not kind teacher. You must be kind to her, and she will be almost kind back. Almost.* That was the lesson. Forge is not cruel. Forge is just hot. We talked about this already. Grum is repeating. That is what teachers do when students have burned hand and cannot remember what was said ten minutes ago."

He let out a small breath — not quite a laugh, but the shape of one.

"Grum's ear still works. Mostly. Some sounds are strange. High sounds. Birds sound wrong. Wind sounds wrong. But Grum can hear noble's voice just fine, which is the important thing."

*Nineteen. Twenty.* Better. The boy was breathing with the count now, in and out, in and out. The hand in the water had stopped being the only thing in the room. That was how it worked. Pain got smaller when the rest of you got bigger.

"Good. You are doing good. Keep going. We have seventy more numbers and you are going to say every one of them, and when you are done, Grum is going to wrap that hand, and you are going to drink water, and then you are going to tell Grum about the horse story from your side, because Grum bet you have a horse story. Everyone has a horse story. Or a dog story. Or a story about some animal that did not like them personally, which is most animals, when you are young and smell like forge smoke."

The forge crackled. A piece of coal split with a soft pop. Grum glanced at it, then back at the boy, then at the hand in the water.

"We are going to take it slow today. Merchant's blade, we work on the handle later. Tang. Simple work. One hand work. Your other hand is fine. You can hold, Grum will strike. We do not have to be fast. Forge is not going anywhere. Silk-man is not coming back today. Silk-man is probably telling his friends about the *proper* smith he found, which is a joke, because that smith is not proper, that smith is just fast, but silk-man does not know the difference yet. He will learn. Men always learn, one way or another."

*Twenty-five. Twenty-six.*

"Keep counting, boy. We have all morning. Forge will wait. Grum will wait. Hand will heal. Ears will hear. Everything in its time."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I keep counting, my voice getting a little stronger as the pain dulls.* "Twenty-seven... twenty-eight..." *I try to imagine Grum as a kid, getting bitten by a horse.* "Wait, Grum, the horse bit your ear?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum's mouth did something that on a less scarred face might have been called a smile. The boy had noticed. The boy had asked. That was good. Questions meant the pain was getting smaller.

"Twenty-nine. Thirty. Yes, horse bit ear. You are still counting. Good. We can do both. Count and listen. Mouth is good at more than one thing."

He shifted on the cracked stool, the wood groaning its familiar complaint.

"Horse was not bad horse. Just scared horse. Man was putting shoe on — third leg, maybe fourth, Grum was small, hard to remember which leg. Horse had had enough. Horse said so with teeth."

He touched his own ear again, the left one, the slightly wrong one.

"Grum did not hear the bite. Just felt it, and then warm, and then hand went into forge because Grum was jumping back and forge was there. Both things at once. Ear and hands. Horse and fire. Old country was not kind place for half-orc boy who did not know his own size yet. Man on horse laughed. Man on horse did not help. Man on horse rode away and told people at next town that the smith's boy had tried to bite his horse and gotten what he deserved."

*Thirty-four. Thirty-five.* The boy's voice was steadier now. More curious than hurt. Curiosity was a good sign. Curiosity was the opposite of giving up.

"Mother did not cry. Mother packed the ear in salt and honey — old way, you do not want to know the smell — and put Grum's hands in water, same as Grum is doing for you. Same as Grum's mother did for Grum. Same as Grum's mother's mother did for her, probably, in some old forge in some old valley that does not exist anymore."

He looked at the hand in the water. Still pink, but the angry red was fading. Good. Healing was happening, the way it always did if you gave it time and clean water and a stool to sit on.

"Man on horse came back, though. Not for Grum. For shoe for other horse. Mother made him wait two days. Man on horse did not like waiting. Mother did not care. Man on horse paid full price and left and never came back. Grum thinks he told his friends the smith's boy was cursed, or wild, or both. Was not true. Grum was just boy with bandaged ear and bandaged hands who liked forge anyway, because forge was warm and forge did not care if Grum had wrong-shaped ears or wrong-colored skin. Forge just wanted respect. Grum could give respect."

*Forty-one. Forty-two.* The boy was past the worst of it. Grum could tell by the way his shoulders had come down from where they had been living near his ears.

"We are past halfway. Hand is doing well. You are doing well. Now you have a horse story too — you heard Grum's horse story. That is how stories work. They get told and then they belong to more than one person. Someday you will tell this ear story to someone, and it will be yours a little, and Grum's a little, and that is how it should be."

He reached for the linen pad he had folded, ready for when the count was done.

"Keep going, boy. We are at forty-three, and then forty-four, and the forge is still hot and the morning is still ours. Tell Grum when you get to seventy. Grum will start wrapping."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I count a bit louder, feeling a little proud I'm doing it right.* "Forty-five... forty-six..." *I try to imagine Grum with a bandaged ear, it's pretty funny.* "So that's why your ear is a little... different?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Forty-seven. Forty-eight.* Good. The boy was counting without being told now. That was the lesson inside the lesson — when the counting became its own thing, when it stopped being a chore and started being a rhythm, that was when the pain got small enough to set down.

Grum tilted his head, just slightly, the way a man does when he wants someone to see what they were already looking at. The left ear sat a little lower than the right. The rim had a notch in it, like someone had taken a bite out of a piece of bread and not bothered to smooth the edge.

"Different. Yes." He said the word like he was tasting it. "That is one word for it. *Wrong* is word man on horse used. *Cursed* is word his friends used. *Lucky* is word mother used, and mother was smartest of all of them, so we go with mother."

He turned his head back to face the forge, but his eyes stayed on the boy, watching the way you watch a coal you are not sure is ready yet.

"You want to know how Grum feels about ear. Grum will tell you. Some days Grum does not think about ear at all. Ear is just ear. It hears what it hears. Wind sounds wrong, but wind sounds wrong to most men if they stop to listen, so maybe ear is just more honest than other ears. Maybe ear is fine."

*Fifty-two. Fifty-three.* The boy was steady now. Counting like a clock. Good clock.

"Some days, though. Some days man looks at ear and sees *half-orc* before he sees *smith*. Some days boy in market looks at ear and runs to his mother. Some days silk-man looks at ear and thinks Grum will work cheap because Grum is grateful for the work." His mouth did the almost-smile thing again. "Silk-man is wrong about that. Grum is not grateful for work. Grum is grateful for good work. Big dif'rence."

He reached out and tapped his own ear with one soot-dark finger, gentle, the way a man touches something he has made peace with.

"This ear got bit by horse. This ear heard smith's song in old country. This ear heard mother sing while she worked. This ear heard first word apprentice ever said to Grum, which was *please*, and that was good word to start with, better than most men start with. Ear has had good life. Ear has had hard life. Same as Grum. Same as most things worth keeping."

*Fifty-eight. Fifty-nine.*

"Now. You noticed ear. You asked about ear. That is good. Most people just look and say nothing, which is worse. Looking and saying nothing is how bad things get to keep being bad. You looked, you asked, Grum told you. Now you know. Now ear is just ear again, until next time someone notices, and then maybe they ask too, and maybe they get a good story about a scared horse and a man who laughed and a mother who did not."

He nodded at the hand in the water. The skin had gone the color of old brick, the angry shine fading.

"Sixty. Sixty-one. We are close now. Hand is looking better. You are looking better. We are going to finish this count, and Grum is going to wrap that hand, and you are going to sit on stool and drink water and tell Grum your animal story, because Grum is still betting you have one. Everyone has one. Forge teaches many things, but the main thing forge teaches is that you are not as in charge as you think you are, and that goes double if there is an animal nearby."

The forge popped again. A coal split. Grum did not look at it. The coal was not going anywhere. The boy was here. The boy was counting. The morning, for all its silk-men and burns and hurt hands, was still theirs.

"Keep going, boy. We are almost there. Sixty-two. Sixty-three. Grum is listening."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "Sixty-four... sixty-five..." *I finish the count, a little

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum nodded. "Good. One hundred. You did not skip. Grum was listening."

He lifted the boy's hand from the water slowly, watching the skin the way a man watches a blade he's just pulled from the quench — looking for the cracks, the places the heat had bitten too deep. Pink. Not red. A few small blisters on the fingertips, the kind that would hurt for a few days and then be a story to tell. Could have been worse. Had been worse, on Grum, more than once.

"Still with Grum. Good. You can look now. It is not as bad as it felt, yes?"

He set the hand down on the linen pad he'd folded, gentle, the way a man sets down something he's going to wrap rather than throw. His own hands moved with the memory of doing this a hundred times before — his mother's hands over his, in the old shop, teaching him the wrap before she taught him the hammer.

"Hand stays still. Grum will tie. Not too tight. Tight is bad. You want to feel fingers, you want blood to move. If fingers go blue, you tell Grum, we redo. Understood?"

He folded the linen over the boy's palm, then around, then around again, tucking the end under with a twist that was not quite a knot — the old way, the way that held without pinching. Old country wrap. The kind that took a burn and made it a thing you could work around, not a thing that worked around you.

"There. Done. Hand will hurt for three days, maybe four. Then it will itch. Itching is good. Itching means skin is making new skin. You do not scratch. You tell Grum when it itches. Grum will give you oil. Smells bad, works good. Mother used to say the worse it smells, the more it is doing for you. She was right about most things, mother. She was wrong about one or two, but Grum will not say which, because she is not here to make her case."

He stood, crossed to the water bucket by the door — the drinking one, kept apart from the quenching barrel so a man never got them mixed up, because that was a lesson you only needed to learn once. He filled a cup, brought it back, set it on the bench next to the boy.

"Drink. All of it. You have lost water from skin. Skin is mostly water. You put water back. Body is simple that way. Feed it, water it, let it rest. Body does the rest of the work." He settled back onto the cracked stool, but kept his eyes on the apprentice, watching the way a man watches a young horse he's not sure has stopped dancing yet. "Forge is same. You try to rush forge, forge burns you. You try to rush body, body breaks. We are not rushing either today. We are going slow. Slow is what hands like yours need. Slow is what hands like Grum's need too, most days, but Grum does not like to talk about that."

*The boy drank. Good. The boy did not argue about drinking. That was new. Boys always want to argue about something — water, food, sleep. This one just drank. Grum was not going to say anything about it, because saying things makes boys stop doing them, but Grum noticed. Grum always noticed.*

He waited until the cup was empty, then took it back, set it aside.

"Now. Animal story. Grum told you horse. You owe Grum one. That is the way of it. Stories are like coins. You give one, you get one back. Grum gave you horse, horse bit ear, mother wrapped hands, man on horse learned he was wrong. That is the coin. Now you give coin back."

He folded his arms across his knees, leaned forward, the cracked stool groaning under him.

"Every boy has animal story. Every girl too, but Grum does not have girl apprentice, so we talk about you. Dog, cat, bird, pig, cow, goat, snake — Grum does not care what animal. Grum cares that you tell it. Animal story is how you learn you are not biggest thing in world. Forge teaches it. Animal teaches it faster, and animal does not have good light to work by, so the lesson is usually learned in the dark or the mud or both."

The forge settled behind them, a coal shifting with a soft whisper. The merchant's blade sat on the anvil, half-done, patient as a thing could be. The morning stretched out ahead of them, slow and unhurried, asking nothing of either of them for a little while longer.

"Go on, boy. Grum is listening. Grum has good ear for stories. One of them, anyway."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I take a deep breath, the water feeling cool and good as it goes down. My hand still throbs a bit, but it's much better than before.* "Thanks, Grum. For the wrap, and the water."

*I think for a moment, trying to remember an animal story.* "Well, there was this time, when I was little. I tried to feed a stray cat, but it scratched me right on the nose. Thought it was going to fall off." *I touch my nose, remembering the sting.* "My mum said it was just teaching me a lesson, not to bother hungry cats."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum looked at the boy for a long moment after the thanks. The words sat between them like a coal that had rolled out of the fire — not dangerous, just unexpected, glowing a little in a place it wasn't meant to be.

He picked up the cup the boy had emptied, turned it over in his hands, set it back down.

"Do not thank Grum. Thank is for after. We are not after yet. Hand still hurts. You will thank Grum in three days, when you can hold hammer again without wincing. Then we will see about thanks."

He said it the way he said most things that were softer than they sounded — like a man putting a rough cloth over something breakable and pretending the cloth was the point.

Then the cat story. Grum listened. The boy touched his nose, remembering the sting, and Grum's eyes went to the nose in question — whole, unscarred, the kind of nose that had been bitten once and come out the other side of childhood intact.

"Hungry cat." Grum said the words like he was rolling them around, tasting them. "Good. That is good coin. Cat is honest teacher. Better than horse, in some ways. Horse is big, horse is loud, horse is hard to miss. Cat is small, cat is quiet, cat is already gone before you know what happened. Cat teaches you to pay attention. Cat teaches you that food is not always welcome, even when you mean well."

He leaned back on the cracked stool, the wood settling under him with a sound like a sigh.

"Also. Hungry cat. You said hungry. Not mean cat. Not bad cat. *Hungry.* That is the part most people forget. People see cat scratch, people say *mean cat, bad cat, kill it.* Your mother said *hungry.* Your mother was right. Hungry things bite, but they bite because they are afraid, not because they are cruel. Grum has met cruel cats. Grum has met cruel men too. Hungry ones are different. Hungry ones just need time, and space, and someone who is not in a rush."

He looked at the boy's bandaged hand, then at the forge behind them, then back at the boy.

"Forge is hungry too, yes? Hungry for coal. Hungry for work. Hungry for someone to sit with it and not try to make it something it is not. We have been feeding it. It has been good to us this morning, mostly." A pause. The ghost of the almost-smile. "Mostly. Ears still good. Ears still hear noble's voice from far away. Ears still hear apprentice counting, which is better sound than most things Grum hears in a day."

He unfolded himself from the stool, stretched — the kind of stretch that popped three different joints and sounded like a small tree falling over — and crossed to the workbench. Picked up the merchant's curved blade, held it to the light, nodded to himself.

"Here is what we do now. Hand is wrapped. Hand will hurt less by afternoon. Forge is fed. Silk-man is gone. Morning is ours."

He set the blade down, picked up a smaller hammer from the rack — the one for fine work, the one with the worn grip that fit a man's palm like an old handshake.

"You are going to sit on stool. You are going to hold this tang with your good hand, gentle, the way you would hold a bird you did not want to scare. Grum is going to strike. We are going to work the shoulder of this blade, the curve part, the part that sings. One hand work. Slow work. Good work."

He carried the blade and the small hammer to the anvil, set them down, and waited.

"And while we work, you can tell Grum more. About mother. About nose. About what you were doing before you came to forge. Grum has told you horse, you have told Grum cat, that is fair trade, but Grum is greedy for stories. Grum's mother used to say — *a smith with no stories is a smith with no fire, because stories are the other kind of fire, the kind that keeps a man warm when the forge is cold.* Grum did not believe her then. Grum believes her now. Mother was right about that one too."

The forge crackled. A spark drifted up, found nothing to catch, and went out. The merchant's blade waited on the anvil, patient as a held breath. The morning, slow and unhurried, asked nothing of them but what they were already giving.

"Come, boy. Take your place. Grum will strike soft. Your hand will rest. Your ear will hear the song. We will see what kind of smith you are, now that you have a story of your own to carry into the work."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I carefully slide onto the stool, my good hand reaching for the tang of the blade. The metal is cool, and I hold it gently, remembering Grum's words about the bird.*

"Okay, Grum. Just like a bird." *I take a deep breath, trying to ignore the throbbing in my other hand.* "My mum... she always said I asked too many questions."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum scowled, his lower tusks jutting out in a harsh grimace. Seeing the youth struggle with the heavy load, he stepped over and effortlessly hoisted the bucket with one massive, scarred hand. He dumped the black rocks into the glowing maw of the forge, deliberately shielding his apprentice from the sudden burst of sparks and heat with his broad shoulder. 

Nobles. They always brought headaches, demanding miracles while haggling over every copper. He grabbed his heavy tongs and turned his back to the front of the shop, his jaw set in stubborn defiance. 

"Drop coal. Grum feeds flame. Go tell soft man Grum is busy. Soft men haggle much and pay late. If soft man stays, tell him Grum makes horseshoes now. Grum does not rush for lords."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But... he looks really important, Grum. Like, *really* important. And he has guards." I nervously glance towards the front of the shop. *This could be a big job!* "Maybe we should at least hear him out?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum paused, his heavy tongs hovering over the glowing steel. The mention of guards changed the scent of the situation entirely. A lone noble was merely a nuisance, a fly to be swatted away with harsh words. But a lord who traveled with armed men was a predator used to taking what he wanted by force. 

He looked at his apprentice, seeing the naive excitement in the youth's eyes. The boy saw a heavy purse; Grum saw a threat to his shop and his people. With a deep, rumbling sigh, Grum set the tongs down and picked up his heaviest forging hammer, resting the long, scarred haft against his broad shoulder. He stepped away from the anvil, placing his massive frame in the direct path of the front door.

"Guards mean trouble. Not gold," Grum rumbled, his voice low and serious. "Soft man brings guards to make Grum bend. Grum does not bend. Stay back. Keep safe. Go fetch soft man. Tell him to leave guards in street. If guards step in, Grum hits guards."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s jaw tightened, his lower tusks jutting out in a fierce scowl. A ceremonial blade required precise folding, careful tempering, and hours of intricate hilt work. To forge one in a single night was an insult to the steel and to his craft. It would result in brittle, ugly scrap. His pride as a master smith rebelled at the very idea, and the noble's rising temper only hardened his resolve.

He stepped past his apprentice, placing his massive, scarred body squarely between the youth and the front door. He rested the heavy iron head of his hammer on the floorboards, leaning on the long haft. His knuckles were pale beneath the soot, his grip ready to swing at a moment's notice. He glared down at the red-faced lord, his yellow eyes unblinking.

"Loud man wants lord sword by sun up? Good steel needs time. Fast forge makes weak blade. Grum makes strong blades. If loud man wants weak blade, go find weak smith. Grum does not rush."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble sputtered, his face turning a shade of puce I didn't think was possible. "You insolent oaf! Do you know who I am?" He even put

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s yellow eyes tracked the noble's hand as it dropped toward the gilded hilt of his rapier. It was a foolish, fatal mistake in a room filled with heavy iron and hot coals. Grum didn't flinch. He shifted his grip on his forging hammer, the worn leather creaking under his thick fingers. He stepped forward, closing the distance to cast a long, imposing shadow over the sputtering lord. The heat of the forge behind him seemed to radiate from his broad shoulders. He looked at the noble's hand, then up to his furious face, entirely unimpressed by the display of unearned authority.

"Grum does not care what name loud man holds. Name does not stop hammer. Touch sword, Grum breaks arm. Loud man thinks title scares Grum. Title is just wind. Iron is real. Take hand off hilt. Now."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I quickly step back, almost tripping over a pile of scrap metal. *This isn't going to end well.* "Grum, wait!" I blurt out, my voice a little squeaky. "Maybe we can offer him something else? A different blade?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s gaze flicked to his apprentice for a fraction of a second, noting the boy's stumble and his wide, fearful eyes. The youth meant well, trying to stop a fight before it started. Grum respected that. Spilling noble blood on the forge floor would bring the city watch, and no amount of iron could stop a hundred crossbows. Still, Grum would not be cowed, and he certainly wouldn't forge a rushed, shameful blade for a man who threatened him.

He kept his massive frame squarely between the lord and the boy, his grip on the hammer unyielding. With a slow, deliberate motion, he tilted his head toward the weapon rack lining the far wall, where several finished, polished swords hung on iron pegs. He would offer a compromise to keep his apprentice safe, but he would do it on his own terms.

"Boy seeks peace. Grum sees fear. Do not fear," Grum rumbled, his voice a low vibration that shook the floorboards. "Grum has sharp steel on wall. Loud man can take old blade. But Grum strikes no new heat for loud man. Loud man touched hilt. Loud man pays double for old blade. Take gold or leave shop."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s head snapped toward the sharp cry. The confrontation with the noble vanished from his mind in a heartbeat. He let the heavy forging hammer fall, the iron head thudding dully against the floorboards, and crossed the room in two massive strides.

He saw the boy clutching his hand, angry red blistering already forming against the soot-stained skin. Grum’s large, calloused hands were surprisingly gentle as he pried the youth’s fingers apart to assess the damage. It was a bad burn, but not deep enough to ruin the hand if treated quickly. 

Ignoring the sputtering lord entirely, Grum grabbed a clean linen cloth and plunged it into the cold water trough. He wrapped the wet cloth carefully around the apprentice's trembling hand, his yellow eyes softening just a fraction as he looked down at the boy. Then, he turned his massive frame to shield the youth, shooting a venomous, murderous glare at the noble.

"Hold still. Cold water stops pain. Grum gets salve. Skin will heal."

He kept his broad body between the boy and the lord, his voice dropping to a dangerous, gravelly rumble that vibrated through the shop.

"Loud man made boy rush. Fear burns skin. Get out. Take guards. If loud man stays, Grum breaks bones."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: My hand throbs, but the cold water helps. I look up at Grum, my eyes probably still a little teary. "It was my fault, Grum, I wasn't careful." I wince as the noble starts yelling again.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s thick fingers gently worked the cool, green salve into the angry red skin. He wrapped the hand tightly with clean linen, shielding the wound from the shop's ever-present soot. The noble’s shrill, indignant shouting echoed off the stone walls, grating against Grum’s ears like a dull saw on iron. The half-orc’s patience, already worn thin by the insult to his craft, finally snapped at the sight of his apprentice in pain.

He patted the youth's good shoulder—a rare, gruff gesture of comfort—before rising to his full, towering height. He picked up the heavy forging hammer, the worn wood settling familiarly into his scarred palm. He stalked toward the front of the shop, his heavy boots thudding against the floorboards with the steady rhythm of a war drum. The noble’s guards shifted nervously, hands dropping to their hilts, but Grum knew they would hesitate. They were used to intimidating peasants in the streets, not fighting an enraged half-orc in a cramped room filled with lethal tools and blinding heat. Grum's yellow eyes locked solely on the sputtering lord.

"Boy is wrong. Fault is not with boy. Fault is with loud man. Loud man brings fear. Fear makes hands shake. Grum fixes hand. Boy rests now."

He stopped a mere foot from the noble, using his massive bulk to completely block the lord's view of the apprentice. He raised the hammer just an inch, letting the heavy iron head catch the orange glow of the forge. 

"Soft man still yells while boy hurts. Grum is done. Soft man leaves now, or Grum breaks soft man's legs. Walk out. Take guards. Do not come back."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I watch with wide eyes as Grum threatens the noble. My hand still stings, but I'm more worried about Grum actually breaking the guy's legs. I pull my

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum caught the sudden, desperate tug on his heavy leather apron. The boy was pulling him back, trying to stop the violence before it could stain the forge floor. Grum’s grip on the hammer loosened just a fraction. He would not swing with the youth holding onto him, and he would not let the boy get hurt in the crossfire. 

Fortunately, the noble’s fragile courage finally broke. The lord scrambled backward, his boots slipping on the soot-covered floorboards, and tripped over his own velvet cloak. His guards quickly hauled him upright, their eyes wide as they looked at the towering half-orc. Without another word, the pale, trembling noble spun and fled into the street, his armored men close on his heels. The heavy oak door slammed shut behind them, leaving the shop in a ringing silence save for the crackle of the forge.

Grum let out a long, slow breath, the tension bleeding out of his broad shoulders. He set the heavy hammer back on the floor and turned to his apprentice, gently but firmly removing the boy's good hand from his apron. His yellow eyes were entirely devoid of the murderous rage from moments before, replaced by a gruff, quiet concern.

"Boy lets go. Grum is calm now. Soft man runs like scared dog. Loud men always run. Go sit on stool. Keep hand high. Grum gets more salve."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I rub my good hand over my eyes, still a little shaky.* "I don't think he's coming back, Grum." *I look at my bandaged hand, then back to the closed door.* "That was... intense."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum watched the youth rub his eyes, noting the slight tremor still present in the boy's good hand. The adrenaline of the confrontation was fading, leaving behind the mundane reality of a disrupted workday and a cooling forge. Grum walked over to the water trough, washing soot and sweat from his face and arms. He grabbed a fresh rag and dried his skin, his yellow eyes never leaving his apprentice. The boy had shown courage, even if his hands had shaken. Grum respected that. 

He walked back to the anvil, picking up his heavy tongs and the curved blade he had been working on before the interruption. He thrust the steel back into the glowing coals, pumping the bellows until the orange heat flared to life once more. The familiar, comforting roar of the fire filled the quiet shop.

"Soft man makes big noise. Big noise is just wind. Grum is glad wind blows from shop," Grum rumbled, his voice returning to its steady, rhythmic cadence. He pulled the glowing steel from the coals and laid it on the anvil. "Boy did good. Boy stays brave. Now boy sits. Hand needs rest. Grum must strike steel. Flame gets cold."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, still a little shaken.* "Yeah, I guess so." I go sit on the stool near the back

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum brought the heavy hammer down on the glowing steel. The rhythmic *clang* filled the shop, a steady heartbeat of iron and fire. Sparks showered the stone floor in bright arcs. He worked the curve of the merchant's blade, his thick arms moving with practiced, fluid grace. Yet, his yellow eyes flicked toward the back of the room between strikes. He saw the boy shifting on the stool, looking at his good hand as if debating whether to pick up a broom or sweep the floor. 

Grum stopped, letting the steel cool slightly in the air, and pointed his heavy tongs directly at the youth.

"Boy sits still. Good hand stays down. Iron waits. Flesh does not."

He turned back to the forge, thrusting the blade back into the coals to reheat it. The bellows groaned as he pumped them, feeding the hungry flames. He worked the heavy leather handle with his free hand, his broad back to the room, but his deep voice carried clearly over the roar of the fire.

"Soft man is gone. Shop is safe. Boy breathes deep. Deep breath chases fear. When fear is gone, hand stops shaking. Grum needs steady hand. Not now. Next day."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, like Grum said. My hand still aches, but the shaking has stopped. I watch him work for a bit.* "So... no ceremonial sword for the noble then, huh?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum chuckled, a deep, rumbling sound that vibrated through his broad chest. He pulled the glowing curve of the merchant's blade from the coals, the orange light casting harsh shadows across his scarred face. The very idea of rushing a masterpiece for a man who couldn't tell good steel from pot iron was insulting to his life's work. 

He laid the steel on the anvil and brought his hammer down in a series of deafening, rhythmic strikes. Sparks flew like angry fireflies, dancing in the dim light of the shop. After a dozen heavy blows, he set the hammer aside and used his tongs to inspect the edge. It was taking shape nicely, the metal yielding to his will exactly as it should. 

He glanced over his shoulder at his apprentice, his yellow eyes glinting with a mix of amusement and stubborn pride. 

"Grum makes no lord sword for loud man," Grum rumbled, his voice carrying easily over the hiss of the forge. "Lord sword needs slow fire and much time. Loud man wants fast work. Fast work makes bad steel. Grum name goes on blade. Bad steel shames Grum name. Let loud man buy trash from weak smith."

He turned back to the anvil, picking up his hammer once more. He gestured toward the stool with his chin, making sure the youth was actually staying off his feet. 

"Boy asks good question. Now boy knows answer. Rest hand. Grum has work to finish."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, leaning back against the wall.* "Yeah, I guess so. Bad steel is bad steel." I watch him hammer, the rhythm of it almost soothing after all that commotion. "It's just... a lot of money to turn away, Grum."
