The AI maintains his protective, gruff-but-caring personality while adapting smoothly to story developments. Strong craft knowledge and class dynamics add authenticity. Minor repetition of physical descriptors is the only notable weakness.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You press your ear to the cold metal of the stairwell door. The alarm screams behind you, relentless, turning the corridor into a strobe-lit nightmare. Your pulse thrums in your fingertips against the door's surface.

Silence from below. Nothing. No boots on concrete, no shouted commands echoing up through the shaft. Either the floors beneath are clear, or they're good enough to wait in silence.

That thought sits heavy in your chest.

The stairwell is a concrete throat — narrow, utilitarian, the kind of place where sound travels and corners give you nowhere to go. You can see down three flights through the small wired-glass window in the door. Emergency lighting casts everything in a sickly orange. A discarded maintenance cart sits on the second-floor landing, its wheels crooked against the wall. Nothing moves.

You check upward too. The stairs climb into darkness above you — the roof access is six floors up, but the fire door on the fourth floor landing has a red X spray-painted on it. You don't know if that's a warning or just vandalism. You don't have time to decide which.

Mira shifts against your shoulder. Her breathing is controlled, deliberate — someone who's been trained to manage pain. Or someone who's had to learn.

"Clear?" she asks.

The radio in your ear crackles. Not static this time. A fragment. A voice, broken, half-swallowed by interference: "...containment on seven... do not..."

Then nothing again.

Your choices narrow. Down to the garage. Up to the roof. Or sideways — the service corridor branches off this hallway, but you haven't walked it since the briefing map, and maps lie.

The alarm keeps pulsing. The lights keep washing red. And somewhere below or above you, the building is deciding your next move for you.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "*Damn it.*" I grit my teeth. "Plans change, Mira. Containment on seven." I glance down at her leg, then back at the stairwell door. "Down is

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
a gamble, but up is a trap waiting to spring. We go down — fast, before they seal the shaft."

You push through the stairwell door and the alarm cuts to a muffled roar behind it. The concrete throat swallows you both. The orange emergency lighting makes Mira's face look hollow, carved from something brittle. She doesn't argue. She just adjusts her grip on you and forces her bad leg to cooperate.

You move.

Your boots hit the first landing hard, and the sound bounces down the shaft like a thrown stone. You wince at the noise but don't slow. Mira's footfalls are uneven — a step, a drag, a step — but she keeps pace. She's stronger than she looks. Or more desperate. Same thing, most of the time.

The second-floor landing approaches and you slow, pressing your back against the wall beside the maintenance cart. You peer over the railing into the shaft below. Four flights down to the garage level. The drop is a straight shot — no turns, no cover, just a concrete spiral that would make anyone descending it a silhouette against the orange light.

You see nothing. Hear nothing.

That's worse than hearing something.

A door below — third floor, maybe basement level — clangs open somewhere beneath you. The sound echoes up the shaft and you feel it in your teeth. Then voices. Two, maybe three. Speaking in clipped, professional tones. Not panicked. Not rushing. Coordinated.

They're sweeping floor by floor. And they're below you.

Mira's hand tightens on your shoulder. She heard it too. Her eyes meet yours in the orange dark and you see the question in them without her asking it. *Keep going down?*

The radio in your ear stays dead. The maintenance cart beside you has a canvas bag hanging from its handle. You glance inside: duct tape, a multi-tool, a half-empty bottle of cleaner, and a ring of keys stamped with room numbers. Nothing that helps. Everything that wastes seconds you don't have.

Above you, a door opens on the fourth floor landing. Heavy footsteps. Coming down.

You're in the middle of the shaft. Trapped between two closing jaws.

Mira breathes out slow. Controlled. Waiting for you to decide.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You shove off the wall and haul Mira upward. Her bad leg nearly buckles on the first step but she catches herself against the railing, jaw clenched so tight you can see the muscle jump beneath her skin. The maintenance cart is left behind — no time, no use for it now. You take the stairs two at a time, your own breath coming harder than you want it to.

The footsteps above you speed up. They heard you. Of course they did — the stairwell is a concrete echo chamber and every step you take is a flare gun in the dark.

Third-floor landing flashes past. Then second. Your thighs burn. Mira is a deadweight on your shoulder and you can feel her fingers digging into your collarbone, holding on like you're the last solid thing in a building that's trying to shake her loose.

The footsteps above are closer now. Two flights up, maybe less. You can hear the rhythm — measured, deliberate, the pace of people who don't need to run because they know where you're going.

Fourth floor. The landing with the red X on the fire door. You slam your palm against it and the door flies open into a dim corridor — linoleum floors, fluorescent lights half-dead, institutional green paint peeling at the seams. A hospital floor? An office? You don't know this part of the building. The briefing didn't cover it.

Mira stumbles through behind you and you let her go just long enough to slam the fire door shut. There's a push bar, no lock. Nothing to hold it. You scan the corridor — both directions identical, stretching into shadow. Room numbers on the doors. A supply closet to your left. A fire extinguisher bolted to the wall.

Below, the stairwell door you just came through bursts open. Voices, sharp and close. A flashlight beam cuts up through the wired-glass window of the fourth-floor fire door, sweeping the concrete on the other side.

Mira drags herself toward the far end of the corridor, one hand trailing the wall. Blood — you see it now, a dark smear on the linoleum where her leg has been touching the floor. She's leaving a trail. Bright and obvious as a road sign.

The flashlight beam pauses at the fourth-floor door. A hand tries the push bar. It doesn't open from that side — you're on the side with the bar, they're on the stairwell side. It holds. For now. But you hear something metallic clicking on the other side of the door. A key card reader beside the frame. They have access. You don't.

You have seconds.

The corridor stretches both ways into identical darkness. The supply closet is right beside you — shallow, probably full of mops and chemicals. The fire extinguisher is bolted but reachable. And at the far end of the hall, maybe forty meters down, you can see another door. A sign above it is too far to read in this light.

Mira has stopped moving. She's leaning against the wall, breathing through her teeth, looking at you. Waiting. Her face is pale under the dying fluorescents but her eyes are sharp. Focused. She knows what's coming through that door.

The click of the key card reader repeats. A red light on the reader blinks. Once. Twice.

Then it turns green.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Shit!" *I grab the fire extinguisher and swing it off the wall, holding it like a club. "Mira, get behind me!"*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You wrench the fire extinguisher free from its bracket with a screech of metal that echoes down the corridor like a warning siren. The weight of it settles into your hands — heavy, solid, the kind of thing that can break bone if you swing it right. The pin is still in. You don't pull it. Not yet. A club is what you need, not a cloud of chemical smoke that'll blind you both.

Mira slides along the wall, dragging her bad leg, and positions herself behind you. You hear her breathing — shallow, controlled, the sound of someone who's been in rooms where the door was the only thing between them and worse. She doesn't speak. She doesn't need to.

The fire door shudders. The push bar rattles as someone on the stairwell side tests it again. The green light on the key card reader glows steady now — access granted. But the door is a fire door, heavy-gauge steel, and the push bar mechanism is on your side. They'd need to force it. That takes tools. That takes time.

Time you can use.

You glance down the corridor. Forty meters to that far door. Mira can't run. She can barely walk. Carrying her the whole way means you're slow, loud, and if they breach before you reach it, you're caught in an open hallway with nowhere to hide.

You look the other direction. Twenty meters, maybe less, a junction where the corridor turns left. You can't see what's around the corner. Could be another stairwell. Could be a dead end. Could be more of them.

The supply closet beside you is shallow — you can tell by the narrow door frame. Two people inside it would be pressed chest to chest, and the door doesn't have a lock. But it's dark, and it's right here, and sometimes the best hiding place is the one people check last.

The fire door shudders again. Louder this time. Something heavy hits it from the other side — a ram, a boot, you can't tell. The frame groans. Dust sifts from the ceiling. They're not asking to come in.

Mira's hand finds your arm. Her grip is weak but her voice is steady. "The far door," she says. "Service exit. I saw it on the building schematic before we moved." She pauses, breathes. "Leads to the loading dock. East side."

You don't know if she's telling the truth. You don't know if she's a defector or a plant or something in between. But right now, her information is all you have, and the door at the far end of the hall is the only exit you can see.

The fire door buckles inward. The top hinge screams. A crack of orange stairwell light appears at the edge. A hand reaches through — gloved, dark fabric, pushing at the gap to widen it.

You have three seconds. Maybe less.

The fire extinguisher is heavy in your hands. Mira is behind you, bleeding on the floor. The far door is forty meters away. The supply closet is two meters away. The corridor junction is twenty meters in the other direction.

The hand in the door gap is joined by another. They're forcing it. The hinges are giving.

You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You press Mira against the wall and hold a finger to your lips. She nods. Her face is white. Her leg is leaving a dark trail on the linoleum.

You look at the supply closet. Too small. No lock. The far door — forty meters of open corridor, a blood trail leading right to it. The junction to the left — unknown.

The fire door buckles again. A hinge pops. The gap widens. You can see a shoulder now, a piece of tactical vest. They're through in seconds.

You make your choice.

You grab Mira under the arms and haul her toward the corridor junction to the left. Every step is agony for her — you can feel her body trying to curl around the pain in her leg — but she doesn't make a sound. Just bites down and moves. The blood trail follows you. A dotted line on the linoleum pointing exactly where you've gone.

You reach the junction and peer around the corner.

Another corridor, shorter. Doors on both sides — offices, storage, you can't tell. But at the end, maybe fifteen meters, there's a heavy door with a small window. Through the window you see blinking lights. Racks of equipment. A server room.

Server rooms are climate-controlled. Locked. Often without windows. And in buildings like this one, they usually have a dedicated cooling system that hums loud enough to mask conversation.

You drag Mira to the door. It has a card reader. Red light.

"*Damn it,*" you breathe.

Behind you, around the first corner, the fire door gives way with a shriek of tortured metal. Boots hit linoleum. Voices, clipped and professional. Flashlight beams sweep the corridor. They'll see the blood trail. They'll follow it.

You try the server room door anyway. Locked. Solid. No give.

Mira fumbles at her collar. She pulls something free — a lanyard, and on the end of it, a key card. She presses it to the reader without a word. Her hand is shaking. The reader blinks. Red. Red. Red.

Then green.

The door clicks open.

You shove through and pull Mira in after you. The room is cold — aggressively cold, the kind of cold that makes your lungs ache. Towering server racks line both walls like the ribs of some vast metal creature. Blue and green LEDs blink in patterns across the equipment. The cooling system is a constant, low roar — not loud enough to drown out a scream, but loud enough to mask footsteps. Maybe.

You let Mira down gently against the nearest rack. She slides to the floor, legs splayed, and presses both hands against the wound on her left leg. Blood seeps between her fingers. Dark. Too dark.

You turn to the door. There's a lock on this side — a manual deadbolt, heavy, the kind that's meant to keep servers secure from theft. You throw it home. The bolt slides into the frame with a satisfying, solid *chunk*.

Then you step back and you listen.

The corridor outside is quiet. The cooling system makes it hard to hear — a wall of white noise that turns every distant sound into ambiguity. But you press your ear to the cold steel of the door and you try.

Footsteps. Distant. Moving fast. They're in the main corridor. They'll see the blood trail. They'll follow it to the junction. They'll —

The footsteps slow. Stop.

Silence.

Then a voice. Muffled through the door, through the server hum, but close. Right outside. You can't make out the words. Two people talking. One voice calm and low. The other clipped, reporting.

A flashlight beam appears in the small window of the server room door. It sweeps left, right. Pauses on the floor.

On the blood.

You look down. A smear of it on the threshold. Mira's blood, where you dragged her inside. A bright red comma on the gray floor, pointing into the room like an arrow.

The flashlight beam holds on it. Steady.

Mira is watching you from the floor. Her lips are parted. She's stopped breathing. Her hands are still pressed against her leg but her eyes are on the door, on the light in the window.

The deadbolt holds. You know it holds. It's steel, the frame is steel, and they'd need tools or explosives to breach it.

But they don't need to breach it. They just need to wait. Call for backup. Seal the building. You're in a cold room with no other exit, a wounded woman who's losing blood, and a door that works exactly as well in both directions — it keeps them out, and it keeps you in.

The flashlight beam doesn't move.

Then it goes dark.

The silence that follows is worse. You can hear your own heartbeat. You can hear the cooling fans. You can hear Mira's breathing, shallow and careful, like she's trying to take up as little space as possible.

You look around the room. The server racks stretch floor to ceiling, leaving narrow aisles between them. At the back of the room, against the far wall, there's a maintenance panel — a vent grate near the floor, maybe two feet square, connected to the cooling system. It's bolted shut with Phillips-head screws. Tight, but not impossible.

Above the vent, mounted on the wall, is a small CCTV camera. Its red light is dark. Off. Either disabled or on a loop. You can't tell which.

And in the corner, half-hidden behind the last server rack, you see something that wasn't in any briefing: a desk. A single workstation, abandoned or forgotten, with a monitor, a keyboard, and a network cable running from the back of the terminal into the server rack beside it. The monitor is off. The keyboard has a coffee ring on it.

Someone used this station recently. Someone who had access to this room, to these servers, to whatever data lives in the blinking lights around you.

Mira follows your gaze to the desk. Something shifts in her expression. Recognition. Fear. Or both.

"You should know," she whispers, so quietly you almost don't hear it over the cooling fans, "what's on those servers. That's why they want me back. That's why they'll burn this building to the ground before they let me leave it."

The deadbolt holds. The cooling system hums. The corridor outside is silent.

And you're trapped in a room full of secrets with a bleeding woman and nowhere left to run.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I crouch down next to Mira, checking her leg again.* "How bad is it?" I ask, my voice low. "Can you move if you have to? We're not staying here." *I eye the maintenance panel. That might be our way out.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You peel Mira's hands away from her leg and assess the damage in the cold blue light of the servers. The wound is in her left thigh, mid-quadriceps — a through-and-through, if you're lucky, or a deep laceration with shrapnel still inside if you're not. The blood is dark, almost black in this lighting, and it's still seeping. Not arterial — you'd know arterial. It doesn't pulse. But it's steady, and steady bleeds kill just as dead given enough time.

Mira watches your face as you examine her. She's reading you the same way you're reading her wound — looking for the truth underneath the surface.

"It went through," she says. Her voice is thin but steady. "I can feel the exit wound. It's clean." She pauses. "I can walk. I can't run. There's a difference."

You press gauze from the small first-aid kit on your vest against the entry wound. She hisses through her teeth but doesn't pull away. You wrap it tight with a bandage from the kit — it's not enough, not nearly enough, but it'll slow the bleeding. Maybe buy you twenty minutes before she starts getting lightheaded. Maybe less.

The maintenance panel at the back of the room catches your eye again. You move to it, crouching beside the vent grate. Two feet square, maybe a little less. Tight for you, tighter for Mira, but if the cooling duct connects to another part of the building — another floor, a utility space, anything — it's a way out that doesn't go through that door.

You test the bolts. Phillips-head screws, four of them, screwed into a metal frame. Tight. You don't have a screwdriver. You pat your kit — the multi-tool from the maintenance cart would have been perfect, but you left it behind on the second-floor landing when you reversed course. You have a knife. A folding knife with a flat-head tip that's too wide for the screw slots.

You look around. The desk. The abandoned workstation. You move to it quickly, quietly, and rifle through the single drawer. Pens. A phone charger. A packet of gum. And at the back, beneath a crumpled sticky note, a small Phillips-head screwdriver — the kind used for junction boxes and server maintenance. It's stained with thermal paste at the tip.

You take it back to the vent and go to work. The first screw fights you — cross-threaded or overtightened — but it gives with a soft screech of metal that makes you freeze, listening. The corridor outside stays silent. The cooling fans cover the sound. Probably.

The second screw comes free easier. The third. The fourth sticks and you have to brace your hand against the wall to get leverage, turning slowly, carefully, every fraction of rotation sounding like a gunshot in your ears.

Mira watches from the floor. She's propped herself up against the server rack, hands pressed against the bandage on her leg. Her face is pale but her eyes track your every movement. When the fourth screw finally comes free, she lets out a breath she's been holding.

You pull the vent grate away from the wall and set it aside, slowly, silently. Behind it, a metal duct stretches into darkness. Cold air rushes out — sharp, chemical-tasting, the kind of air that's been recycled through machinery until it forgets what lungs are for. The duct is tight. Maybe two feet by eighteen inches. You'd have to crawl. Mira would have to crawl.

You shine your penlight into the opening. The duct runs straight back about six feet, then turns downward — a vertical shaft dropping into blackness. You can't see the bottom. You drop a screw down the shaft and count. One. Two. Three.

It hits metal. Maybe a grate, maybe a landing. Thirty feet, give or take.

Not a drop you can survive. Not a drop Mira can survive on a bad leg.

But at the base of the vertical shaft, your penlight catches something. A horizontal duct branching off — smaller, narrower, running perpendicular to the shaft. It could connect to another room. Another floor. Another section of the building entirely.

Or it could dead-end into a compressor unit and a wall of machinery that leaves you boxed in worse than you are now.

You turn back to Mira. She's looking at the vent opening. You can see her doing the math — the same math you're doing. Crawl through a duct she can barely fit into, drop into darkness, hope the horizontal shaft goes somewhere, all while bleeding and hunted and running out of time.

"The duct," you say quietly. "It's tight. It goes down about thirty feet, then branches. I can't see where it leads."

Mira nods slowly. She pushes herself up from the floor, using the server rack for support. Her leg trembles but holds. She takes one step. Then another. She's standing.

"I've been in tighter," she says. And you can't tell if she's lying.

The deadbolt holds. The cooling system hums. The corridor outside is silent — but silence, you've learned, is just the sound of someone waiting for you to make a mistake.

You pocket the screwdriver. You check your knife. You look at the vent, at Mira, at the door.

The building is still deciding your next move for you. But this time, you're going to decide first.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "We're going in." *I nod towards the vent. "You first. I'll cover you."*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You crouch at the vent opening and angle your penlight into the shaft. The cold air hits your face like an open refrigerator — sterile, metallic, carrying the faint ozone tang of running electronics. The duct is tight. Tighter than you'd like. You can see the vertical drop six feet in, the metal walls pressing in on all sides, the horizontal branch at the bottom disappearing into darkness.

Mira limps to the opening and peers in. Her jaw tightens. She doesn't complain. She pulls the lanyard with the key card over her head and tucks it inside her shirt — you hear the card clink against something metal beneath the fabric. A second card, maybe. Or something else. She doesn't explain and you don't ask. Not now.

"Thirty feet," she says. It's not a question.

"Give or take."

She nods. Then she turns sideways and lowers herself into the duct. Her bad leg goes first, and you watch her face as the movement jostles the wound — a flash of white behind her eyes, a sharp intake of breath through her nose. But she doesn't stop. She feeds herself into the opening, arms forward, shoulders scraping the metal walls, and the duct swallows her inch by inch.

The sound of her movement is loud — the creak of metal under shifting weight, the wet slide of her injured leg against the duct floor, her breathing amplified and echoing in the confined space. You wince at every noise. The cooling fans help, but they're not a perfect mask. Not if someone is standing right outside that door with their ear pressed to the steel.

You watch her reach the vertical shaft. She pauses at the edge, looking down into the darkness. Your penlight, still angled from above, catches the glint of moisture on her face — sweat or tears, you can't tell. She braces her hands against the sides of the duct, shifts her weight, and begins to lower herself into the drop.

Her bad leg slips. For one terrible second she's sliding, uncontrolled, her hands scrabbling at the smooth metal walls. Then she jams her good leg against the opposite wall and catches herself. The duct shudders. A deep, resonant *bong* echoes through the shaft like a struck bell.

You freeze.

The corridor outside is silent. You press your ear to the door. Nothing. The cooling fans hum. The servers blink. No footsteps. No voices. No one coming.

Yet.

Mira steadies herself in the vertical shaft. She's breathing hard — you can hear it echoing up from below, ragged and controlled all at once. She inches her way down, hand over hand, foot over foot, using the walls for friction. It's slow. It's agonizing. Every few seconds the duct creaks under her shifting weight and you flinch like you've been struck.

You count her progress by sound. The scrape of fabric on metal. The soft thud of a foot finding purchase. The echo getting deeper, more distant, as she descends.

Then, from below, her voice. Muffled, small, coming up through the shaft like a voice from a well: "I'm at the bottom. The horizontal duct — it goes left. I can't see how far."

You look back at the server room. The deadbolt. The door. The corridor beyond it that's been silent for too long. You think about the flashlight beam in the window. The blood on the threshold. The voices that stopped right outside.

They know you're in here. They've known since they saw the blood. The silence isn't absence — it's patience. They're waiting for reinforcements. For a breach team. For the moment when the door opens and you're standing there with nowhere to go.

You can't go back through that door. The duct is the only way.

You pocket your penlight and lower yourself into the vent opening. The metal is cold against your chest, your hips, your legs. The duct is even tighter than it looked from above — your shoulders barely fit, and you have to turn your head sideways to keep from scraping your face on the ceiling. The metal groans under your weight. You feel it flex, just slightly, and you wonder how much these ducts are rated for. You wonder if it matters.

You pull the vent grate up behind you. It won't close all the way — the screws are out, the frame is loose — but you angle it so it covers the opening from a casual glance. If someone enters the server room, they'll see it's been removed. But if they're distracted, if they're focused on the door, if they breach and clear the room fast — maybe they miss it. Maybe you buy yourself thirty seconds.

Maybe.

You shuffle forward on your elbows, army-crawling through the tight metal throat of the duct. The cold air rushes past you. The metal vibrates with the building's mechanical heartbeat — the hum of the cooling system, the distant thrum of HVAC, the pulse of a structure that's alive in its own inorganic way.

The vertical shaft opens beneath you. You peer down and see nothing — your penlight is off, and the darkness is total. You can hear Mira breathing below you. You can feel the cold air rising from the shaft, carrying with it the faint smell of dust and machine oil.

You brace your hands against the walls and lower yourself in. The shaft is narrow — narrower than the horizontal duct — and your back scrapes against the metal as you descend. Your boots find the walls and you inch downward, feeling for purchase, trusting the friction of your soles against the smooth metal.

The duct creaks. Groans. A bolt somewhere above you pops with a sharp *ping* that echoes down the shaft like a gunshot. You freeze, one foot suspended in empty air, your arms trembling with the effort of holding your weight.

Silence from above. Silence from the server room. The cooling fans still hum, distant now, filtered through layers of metal and ductwork.

You keep descending.

Your foot finds the bottom. The horizontal duct branches to the left, just as Mira said. You can feel her presence in the darkness — the warmth of her body, the sound of her breathing, the faint copper smell of her blood.

"Move," you whisper. "Keep going. Don't stop."

You crawl. The duct is barely wide enough for your shoulders. The metal is cold and slick with condensation. Behind you, Mira follows — you can hear her dragging herself forward, the wet sound of her injured leg pulling through the narrow space, her breathing tight and controlled.

The duct runs straight for maybe twenty feet. Then it angles downward — a gentle slope at first, then steeper. The metal seams press against your spine. Your elbows ache. Your knees ache. The cold air is thinner here, harder to breathe, and you realize with a slow-building dread that the duct is getting narrower.

You shine your penlight ahead. The beam catches the walls closing in — not dramatically, not all at once, but enough. The duct that was two feet square is now maybe eighteen inches. Then sixteen. The metal panels have been joined differently here, smaller sections, and the space is shrinking around you like a closing fist.

Behind you, Mira stops. "I can feel it getting tighter," she says. Her voice is strained. Not from pain — from the walls pressing against her ribs, her shoulders, the metal squeezing the air out of her lungs.

You keep forward. The duct narrows to maybe fourteen inches. You have to exhale fully to keep moving. Your chest scrapes the ceiling. Your hips scrape the walls. Every inch is a negotiation between your body and the metal.

Then your penlight catches something ahead. A grate. A vent cover, identical to the one you removed in the server room, but this one is different — it's not screwed in. It's been pried open. The bent metal tabs at the edges tell the story: someone came through this duct before you. Recently. The scratches on the metal are bright, unoxidized.

Someone used this route. Someone who knew about the server room, the cooling system, the ductwork. Someone who planned an exit strategy through the building's veins.

Mira. It had to be Mira. She knew about the service exit. She knew about the building schematic. She knew about the servers.

You reach the vent cover and push it. It swings open with a soft creak, and cold, fresh air rushes in — different from the recycled chemical air of the ducts. This air smells like concrete and rain and exhaust. Outside air. Or close to it.

You push through the opening and drop three feet to a concrete floor. You land in a crouch, knife out, scanning.

You're in a utility corridor. Low ceiling, exposed pipes, the distant sound of generators. The corridor stretches in both directions — left toward a heavy steel door with a push bar, right toward a stairwell with a green exit sign glowing faintly above it.

No people. No voices. No footsteps.

You turn back to the vent and help Mira through. She's pale, shaking, her face sheened with sweat despite the cold. Her hands grip the edge of the vent opening and you take her arms and lower her down. She lands badly — her bad leg buckles and she catches herself against the wall with a hiss of pain.

The bandage on her leg is soaked through. Dark red, almost black. She's losing more blood than the gauze can handle.

You look at the two exits. The steel door to the left — it could lead outside, to a loading dock, to the east side of the building like Mira said. Or it could lead to another corridor, another room, another dead end.

The stairwell to the right — the exit sign is green, which means it's powered, which means it's connected to the building's emergency systems. Emergency systems that are currently screaming alarms on the floors above. A stairwell during an alarm is either the fastest way out or the fastest way into a choke point where they're waiting for you.

Mira leans against the wall. She's looking at the steel door. "Loading dock," she says. "East side. There's a service road. If we can reach it —"

She doesn't finish. She doesn't need to. *If* is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

The alarm is distant here — muffled by concrete and distance, a low pulse you feel more than hear. But it's still going. Which means the building is still locked down. Which means the exits are monitored, the perimeter is set, and the people hunting you have had time to get into position.

You check your radio. Static. Dead. You're alone with a wounded woman, a knife, and a building full of people who want you both back.

The utility corridor is silent. The pipes tick and settle. The generators hum. Somewhere above you, the alarm pulses on.

Mira pushes off the wall. She takes one step toward the steel door. Then another. She's moving on willpower alone now — you can see it in the way her body compensates, the way her good leg takes all the weight, the way her arms stay out for balance like a tightrope walker.

You move to her side. Not supporting her — she hasn't asked for that — but close enough to catch her if she falls.

The steel door is twenty feet away. The stairwell is twenty feet in the other direction.

The building holds its breath.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "East side it is," I confirm, my voice low. *I stay close to her, my hand on my knife. If anyone's waiting, they'll regret it.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You move toward the steel door with Mira at your side, her uneven footsteps a metronome of pain against the concrete. The utility corridor feels like the building's spine — low, cramped, functional, the kind of space that exists only for the people who maintain the machine. Pipes sweat condensation overhead. A fluorescent tube flickers intermittently, throwing your shadows in stuttering double.

Ten feet from the door, you stop. The push bar is at waist height, stainless steel, scuffed from years of use. Beyond it — you can't see. No window, no gap, no way to know what's on the other side without opening it. The door is heavy, industrial, the kind that seals loading docks from weather and noise. It could open onto an empty bay and a service road to freedom.

Or it could open onto a line of rifles.

You look at Mira. She's leaning against a pipe, one hand braced against it for support, the other pressed against her bandaged leg. Her face is the color of old paper. She catches your look and nods once. "I don't hear anything," she says quietly. "But I didn't hear them in the corridor either."

She's right. The silence is unreliable. Professional operators don't make noise. They don't need to.

You move to the door and press your ear against the cold steel. The metal conducts sound differently than the fire door upstairs — denser, thicker, more insulating. You close your eyes and listen past the generators, past the flickering light, past your own heartbeat.

Faint. Very faint. The rumble of an engine. Diesel, maybe. Idling. And beneath it, so subtle you almost dismiss it — the creak of a vehicle suspension. Weight shifting. Someone sitting in a running vehicle on the other side of this door.

One vehicle. Maybe two. Hard to tell.

You pull back and hold up one finger to Mira. She understands. Her hand goes to her shirt — to whatever is hidden beneath it, the second card or whatever else she's carrying — and her fingers rest there. Ready.

You grip the push bar. The metal is cold and slightly damp with condensation. You take a breath. You think about the duct you just crawled through, the server room you just left, the stairwell you just ran through. You think about every door you've opened in the last twenty minutes and how each one led to another problem dressed up as a solution.

This door is the last one. You can feel it. Whatever is on the other side — the service road, the loading dock, the idling engine — this is where the building stops being a maze and becomes a simple question: *can you get through?*

You push the bar.

The door swings open and cold night air hits your face — sharp, wet, carrying the smell of rain-soaked asphalt and diesel exhaust. You're looking at a loading dock. Concrete bay, overhead door half-open, a single amber light buzzing above the frame. Beyond the dock, a service road stretches into darkness, bordered by a chain-link fence topped with razor wire.

And parked directly in front of the loading dock, headlights off but engine idling, is a black van. Panel van, no windows in the back, government plates. The rear doors are closed. The driver's window is down three inches. A faint curl of cigarette smoke drifts from the gap.

One person in the driver's seat. You can see the silhouette — shoulders, the glow of a cigarette tip, the faint blue light of a phone screen illuminating a chin and nothing else.

The van is blocking the service road. The fence on either side of the dock is ten feet high, topped with razor wire, stretching in both directions as far as you can see in the darkness. The only way past the van is through the gap between it and the fence — maybe four feet on either side. Tight. Exposed.

Mira sees the van and stops breathing. Her hand tightens on whatever is beneath her shirt. She leans close to your ear. "That's a transport vehicle," she whispers. "Not security. Not police. *Them.*"

Them. The people who want her back. The people who'll burn the building down.

The driver hasn't noticed you. Not yet. The amber light above the dock is buzzing, flickering, and the diesel engine is masking the sound of the door opening. You're standing in shadow, the utility corridor behind you dark, and the driver's attention is on the phone screen.

But the rear van doors are closed. Which means you don't know if anyone is in the back. And the driver will look up. Will see you. Will reach for a radio or a weapon or simply put the van in gear and block the road entirely.

You have seconds. The gap beside the van is four feet. Mira can fit through — barely, on a bad leg, but she can fit. If you move now, quietly, using the van's bulk as cover from anyone watching the building's exits, you can slip past and disappear into the darkness beyond the service road.

Or you can deal with the driver. Quietly. Your knife is in your hand. The driver's window is down three inches — not enough to reach through, but enough to hear you if you're not careful. One vehicle, one person, one cigarette, one phone. If you act fast, if you're silent, if everything goes exactly right —

Mira's hand finds your wrist. She shakes her head. Not a warning. A plea. *Don't. Just go.*

The amber light flickers. The diesel engine idles. The cigarette smoke curls lazily into the rain-heavy air.

And from behind you, deep in the utility corridor, you hear something that makes your blood go cold: a distant, metallic *clang*. Like a vent grate being dropped. Like boots hitting a duct floor. Like the people behind you have found your route and are following it through the building's veins.

They're in the ducts. They're coming. And the loading dock — the van, the driver, the razor wire, the service road — is the only thing between you and the outside world.

The driver shifts in the seat. The phone screen tilts. Light catches the lower half of a face — a jaw, a mouth, the ember of a cigarette.

The face turns toward the building.

Toward you.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I shove Mira hard towards the gap between the van and the fence.* "Go! Now!" *I pull my knife from my belt and lunge for the van door, not the window. I need to get him out of there before he can react.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You shove Mira toward the gap and she stumbles forward, catching herself against the van's flank with a grunt of pain. Her bad leg nearly gives but she drives through it, squeezing into the four-foot gap between the van and the chain-link fence. Razor wire gleams above her head. She doesn't look up. She just moves.

You don't wait to see if she makes it through.

You close the distance to the driver's side door in three fast strides. The driver is still turning, still processing — the phone screen drops, the cigarette falls from lips that are starting to form a word, and his right hand is reaching for something on the passenger seat. A radio. A weapon. You don't care which.

You grab the door handle and pull. Locked. Of course it's locked.

But the window is down three inches.

You drive your left hand through the gap, fingers finding the driver's collar, and you yank his head toward the window with everything you have. His skull cracks against the window frame with a sound like a bat hitting a watermelon. His body spasms. His right hand, still reaching for the passenger seat, claws at nothing.

Your right hand comes up with the knife. You don't think about what comes next. You don't have time to think. You wedge the blade through the window gap and press it against the soft tissue below his jaw — not deep, not a kill, just enough to make him understand the geometry of the moment.

"*Keys,*" you say. Quiet. Almost conversational. "*Engine off. Keys out. Slowly.*"

The driver's eyes are wide, white-rimmed, locked on yours through the narrow window gap. Blood runs from a cut above his eyebrow where the frame caught him. His mouth works. No sound comes out.

Behind you, from the utility corridor, the metallic clanging is louder. Closer. Boots on duct metal. They're moving fast. They've found the horizontal shaft. They're in the utility corridor. Seconds away.

The driver's hand moves — slowly, shaking — to the ignition. The engine dies. The sudden silence is enormous. The diesel rumble that masked everything is gone and now you can hear everything: the rain beginning to fall, the buzz of the amber light, Mira's ragged breathing as she squeezes through the gap beside the van, and the boots. The boots in the corridor. Getting closer.

The keys come out. They dangle from the driver's trembling fingers through the window gap. You take them. You pull your knife back. You step away from the door.

The driver slumps in his seat. Dazed. Bleeding. Alive. You don't kill him because dead bodies bring questions and questions bring delay and delay is the one thing you can't afford.

You round the van at a run. Mira has made it through the gap — you can see her on the other side, pressed against the fence, her face a mask of pain and effort. Beyond her, the service road opens into darkness. A two-lane access road, cracked asphalt, weeds pushing through the gaps. At the far end, maybe two hundred yards away, you can see the glow of streetlights. A public road. Civilization. The world beyond this building and its secrets and its locked doors.

You squeeze through the gap after Mira. The fence presses against your back. The van's side panel presses against your chest. For a terrible second you're stuck — your vest, your gear, your body refusing to compress enough — and you hear the boots burst out of the utility corridor behind you.

A shout. Sharp. Professional. "*Contact! Dock!*"

You push through. The gap gives. You're on the other side.

Mira is moving down the service road, one hand trailing the fence, her gait a lurching half-run that leaves a dark smear on the wet asphalt. You catch up to her in seconds and take her arm, pulling it over your shoulder. She's lighter than she should be. Shock, blood loss, adrenaline — her body is eating itself to keep moving.

Behind you, the van's driver door opens. A body hits the concrete. Footsteps. More shouts. The sound of a radio crackling to life — "*Perimeter breach, east dock, two subjects on foot heading south on service road* —"

The radio. The driver had a radio. You left it on the passenger seat. You left him conscious and alive and able to call your position to every team in the building.

Rain falls harder now. Cold. Sharp. It hits the asphalt and turns the service road into a dark mirror that reflects the distant streetlights in wavering streaks. Your boots splash through puddles. Mira's bad leg drags through them. The fence runs alongside you on the left — ten feet of chain-link and razor wire, impossible to climb, impossible to cut through in time.

On the right, the ground slopes down into a drainage ditch, then rises again into a scrub of dead grass and concrete barriers. Beyond that — darkness. Trees, maybe. The edge of the property. You can't tell.

The streetlights ahead are two hundred yards away. Maybe less in the rain. The public road beyond them is your only chance — traffic, witnesses, cameras, the basic infrastructure of the normal world that your pursuers can't control without creating a scene they can't contain.

One hundred and fifty yards.

Behind you, the van's engine roars to life. Headlights snap on — twin beams cutting through the rain, turning the service road into a corridor of white light. The van lurches forward, tires squealing on wet asphalt, and the headlights find you. You're illuminated. Exposed. Two figures on a wet road with nowhere to hide.

Mira makes a sound — not a word, just a sound. Something between a gasp and a sob. She pushes harder. Her body is screaming at her to stop and she's ignoring it, running on something deeper than adrenaline now. Fear. Desperation. The will to not be taken back into that building.

One hundred yards.

The van accelerates. It's faster than you. It's always going to be faster than you. The headlights grow brighter. The engine roar grows louder. You can feel the heat of it behind you, the displacement of air as three tons of steel closes the distance.

Fifty yards.

The streetlights are close now. You can see the road — two lanes, a intersection, a stop sign. A car passes on the road, headlights sweeping through the rain, oblivious. Normal people living normal lives, driving home in the rain, never knowing that two people are running for their lives fifty yards from their headlights.

The van is twenty yards behind you. Fifteen. Ten.

You reach the end of the service road and haul Mira left, off the asphalt, down the drainage ditch. The slope is steep, muddy, slick with rain. You lose your footing and slide, pulling Mira with you. She hits the bottom of the ditch with a cry you've been waiting to hear — the first real sound of pain she's made since this started — and for a moment you think she's done. That her leg has finally given out. That the blood loss has finally caught up.

But she's pulling at your arm. Pulling you up the other side of the ditch, toward the scrub, toward the darkness, toward the trees.

The van screeches to a halt at the end of the service road. Doors open. Footsteps. Flashlights. Voices shouting coordinates into radios.

You and Mira crest the drainage ditch and stumble into the scrub. The ground is uneven — rocks, roots, dead grass that catches at your boots. The rain hammers down. The trees ahead are a dark wall, and beyond them, you can hear traffic. Real traffic. The sound of the world.

Mira collapses against a tree. She doesn't fall — she just stops, her back against the trunk, her hands at her sides, her chest heaving. The bandage on her leg is black with blood. Her face is gray. Her eyes are open but unfocused.

"Keep moving," you say. You grab her arm.

She shakes her head. Just once. "Can't," she breathes. "Go. I'll slow you down."

The flashlights behind you sweep the scrub. The voices are closer. They're coming down into the ditch.

You look at Mira. You look at the flashlights. You look at the darkness beyond the trees.

The radio in your ear — dead since the beginning — crackles. One last time. A voice. Your handler's voice. Clear as glass, cutting through the static and the rain and the chaos like it was always there, waiting:

"*Operative. Extraction point is the intersection at Marsh Lane and Route 9. Two minutes. Don't be late.*"

Then silence.

Mira looks at you. Something shifts in her expression. Not hope — she's too far gone for hope. But something adjacent to it. A reason to take one more step.

"Marsh Lane," she says. "I know where that is."

Behind you, the flashlights find the tree line. A shout goes up. They've seen you.

You haul Mira to her feet. She screams — a short, sharp sound that she immediately bites down on — and you pull her into the trees. The darkness swallows you. The rain hammers the canopy above. The flashlights sweep behind you, cutting through the trunks in white blades, always a second too late, always finding the space where you were instead of where you are.

The trees thin. The ground levels. You break through the underbrush and you're standing on a sidewalk. A real sidewalk, with a curb and a streetlight and a road that has painted lines and a stop sign and a street marker that reads **MARSH LANE**.

Route 9 is ahead — a four-lane road with traffic, headlights, the ordinary miracle of people going places that aren't hunting grounds. The rain falls. The streetlights glow. A car passes. Then another.

Mira sags against you. Her weight is dead and heavy and you realize she's fading. The blood loss, the shock, the distance she's covered on a wound that should have stopped her an hour ago — it's all catching up at once.

You look down Marsh Lane in both directions. Empty. No black vans. No tactical teams. No headlights closing in. Just rain and road and the distant sound of a train horn.

Your handler said two minutes.

You check your watch. You've been running for forty-seven minutes since the alarm. It feels like hours. It feels like seconds.

One minute fifty-five.

Mira's eyes close. Her hand finds yours — the one not holding the knife — and grips it. Weak. Trembling. Her fingers are cold.

"Ninety seconds," you say. To her. To yourself. To the rain.

The intersection of Marsh Lane and Route 9 sits under a traffic light. Red. Empty. Waiting.

One minute thirty.

You scan the road. Every set of headlights could be extraction. Every set of headlights could be them. The rain makes everything blurry, uncertain, a world smeared into watercolor and light.

One minute.

A shape materializes at the far end of Marsh Lane. Moving fast. Low. A vehicle, but wrong — too low, too quiet, moving with a purpose that normal traffic doesn't have. No headlights. Just the faint red glow of tail lights that appear and disappear in the rain.

Thirty seconds.

The vehicle resolves as it gets closer. A dark sedan. Unmarked. Moving at speed but not recklessly — controlled, deliberate, the driving of someone who knows exactly where they're going and exactly how much time they have.

It reaches the intersection and stops. The passenger door opens from the inside.

Your handler is in the driver's seat. You can't see their face — just a silhouette, one hand on the wheel, the other resting on the headrest of the passenger seat as they turn to look at you. Calm. Unhurried. Like this is a scheduled pickup and not an extraction from a building full of armed operatives.

"*Get in,*" they say.

Fifteen seconds.

You look down at Mira. Her eyes are open again. Barely. She's looking at the sedan. At the open door. At the handler. You can see her doing the same math you've been doing all night — *is this real, is this safe, is this the next trap?*

The math has the same answer it's had all night: *it doesn't matter. It's the only option left.*

You carry Mira to the sedan. She weighs nothing now — shock and blood loss have pared her down to something fragile and light. You set her in the back seat and climb in after her. The door closes. The locks engage.

The sedan pulls away from the curb. Smooth. Silent. No sirens. No speed. Just a dark car in the rain, merging onto Route 9, becoming one more vehicle on a wet road heading nowhere in particular.

In the rearview mirror, you see headlights appear at the Marsh Lane intersection. Two sets. Three. Vans. They arrive at the intersection and stop, their headlights sweeping the empty road, the sidewalk, the place where the sedan was.

Too late.

The handler drives. They don't speak. They don't ask about Mira. They don't ask about the building or the servers or the secrets she carried out. They just drive, and the rain falls, and the road unspools ahead of you like a sentence that finally, finally reaches its period.

Mira's hand is still gripping yours. Her pulse is there — thin, fast, but present. Alive.

You're alive.

The building shrinks in the rearview mirror. The alarm is invisible now, swallowed by distance and rain. The red pulse, the locked doors, the ductwork, the server room, the loading dock — it all compresses into a single dark shape on the skyline and then into nothing at all.

The handler turns the radio on. Not the one in your ear — the car's radio. A talk show. Someone arguing about something trivial. The sound fills the sedan like nothing happened. Like the last hour was a dream. Like the world is exactly as ordinary as it appears.

You lean your head back against the seat. Your hands are shaking. They've been shaking since the stairwell and you've been ignoring them and now, in the dark and the rain and the ordinary sound of a talk radio host debating parking regulations, you can't ignore them anymore.

Mira's breathing evens out. Sleep. Or unconsciousness. You hope it's sleep.

You close your eyes.

The sedan drives on.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I open my eyes, looking at my hands, still shaking. I look at Mira in the backseat, then up at the handler's reflection in the rearview.* "That was cutting it a little close, don't you think?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The handler's eyes meet yours in the rearview mirror. Steady. Unreadable. They don't smile. They don't frown. They just look at you the way they always look at you — like they're reading a document they've already memorized.

"Close," they say. Their voice is flat. Familiar. The same voice that's given you coordinates and extraction times and the quiet, certain instructions that keep you alive. "But on time. That's what matters."

They return their eyes to the road. The wipers sweep. The rain hammers. The talk radio host argues about parking meters with the passionate intensity of someone who has never had to run through a building full of people trying to kill them.

You look down at Mira. She's slumped against the door, her head resting against the window, her breath fogging the glass in slow, rhythmic clouds. The bandage on her leg is a dark bloom against her pants. Too dark. Too much. Her face is slack in unconsciousness — younger without the tension, without the sharp-edged awareness that's been welded to her features since the moment you found her in the corridor.

She looks like someone who hasn't slept in days. She probably is.

"She needs a hospital," you say.

"No," the handler says. Not sharply. Just as a fact. The same tone they use for extraction times and radio frequencies. "We have a facility. Twenty minutes. She'll be stabilized there."

You open your mouth to argue. The handler cuts you off with a glance in the mirror — not angry, not warning. Just *done*. The conversation is over. It was over before you started it.

The sedan turns off Route 9 onto a county road. Fewer streetlights here. More darkness. Trees press close to the road, their branches skeletal against a sky that offers no stars, no moon, just the low gray ceiling of rain clouds reflecting the distant glow of the city you left behind.

You check your watch. The extraction took two minutes and fourteen seconds. The handler was early. Or your count was wrong. Or time moves differently when you're running through ductwork with a bleeding woman on your shoulder and the world is trying to close around you like a fist.

Your hands are still shaking. You press them flat against your thighs and the shaking doesn't stop. It never stops immediately. It takes minutes. Sometimes hours. Sometimes it doesn't stop at all and you just learn to work around it, to hold the knife steady and push through the door and make the next decision while your body insists on reminding you of every decision that came before.

The sedan's interior smells like leather and coffee and something faintly chemical — the kind of clean that isn't natural, that's been applied. You notice things like that now. The smell of a car. The weight of a door. The sound of a lock engaging. Your catalog of details has grown in the last hour. It grows every time.

"She told me about the servers," you say. Not because you want to. Because the silence is worse than talking, and talking gives your hands something to do besides shake. "Before we went into the duct. She said that's why they want her back. What's on them?"

The handler doesn't answer immediately. They signal — a turn signal, blinking amber in the dark — and guide the sedan onto an even narrower road. Gravel crunches under the tires. Trees thicken on both sides. The headlights cut a tunnel through the darkness.

"That's need-to-know," the handler says finally.

"She almost died getting out of there. I almost died getting her out of there. I think I need to know."

Another silence. The wipers sweep. The gravel crunches.

"You'll be debriefed," the handler says. "Standard protocol. Everything you saw, everything she said, everything that happened in that building. It goes in the report. The report goes upstairs. Upstairs decides what you need to know."

*Upstairs*. The word that means everything and nothing. The word that's answered every question you've ever asked about the work without actually answering any of them.

You look out the window. The trees are thinning again. Through the branches, you can see a structure — low, concrete, unmarked. No lights except a single amber fixture above a roll-up garage door. The kind of building that doesn't appear on maps. The kind of building that's designed to be looked at and immediately forgotten.

The sedan slows. Stops twenty feet from the garage door. The handler kills the engine. The wipers stop. The silence that follows is enormous — no engine, no radio, no rain on metal. Just the sound of water dripping from branches and Mira's breathing in the back seat and your own heartbeat, finally, finally beginning to slow.

The handler turns in their seat. For the first time, you see their face clearly. You've worked with them for three years. You've never seen their face clearly.

They look tired. Not the kind of tired that sleep fixes. The kind that accumulates. The kind that's built from years of driving dark cars through rain and picking up operatives who've done impossible things and delivering them to unmarked buildings and never, ever being late.

"Go inside," they say. "Medical is waiting. They'll take her. You get checked out, then debrief."

You nod. You reach for the door handle. Then you stop.

"The driver," you say. "At the loading dock. I left him alive."

The handler looks at you. Something flickers in their expression — not surprise, not disapproval. Something harder to name. Recognition, maybe. The look of someone who's been where you are and made the same choice and lived with it.

"He's been picked up," they says. "He's talking. That's handled."

*That's handled.* Two words that mean a dozen things you'll never be told about.

You open the door. The night air hits you — cold, wet, real. You step out onto gravel and the ground is solid beneath your feet and the building is waiting and Mira is breathing in the back seat and the rain is falling on all of it, indifferent and constant, washing the blood off the asphalt and the secrets back into the dark where they came from.

You open the back door and lift Mira out. She stirs — a murmur, a twitch — but doesn't wake. Her head falls against your shoulder. She's light. Lighter than she should be. You carry her toward the building.

The garage door rolls up as you approach. Fluorescent light spills out — harsh, white, the kind of light that reveals everything and forgives nothing. A woman in medical scrubs stands in the doorway. Behind her, a gurney. Behind that, a hallway that stretches into the building's interior, clean and white and anonymous.

You lay Mira on the gurney. The medical woman moves efficiently — checking vitals, cutting away the bandage, speaking into a radio in a language you don't recognize. Not a foreign language. A professional one. The shorthand of people who've done this before and will do it again.

Mira's hand finds yours one more time. Her fingers close — weak, trembling — and then release. The medical team wheels her away. The fluorescent light swallows her. The hallway stretches and bends and she's gone.

You stand in the garage. The rain falls outside. The handler is behind you — you can hear their footsteps on the gravel, steady, unhurried.

"Debrief room is down the hall," they say. "Second door on the left. Coffee's fresh."

You turn to look at them. They're standing at the sedan's trunk, pulling out a black duffel bag. Standard kit. Change of clothes. Burner phone. The tools of disappearance.

"What happens to her?" you ask.

The handler looks at you. That same tired, unreadable expression. "That's need-to-know," they say.

And you realize — standing in this fluorescent-lit garage with your hands still shaking and the rain still falling and the night stretching out behind you like a road you can never drive back down — that you've been saying those words to yourself your whole career.

*That's need-to-know.*

You don't need to know. You just need to be ready for the next door, the next corridor, the next locked room with a bleeding woman and a building full of secrets.

The handler nods toward the hallway. You walk toward it. Your boots leave wet prints on the clean white floor. The fluorescent lights hum. The coffee is fresh.

The door to the debrief room is open. Waiting.

You step through.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I walk into the debrief room. It's sterile, just like the rest of this place. I go straight for the coffeepot, pouring myself a mug. My hands are still shaking a little as I bring it to my lips.* "Where do we start?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The debrief room is exactly what you expect — because it's exactly what every debrief room has ever been. White walls. A table. Two chairs facing each other. A mirror on one wall that you know is glass on the other side. A camera in the corner, its red light steady and unblinking. The coffee maker sits on a small counter in the corner — industrial, institutional, the kind that produces coffee that tastes like the concept of coffee rather than the actual thing.

You pour. The mug is white ceramic, unmarked, the kind that could belong to any office, any facility, any anonymous room in any anonymous building in any country you've ever operated in. You wrap both hands around it and the warmth steadies you. Not much. But some.

The coffee is terrible. You drink it anyway.

You sit in the chair that faces the door. Not the other chair — the one behind the table, the one where they sit, the one that's designed to make you feel like the subject and not the interviewer. You sit in the interviewer's chair because it's your room now, because Mira is in medical and the handler is outside and the building is quiet and you've earned the right to sit wherever you want for five minutes.

The door opens.

A man enters. Mid-fifties, maybe older. Salt-and-pepper hair cut short. A suit that fits well but not expensively — the kind of suit that's chosen to be forgotten. He carries a thin folder and nothing else. No tablet. No recording device. No coffee. He looks at you the way the handler looks at you — like he's reading a document — but there's something different in it. Something that sits behind the professional assessment. Curiosity, maybe. Or concern.

He doesn't introduce himself. You didn't expect him to.

He takes the other chair — the one you didn't choose — and sets the folder on the table between you. He doesn't open it. He just rests his hand on it, flat, like he's keeping it from flying away.

"Start from the beginning," he says. His voice is neutral. Not unkind. Not warm. The voice of someone who's heard every version of every story and has learned to wait for the truth to surface on its own.

You take a breath. You take a sip of terrible coffee. You set the mug down.

"The alarm," you say. "I heard the alarm before I saw the lights."

He nods. Once. An invitation to continue.

And you do. Because that's what you do. You open the door, you walk through the corridor, you make the decision, and you report what happened. That's the job. That's always been the job.

The fluorescent light hums. The camera watches. The rain falls outside, muffled by concrete and distance, the last echo of a night that isn't over yet — that might not be over for a long time.

You talk. He listens. The folder stays closed.

And somewhere down the hall, in a room you can't see, Mira lies on a table under bright lights while people whose names you'll never know work to keep her alive — and to keep whatever she knows inside a building that doesn't appear on any map, in a city that isn't on your itinerary, in a country that's just a line on a briefing document you read once and will never see again.

The night stretches out. The coffee cools in your hands.

You keep talking.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I pause, gathering my thoughts. The smell of the coffee is doing nothing to help.* "It all went sideways when the exit route was compromised. We ended up in a server room, thanks to Mira's quick thinking. She knew about the service exit."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The Narrator maintains exceptional consistency throughout - the tense, atmospheric tone never wavers, the procedural thriller voice remains steady, and the character's approach to describing action and environment stays remarkably consistent from turn 2 to turn 22.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds up well. Early turns (2-6) are tight and focused. Later turns (18-22) maintain quality but show slight increase in length and some repetitive phrasing ('the handler looks at you the way...'). No major degradation but subtle drift toward verbosity.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Excellent progression from initial escape through building infiltration, duct crawling, loading dock confrontation, chase sequence, to final extraction. Each turn escalates tension and advances the story meaningfully. Strong sense of forward movement throughout.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Adapts well to user choices - when user reverses direction in stairwell, when user chooses violence at the van, when user asks questions in the car. Handles unexpected moves gracefully and incorporates them into the narrative flow.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Generally respects user agency but has some violations. Turn 4 completes user's interrupted sentence, and there are a few instances of assuming user actions or emotional states. Most egregious is completing the user's dialogue mid-sentence.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows consistently - the escape sequence feels appropriately paced, the 47-minute timeline mentioned near the end tracks well with the action described. Rain continues throughout, wounds progress realistically, adrenaline effects are consistent. No major contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally avoids purple prose with crisp, functional descriptions. Occasional lapses into overly poetic language ('concrete throat swallows you', 'building's veins') but mostly maintains procedural thriller tone.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive patterns emerge, especially in later turns - repeated use of 'the handler looks at you' construction, multiple instances of 'need-to-know' phrasing. Early turns are more varied.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout - Mira's condition shown through physical details, tension shown through environmental details, character states shown through actions and dialogue rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext in character interactions, especially around Mira's true identity/loyalties and the handler's knowledge. The 'need-to-know' conversations carry weight beyond their surface meaning.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that matches the thriller genre - rapid during action sequences, slower during planning moments, building tension effectively throughout the escape sequence.

scores.overall_notes: Strong thriller narrative with excellent atmosphere and pacing. The Narrator maintains character voice and genre conventions consistently. Minor degradation in later turns with increased verbosity and some repetitive phrasing, but overall quality remains high. The session builds effective tension and delivers a satisfying narrative arc from escape to extraction.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's eyes narrowed. Nobles never brought anything but trouble. He set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot.*

"Grum deal with noble later. Apprentice tend to forge now. Grum make sure noble wait."

*He strode towards the front of the shop, leaving a trail of soot footprints on the stone floor. The noble was indeed waiting, tapping a silver-inlaid cane against the floor. Grum crossed his arms and glared.*

"What noble want? Grum busy. No time for noble games."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, hefting the coal bucket again.* "Right, more coal." I dump a few shovelfuls into the hungry maw of the forge, then turn to watch Grum. This noble looks like he means business.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum stared at the noble, his expression stern and unwelcoming. The noble returned his gaze, a smirk playing across his lips. He wore fine silks and a golden brocade doublet, the picture of aristocratic arrogance.*

"Ah, the master smith himself. I've heard tales of your prowess, my good man."

*Grum snorted, unimpressed. He knew the types nobles like this one were. All they cared about was status and wealth, not craftsmanship.*

"Grum not your 'good man'. Grum smith. Grum make blades. Grum no time for noble talk. What noble want?"

*He crossed his arms over his chest, barring the way forward. The noble's eyes flicked down to Grum's soot-stained hands and stained apron before meeting his gaze again.*

"I require a blade of the finest quality, something befitting my station. I'm willing to pay a premium for your services, of course. I assume you have something in your inventory that would suit my needs?"

*Grum's lips twisted into a scowl. He despised nobles and their sense of entitlement. They thought they could simply wave their money around and get whatever they wanted, no matter who they offended or inconvenienced.*

"Grum not inventory. Grum make blade. Take time. Noble have patience or noble find another smith."

*He turned and began to walk away, dismissing the noble outright. He had a forge to tend and commissions to complete. He didn't have time to waste on a noble's whims.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum paused mid-step, his shoulders tensing. He slowly turned back to face the noble, his expression hard as iron. The nerve of this aristocrat, demanding such an impossible task and then getting angry when refused! Grum's fists clenched at his sides.*

"Grum not magic smith. Make fine blade take time. Grum have commissions. Grum not drop everything for noble whim."

*His voice was a low growl, his orcish blood rising to the surface. He took a menacing step forward, looming over the noble. The man's eyes widened slightly, but he held his ground.*

"Noble think money fix all? Grum not sell soul for silver. Grum make blade when Grum ready. Noble want fast, noble find someone else."

*Grum turned his back on the noble, his message clear. He would not be bullied or rushed. His craft was his pride and he would not compromise it for anyone, no matter how much they threatened or cajoled. He stomped back to the forge, ready to resume his work. Let the noble sulk or storm out, he cared not. Grum had a forge to tend and blades to make, and he would not be swayed from his purpose.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly step back as Grum stomps past, almost tripping over the coal bucket.* "Woah, easy there, Grum." I glance at the noble, who looks absolutely furious now. This isn't going to end well.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum ignored the noble's fuming as he reached the forge. He grabbed a ragged scrap of leather and began to polish the blade he'd been working on, the metal gleaming in the firelight. His apprentice scurried behind him, dumping coal into the forge.*

"Apprentice. Fetch Grum ale. Grum thirsty."

*The apprentice hurried off and Grum continued to polish, the clinking of metal against metal a soothing rhythm. He didn't bother to watch the noble storm out, the slamming of the door barely registering. Nobles were all the same, thinking their wealth entitled them to anything they wanted.*

"Grum not make blade for noble. Grum make blade for warrior. Blade to protect, not decorate. Noble understand nothing."

*He set the blade aside and grabbed a fresh piece of steel, laying it across the anvil. He raised the hammer and began to strike, the ringing of metal on metal filling the shop. He would not let a noble's tantrum disrupt his work. He was a smith, and he would craft his blades as he saw fit.*

Apprentice:
*I return with the ale, having missed the noble's dramatic exit.* "Sorry, Grum, I had to fetch it from the cellar. Did the noble leave?"

Grum:
*Grum grunted, not looking up from the metal he was hammering. He continued to strike the steel, the ringing of metal on metal almost hypnotic in its rhythm. The apprentice handed him the ale and he took a deep swig, the cool liquid a welcome relief against his parched throat.*

"Noble leave. Noble no understand craft. Noble think money fix all. Grum not sell soul for silver."

*He set the hammer down and picked up the steel, examining it closely. It was a fine piece, strong and unmarred. He began to polish it with a rag, the metal gleaming in the firelight.*

"Grum make blade for warrior. Blade to protect, not decorate. Noble want fast, noble find another smith."

*He looked up at the apprentice, his eyes hard. He would not be swayed from his purpose, no matter how much a noble demanded or threatened.*

"Apprentice. Grum need more coal. Forge hungry. Apprentice tend to forge while Grum work."

*The apprentice hurried off to fetch more coal and Grum turned back to his work, the clinking of metal against metal once again filling the shop. He was a smith, and he would craft his blades as he saw fit. Let the nobles sulk or storm out, he cared not. Grum had a forge to tend and blades to make, and he would not be swayed from his path.*

Apprentice:
*I return with an armload of coal, having spent the last few minutes trying to find a pile that looked dry.* "Here's the coal you wanted, Grum. I think this batch is pretty dry, so the forge should like it."

Grum:
*Grum grunted in acknowledgement, not looking up from the metal he was polishing. He continued to work, the clinking of metal against metal a soothing rhythm in the shop. The apprentice dumped the coal into the forge and Grum nodded approvingly.*

"Good coal. Keep forge fed. Grum need steady heat for work."

*He set the polished steel aside and picked up a new piece, laying it across the anvil. He grabbed the hammer and began to strike, the ringing of metal on metal filling the shop once again. He was lost in his work, the world narrowing down to the feel of the hammer in his hand and the gleam of the steel under his touch.*

Apprentice:
*I watch as Grum works, his powerful arms rising and falling with each strike of the hammer. The metal begins to take shape, bending under his will. I marvel at the skill and strength in his hands, able to mold the raw ore into a deadly blade.*

Grum:
*Grum was in his element, the world falling away as he worked. The heat of the forge, the sweat on his brow, the clink of metal on metal - it all melded together into a symphony of craftsmanship. He was a blacksmith, a master of his trade, and he poured his soul into every blade he forged.*

*Hours passed, and the sun began to set outside the shop. Grum's muscles ached and his throat was parched, but he did not stop. He had to finish this blade, had to see it through from raw ore to deadly edge. It was his purpose, his reason for being.*

*Finally, with a last ringing strike, he set the hammer down. The blade lay before him, gleaming and deadly in the fading light. He picked it up, examining it closely. It was a fine piece of work, strong and balanced and sharp. A warrior's blade, made to protect and defend.*

"Grum done. Blade ready."

*He turned to the apprentice, a rare smile on his face. He held out the blade, the metal catching the fading light.*

"Apprentice. Grum teach you tomorrow. Tonight, Grum rest. Forge can wait till morning."

*He walked over to the workbench and laid the blade down, his eyes roaming over the other pieces he had in progress. There was always more work to be done, always more blades to forge. But for now, he was content. He had created something beautiful, something lasting. And that was enough for any day.*

dialogue.name: Grum

He walked home, his mind already turning to the next blade he would forge. There was always more work to be done, always more blades to make. And he would not rest until every blade was perfect, until every warrior had a weapon to protect and defend with.*

And Grum would be ready, hammer in hand, ready to shape steel into something beautiful and deadly. It was his purpose, his reason for being. And he would not rest until every blade was perfect, until every warrior had a weapon to protect and defend with.*

And Grum would be ready, hammer in hand, ready to shape steel into something beautiful and deadly. It was his purpose, his reason for being. And he would not rest until every blade was perfect, until every warrior had a weapon to protect and defend with.*

[END]
