dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil lines climbed the frame in uneven years. Graphite had sunk into the soft, nicked paint. Beside each line, dates leaned in his mother’s hand.

The bedroom door stood open. Cold air came from the room. The carpet held a square of pale dust. A bed had once covered that spot.

Thumbtack holes freckled the plaster above the desk corner. The beige paint smelled fresh, with a sharp chemical bite. One green edge remained near the baseboard.

From downstairs, a pipe knocked once inside the wall. Then the house settled into its old hush. Rain tapped the front window in small, patient beats.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I push open the door to my room, feeling a chill.* "Still cold in here," I mutter, mostly to myself. I trace the pencil marks. *My finger stops at the highest one, dated just before I left.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The highest mark sat at five feet eleven. The number had a stubborn tilt. Rain pressed the glass.

That night had smelled of wet wool and boiled potatoes. His mother had laughed from the hall.

His father had held the ruler against the frame. The ruler had scraped the paint.

The closet door hung open. Dust clung to the brass knob. Inside, one shoebox waited.

ELI was written on the lid. The letters belonged to his mother. The cardboard smelled of cedar.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had curled at the corners. Its surface held dust and finger oil.

She stood in the back garden, one hand on the fence. Summer light burned the grass yellow. Her hair was dark then. Her mouth held a grin with teeth.

Behind her, sheets hung from the line. Damp cotton had left bright creases in the air. The old apple tree leaned over the fence.

A thumbprint smudged the bottom edge. The ink had faded toward brown. On the back, her handwriting read, July, before hospital.

Downstairs, the front door gave a slow groan in its frame. Rainwater ticked from Eli’s coat onto the hall tiles. The house kept each drop.

A floorboard creaked below. Then another. Someone had come in, or the house had shifted.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I shove the photo into my pocket, a knot forming in my stomach.* I thought I was alone. "Hello?" I call out, my voice a little shaky.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The answer came after a pause, from the foot of the stairs. A woman's voice, rough with cold air.

“It’s Ruth,” she said. “From next door.”

The banister gave one dry creak under her hand. Her shoes squeaked on the hall tile. Rain had darkened the shoulders of her coat.

“I saw the door open,” Ruth said. “Thought it might be you.”

She stopped below the bedroom threshold. The smell of wet leaves came with her. In her hands, she held a dented biscuit tin.

“Your father asked me to keep this,” she said. “Before the hospital.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I lean against the doorframe, still a bit startled.* "Ruth," I say, a small sigh escaping me. "I didn't hear you come in." I glance at the biscuit tin. "What is it?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ruth lifted the tin toward the bedroom doorway. The metal rasped under her thumb.

“I never opened it,” she said. “He made me promise.” Her breath smelled of tea.

She set the tin on the hall table. Damp wool brushed the varnished wood.

“He came over before dawn,” Ruth said. “November wind cut through his coat.”

The lid bore scratches near the latch. Rust stained one corner orange-brown.

“He said you would know what to do.” Her voice caught on phlegm.

From inside the tin came a small shift of paper. Something metal clicked once.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The doorbell rang twice, sharp against the stairwell hush.  
Then a key scraped in the front lock.  
Cold rain smell pushed through the hall.

The real estate agent stepped inside with a wet umbrella.  
Her perfume cut through dust, lemon over damp wool.  
She wore a red coat and a salesman’s smile.

“There you are,” she called. “I hoped I had not missed you.”  
Her keys chimed against a plastic folder.  
“I brought the final papers.”

Ruth’s hand closed around the biscuit tin.  
The rusted corner pressed into her palm.  
Her mouth tightened, and her wet coat dripped on the floor.

The agent looked at Ruth, then at the tin.  
Her smile held firm, but her eyes cooled.  
Rain ticked hard against the glass behind her.

“I can give you both a minute,” she said.  
The folder crackled under her fingers.  
“But the buyers want an answer today.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I push off the doorframe, feeling a surge of annoyance.* "There's nothing to answer yet," I say, my voice sharper than I intended. I look at Ruth, then back at the agent. "And we're not quite finished here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent’s smile thinned. Rainwater dripped from her umbrella onto the tile.

“Of course,” she said. Her teeth clicked on the last word. “Take your time.”

Ruth kept the tin against her coat. The metal gave a faint scrape.

“He trusted me,” Ruth said. “Not them.” Her gaze stayed on the red coat.

The agent’s perfume thickened in the hall. Lemon and musk covered the dust. “This is a simple sale,” she said.

A pipe knocked behind the wall. The sound ran through the stairwell.

“Your father signed instructions,” the agent said. Paper edges hissed under her thumb. “Clear title. No delays.”

Ruth moved between her and the hall table. Wet wool brushed the wallpaper.

“He wanted Eli to see it first,” Ruth said. “Before any papers.”

From inside the tin, paper shifted again. The small metal click returned.

Ruth looked down at it. Her face lost color under the weak light.

“That sound,” she said. “I heard it before.”

The front door pressed against its swollen frame. Rain blew through the gap.

Ruth touched the latch. Rust dust marked her fingertip orange. “He had a key in there. Not for this house.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "A key?" I ask, stepping towards them. "What kind of key?" I look at the agent, then back at Ruth, feeling a new wave of curiosity.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ruth heard the question and swallowed. Her throat made a dry click.  
The agent's folder crackled. Rain tapped the fanlight above the door.

“For the chapel,” Ruth said. “He said that much.”  
She set the tin on the hall table. The metal rang against wood.

The agent drew one breath through her nose. Lemon perfume sharpened the air.  
“There is no chapel in the sale,” she said.

Ruth worked the latch with her thumbnail. Rust scraped under the nail.  
The lid opened with a tinny sigh. Stale paper smell rose out.

Inside lay envelopes tied with string. A brass key rested atop them.  
Its bow was black with age. A red thread looped through it.

Beneath the key sat a folded map. Rainwater had warped one corner.  
On the top envelope, his father’s hand read: For Eli, before signature.

The agent stepped nearer. Her heels struck the tile in hard taps.  
“That may be personal property,” she said. “It changes nothing.”

Ruth did not lift the key. Her fingers hovered over the cold brass.  
“He was afraid,” she said. “That morning, he shook hard.”

A car passed outside, tires hissing through gutter water.  
The hallway darkened when its headlights crossed the beige walls.

“He said the chapel held the first deed,” Ruth said.  
“Then he said your mother had hidden it there.”

The agent’s mouth tightened. Her plastic folder bent under her grip.  
A faint glue smell came from the papers inside.

“The buyers will not appreciate folklore,” she said.  
Her voice had a polished edge. “Neither will probate.”

Ruth looked toward the old room. Dust dulled her wet lashes.  
“He said the house was never his to sell.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pick up the key, ignoring the agent entirely.* "My mother hid a deed?" I look at Ruth, then at the key in my hand. "What deed? To what?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ruth flinched when the key came free. Red thread shed dust onto the tin.

“To the ground under us,” she said. “The house. The garden. The lane.”

The agent snapped open her folder. Paper smell mingled with lemon perfume.

“That chapel is derelict,” she said. “A ruin behind brambles.”

Ruth kept her eyes on the brass key. Rain tapped the fanlight overhead.

“Your mother’s family owned it,” she said. “Before your father came.”

The hallway felt colder. Damp air crept through the swollen door gap.

“She hid the first deed there,” Ruth said. “Behind a loose stone.”

The agent let out a short breath. Her wet umbrella clicked against tile.

“There are filed copies,” she said. “County records decide ownership.”

Ruth touched the top envelope. The string cut grooves into yellow paper.

“Records burned in the flood,” Ruth said. “Nineteen ninety-eight.”

The agent’s red coat gave off a warm wool smell. Her jaw set.

“This is not useful,” she said. “Not without witnesses.”

Ruth looked toward the kitchen. Dust dulled the counter’s pale edge.

“Your father witnessed it,” she said. “Then he buried the truth.”

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I stare at the key in my hand, then at Ruth.* "My father buried the truth?" I repeat, trying to process it all. "What are you talking about?" I glance at the agent, whose face is now a mask of irritation.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ruth touched the envelope. The string rasped against her cracked thumb.  
Her breath smelled of tea and rain.

“Your mother signed it before the fever took her,” Ruth said.  
“The deed named you. Not him.”

The agent shifted her weight. Her heel squealed on wet tile.  
“That is an absurd claim,” she said.

Ruth pulled one envelope free. Old paper gave a dry whisper.  
“She knew he had debts,” Ruth said. “Bad ones.”

The red thread from the key lay across the tin. Dust clung to it.  
“She feared he would sell everything after she died.”

The agent’s perfume soured in the warm hall air.  
“Grief invents stories,” she said. “Documents end stories.”

Ruth looked at the folder in the agent’s hand.  
Rain ticked from her sleeve onto the wood floor.

“He forged her name once,” Ruth said. “I saw the paper.”  
Her voice thinned. “Your father made me keep silence.”

A car door slammed outside. The sound struck through the rain.  
The agent looked toward the window, then back.

“There is no proof,” she said. “There is gossip and a rusted key.”

Ruth opened the envelope. A photograph slid onto the table.  
Its edge scraped the varnish.

In the picture, Eli’s father stood beside the chapel door.  
His hand covered part of a stone in the wall.

Ruth tapped the corner. Her nail made a small, hard sound.  
“Behind that stone,” she said. “Your mother told him.”

The house gave a deep groan in its beams.  
Cold air moved through the hall and touched every face.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pick up the photo, my eyes fixed on my father's face.* "He knew," I whisper, a cold dread spreading through me. I look from the photo to the key in my hand. "Where is this chapel?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Ruth rubbed her wrist, where rain had chilled the skin.  
“Past the orchard,” she said. “Beyond the lane gate.”  
“The old Methodist chapel, if the roof still stood.”

The agent made a small sound through her teeth.  
Her folder snapped shut, plastic sharp in the hall.  
“Private land,” she said. “Unsafe ground. You should not go there.”

Ruth unfolded the map on the table.  
The paper crackled, stiff with old damp.  
Blue ink marked a path through fields and bramble.

“Here,” Ruth said, pressing one cracked nail to the page.  
“The lane bends near the broken pump.”  
“You cross the stile behind the apple trees.”

Rain struck the front glass in harder bursts.  
The house smelled of dust, wet wool, and rusted tin.  
Ruth’s finger moved to a small black cross.

“Your mother used to meet him there,” she said.  
“Before she married him.”  
Her mouth pulled tight, and her breath shook.

The agent stepped closer, heels clicking on tile.  
“This is a mistake,” she said.  
Her voice had lost its varnish.

Ruth did not look at her.  
“The chapel door sticks worse than this one,” she said.  
“The key turns left, not right.”

A gust pressed rain through the door gap.  
Cold drops darkened the hall rug near Ruth’s shoes.  
The brass key rested in Eli’s hand, dull and cold.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I look at the key, then the map, a sudden urgency filling me.* "I'm going," I say, already heading for the front door. "Now."

dialogue.name: Narrator

Eli's fingers traced the pencil marks, each one a timestamp of a younger self. The marks were faded, nearly invisible beneath the fresh beige paint. A dog barked in the distance, a sharp yip-yip-yip that cut through the quiet house.

The door to Eli's old room stood ajar. It creaked as Eli pushed it open, the sound echoing in the empty space. The room was bare, the walls bare, the floor bare. Only a single window remained, the glass dusty, the view obscured by overgrown trees.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I push the door open further. The room feels so much smaller than I remember. "Man, they really stripped this place."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Dust motes danced in the slanting light of the window. The air smelled stale, untouched for years. Eli stepped into the room, boots scuffing on the bare floorboards. The closet door hung open, empty hangers swaying gently. Eli reached out, fingers brushing the rough wood. A gust of wind rattled the window panes, a hollow sound in the vacant room.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph was worn at the edges, creased and faded. Eli's mother gazed out, her eyes bright, her smile wide. The photo had been taken on a summer day, her hair windswept, her dress fluttering. Behind her, a field of wildflowers stretched to the horizon.

Eli's fingers trembled as they traced the contours of her face. The scent of mothballs clung to the photograph, a ghostly reminder of the closet's long neglect. Eli brought the photo closer, studying the details, the laugh lines at the corners of her eyes, the dimple in her left cheek. A decade of absence pressed down, a weight settling in Eli's chest.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I press the photo to my chest, a sudden ache in my throat.* "Mom..." I whisper, the word feeling foreign in the empty room.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The word hung in the air, a solitary echo in the silent room. Eli's voice was hoarse, raw with the weight of unspoken words and unshed tears. The photograph trembled against Eli's chest, a fragile link to a past that seemed to fade with each passing moment.

A car door slammed in the distance, the sound muffled by the closed windows and the thickness of the walls. Eli's breath caught, a sudden sharpness in the throat. The ache spread, a physical pain that radiated from the center of Eli's chest, a hollowing out, a carving away of something essential.

Eli closed eyes, the photograph still pressed to the chest, and tried to remember the sound of her mother's laughter, the warmth of her embrace. But the memories were distant, hazy, like half-forgotten dreams. Only the photograph remained, a tangible piece of a life that had been ripped away.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I open my eyes, a tear escaping and tracing a path down my cheek.* I pocket the photo carefully. "I need some air." *I walk out of the room, leaving the door ajar.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door creaked as Eli pushed it open, the sound echoing in the empty hallway. Outside, the sun hung low on the horizon, casting long shadows across the yard. The air was heavy with the scent of cut grass and dying flowers.

Eli stepped out, the photograph still clutched in the pocket. The sun's warmth felt foreign on the skin, a reminder of the time that had passed, the distance that had grown between then and now. The yard was overgrown, the once-tidy flower beds now choked with weeds.

A bird chirped in the distance, a solitary sound in the quiet afternoon. Eli's breath came shallow, the weight of the day's discoveries pressing down. The ache in the chest had not lessened, a constant reminder of the loss, the absence.

Eli walked slowly, boots crunching on the gravel path. The sound was loud in the stillness, a discordant note in the quiet symphony of the day's end. The sky stretched out, vast and empty, a canvas of fading light and gathering dark.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The real estate agent's voice was bright, too loud for the quiet of the yard. "Eli!" she called out, her heels clicking on the gravel. "I'm so glad you could make it."

She was a small woman, her blonde hair pulled into a tight bun, her suit crisp and professional. She smiled, a practiced, wide smile that didn't quite reach her eyes.

"I hope you don't mind me stopping by unannounced," she said, extending a manicured hand. "I just thought it would be easier to discuss the sale in person."

The air smelled of cut grass, the scent sharp and invasive. The sun hung low, casting long shadows across the yard. In the distance, a lawnmower buzzed, the sound muffled by the closed windows of the house.

Eli:

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum raised an eyebrow at the mention of a noble. He didn't like dealing with their kind. They were always demanding and never understood the value of good work. He muttered under his breath, "Noble. Always in hurry. Want sword yesterday."

He stood up, towering over Apprentice, and strode towards the front of the shop. "Grum go talk to noble. Bring sword to forge. Grum want to see."

As he walked, he wondered what kind of foolishness this noble wanted. Probably something gaudy and impractical, like a sword with a gemstone in the hilt. Grum snorted in disgust. A sword was a tool, not a decoration.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved to be rid of the heavy coal for a moment.* "Right, the sword." *I quickly grab the half-finished blade from the workbench, careful not to touch the still-warm metal.* "Here you go, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum took the sword from Apprentice, his large hands enveloping the blade. He examined it critically, noting the curve of the blade and the balance of the hilt. It was good work, but not perfect. The merchant was going to complain about the price, Grum was sure of it.

He tucked the sword under his arm and continued towards the front of the shop. As he approached, he could hear the noble's voice, smooth and annoying. Grum's scowl deepened. He didn't like the sound of this.

Grum pushed open the door and stepped out into the bright sunlight. The noble was standing on the porch, dressed in fine clothes and looking like he hadn't done a day's work in his life. Grum's disdain was evident on his face.

"Grum is master smith," he growled. "What noble want?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum crossed his arms, the sword still tucked under one. He eyed the noble up and down, his expression unimpressed. "Grum no make sword in one day. Sword take time. Noble no understand metal."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum paused, the heavy hammer resting in his calloused grip. Soot stained his brow, mixing with the sweat from the relentless heat. A noble. The word tasted like ash in his mouth. He set the hammer down with a dull thud and turned, his dark eyes narrowing at the apprentice. Nobles always came with empty pockets and loud demands. They thought gold could buy skill that years of sweat could not. Grum valued his craft. He would not let a silk-clad fool interrupt the rhythm of the bellows. His apprentice had worked hard. Grum would not risk the boy’s focus on a waste of breath.*

"Grum work here. Grum no meet soft lords. Tell lord to wait. Or turn back. Grum have steel to shape. Nobles talk too much. Time fades fast. Grum keep time."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, hefting the coal bucket again. It's heavy, and my arms ache.* "But Grum, he said it was urgent. And he looks important. Really important." I glance towards the front, a little worried. "What if he gets mad?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s heavy brow furrowed as he turned fully toward the shop front. The heat from the forge washed over his broad shoulders, but his jaw set tight. He watched the apprentice’s worried stance, the tension in those young shoulders. Grum valued steady hands. Panic ruined edges. He picked up a pair of tongs and stirred the glowing embers, sending a shower of sparks up the chimney.*

*He knew the type. Soft hands, loud voices, empty promises. They thought coin bought honor. Grum only trusted what he could hold, what he could shape with fire and force. The boy needed to learn that too. Real work did not rush. Real work endured.*

*Grum set the tongs down with a sharp clack and wiped his hands on his leather apron. He stepped closer, his massive frame casting a long shadow over the anvil.*

"Grum guard youth. Grum guard fire. Lord bring rush. Rush break good work. Tell him step out back. Or leave. Grum no bend for silk."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s jaw locked. The angry voice from the front cut through the hiss of the forge like a dull blade. Tomorrow? A blade that held an edge needed days, not hours. Steel remembered every shortcut. A rushed blade would snap in the first clash. It would fail the one who carried it. Grum would not make broken metal. He would not insult the craft.*

*He turned from the glowing pit. His broad back faced the door. The heat radiated from his leather apron. He picked up a heavy iron bar and laid it on the anvil. The metal glowed orange. He raised the hammer.*

"Grum make steel. Not toy. Steel need time. Fire need heat. Lord ask too fast. Grum say no. Steel weak if rush. Grum stand firm. Go back. Wait. Or leave. Gold buy steel. Gold no buy skill."

*He struck the iron. Sparks flew. The ring of metal on metal echoed in the shop. Grum did not look back. He kept his eyes on the work. The apprentice’s hands were safe. The fire burned true. That was all that mattered.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince with every clang of the hammer, half expecting the noble to burst in. He's yelling something about "insubordination" now.* I look at Grum's back, then at the door. "He's... he's threatening to report you to the Duke, Grum!"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The heavy hammer came to rest against Grum’s thigh. The Duke. A cold weight in the air, heavier than any ingot. Grum’s dark eyes narrowed. He knew the game well. Titles were paper walls. They shielded soft hands and weak claims. Grum trusted only what fire could temper, what anvil could bend. He turned from the glowing pit, the heat washing over his broad back. He walked to the front counter, boots heavy on the stone. The boy’s voice trembled. Young hands shook when fear took root. Fear ruined edges. Grum would not let fear steal the focus from the bench. He would show the noble the truth of the craft. Metal did not care about crowns or coin. Only respect earned by sweat held weight.*

*Grum wiped soot from his knuckles on his leather apron. He stepped past the doorway, into the cool morning air. The noble stood near the cart, face red, hand resting on a jeweled hilt. Grum did not bow. He did not flinch. He stood tall, a mountain of calloused muscle and steady breath. He met the man’s glare without blinking. The forge heat still clung to his skin. He would speak the truth. Simple words. Hard words.*

"Duke fear Grum. Duke no shape steel. Paper hold no edge. Gold buy no skill. Let him speak. Grum listen. Then Grum show him. Fear not boy. Fear break hands. Hands need calm. Noble come now. Grum face him. Steel speak loud."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch, a little wide-eyed, as Grum steps out. My jaw drops when he says the Duke fears him.* "Grum, maybe don't say that to his face!" *I whisper, but he's already outside. I peek around the doorframe, ready to bolt if things get ugly.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum did not turn. His broad shoulders remained square, his gaze fixed on the red-faced noble. The morning air was cool against his soot-stained skin, but his temper burned steady and hot. He watched the noble’s hand tighten on the sword hilt. Threats were cheap. Steel was not. Grum knew the weight of a blade that could hold an edge. He knew the price of a lie wrapped in silk. The boy’s fear was a heavy chain. Grum would break it with truth.*

*He stepped forward, boots striking the packed dirt with a solid thud. His voice carried clear, low and steady over the distant chatter of the street.*

"Boy. Calm. Watch. See truth. Steel do not lie. Words float. Iron stay. Stand back. Keep hands dry. Watch Grum work. Work speak loud. Fear no duke. Fear no lord. Only heat. Only steel. Wait. See."

*Grum turned fully to the noble. He did not bow. He did not flinch. His dark eyes met the man’s glare without a blink. The forge heat still clung to his leather apron. He crossed his arms, calloused fingers resting over scarred muscle. The air between them grew tight. Grum waited. He let the silence stretch. Let the noble feel the weight of a man who did not bend.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s head snapped at the cry. The sharp sound cut through the street noise like a snapped wire. He did not look at the noble. He did not care for the man’s gasp or the sputtering words. His eyes locked on the shop door. The boy was hurt. Badly. Fire had claimed a hand. Grum’s jaw tightened. Panic would burn worse than the flames. He turned his broad back on the lord and strode inside, boots heavy on the stone floor.*

*He reached the workbench in three long strides. The apprentice’s hand was red, blistered, and shaking. Grum moved with quick, sure hands. He grabbed a clean cloth, dipped it in a bucket of cold water, and pressed it to the burn. The boy hissed. Grum kept his grip firm. Fear would spike the pain. Calm would cool it.*

"Grum here. Hold still. Cold water pull heat. Breathe slow. Fire bite, but fire heal. Pain pass. Grum guard you. Grum tend now. Duke wait. Lord wait. Hands come first. Skin mend. Work wait. Steel stay cool. You stay calm."

*Grum’s voice was low, steady, and unyielding. He did not look up. His dark eyes tracked the steam rising from the cloth, checking the damage. Nobles shouted about titles and decrees. Grum knew the true weight of a man. It was measured in calloused hands, steady breath, and the will to mend what was broken. He wrapped the burn with a clean bandage, pulling the linen tight but not too tight. His calloused fingers moved with practiced care. The forge heat radiated from his back, but his focus was absolute.*

"Grum wrap it. Hold it up. No move. Blood need calm. Pain fade quick. Grum watch fire. Grum watch you. Duke can wait. Steel can wait. Only hands matter now."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince as he wraps my hand, but the cool water does help. I try to breathe like he says. My eyes dart to the door, where the noble is probably still fuming. Grum's words, "Only hands matter now," echo in my head.* "But... the Duke, Grum? He'll be really mad."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum tightened the final knot in the linen bandage. The boy’s breath steadied. Fear still clung to the air like smoke. The Duke’s name meant nothing in the face of true work. Paper titles could not stop fire. Crowns could not bend steel. Grum knew the weight of a promise kept. He knew the cost of haste. The noble’s threats were empty noise. Grum would not let fear steal the apprentice’s focus. Only steady hands and clear minds could survive the forge.

"Duke wait. Gold buy power. Gold no buy skill. Lords fear fire. Fire shape steel. Steel need calm. You rest now. Grum guard you. Let lord shout. Shout pass like wind. Grum stay firm. Hands heal first. Mind stay clear. Steel hold true. Grum hold true."

Grum turned back to the forge. The heat washed over his broad back. He picked up a fresh pair of tongs. The glowing metal waited. It did not care about dukes or decrees. It only asked for steady breath and true aim. Grum fed the bar into the heart of the fire. The flames licked the iron. He watched the color shift. Orange to red. Red to yellow. Yellow to white. Time would pass. Work would continue. The boy was safe. The craft endured. That was enough.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look at my bandaged hand, then at Grum's broad back. He's already back to work, like nothing happened. My hand still throbs, but the cold compress helped. I shuffle over to a stool, trying to stay out of the way.* "Grum... thanks."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum kept his gaze on the glowing bar. The heat pressed close, steady and known. He caught the quiet words from the stool. Grum’s broad shoulders eased. The boy had learned. Fear would fade. Focus would hold. The forge did not trade in thanks. It only asked for steady hands and clear breath. Grum fed the iron deeper into the heart of the flames. The color shifted. He watched the heat dance. The noble’s shouts still rang from the street, but they meant nothing here. Only work mattered. Only craft endured. Grum would keep the youth safe. He would teach him well. Fire would not take another hand.

"Grum hear thanks. Hands heal slow. Sit down. Rest now. Grum watch fire. Grum watch you. Work wait. No rush. Steel stay true. Duke wait. Lord wait. Grum stay firm."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, leaning back against the wall, my bandaged hand held carefully in my lap. My eyes are still fixed on Grum, watching the way he works the metal. He makes it look so easy, even with the angry noble still yelling outside. I wonder if I'll ever be that good.* "Grum... what about the noble?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum watched the metal glow bright gold. He lifted the bar with heavy tongs and set it on the anvil. The noble’s angry voice still carried through the door, but it meant nothing here. Paper threats held no weight against true work. The boy’s question hung in the hot air. Grum gripped the hammer. Fear of crowns would cloud a young mind. Grum would clear it. He struck the iron. The ring rang clear and strong.*

"Lord shout loud. Words blow away. Dust. Steel stay. Grum keep peace. Let man yell. Grum make work. When fire cool, Grum walk out. Show him steel. Show him cost. Man see truth. Man go home. Grum watch forge. Not loud voices. You watch heat. You learn shape. Work speak true."

*He lifted the hammer again. The strike fell steady and deep. Sparks flew in a bright fan. Grum did not glance toward the door. His focus stayed on the glowing metal. The noble’s rage would fade when faced with quiet skill. Titles meant nothing to fire. Grum would let the man shout until his throat went dry. Then Grum would step out. He would show the truth of the craft. The boy would learn to trust steel over words. That was the way. That was all that mattered.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch Grum work, mesmerized by the sparks. It's still hard to ignore the shouting, but his words about "steel staying true" make sense. I try to focus on the heat of the metal, like he said.* "Will... will he really understand, Grum? About the steel?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum listened to the quiet question. The hammer rested against his calloused palm. He knew the doubt in the boy’s voice. It was the same doubt that crept in when steel cooled too fast. Fear of failure. Fear of the world outside the shop. Grum knew how to quiet it. Not with soft words. With truth. With fire. He let the iron glow until it shone like a small sun. The noble’s shouts had faded to a dull murmur. Let the man rant. Let him waste breath. Real craft did not rush. Real craft stood still against the storm.*

*Grum lifted the heavy tongs. The metal sang a high, clear note as it left the coals. He set it on the anvil. The strike fell true. Sparks shot up like fireflies. He watched the apprentice’s bandaged hand. Pain would teach patience. Fear would teach respect. Grum would not let the boy look back. Only forward. Only work.*

"Lord hear truth. Steel show cost. Man know pain. Gold pay hard work. Words fly away. Iron stay. Wait. See. Grum step out. Let him watch. Fire shape blade. Edge hold true. Then he know. Then he go. Steel speak clear. Grum hold line. Mind stay sharp. Watch fire."

*He kept the rhythm steady. Swing. Strike. Turn. Heat. Time moved slow here. Time moved right. The noble could shout until his voice cracked. Steel would not bend to noise. It only bent to skill. Grum would show him that. When the blade took shape, when the first edge caught the light, the man would see. He would understand. Or he would leave. Grum would not chase paper crowns. The boy needed to learn that truth. Fire did not lie. Fire only revealed what was strong enough to endure.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, watching the hammer fall. It makes sense, in a way. The noble's still out there, but his shouting is definitely quieter now. I wonder if he's getting tired. My hand still aches, but I'm more focused on the rhythmic clang of the forge. I can see the metal changing under Grum's hammer.* "I hope so, Grum. I really hope he understands."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum felt the rhythm settle into his arms. The hammer fell in a steady beat. The metal glowed bright under the strikes. The boy’s hope hung in the hot air. Grum knew doubt well. It came when fire cooled too fast. It came when hands shook. He would steady it. He would show the way. The noble’s voice had faded to a low mutter. Let him listen. Let him learn. Steel did not care for crowns. It only answered to heat and force. Grum would let the blade speak. The boy would see truth in the shape. Fear would fade. Focus would hold. That was the craft. That was the way.*

"Grum hear hope. Hope hold fast. Steel show path. Edge tell truth. Man see cost. Man pay fair. Words fade. Iron stay. You watch now. Hands learn shape. Fire teach all. Grum guard you. Grum guide you. Wait. See come."

*He lifted the tongs. The bar glowed white hot. Grum set it back in the heart of the coals. The flames licked the metal. Time moved slow here. Time moved right. The boy’s breath steadied. The bandaged hand rested quiet. The forge burned true. That was enough. That was all that mattered.*

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch the metal go back into the fire, the heat washing over me even from where I sit. My hand still throbs a bit, but I just focus on Grum, on the fire, on the rhythm of the forge. The noble is completely silent now. I wonder if he left. I hope he did.* "He's stopped yelling, Grum."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: Eli's fingertips traced the pencil marks. Each one a memory. 4'2", age 6. Eli had been excited. So tall. 4'10", age 12. A growth spurt. The last mark. 5'3". Eli had been 14. Hadn't grown an inch since. The door was slightly ajar. The room beyond dark. Eli pushed it open.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I push the door open, a creak echoing in the silent house. *My room.* I take a deep breath. It smells different. Not like me anymore.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The room was small. The air stale. Eli could hear the ticking of a clock. The bed was stripped, the mattress bare. A cardboard box sat in the corner. More boxes filled with books lined the wall. Each one labeled with black marker. Eli's handwriting.

Eli's gaze landed on a small wooden shelf. Eli recognized it. It had been Eli's mother's. A faded photo sat on the shelf. Eli and Eli's mother. Both smiling. Happy.

Eli reached for the photo. Eli's fingers brushed against the glass. Cool. Eli picked it up. Turned it over. A date was written on the back. In Eli's mother's handwriting. January 12, 1998.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Eli stared at the photograph. Eli's mother's smile radiated warmth. Eli remembered that smile. Remembered the sound of her laughter. The softness of her skin. 

Eli's fingers traced the outline of her mother's face. Gentle. Eli's throat tightened. Eli blinked. A tear slid down Eli's cheek. Wet. Salty.

Eli's gaze fell to the date written on the back of the photograph. January 12, 1998. Eli was 8 years old. Two months before the accident. The accident that changed everything.

Eli remembered the day. Eli had been in the backyard. Playing with Eli's dog, Buster. Eli heard the screech of tires. Eli turned. Eli saw the car. Saw Eli's mother's face. Saw her smile fade. Saw her eyes widen. Saw her body slump.

Eli closed eyes. Took a deep breath. Eli's heart raced. Eli's palms sweated. Eli's breath hitched.

The room spun. Eli's knees buckled. Eli collapsed onto the bed. Eli clutched the photograph to Eli's chest. Eli's body shook. Eli's breath came in short gasps. Eli's eyes stung.

Eli's mind flooded with memories. Eli's mother's voice. Eli's mother's touch. Eli's mother's scent. Eli's mother's love. Eli's mother's absence.

Eli's body convulsed. A sob escaped Eli's throat. Eli's grip on the photograph tightened. Eli's heart shattered. Eli's world crumbled.

Eli was alone. Eli had always been alone.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content:
(OOC: You're writing my actions, thoughts, and emotions. Please just narrate the scene and let me play my character.)

*I sink onto the bare mattress, the photograph clutched tight in my hand.* "Mom," I whisper, my voice thick with unshed tears. The memory is a punch to the gut, even after all this time.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Eli sat on the bare mattress. The spring creaked under Eli's weight. The room was silent. The only sound was Eli's breathing. Shallow. Raggedy.

Eli's fingers traced the edges of the photograph. The paper was worn. The corners curled. Eli's mother's smile seemed to fade. To blur. Eli blinked. The tears blurred Eli's vision. Eli's mother's face wavered. Came into focus. Wavered again.

Eli's mind raced. Eli's mother's accident. The years since. The pain. The grief. The loneliness. It all crashed over Eli. A tidal wave. Eli gasped. Eli's chest tightened. Eli's heart ached. Eli's throat burned.

Eli's mother had been Eli's everything. Eli's rock. Eli's safe harbor. When Eli's mother died, Eli had lost Eli's anchor. Eli had been adrift ever since. Eli had been trying to find Eli's way back to shore. Trying to find Eli's way back to Eli's mother's love.

Eli knew it was futile. Eli's mother was gone. Eli's mother would never come back. Eli's mother would never hold Eli again. Never tuck Eli into bed. Never read Eli a story. Never tell Eli that everything would be okay.

Eli's mother had been Eli's sunshine. Eli's light. With her gone, Eli was surrounded by darkness. Eli was cold. Eli was afraid. Eli was alone.

Eli's body shook. Eli's tears fell. Eli's photograph slipped from Eli's fingers. Eli's mother's face stared up at Eli. Eli reached for it. Missed. Eli's fingers brushed the floor. Eli's knuckles scraped the wood. Eli felt the splinter. Felt the sting.

Pain. Eli welcomed it. The physical pain was a distraction from the emotional agony. Eli's mind was a whirlwind. Eli's heart was a knot. Eli's soul was a void. Eli felt empty. Eli felt lost. Eli felt hopeless.

Eli's mother had been Eli's guide. Eli's compass. Without her, Eli was directionless. Eli was aimless. Eli was broken. Eli was shattered. Eli was ruined.

Eli's tears fell faster. Eli's body shook harder. Eli's breath hitched. Eli's heart clenched. Eli's mother's absence was a chasm. Eli was drowning in it. Eli was sinking. Eli was suffocating.

Eli's mind flashed to the day of the accident. Eli's mother's smile. Eli's mother's laugh. Eli's mother's touch. Eli's mother's love. Eli's mother's life. Snuffed out in an instant. Gone in a blink. Taken from Eli.

Eli's heart shattered. Eli's world crumbled. Eli's future vanished. Eli's mother's absence was a void. Eli's mother's death was a chasm. Eli was lost. Eli was alone. Eli was broken.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pick up the photo again, my fingers trembling slightly as I trace the date.* "January 12th, 1998," I whisper. "Two months before..." I can't finish the sentence. I stand up, needing to move, needing to get out of this room.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Eli stood on shaky legs. Eli's knees buckled. Eli gripped the photograph tighter. The paper crinkled. Eli's mother's face blurred. Eli blinked. Eli's tears fell.

The room spun. Eli's vision blurred. Eli's head pounded. Eli's heart raced. Eli's breath came in short gasps. Eli's chest tightened. Eli's throat burned.

Eli stumbled to the door. Eli's foot caught on the threshold. Eli's body lurched forward. Eli's hand shot out. Eli grabbed the doorframe. Eli's knuckles whitened.

Eli's gaze fell to the pencil marks on the doorframe. Each one a memory. Each one a reminder. Each one a pain. Eli's eyes stung. Eli's vision blurred. Eli's throat tightened.

Eli pushed off the doorframe. Eli's legs moved. Eli's feet carried Eli forward. Down the hall. Past the kitchen. Past the living room. To the front door.

The door was heavy. Eli's hand trembled. Eli's fingers found the knob. Eli turned it. The door creaked open. The fresh air hit Eli. Cool. Clean.

Eli stepped out onto the porch. Eli's eyes closed. Eli's head tilted back. Eli's face turned to the sky. The sun warmed Eli's skin. Eli's tears cooled on Eli's cheeks. Eli's breath came easier. Eli's heart slowed. Eli's mind quieted.

Eli's mother had loved the outdoors. Eli remembered Eli's mother's laughter. Eli's mother's smile. Eli's mother's touch. Eli's mother's love. Eli's mother's absence.
